The course in one story

Computers can’t read. They can only work with numbers. So the whole course is about one question: how do you turn text into numbers, so that a computer can find patterns in lots of text, far more than a human could read?

The course tells this story in three steps. Each step is smarter than the one before.

  1. Step 1 — Count words (Bag-of-words). Throw all the words of a document into a bag and count them. Word order is lost: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look the same. It’s crude, but it works surprisingly well. Methods built on counting:
    • word lists (“dictionaries”): you choose the words to look for, for example “uncertain”, “risk”, “crisis”;
    • sorting documents into groups (e.g. spam or not spam);
    • finding hidden themes in a pile of documents (topic models).
  2. Step 2 — Give each word a meaning-location (Word embeddings). Instead of only counting, give each word a set of coordinates, like a spot on a map, so that words with similar meanings sit close together: “king” sits near “queen”, and “apple” near “banana”. The computer learns these spots by noticing which words appear near each other in lots of text.
  3. Step 3 — Read words in context (Large Language Models, like ChatGPT). In step 2, a word has one fixed spot. But “bank” means different things in “river bank” and “bank loan”. LLMs read the whole sentence and adjust each word’s meaning to its neighbours. They learn this by reading huge amounts of text and practising guessing the next word, billions of times.

The exam asks about all three steps, then gives you a business problem and asks which tools you would use.

Mini-dictionary: words that come up again and again

You don’t need maths for any of these. Each one is just an idea.

  • Document: one piece of text you analyse. One email, one speech, one survey answer, one news article.
  • Corpus: your whole collection of documents. For example, 1,000 survey answers.
  • Variable: anything you measure that can change from case to case. Examples: price, age, or “is this email spam?”.
    • Continuous variable: a number on a smooth scale that can take any value. Height, price, temperature.
    • Categorical variable: a label from a fixed set. Spam / not spam; party A / party B; happy / angry / neutral.
  • Model: a recipe the computer follows to turn inputs into an answer. “Look at the words → guess if it’s spam.”
  • Estimate / train a model: let the computer tune the recipe’s settings by looking at examples, until it gets the examples mostly right. Like adjusting the oven temperature until the cake comes out right.
  • Parameters / weights: those settings, the numbers inside the recipe that get tuned. A big LLM has billions of them.
  • Regression: predicting a number from other information by finding the best-fitting line. Example: predicting a house’s price from its size. In a “text regression”, the information is word counts.
  • Classification / classifier: predicting a category instead of a number. Spam or not spam? Positive or negative review? Naive Bayes is one classifier taught in the course, a spam-filter-style method (explained in question 1(g)).
  • Supervised learning: you give the computer examples with the right answers attached, for example 500 emails a human has already marked “spam” or “not spam”, and it learns from those. Like a student learning from a workbook with an answer key.
  • Unsupervised learning: you give the computer data with no answers, and it finds structure on its own, for example sorting comments into themes nobody named in advance. Like sorting a pile of photos into groups without being told what the groups are.
  • Self-supervised learning: the answers come free from the data itself. Hide the next word of a real sentence and ask the computer to guess it; the real text is the answer key. This is how LLMs learn.
  • Matrix: a table of numbers, like a spreadsheet, with rows and columns. Nothing more.
  • Vector: a list of numbers, like one row of that spreadsheet, e.g. (3, 0, 1). You can draw a short list as an arrow on a graph: (3, 1) means “3 steps right, 1 step up”.
  • Dimension: one position in that list, or one column of the spreadsheet. “300 dimensions” means a list of 300 numbers.
  • Token: the pieces an LLM actually reads. Often a whole word, sometimes a piece of a word (“un” + “believ” + “able”).
  • Layer: one processing step inside a model. Models pass the text through many layers in a row, like a factory line where each station adds something.

In plain words. If a word on this guide ever stops you, look for it here or in the “What the words mean” box in that chapter. If it isn’t in either place, that’s a gap in this guide, not in you.

Part I — Turning text into numbers

1. What “text as data” is, the workflow, and the four challenges (Lecture 1)

Exam priority: ★ Low — background, but it feeds the ethics/ESG question and the business-case reflection

Start from zero

The problem. Picture a phone company that gets 10,000 online reviews every month. The boss asks: “Are customers happier this month than last month? What do they complain about most?” Nobody has time to read 10,000 reviews. A computer could do it in seconds, but a computer cannot read. It can only work with numbers. So someone has to turn the reviews into numbers first. That whole job, from raw text to an answer, is what this course calls “text as data”.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Collect the text. Copy the reviews from the website into a file on your computer.
  2. Clean the text. Make everything lowercase, remove the “!!!” and the smileys, and cut each review into single words.
  3. Turn the words into numbers. For each review, count how often each word appears. Now every review is a row of numbers, like a row in a spreadsheet.
  4. Let a method find the pattern. For example, a rule or a computer program that has learned from examples labels each review as “happy” or “unhappy”.
  5. Check the result. Read a few reviews yourself. Did the computer get them right? If not, find out which step went wrong.

A tiny example by hand. Take two reviews. Review 1 is the one used later in this chapter: “Great phone!!! but the battery is NOT good :(”. Review 2 is our own: “Bad phone.”

Step 2, cleaning. Review 1 becomes 8 words: great, phone, but, the, battery, is, not, good. Review 2 becomes 2 words: bad, phone.

Step 3, counting. Make a small table. Each row is a review. Each column is one word we care about: great, good, bad. Each cell says how many times that word appears in that review.

Review ↓ / Word → great good bad
Review 1 1 1 0
Review 2 0 0 1

Work out one cell out loud: row “Review 1”, column “great”. The word “great” appears once in review 1, so the cell is 1.

  • Step 4, a very rough rule (our own illustration): score = (number of happy words, “great” and “good”) minus (number of unhappy words, “bad”). Review 1: 1 + 1 − 0 = 2, so “happy”. Review 2: 0 + 0 − 1 = −1, so “unhappy”.
  • Step 5, checking. Review 2 is right. Review 1 is wrong: a human sees that the customer is unhappy with the battery. The word “not” flipped the meaning, and our counting missed it. This is exactly why the checking step exists.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: reading huge amounts of text fast and in the same way every time.
  • Good at: spotting trends over time, such as “complaints about the battery doubled this month”.
  • Breaks when: the meaning hides in context, like “not good”, sarcasm, or a word with two meanings.
  • Breaks when: the text it learns from is unfair or private, so the results can be unfair or break privacy rules.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • text as data: treating written text as something you can count and measure, like numbers in a spreadsheet. Example: counting how many reviews mention “battery”.
  • data: any collected facts or records. Example: a list of all reviews with their dates.
  • document: one piece of text you study, such as one review, one email or one speech.
  • corpus: the whole collection of documents. Example: all 10,000 reviews together.
  • workflow: the fixed order of steps you follow, like a recipe.
  • text collection: getting the text onto your computer.
  • scraping: a program that visits web pages and copies the text off them, like a very fast copy-paste.
  • API: a “service door” a website offers so programs can ask it for data directly. Example: a news site that hands you articles in a neat file when your program asks.
  • database: an organised digital filing cabinet where data is stored.
  • JSON: a simple text format for storing data in labelled boxes, such as “review: …, date: …”.
  • preprocessing / cleaning: tidying the text before counting. Example: making “Great” and “great” the same.
  • tokenization: cutting text into small pieces, usually single words.
  • token: one of those pieces. “Bad phone” has 2 tokens.
  • lemmatization: turning each word into its dictionary form. Example: “studies” becomes “study” (Chapter 2).
  • normalization: making different spellings count as the same thing. Example: turning an emoji into a word, or fixing “gud” to “good”.
  • feature extraction: turning cleaned text into numbers the computer can use.
  • feature: one number that describes a document. Example: “how many times ‘battery’ appears”.
  • bag-of-words: counting words and ignoring their order (Chapter 3).
  • document-term matrix: the table of those counts, one row per document, one column per word (Chapter 3).
  • TF-IDF: a way of re-weighting word counts so that rare, telling words count more (Chapter 4).
  • word embeddings: a way to give every word a list of numbers so that words with similar meanings get similar numbers (later lectures).
  • model / modeling: a method that takes the numbers and produces an answer, such as a label or a group. Example: a rule that says “happy” or “unhappy”.
  • training data: the examples a model learns from. Example: 1,000 reviews that a human has already marked as happy or unhappy.
  • algorithm: a fixed list of instructions a computer follows, like a recipe.
  • text classification / classifier: putting each document into a box from a fixed list, such as “spam” or “not spam”. The classifier is the method that does it.
  • clustering: letting the computer put similar documents into groups without being told the groups in advance.
  • topic modeling: a method that finds the main themes running through many documents.
  • LLM (large language model): a very large program trained on huge amounts of text that can read and write language, such as ChatGPT.
  • interpretation and evaluation: asking “does this result make sense, and is it correct?”
  • sentiment analysis: measuring whether a text is positive or negative in mood.
  • big data: so much data that one normal computer struggles to store or process it.
  • parallel / distributed computing: splitting a big job over many computers at the same time, like many cashiers instead of one.
  • unstructured / noisy text: text with no fixed form and lots of mess, such as typos, slang and “lol”.
  • ambiguity: when a word or sentence can mean more than one thing.
  • context: the words and situation around a word that tell you what it means. Example: “bank” next to “river” or next to “loan”.
  • word sense: one of the meanings a word can have. “Bank” has at least two senses: a money bank and a river bank.
  • sarcasm: saying the opposite of what you mean, like “Great, it broke again.”
  • ethics: questions of right and wrong. Example: is it fair to judge job seekers by a computer that learned from unfair old decisions?
  • pitfall: a hidden trap that makes your result wrong if you don’t watch for it.
  • bias: an unfair tilt. If a model learns from unfair examples, it repeats the unfairness.
  • privacy / consent: privacy is keeping personal information safe; consent is the person saying “yes, you may use it”.
  • transparency / black box: a model is transparent if you can see why it decided something; a black box gives answers without showing its reasons.
  • ESG: Environmental, Social and Governance, a way of judging a company’s effect on the planet, people and how it is run.
  • carbon footprint: how much greenhouse gas an activity releases. Training a big LLM uses a lot of electricity.
  • copyright: the legal right of an author to control copies of their work.
  • Python / Jupyter / library: Python is a programming language; Jupyter is a notebook where you mix code and notes; a library is a ready-made toolbox of code. NLTK, spaCy and Pandas are libraries (the first two for text, Pandas for tables).
  • True/False item: an exam question where you say whether a statement is true or false.

The idea in plain words

Computers are good with numbers and bad with words. “Text as data” means turning written text (news, reviews, speeches, emails) into numbers, so a computer can count, compare and find patterns in it.

Example: you have 10,000 customer reviews. You cannot read them all. If you turn each review into numbers, a computer can tell you which reviews are angry, which topics keep coming up, and how this changes month by month.

Analogy Think of a huge pile of letters in a language the computer cannot read. Text as data is the step where you sort the letters, clean them up, and turn each one into a row in a spreadsheet. After that, the computer can do maths on the spreadsheet, even though it never “understands” the letters.

Source: Lecture 1, slides 10–11.

The exam definition

Lecture 1, slide 10 (“What is Text as Data?”):

  • “Text data refers to information captured in written form (e.g., documents, emails, social media, etc.)”
  • “Using computational techniques to analyze and extract meaningful patterns from text”
  • “Popular in various domains like finance, political science, marketing, and more”

Motivating examples (slide 11): predicting stock prices from news articles; sentiment analysis of customer reviews; analysing political speeches to understand policy positions; detecting fake news from language patterns.

The workflow (slide 12, “Text as data workflow: Key Steps”):

  1. Text Collection (Scraping, APIs, Databases)
  2. Preprocessing (Cleaning, Tokenization, Lemmatization)
  3. Feature Extraction (Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, Word Embeddings)
  4. Modeling (Text Classification, Clustering, Topic Modeling, LLMs)
  5. Interpretation and Evaluation

(In plain words: get the text, tidy it, turn it into numbers, run a method on the numbers, then check the answer. Every tool named in brackets is explained in “What the words mean” above.)

The four challenges (slide 13), with the details from slides 14–17:

Challenge (slide 13) What it means (slides 14–17) Course example
1. Handling large datasets (Big Data) Volume (huge amounts of text), storage (needs efficient data management), processing (needs parallel and distributed computing) “analysing billions of tweets or entire internet archives”
2. Noisy, unstructured text Typos, slang, abbreviations; no clear rules for punctuation or grammar; needs cleaning, tokenization, normalization (emojis, misspellings) informal social media posts or comments
3. Language ambiguity and context A word can mean different things in different contexts; sentiment, tone and intent need context “bank” = financial institution or riverbank; sentiment analysis “may misinterpret sarcasm or humor”
4. Ethical concerns Bias in data (“Algorithms may pick up biases present in the training data”); privacy (personal data without consent); transparency (“black-box models”) “Predictive models for hiring based on biased language data in resumes”

(Rows = the four challenges from slide 13; columns = what each means and the slide’s own example.)

Source: Lecture 1, slides 10–17.

A tiny worked example

Take the course’s own running motivation: “sentiment analysis of customer reviews” (slide 11). Follow one review through the five steps.

Workflow step (slide 12) What happens to the review “Great phone!!! but the battery is NOT good :(”
1. Collection The review is scraped from a website, or pulled through an API, and stored (slide 4 of Lecture 2a says JSON, a simple labelled text format, is a good storage format).
2. Preprocessing Lowercase, remove punctuation, split into tokens: great, phone, but, the, battery, is, not, good.
3. Feature extraction Count the words into a row of a document-term matrix (Chapter 3), maybe re-weight with tf-idf (Chapter 4).
4. Modeling A classifier (a method that sorts each text into one of a few boxes) labels the review as positive or negative.
5. Interpretation and evaluation Check: did the model get it right? Here challenge 3 bites: “great” and “good” look positive, but the “not” flips the meaning.

(Rows = the five steps; the column shows what happens to this one review. The review sentence is our own illustration.)

Reading the course code

Not relevant for this chapter. The lecture names Python and Jupyter as the course tools (Lecture 2b, “Why Python?”: libraries such as NLTK, spaCy and Pandas).

How this shows up on the exam This topic will probably not get its own 5-point question. It comes in through three side doors:

  1. The ethics question about LLMs (large language models, the ChatGPT-style tools). In 2025 this was Q4(a), on ethics and ESG (environmental, social and governance concerns). The official marking guide wanted two answers: these models use a lot of energy (a big carbon footprint), and they learn from huge piles of text “often used without permission/copy right issues”. The guide also says “Other answers might also be ok, but need to be well grounded”. So bias, privacy and transparency from this lecture can earn extra marks, as long as you explain them well.
  2. The business-case reflection question (2025 Block 5), where you think through a real company problem. Here, walk through the workflow steps in order: collect the text → clean it → turn it into numbers (features) → fit a model → check the results (collect → clean → features → model → evaluate).
  3. True/False items, for example “TF-IDF is a modeling step”. That is FALSE. Slide 12 puts tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more) under feature extraction, the “turn text into numbers” step.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The five workflow steps in the right order, with one example tool for each step.
  • For each challenge (something that makes text hard for computers): name it, say why it happens, and give the slide’s example. The examples are “bank” (river bank or money bank?), sarcasm (saying the opposite of what you mean), and biased resumes (a hiring model copying unfair patterns).
  • In the reflection question, say at which step of the workflow each pitfall (trap) bites. For example, ambiguity (a word or sentence with more than one meaning) hurts at the modeling step. Bias hurts at the interpretation step, when you read the results.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Putting tf-idf or bag-of-words (two ways of turning text into word counts) under “modeling”. They belong to feature extraction, the “turn text into numbers” step.
  • Putting lemmatization (turning a word into its dictionary form, e.g. “ran” → “run”) under feature extraction. It belongs to preprocessing, the cleaning step.
  • Writing “ethics” without saying which kind (bias, privacy or transparency) and why it happens.

Key terms to use

  • text as data (treating written words as numbers to analyse)
  • corpus (the whole collection of texts you study)
  • workflow (the fixed order of project steps)
  • collection (gathering the texts)
  • preprocessing (cleaning the text before counting)
  • feature extraction (turning cleaned text into numbers)
  • modeling (running a statistical method on those numbers)
  • interpretation and evaluation (reading results and checking they hold)
  • noisy/unstructured text (messy text: typos, slang, no fixed format)
  • ambiguity (one word, several possible meanings)
  • context (surrounding words that fix the meaning)
  • word sense, e.g. “bank” (which meaning of a word is meant)
  • bias (unfair patterns copied from training text)
  • privacy (personal details in texts need protecting)
  • transparency (being able to explain a model’s decisions)
  • black box (a model whose reasoning you cannot see)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “Lemmatization is part of the preprocessing step.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Lemmatization means turning each word into its dictionary form (“ran” → “run”, “mice” → “mouse”). Preprocessing is the cleaning stage, before any counting happens. Does the first belong inside the second?

    True. Why: Lemmatization tidies words up before you count them, like sorting laundry before you wash it. The slide lists it under Preprocessing, next to cleaning and tokenization (splitting text into single words). (Source: Lecture 1, slide 12.)

  2. True or false: “TF-IDF is a modeling technique in the text-as-data workflow.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: TF-IDF is a way to score words: a word that shows up a lot in one text but rarely in others gets a high score. A “modeling technique” is a method from the later stage, where you use the numbers to predict or find patterns. Does TF-IDF belong to that later stage?

    False. Why: TF-IDF only turns text into numbers. It is like weighing the ingredients, not cooking them. The workflow calls that step feature extraction, and modeling comes after it. (Source: Lecture 1, slide 12.)

  3. True or false: “Sarcasm is an example of the ‘noisy text’ challenge.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean (“Great, my train is late again”). “Noisy text” is the course’s label for messy writing. Is sarcasm filed under that label?

    False. Why: Noisy text means messy spelling and wording: typos, slang and abbreviations like “gr8”. A sarcastic sentence can be spelled perfectly. Its problem is the meaning, so the slides file it under language ambiguity and context (words whose meaning depends on the situation). (Source: Lecture 1, slides 15 and 16.)

  4. Explain in 2–5 sentences: Why is ethics a challenge in automated text processing?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Automated text processing” means letting a computer read and judge text for us. Why can that be unfair or harmful?

    Model answer: Models learn from training text, so they can pick up the biases in it. For example, a hiring model trained on biased language in resumes can treat candidates unfairly (Lecture 1, slide 17). Text often contains personal data, which raises privacy issues if it is collected without consent. Many models are black boxes, so it is hard to explain why they made a decision.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: A computer learns from old text and copies its unfairness, the way a child picks up a parent’s prejudices. If past hiring favoured one group, the model will too. Text often holds personal details, so collecting it without asking is a privacy problem. And many models cannot tell you why they decided something.

Sources: Intro_to_text_as_data.pdf (Lecture 1), slides 7 and 10–17

2. Preprocessing: cleaning, tokenization, stop words, stemming vs lemmatization, n-grams, and search as a measurement choice

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — likely as True/False items (“not” as a stop word, stemming vs lemmatisation, n-grams) and as pitfalls in the reflection question

Start from zero

The problem. A history researcher wants to know: did American presidents talk about war more in some decades than others? She has every State of the Union speech (the yearly speech a US president gives to Congress). She asks the computer to count “war”. But the computer sees “War”, “war” and “WAR” as three different things. It also finds “war” hidden inside “toward” and “warm”. And it counts words like “the” and “of” thousands of times, which tells her nothing. Before any counting makes sense, the text has to be tidied. That tidying is called preprocessing.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Make everything lowercase, so “War” and “war” become the same word.
  2. Remove punctuation such as full stops, commas and “!”.
  3. Cut the text into words at the spaces. Each piece is called a token.
  4. Remove stop words. These are very common little words like “the”, “of” and “is” that appear everywhere. A ready-made list tells the computer which ones to drop.
  5. Remove numbers, if you don’t need them.
  6. Shrink words to a base form (optional). “Studies” and “study” should count as one word. Two ways: chop the ending off by rules (stemming), or look up the dictionary form (lemmatization).
  7. Optionally keep word pairs (n-grams), so “not good” stays together as one item.
  8. Check what you threw away. Every step deletes something. Ask: did I delete something my question needs?

A tiny example by hand. Take the sentence this chapter uses below, from President Ford’s 1975 speech: “the state of the Union is not good.”

  • Lowercase: “the state of the union is not good.”
  • Remove punctuation (the full stop): “the state of the union is not good”
  • Cut into tokens: the, state, of, the, union, is, not, good. That is 8 tokens. “the” appears twice, so there are 7 different words. The list of different words is called the vocabulary, so the vocabulary size here is 7.
  • Remove stop words. The standard English list contains “the”, “of”, “is” and also “not”. Drop all of them and 3 tokens are left: state, union, good.

The sentence said “not good”. After cleaning it says “good”. A bad message turned into a good one, only because “not” sat on a stop-word list.

Now try word pairs instead (2-grams). With 8 tokens there are 7 neighbouring pairs: “the state”, “state of”, “of the”, “the union”, “union is”, “is not”, “not good”. The pair “not good” survives as one item, so the meaning is kept.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: making the same word count as the same word, so counts become fair and the table of words gets smaller.
  • Good at: removing junk that carries no meaning for your question.
  • Breaks when: a cleaning step deletes the very thing you care about, like “not”, numbers such as “8%”, or “US”.
  • Breaks when: you search sloppily, so “war” also matches “toward”, or long speeches look “more about war” only because they are longer.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • preprocessing: tidying raw text before you count anything.
  • pipeline: a fixed chain of steps, where the output of one step goes into the next, like a factory line.
  • lowercasing: turning every capital letter into a small letter. “Hello” becomes “hello”.
  • punctuation: marks such as . , ! ? : ; and quotes.
  • tokenization / token: cutting text into pieces; each piece is a token. On these slides a token is a word. In Lecture 7 a token can also be part of a word, like “un” in “unbelievable”.
  • stop words: very common words like “the”, “and”, “is” that are often removed because they appear everywhere.
  • stop-word list: a ready-made list of stop words. The one from NLTK includes “not”, which causes trouble.
  • NLTK: a free Python toolbox for working with text. It holds the stop-word list, the stemmer and the lemmatizer used here.
  • stemming: cutting word endings off by fixed rules. “studies” becomes “studi”. Fast, but the result may not be a real word.
  • PorterStemmer: the name of a well-known stemming tool in NLTK.
  • lemmatization: replacing a word by its dictionary form. “studies” becomes “study”, “was” becomes “be”.
  • WordNetLemmatizer and pos=“v”: the lemmatization tool in NLTK; pos=“v” tells it to treat each word as a verb (“pos” means part of speech, such as noun or verb).
  • vocabulary: the list of different words in your texts. “the cat saw the dog” has 5 tokens but a vocabulary of 4 words.
  • n-gram: a group of n neighbouring words. 1-gram = one word, 2-gram (bigram) = a pair like “low unemployment”, 3-gram = three words in a row.
  • word order: the sequence in which words appear. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” use the same words in a different order.
  • string: what programmers call a piece of text, such as “hello world”.
  • substring: a piece of text found inside a longer text. “war” is a substring of “toward”.
  • whole-word match / word boundary: a search that only counts “war” when it stands alone as a word, not inside “toward”. In code, \b marks the edge of a word.
  • pattern (regular expression): a small search rule written in code. \w* means “any letters here, or none”.
  • case: whether letters are capital (upper case) or small (lower case). “Ignore case” means treat “War” and “war” the same.
  • normalise by document length: dividing a count by how long the text is, such as “mentions per 1,000 words”, so long and short speeches can be compared fairly.
  • index: one number tracked over time that sums something up, like “war mentions per 1,000 words, year by year”.
  • trend: the direction a number moves over time, up or down.
  • measurement choice: a decision about how you measure that changes the answer you get. Example: whether “toward” counts as “war”.
  • research question: the exact question your study tries to answer. It should decide which cleaning steps you use.
  • sentiment / sentiment index: sentiment is the positive or negative mood of a text; a sentiment index tracks that mood as one number over time.
  • earnings call: a phone meeting where a company’s bosses talk to investors about its results.
  • Boolean search: a keyword search with AND, OR and NOT, like “oil AND price NOT olive”.
  • notebook / cell / saved output: a notebook is a file that mixes code and notes; a cell is one block in it; saved output is the result stored after the code was run.
  • helper function: a small, reusable piece of code that does one job, such as “count this word”.
  • alphabetic: made only of letters, with no digits or symbols.
  • set (curly brackets { }): a collection of items in no particular order, such as {“hello”, “world”}.
  • State of the Union: the yearly speech in which the US president reports to Congress. The course uses a collection of them as its example texts.
  • bag of words: counting words while ignoring their order (explained fully in Chapter 3).

The idea in plain words

Raw text is messy. “The”, “the” and “THE” are the same word to you, but three different strings to a computer. Preprocessing tidies the text so that the counting later on makes sense.

But every cleaning step throws something away. Sometimes what you throw away is exactly what mattered. That is the main lesson of this chapter.

Analogy Preprocessing is like peeling vegetables before cooking. Peeling the potato is sensible. But if you “clean” a strawberry the same way, you lose the fruit. The course’s rule: “clean with purpose, not on autopilot” (Interactive 1, cell 16).

Source: Interactive 1, cells 16 and 27.

The exam definition

The standard pipeline (Interactive 1, cell 11): “lowercase → remove punctuation → tokenize → drop stop words → drop numbers → (stem or lemmatize)”.

The steps, as the slides define them (Lecture 2a, slides 6–7):

Step Slide definition Slide example
Lowercasing “Convert all text to lowercase to ensure uniformity.” "Hello World!" → "hello world!"
Removing punctuation “Strip out punctuation marks using string.punctuation.” "hello world!" → "hello world"
Tokenization “Split text into individual words (tokens) using text.split().” "hello world" → {"hello", "world"}
Removing stop words “Eliminate common words (e.g.,”the”, “and”).” {"this", "is", "a", "test"} → {"test"}
Removing numbers “Discard tokens that are purely numeric using word.isnumeric().” {"room", "101"} → {"room"}

(Rows = cleaning steps; columns = the slide’s definition and the slide’s example.)

(The code names in the table are small Python tools: string.punctuation is a ready-made list of punctuation marks, text.split() cuts text at the spaces, and word.isnumeric() asks “is this token made only of digits?”)

On these slides a token is a word split on spaces. Later, in Lecture 7 (LLMs and tokenization), tokens can be pieces of words: “one word need not equal one token”, e.g. unbelievable → un | believ | able (Lecture 7, slides 13 and 29). That difference is what the “tokens vs words” questions ask about.

Stemming vs lemmatization. Both reduce different forms of a word to one form, so that “study” and “studies” are counted together. The course notebook uses NLTK’s PorterStemmer for stemming and WordNetLemmatizer(pos="v") for lemmatization (Interactive 1, cell 4). (pos="v" tells the lemmatizer to treat each word as a verb.)

  • Stemming chops off word endings by rules. Example: “studies” → “studi”. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • Lemmatization looks the word up and returns its dictionary form. Examples: “studies” → “study”, “was” → “be” (as verbs). [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • The notebook asks which gives the smaller vocabulary and which gives tokens you can still read (cell 14). Usually stemming gives a smaller but less readable vocabulary. [Not in course files — general knowledge]

N-grams (Lecture 2a, slide 12). A 1-gram is a single word. A 2-gram (bigram) is a pair of neighbouring words: “all the, the words, words in, …”. A 3-gram is three words: “all the words, the words in, …”. The slide’s callout: n-grams “Can handle”low unemployment” versus “high unemployment”“. They keep a little bit of word order.

Search is a measurement choice (Interactive 1, cell 27): “A text search is a measurement choice: substring vs whole word, case, and normalising by document length can change both the level and the trend of an index.” (In plain words: the exact way you search, such as whether “toward” counts as “war”, whether “War” counts, and whether you divide by speech length, changes the numbers you get and even whether they seem to go up or down over time.)

Source: Lecture 2a slides 6, 7, 12; Interactive 1 cells 4, 11, 14, 27.

A tiny worked example

Example 1: the Ford “not good” trap (Interactive 1, cells 13–14). President Ford’s 1975 State of the Union contains: “I must say to you that the state of the Union is not good.” The word “not” is in the NLTK English stop-word list. Turn stop-word removal on, and the part “the state of the Union is not good” shrinks to “state union good”. The meaning has flipped from bad to good.

The Practical Day 1 notebook shows the same thing with its own cleaner (lowercase, keep alphabetic words of at least 3 letters, remove stop words). Saved output, cell 8:

Original sentence After cleaning
Inflation fell from 8% to 3%. inflation fell
The US economy is not growing. economy growing
Banks bank on lower interest rates. banks bank lower interest rates

(Rows = the three test sentences; columns = before and after the notebook’s cleaner.)

What went wrong, row by row: the numbers (the main economic information) vanished; “not” vanished, so the meaning flipped; “US” vanished; and “interest rates” survived only as two separate words. The notebook’s conclusion: “Preprocessing should follow the research question.” (cell 9)

Example 2: the case trap (Interactive 1, cell 14). The stop-word list is all lowercase. If you skip lowercasing, “The” is not removed, and the vocabulary grows, because “The” and “the” now count as two different words.

Example 3: the war search trap (Interactive 1, cells 7–10). Our own test sentence: “War came. We moved toward the warm south, but the war went on.” (13 words). Three ways to count “war”:

Search method What it matches Count
Substring, like .count("war") toward, warm, war 3
Whole word \bwar\b war 1
Whole word, ignore case War, war 2

(Rows = search methods; columns = what is matched and how many. Counts checked in Python.)

Only the last one is right. The notebook warns about the same problem with “oil”, which also matches “soil”, “toil” and “spoil”. A third fix is to divide by document length (counts per 1,000 words), because State of the Union speeches in the 1940s–1970s were much longer. Longer speeches give higher raw counts, which can create a fake “trend” (cell 10).

Reading the course code

From Interactive 1, cell 4 (the helper functions):

pattern = r"\w*" + word + r"\w*"     # whole_word=False: substring search
pattern = r"\b" + word + r"\b"       # whole_word=True: word boundaries
text = text.translate(str.maketrans("", "", string.punctuation))
tokens = [t for t in tokens if t not in STOPS]
tokens = [stemmer.stem(t) for t in tokens]
  • Line 1: the substring pattern. \w* means “any letters before or after”, so searching for “war” also catches “toward”.
  • Line 2: \b means “word boundary”. It only matches “war” as a whole word.
  • Line 3: deletes every punctuation mark listed in string.punctuation.
  • Line 4: keeps only tokens that are not in the stop-word list STOPS. The code comment warns: “STOPS is all lowercase!”
  • Line 5: replaces each token by its Porter stem. The other option is lemmatizer.lemmatize(t, pos="v").

The notebook has no saved outputs. When run, cell 15 would show a “ladder” table with the number of tokens and the vocabulary size after each extra cleaning step.

How this shows up on the exam Mostly as True/False items, for example:

  • “Removing stop words never changes the meaning of a sentence” (False). Stop words are very common little words like “the”, “is” and “not” that are often deleted.
  • “N-grams can distinguish ‘low unemployment’ from ‘high unemployment’” (True). N-grams are short runs of neighbouring words kept together as one unit.

In the reflection question (2025 Block 5), your cleaning choices are a strong “pitfall” (trap) to discuss. For example, if you measure whether customer survey answers are positive or negative (sentiment), deleting “not” would turn negative answers into positive ones. This chapter also helps with 2025 Q2(c) on Boolean search (keyword search with AND/OR/NOT). A keyword search needs whole-word matching (so “war” does not match inside “toward”) and length normalisation (dividing by text length, so long texts do not win only by being long).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The cleaning steps (the pipeline) in the right order.
  • At least one real course example of cleaning going wrong: Ford’s “not good” (deleting “not” leaves “good”), or “The US economy is not growing” → “economy growing”.
  • The rule that cleaning choices should follow your research question (what you are trying to find out).
  • For search, the three choices: substring vs whole word (does “war” count inside “toward”?), case (does “War” equal “war”?), and per-length normalisation (dividing counts by text length).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying stop-word removal is “always safe”.
  • Saying that keeping “not” fully fixes a bag of words (a method that only counts words). It does not: word order is still lost (Practical Day 1 cell 9).
  • Mixing up stemming and lemmatization. Stemming chops word endings by fixed rules (“studies” → “studi”). Lemmatization finds the dictionary form (“studies” → “study”).
  • Treating raw keyword counts as comparable across texts of very different length. A long report mentions “war” more than a short note, even if it cares less about war.

Key terms to use

  • preprocessing (cleaning text before counting it)
  • lowercasing (turning every capital letter into a small one)
  • punctuation removal (deleting commas, full stops and similar)
  • tokenization (splitting text into single words)
  • token (one word or piece after splitting)
  • stop words (very common little words, often deleted)
  • stemming (chopping word endings by fixed rules)
  • lemmatization (turning words into their dictionary form)
  • n-gram / bigram (n neighbouring words kept together; bigram = two)
  • vocabulary (the list of different words; its size = number of distinct tokens)
  • word boundary (where a word starts and ends)
  • substring (a piece of text inside a longer word)
  • measurement choice (a decision that changes what you measure)
  • normalise by document length (divide counts by how long the text is)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “In the course notebooks, removing English stop words can turn ‘is not good’ into ‘good’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Stop words are common little words that the computer is told to delete. In the class code, does that deletion also wipe out “is” and “not”, so only “good” is left?

    True. Why: The standard English stop-word list (from NLTK, a Python toolkit for text) includes “not”. So “is not good” loses both “is” and “not”, and a complaint now reads like praise. It is like a censor blacking out “not” in “I do not agree”. (Source: Interactive 1, cell 14.)

  2. True or false: “Searching with "war" in text counts only the word ‘war’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: "war" in text is a line of Python code that checks whether the letters w-a-r appear anywhere in a text. Does it find only the real word “war”?

    False. Why: It looks for those letters anywhere, even inside other words (a substring search). So “toward” and “warm” also match. It is like searching for “cat” and getting “education”. The fix is \bwar\b, where \b means “edge of a word”, so only the whole word counts. (Source: Interactive 1, cell 7.)

  3. True or false: “A 2-gram model keeps some information about word order.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A 2-gram is a pair of neighbouring words treated as one unit, like “low unemployment”. If you count pairs instead of single words, do you keep some sense of which word came next to which?

    True. Why: Counting single words splits “low” and “unemployment” apart. Counting pairs keeps “low unemployment” glued together, so you know “low” came right before “unemployment”. You keep a small piece of the order, not the whole sentence. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 12.)

  4. True or false: “If you do not lowercase, the vocabulary gets smaller.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Lowercasing means turning every capital letter into a small one. The vocabulary is the list of different words the computer sees. If you skip lowercasing, does that list get shorter?

    False. Why: It gets longer. Without lowercasing, “The” and “the” look like two different words to the computer, like counting “Apple” and “apple” as two different fruits. (Source: Interactive 1, cell 14.)

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences: You build a sentiment index from earnings calls. Which preprocessing step would you switch off, and why?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: An earnings call is a company meeting where the bosses talk about results. A sentiment index is a score for how positive or negative they sound. Which cleaning step would you turn off, and why?

    Model answer: I would not remove stop words with the standard list, because it contains “not”. Removing it turns “growth is not strong” into “growth strong” and flips the sentiment (as in Ford’s “not good” example, Interactive 1). I might also keep numbers, since they can carry the main economic information (Practical Day 1). Preprocessing should follow the research question, not be applied on autopilot.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: The usual stop-word list deletes “not”, and that flips the meaning: “not strong” becomes “strong”. So do not use that list here. Numbers may matter too, so keep them. Pick cleaning steps that fit your question instead of running them out of habit.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 6, 7, 12; GRA4164_Interactive_1_Text_as_data.ipynb cells 4, 7–16, 27; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 7–10

3. The bag-of-words assumption and the document-term matrix

Exam priority: ★★★ High — asked directly in 2025 Q2(a) (5 points)

Start from zero

The problem. A newspaper has 50,000 old articles and wants to find all the ones about the economy, or see which articles are alike. A computer can add, compare and sort numbers, but it cannot do any of that with words. “Inflation” is not a number. So we need one fixed way to turn every article into a row of numbers, with the same columns for every article. Then the computer can line the articles up and compare them. The simplest way to do this is called bag-of-words, and the table it produces is called the document-term matrix.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Decide what one “document” is. One article? One sentence? All articles from one day? Your question decides.
  2. Clean the text (Chapter 2) and cut it into words.
  3. Make the word list. Write down every different word that appears anywhere in your documents. This list is the vocabulary.
  4. Draw a table. One row for each document. One column for each word in the vocabulary.
  5. Fill each cell with a count: how many times this word appears in this document.
  6. Forget the word order. Only the counts are kept. That is the “bag” in bag-of-words: the words are thrown in a bag and shaken.
  7. Notice the zeros. Most documents use only a few of all the words, so most cells are 0.

A tiny example by hand. Three very short documents. The first two come from this chapter’s analogy; the third is our own.

  • Doc A: “dog bites man”
  • Doc B: “man bites dog”
  • Doc C: “dog barks”

The vocabulary (every different word, in alphabetical order) is: barks, bites, dog, man. That is 4 words, so the table has 4 columns. There are 3 documents, so it has 3 rows.

Document ↓ / Word → barks bites dog man
Doc A 0 1 1 1
Doc B 0 1 1 1
Doc C 1 0 1 0

Rows are documents. Columns are words. Each cell is “how many times this word appears in this document”.

Work out one cell out loud: row Doc C, column “dog”. Doc C is “dog barks”. “dog” appears once, so the cell is 1. Next to it, row Doc C, column “man”: “man” does not appear in “dog barks”, so the cell is 0.

Two things to notice:

  • Rows A and B are exactly the same: 0, 1, 1, 1. The table cannot tell “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”. That is the price of ignoring word order.
  • Count the zeros: 1 in row A, 1 in row B, 2 in row C, so 4 zeros out of 12 cells. That is already one third. With a real vocabulary of thousands of words, almost every cell is 0. That is what “sparse” means.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: turning any text into numbers in a fast, simple and repeatable way.
  • Good at: questions where word counts are enough, such as “how often does this article mention inflation?”
  • Breaks when: order matters. “Good, not bad” and “bad, not good” become the same bag, and “dog bites man” equals “man bites dog”.
  • Breaks when: the table gets huge. Thousands of columns and few rows make later statistics unreliable.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a pile of word counts, ignoring order. Like cutting a sentence into single words and throwing them in a bag.
  • assumption: something a method takes as true to keep things simple. Here: “word order does not matter”.
  • corpus: the full collection of texts you study. The slide writes it as \(D\).
  • document: one unit of text in the corpus. It can be a sentence, an article, a paragraph or one day of news. \(D_i\) means document number \(i\).
  • term: one item in the vocabulary, usually a word, sometimes a word pair.
  • vocabulary: the list of all different terms in the corpus. Its length is written \(p\).
  • matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with only numbers in it.
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the table with one row per document, one column per term, and counts in the cells. The slide calls it \(C\).
  • row / column / cell / element: a row goes across, a column goes down, a cell (also called an element or entry) is one box where a row and a column meet.
  • dimension, \(n \times p\): the size of a table: \(n\) rows by \(p\) columns. Read “\(\times\)” as “by”. Our example is \(3 \times 4\).
  • numerical array: programmer talk for “a table (or list) of numbers”.
  • vector: an ordered list of numbers. One row of the DTM is a vector, such as (0, 1, 1, 1).
  • \(c_i\) and \(c_{ij}\): \(c_i\) is row \(i\) (all the counts for document \(i\)); \(c_{ij}\) is one cell (the count of term \(j\) in document \(i\)). The small letters below the line, called subscripts, are addresses: “row \(i\), column \(j\)”.
  • count: how many times something appears.
  • token: one piece of cut-up text, here one word (Chapter 2).
  • stop words: very common words like “the” and “and” that are often removed (Chapter 2).
  • tf-idf: a re-weighted version of the counts that makes rare, telling words count more (Chapter 4).
  • sparse / dense: sparse means mostly zeros; dense means mostly non-zero numbers.
  • n-gram / 1-gram / 2-gram: a group of \(n\) neighbouring words used as one term. A 2-gram column like “low unemployment” keeps a bit of word order.
  • unit (document unit, term unit): what you choose as one row (a sentence, an article, a day) and as one column (one word, or a word pair).
  • CountVectorizer: a ready-made Python tool (from the scikit-learn toolbox) that builds a DTM of counts for you.
  • min_df, ngram_range, stop_words: settings of that tool. min_df=5 keeps only words found in at least 5 documents; ngram_range=(1, 2) adds word pairs; stop_words="english" drops common words.
  • fit_transform: “learn the vocabulary, then build the table” in one command.
  • nnz: short for “number of non-zeros”, the count of cells that are not 0.
  • sparse format: a space-saving way to store a mostly-zero table by writing down only the non-zero cells.
  • regression: a method that finds how one number (for example GDP growth) moves with other numbers (for example word counts), and gives each of those numbers a weight.
  • GDP growth: how fast a country’s total economic output grows from one year to the next.
  • overfit: when a method learns the noise in its examples by heart, so it looks perfect on them but fails on new data. Like memorising last year’s exam answers without understanding.
  • \(p \gg n\): “many more columns than rows”. The symbol \(\gg\) means “much bigger than”.
  • regularisation: a brake that stops a regression from giving big weights to too many columns (Lecture 3).

The idea in plain words

To do maths on text, each document must become a list of numbers. The simplest way: count how often each word appears. Then forget the order of the words. That is the bag-of-words idea.

Put all those counts in one big table: one row per document, one column per word. That table is the document-term matrix (DTM).

Analogy Cut a sentence into single words with scissors and throw them into a bag. Shake the bag. You can still count how many times “data” is in there, but you can no longer read the sentence. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give exactly the same bag.

Source: Lecture 2a, slides 2 and 12.

The exam definition

Why we need it (slide 2): “Computers do not inherently understand words, and we cannot directly apply mathematical operations to them.” “Words need to be transformed into numerical representations for analysis.”

The bag-of-words assumption (slide 12): all the words in the corpus “are treated individually”. The slide’s callout: “The word sequence does not matter!” Only the counts matter.

Corpus and document (slides 4 and 8):

  • “Corpus = all words, sentences and documents”
  • “\(D\) is the raw data”; “\(D_i\) is document \(i\) in \(D\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\)” (in plain words: \(D\) is the whole pile of texts, and \(D_1, D_2, \dots, D_n\) are text number 1, text number 2, and so on up to the last one, number \(n\))
  • “What is a document? Can be a sentence, a day, an article, a paragraph, etc.” The research question decides which.

The document-term matrix (slide 9):

  • “\(C\) is \(D\) represented as a numerical array with dimension \(n \times p\), where \(p\) is the length of the vocabulary” (a table of numbers with \(n\) rows, one per document, and \(p\) columns, one per vocabulary word)
  • “Elements of \(C\) are usually counts of tokens in \(D\): words, phrases, etc.” (each cell holds a count)
  • “\(c_i\) of \(C\) is a numerical vector with counts of tokens in row \(i\) in \(C\)” (one row of the table, written as a list of numbers)

Two facts about it (slide 11): “Typically sparse (many zeros)” and “Typically LARGE (millions of documents, hundred-of-thousands unique terms)”.

Source: Lecture 2a, slides 2, 4, 8, 9, 11, 12.

A tiny worked example

The slide’s own DTM (Lecture 2a, slide 10). Rows are documents, columns are terms (words), and each cell is “how many times this word appears in this document”:

Documents ↓ / Terms → Using text as data …
Doc1 1 1 2 2 …
Doc2 0 3 0 2 …
Doc3 0 0 5 2 …
… … … … … …

Read one cell by hand: row Doc2, column “text” = 3. That means the word “text” appears 3 times in Doc2. Row Doc1 as a vector is the slide’s \(c_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 & 2 & \dots \end{bmatrix}\).

The grid above: rows = documents (\(n\) of them), columns = vocabulary terms (\(p\) of them), each cell = a count. The dashed box is one row, the vector \(c_1\) for Doc1. The faded zeros hint at sparsity.

Why it is sparse. A real vocabulary has thousands of words, but one document uses only a few of them, so most cells are 0. Practical Day 1 (cell 14) built a tf-idf DTM for 72 speeches: shape (72, 8538), with 89,284 non-zero entries. That is \(89{,}284 / (72 \times 8{,}538) \approx 14.5\%\) filled, so about 85% of the cells are zero.

The same corpus can give different DTMs (slides 13–15). You choose (i) the document unit and (ii) the term unit:

Choice Rows Columns Slide
Document level, 1-gram Doc1, Doc2, Doc3 Using, text, as, data 13
Sentence level, 1-gram Sen1, Sen2, Sen3 Using, text, as, data 14
Document level, 2-gram Doc1, Doc2, Doc3 “Using text”, “text as”, “as data” 15

(Rows of this table = the three set-ups on the slides; columns = what becomes a row and what becomes a column of the DTM.)

For example, at sentence level the row Sen1 (“Using text as data is new to most economists.”) is 1, 1, 1, 1, while Sen2 (“However, it is a growing field.”) is 0, 0, 0, 0.

Slide 8 shows that one corpus can be split by sentence, by article, or by day (one day can hold many articles). The slide’s message: the research question should decide what counts as a document.

The formula, symbol by symbol

In words: the whole corpus becomes one table with \(n\) rows and \(p\) columns, and each row is the list of word counts for one document.

\[C \ \text{ has dimension } \ n \times p, \qquad c_i = \begin{bmatrix} c_{i1} & c_{i2} & \dots & c_{ip} \end{bmatrix}\]

  • \(C\) = the document-term matrix (the whole table).
  • \(n\) = how many documents we have (number of rows).
  • \(p\) = “the length of the vocabulary”: how many different terms we have (number of columns).
  • \(c_i\) = row \(i\): the list of counts for document \(i\).
  • \(c_{ij}\) = one cell: how many times term \(j\) appears in document \(i\). (This notation is used on slides 16–17.)

Read aloud: “The corpus becomes a table \(C\) with \(n\) rows, one per document, and \(p\) columns, one per vocabulary term; cell \(c_{ij}\) counts how often term \(j\) appears in document \(i\).”

(The cell notation \(c_{ij}\) comes from slides 16–17; the row-vector layout is the slide-10 \(c_1\) written out in general.)

Reading the course code

Interactive 1, cell 19:

vec = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, NGRAM_MAX), min_df=MIN_DF, stop_words=STOP_WORDS)
X = vec.fit_transform(docs["rawtext"])
share_zero = 1 - X.nnz / n_cells
  • Line 1: sets up the counting machine. ngram_range=(1, 2) would add word pairs as extra columns; min_df=5 keeps only words found in at least 5 speeches; stop_words="english" drops stop words.
  • Line 2: learns the vocabulary and builds the DTM X (one row per speech, one column per term), stored in a sparse format.
  • Line 3: X.nnz is the number of non-zero cells, so this is the share of zeros.

No outputs are saved. Running it would show the share of zeros is very high. The notebook asks you to notice three things (cell 20): columns grow more slowly than rows (new speeches reuse old words); bigrams add many columns and even more zeros; min_df throws out rare words, typos and names.

The notebook’s warning (cell 20): the next notebook regresses GDP growth on this matrix with about 70 speeches but thousands of columns. With far more columns than rows (\(p \gg n\)), a regression (a method that gives each column a weight to predict a number like GDP growth) overfits: it fits the 70 known speeches perfectly but predicts new ones badly. That is why text regressions need regularisation (a brake on the weights; Lecture 3).

How this shows up on the exam 2025 Q2(a) asked exactly this, for 5 points: what is the underlying assumption of bag-of-words (the method that only counts words), and what is a document-term matrix (a table of word counts)? The official marking guide wanted two things:

  • Word occurrences are treated as independent (each word is counted on its own), and context (the surrounding words) is not modelled.
  • Documents in rows, tokens (words) in columns, counts as the entries.

Expect True/False items too: “In a bag-of-words model the order of words matters” (False); “A DTM is typically dense” (False; “dense” means mostly filled with non-zero numbers).

What a top-grade answer must include

  1. The assumption: word order (sequence) does not matter, and each word is treated on its own, so context is lost.
  2. The DTM (document-term matrix): documents in rows, terms (words) in columns, counts in the cells. Its size is n documents by p words (\(n \times p\)), where \(p\) is the vocabulary size (the number of different words).
  3. One consequence: the table is usually sparse (mostly zeros) and large.
  4. A one-line example (“dog bites man” counts the same as “man bites dog”), or the fix: n-grams (neighbouring words kept together) keep “low unemployment” apart from “high unemployment”.
  5. Bonus: what counts as one document (a sentence, an article, a day) is your choice, driven by your research question.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Answering only half: the assumption but not the DTM, or the other way round.
  • Mixing up rows and columns (rows = documents, columns = words).
  • Writing only “it counts words”, with no table size and no mention that word order is ignored.
  • Calling the DTM dense (mostly filled). It is sparse (mostly zeros).
  • Forgetting that the vocabulary size (\(p\)) is usually much bigger than the number of words in any one document.

Key terms to use

  • bag-of-words assumption (word order ignored; only counts matter)
  • word order / sequence ignored (which word came first is lost)
  • document-term matrix (table: documents down, words across, counts inside)
  • rows = documents (each line of the table is one text)
  • columns = terms (each column is one word)
  • counts (how many times a word appears)
  • \(n \times p\) (n documents by p words)
  • vocabulary (the list of all different words)
  • sparse (mostly zeros)
  • large (many rows and very many columns)
  • corpus (the whole collection of texts)
  • document unit (what counts as one “document”)
  • n-grams (neighbouring words kept together as one unit)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “A document-term matrix has dimension \(n \times p\), where \(p\) is the vocabulary size.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A document-term matrix is a table of word counts. “Dimension \(n \times p\)” means it has n rows and p columns. The vocabulary size is the number of different words across all your texts. Is the number of columns equal to the number of different words?

    True. Why: Each document gets one row (n documents, n rows). Each different word gets one column (p words, p columns). Think of a class register: one row per pupil, one column per lesson. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 9.)

  2. True or false: “With 1-grams, ‘the dog bites the man’ and ‘the man bites the dog’ get the same row in the DTM.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “1-grams” means counting single words one at a time. A row in the DTM (document-term matrix) is the list of word counts for one text. Do these two sentences end up with identical counts?

    True. Why: Both have “the” twice and “dog”, “bites” and “man” once each. Counting single words is like tipping the words into a bag and shaking it: the order is gone. The slide says “The word sequence does not matter!” Only 2-grams or longer (pairs like “dog bites”) would tell the two sentences apart. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 12.)

  3. True or false: “A document must always be a full article.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: In text analysis, a “document” is one unit you count words for, so one row in the table. Must that unit always be a whole article?

    False. Why: You choose the unit to fit your question, like choosing to count your steps per hour or per day. The slide says a document “Can be a sentence, a day, an article, a paragraph, etc.” (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 8.)

  4. True or false: “Most cells in a DTM are zero.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A cell is one box in the table: how often one word appears in one document. Are most of the boxes 0?

    True. Why: The table has a column for every word used anywhere in all the texts, but each text uses only a few of them. Picture a receipt that lists every product in the shop: most lines would say 0. The slide says “Typically sparse (many zeros)”. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 11.)

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q2a style): What is the bag-of-words assumption, and what is a document-term matrix?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Two parts. What does the bag-of-words method assume about text? And what is the table of word counts it produces? (This exact question came up in 2025, for 5 points.)

    Model answer: The bag-of-words assumption is that word order does not matter: each word is treated individually, as if the words were thrown into a bag, so context is not modelled. A document-term matrix stores the corpus as numbers: each row is a document, each column is a term from the vocabulary, and each cell counts how often that term appears in that document. Its dimension is \(n \times p\) (\(n\) documents, \(p\) terms). It is typically very large and sparse (mostly zeros), because each document uses only a small part of the vocabulary.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Bag-of-words only counts words and forgets their order. The document-term matrix is the table of those counts: one row per text, one column per word. The table is huge and mostly zeros, because each text uses only a few of all the words.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 2, 4, 5, 8–15, 20; GRA4164_Interactive_1_Text_as_data.ipynb cells 17–20; practical_day_1.ipynb cell 14

4. Normalising the DTM: raw counts, row normalisation, binary, tf-idf

Exam priority: ★★★ High — asked directly in 2025 Q2(b) (5 points); idf calculations possible

Start from zero

The problem. A news website wants to tag each article with its most telling words, so readers can find “articles about inflation”. It already has the table of word counts from Chapter 3. But the raw counts mislead in two ways. A long article uses every word more often than a short one, only because it is long. And words like “the” or “said” are big in every article, so they say nothing about what makes this one special. We need to adjust the counts before using them. This chapter shows four ways: keep the raw counts, turn them into shares, turn them into yes/no, or weight them by how rare the word is (tf-idf).

How it works, step by step.

  1. Raw counts. Keep the table as it is. Easy, but long documents win.
  2. Shares (row normalisation). For each document, add up all its counts to get its total length. Divide every count in that row by the total. Now each cell says “what share of this document is this word”, and long and short documents can be compared.
  3. Yes/no (binary). Replace every count above 0 with a 1. Now a cell only says “does the word appear at all?”
  4. Tf-idf. For each word, count how many documents contain it. Divide the total number of documents by that number: a rare word gives a big result, a word found everywhere gives 1. Press the “log” button on that result to get the rarity weight. Then multiply each count by its word’s rarity weight. Words found in every document end up with weight 0.

A tiny example by hand. We reuse the small table from Chapter 3 (Lecture 2a, slide 10) and pretend these 3 documents and 4 words are the whole corpus. Rows are documents, columns are words, cells are counts.

Document ↓ / Word → Using text as data
Doc1 1 1 2 2
Doc2 0 3 0 2
Doc3 0 0 5 2

Shares. Doc2’s counts are 0, 3, 0, 2. They add up to 5, so Doc2 has 5 tokens. The cell for “text” becomes 3 out of 5, which is 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. In words: 60% of Doc2 is the word “text”.

Yes/no. Doc3 uses “as” 5 times. In the binary table that cell becomes 1. Doc1 uses “as” 2 times; that also becomes 1. The difference between 5 and 2 is gone.

Tf-idf, for the word “Using”. Look down its column: only Doc1 has a non-zero count, so 1 document out of 3 contains it. Total documents ÷ documents with the word = 3 ÷ 1 = 3. The natural log of 3 is about 1.099. Doc1 uses “Using” once, so its tf-idf is 1 × 1.099 = 1.099.

Tf-idf, for the word “data”. All 3 documents contain it. 3 ÷ 3 = 1, and the log of 1 is 0. So every “data” cell becomes 0, however big its count. A word that is everywhere cannot help tell documents apart.

Tf-idf, for “as” in Doc3. Two documents contain “as”, so 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, and the log of 1.5 is about 0.405. Doc3 uses “as” 5 times, so 5 × 0.405 ≈ 2.027.

These match the full tables further down in this chapter.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: shares make long and short documents fair to compare.
  • Good at: tf-idf pushes the telling words up and the everywhere-words down, so very common words matter less.
  • Breaks when: tf-idf boosts words that are rare for boring reasons, such as names of guests in one speech.
  • Breaks when: binary throws away useful “how much” information, and different software (such as scikit-learn) uses slightly different tf-idf formulas, so numbers differ.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • normalise / transformation: changing the numbers in a fixed way so they become fairer to compare. Like turning test scores into percentages.
  • corpus / document: the whole collection of texts, and one text in it (Chapter 3).
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the table of counts with one row per document and one column per word (Chapter 3).
  • vector / document vector: one row of the table seen as a list of numbers, or as an arrow (Chapter 5).
  • raw counts: the plain counts from the document-term matrix, before any change.
  • document length / \(m_i\): the total number of tokens in document \(i\). \(m_i = \sum_j c_{ij}\) means “add up all the counts in row \(i\)”.
  • \(\sum\) (sigma, the sum sign): “add these all up”. \(\sum_j\) means “add over all columns \(j\)”.
  • row normalisation: dividing every count in a row by that row’s total, so each row adds up to 1. Cells become shares.
  • share / proportion: a part of a whole, such as 3 out of 5 = 0.6 = 60%.
  • binary: only two values, 0 or 1, like a light switch.
  • indicator, \(1_{c_{ij} > 0}\): a little switch that is 1 when the condition inside is true (the count is above 0) and 0 when it is false.
  • term frequency (tf): how often a word appears in one document. On slide 17 it is the raw count; slide 19 describes it as a share.
  • document frequency (\(d_j\)): how many documents contain word \(j\) at least once. Not the total number of uses.
  • inverse document frequency (idf): the rarity weight, \(\log(n/d_j)\). “Inverse” because it goes up when the document frequency goes down.
  • \(n\): the total number of documents.
  • log / natural log (ln): a calculator button that shrinks big numbers. Log of 1 is 0. Bigger numbers give bigger logs, but slowly: ln 3 ≈ 1.1, ln 10 ≈ 2.3, ln 100 ≈ 4.6. “Natural log” is one common kind of log, written ln.
  • base of a log: which kind of log you use (natural log, log base 10, and so on). Different bases give different numbers but the same ranking of words. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • tf-idf: term frequency times inverse document frequency. A count multiplied by a rarity weight.
  • distinctive word: a word that is common in this document but rare in others, so it tells you what this document is about.
  • function words: small grammar words like “the”, “of”, “and” that carry little topic meaning.
  • smoothing / smoothed idf: a small tweak (adding 1 in a few places, as in scikit-learn’s version shown below) so that no word gets a weight of exactly 0.
  • L2 normalisation / L2 length: treat a row as an arrow and make its length 1. The length is found by squaring each number, adding them up, and taking the square root (as in Pythagoras for a triangle).
  • square root (\(\sqrt{\ }\)): the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the number inside. \(\sqrt{9} = 3\).
  • scikit-learn: a free Python toolbox for data analysis used in the course. TfidfVectorizer is its tf-idf tool; CountVectorizer is its counting tool.
  • max_df: a setting that drops words found in more than a given share of documents. max_df=0.5 drops words in more than half of them.
  • software default: the setting a tool uses if you don’t choose one yourself.
  • feature selection: keeping only the useful columns and dropping the rest.
  • threshold: a cut-off line. “Drop terms below a threshold” means drop the ones with a score under some chosen number.
  • weighting: giving some words more importance than others in later calculations.

The idea in plain words

Raw counts have two problems.

  1. Long documents win automatically. A 10-page speech uses every word more often than a 1-page speech, only because it is longer. In Practical Day 1, Truman’s 1946 speech has 27,722 words, while Truman’s 1949 speech has 3,397 (cell 5).
  2. Common words win automatically. Words like “the” or “government” have big counts in almost every document, so they tell you nothing about what makes this document special.

So we often transform the counts before using them. The course gives three transformations plus tf-idf.

Analogy Imagine judging which student “talks most about football”. Student A wrote 10 pages and mentions football 10 times. Student B wrote 1 page and mentions it 5 times. Raw counts say A; shares (row normalisation) say B. And if every student mentions “school”, that word is useless for telling them apart: tf-idf gives it a weight of zero.

Source: Lecture 2a, slide 16; Practical Day 1, cell 5.

The exam definition

Lecture 2a, slide 16: “Not uncommon to normalize the raw counts in \(C\)”. “E.g., long documents will have higher counts just because they are longer. We might want to control for this”. “Common transformations are” (normalize = adjust the counts so documents are fair to compare):

In words: three ways to turn a row of counts into new numbers: keep the counts (left), divide each count by the document’s total number of tokens (middle), or write 1 if the word appears and 0 if not (right).

\[x_i = c_i \qquad\qquad x_i = c_i / m_i, \ \text{ with } \ m_i = \sum_j c_{ij} \qquad\qquad x_{ij} = 1_{c_{ij} > 0}\]

“Even more common is perhaps the Term frequency, inverse document frequency (Tf-idf) transformation” (slides 17–18):

In words: take the count of the word in the document, count how many documents contain the word, turn that into a rarity weight with the log, and multiply the count by the weight.

\[tf_{ij} = c_{ij} \qquad\qquad idf_j = \log\left(\dfrac{n}{d_j}\right), \quad d_j = \sum_i 1_{\{c_{ij} > 0\}} \qquad\qquad \mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}_{ij} = tf_{ij} \times idf_j\]

What each one does, and why (slide 19 plus the 2025 evaluation guideline):

Transformation What the cell becomes Motivation Slide 19 comment
Raw counts the count \(c_{ij}\) simplest “Simple representation but sensitive to document length.”
Row normalisation count ÷ total tokens in the document removes dependence on document length “Mitigates the impact of document length differences.” (slide 19’s “Term Frequency (TF)” entry, which describes this share)
Binary 1 if the word appears, else 0 removes dependence on how many times a word is used “Ignores frequency; focuses on term occurrence.”
Tf-idf count × rarity weight down-weights words common everywhere, up-weights distinctive words “Highlights terms that are significant in a document but rare in the corpus.”

(Rows = the four transformations; columns = what the number in each cell becomes, why you would use it, and the slide’s own comment.)

Slide 18 intuition: “Rare terms: High IDF → More significant if term appears in a document.” “Common terms: Low IDF → Less impact on distinguishing documents.” “Balance: TF-IDF balances term frequency with uniqueness.” Uses: “Feature Selection: Drop terms with TF-IDF below a threshold.” “Weighting: Apply TF-IDF scores to emphasize important terms in models.”

Interactive 1’s one-liner (cell 27): “Raw counts describe the language; tf-idf describes the document.”

Slide inconsistency: which TF to write. The slides define TF two ways. Slide 17 says \(tf_{ij} = c_{ij}\), the raw count. Slide 19 says TF “Normalizes raw counts by the total number of terms in the document”, which is the row normalisation \(c_{ij}/m_i\). In the exam: write the tf-idf formula with \(tf_{ij} = c_{ij}\) (the slide-17 formula), and if you mention TF as a share, call it row normalisation and say both versions appear on the slides. Also, slide 24 says tf-idf can “downplay the importance of very rare or common words”, but slide 18 says rare terms get a high idf. Go with slide 18: rare = high idf.

Source: Lecture 2a, slides 16–19, 24.

A tiny worked example

We use the slide-10 DTM and, as an exercise, treat these 3 documents and 4 terms as the whole corpus (we ignore the “…” columns). We use the natural log (ln). The numbers below are our own illustration on the slide’s table, all checked in Python.

Start: raw counts (rows = documents, columns = terms; same as slide 10):

Using text as data row total \(m_i\)
Doc1 1 1 2 2 6
Doc2 0 3 0 2 5
Doc3 0 0 5 2 7

Row normalisation \(x_{ij} = c_{ij}/m_i\) (rows = documents, columns = terms, cells = share of the document’s tokens). By hand for Doc2, “text”: \(3/5 = 0.6\).

Using text as data
Doc1 0.167 0.167 0.333 0.333
Doc2 0 0.6 0 0.4
Doc3 0 0 0.714 0.286

Each row now adds up to 1.

Binary \(x_{ij} = 1_{c_{ij}>0}\) (cells = 1 if the term appears at all):

Using text as data
Doc1 1 1 1 1
Doc2 0 1 0 1
Doc3 0 0 1 1

Doc3’s 5 uses of “as” and Doc1’s 2 uses both become 1.

Tf-idf, slide version. Step 1, document frequency \(d_j\) (count the non-zero cells in each column). Step 2, \(idf_j = \ln(3/d_j)\).

Term \(d_j\) (documents containing it) \(n/d_j\) \(idf_j = \ln(n/d_j)\)
Using 1 3 1.099
text 2 1.5 0.405
as 2 1.5 0.405
data 3 1 0

(Rows = terms; columns = the steps of the idf calculation.)

Step 3, multiply each count by its column’s idf (rows = documents, columns = terms, cells = tf-idf):

Using text as data
Doc1 1.099 0.405 0.811 0
Doc2 0 1.216 0 0
Doc3 0 0 2.027 0

By hand, Doc3 / “as”: \(tf = 5\), \(idf = \ln(3/2) = 0.405\), so \(5 \times 0.405 = 2.027\). And Doc1 / “Using”: \(1 \times \ln 3 = 1.099\).

What happened: “data” is in every document, so \(\ln(3/3) = \ln 1 = 0\) and its whole column becomes 0. “Using” is only in Doc1, so it gets the biggest weight per use. That is tf-idf’s point: words found everywhere cannot tell documents apart.

Tf-idf, scikit-learn version. The software used in the course does two extra things. Practical Day 1 (cell 11): “By default, scikit-learn uses smoothed inverse document frequencies and normalizes each document vector to length one (L2 normalization).” (In plain words: it adds 1 in a few places so no idf is exactly 0, and then shrinks or stretches each row so that, seen as an arrow, it has length 1.) Interactive 1 (cell 24): “scikit-learn adds 1 to every idf, so no word is weighted down to exactly zero”. The exact smoothed formula is \(idf_j = \ln\frac{1+n}{1+d_j} + 1\). [Not in course files — general knowledge]

Term \(d_j\) smoothed \(idf_j = \ln\frac{1+3}{1+d_j} + 1\)
Using 1 \(\ln(4/2) + 1 = 1.693\)
text 2 \(\ln(4/3) + 1 = 1.288\)
as 2 \(\ln(4/3) + 1 = 1.288\)
data 3 \(\ln(4/4) + 1 = 1.000\)

Now Doc1’s raw weights are count × idf: \(1 \times 1.693 = 1.693\), \(1 \times 1.288 = 1.288\), \(2 \times 1.288 = 2.575\), \(2 \times 1 = 2\). The L2 length of this row (square each weight, add them up, take the square root) is \(\sqrt{1.693^2 + 1.288^2 + 2.575^2 + 2^2} = 3.893\). Divide each weight by 3.893:

Using text as data
Doc1 0.435 0.331 0.661 0.514
Doc2 0 0.888 0 0.460
Doc3 0 0 0.955 0.297

(Rows = documents, columns = terms, cells = scikit-learn tf-idf with smoothed idf and L2-normalised rows.)

Note that “data” is no longer 0. This is why “the can survive tf-idf without a stop-word list” in scikit-learn (Interactive 1, cell 24). As the notebook says: “Software defaults are modelling choices too.”

The course’s own scikit-learn example (Practical Day 1, cell 12, saved output). Three sentences: “Inflation and interest rates rose.” / “Interest rates fell as inflation eased.” / “Employment and wages rose.” In document 2, the words found only there (“as”, “eased”, “fell”) get 0.46, while “inflation”, “interest”, “rates” (also in document 1) get 0.349. In document 3, “employment” and “wages” get 0.563, while “and” and “rose” get 0.428. Rarer words get more weight. In document 1, all five words appear in two documents, so they all get the same weight, \(1/\sqrt{5} = 0.447\).

The formula, symbol by symbol

In words: the tf-idf score is “how often the word is used here” times “how rare the word is across all documents”.

\[\mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}_{ij} = tf_{ij} \times idf_j = c_{ij} \times \log\left(\frac{n}{d_j}\right)\]

  • \(i\) = which document; \(j\) = which term.
  • \(c_{ij}\) = how many times term \(j\) appears in document \(i\) (the DTM cell).
  • \(tf_{ij}\) = term frequency; on slide 17 it is the plain count \(c_{ij}\).
  • \(n\) = “Total number of documents.”
  • \(d_j = \sum_i 1_{\{c_{ij} > 0\}}\) = “Number of documents containing term \(j\)”. The \(1_{\{\cdot\}}\) is an indicator: it is 1 when the count is above 0, otherwise 0. Adding it up over documents counts how many documents contain the word.
  • \(\log(n/d_j)\) = the rarity weight. If the word is in all documents, \(n/d_j = 1\) and \(\log 1 = 0\). If it is in only one document, \(n/d_j = n\), the biggest possible weight.
  • \(m_i = \sum_j c_{ij}\) (row normalisation) = the total number of tokens in document \(i\).

Read aloud: “The tf-idf of word \(j\) in document \(i\) is how often the word appears in that document, times the log of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents that contain the word.”

Notes for the exam: the slide writes only “log” with no base, and has no +1 smoothing. Write it exactly as the slide does. If you need a number, say which log you use.

Reading the course code

Interactive 1, cell 23 (simplified):

Vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer if WEIGHTING == "tfidf" else CountVectorizer
X = Vectorizer(stop_words=STOP_WORDS, max_df=MAX_DF).fit_transform(speeches["rawtext"])
  • Line 1: picks the tool. CountVectorizer gives raw counts; TfidfVectorizer gives tf-idf weights (smoothed idf, rows L2-normalised).
  • Line 2: builds the matrix for all 222 speeches. max_df=0.5 would drop words found in more than half the speeches, which the notebook calls “a crude version of the idf idea”.
