No outputs are saved. Run on Lincoln 1862, raw counts without stop-word removal would put function words such as “the” at the top. With tf-idf, words special to that speech would rise. Practical Day 1 (cell 15) shows the catch: tf-idf can also promote rare names. Trump 2018’s top terms include “justin”, “ho” and “ryan” (guests and officials).

How this shows up on the exam 2025 Q2(b), for 5 points: describe three ways to normalise the DTM (adjust the word-count table so texts compare fairly) and the reason for each. The official marking guide:

  • Row normalisation (divide each count by the text’s length) → removes the effect of length.
  • Binary (1 if the word appears, 0 if not) → removes the effect of how many times it appears.
  • Tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more) → gives less weight to common words and more to distinctive ones.

Also likely as True/False: “A term that occurs in all documents gets idf = 0” (True under the slide formula; idf is the “rarity score” half of tf-idf) or “Rare terms get a low idf” (False). A small calculation with the formula \(idf = \log(n/d_j)\) is possible, but none appeared in 2025.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • All three methods by name (row, binary, tf-idf). For each one: its formula or a one-line description, AND its reason.
  • Why normalise at all: “long documents will have higher counts just because they are longer” (slide 16).
  • For tf-idf, its two parts: term frequency (how often the word is in this document) × inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across documents). Give the formula \(idf_j = \log(n/d_j)\) and say what the letters mean: \(n\) is the number of documents, \(d_j\) is the number of documents that contain word \(j\). Then give the effect: a word in every document gets weight 0, and rare words get high weight.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Naming three methods but giving no reason. Half the marks are for the “why”.
  • Giving only two methods when three are asked.
  • Saying tf-idf “removes rare words”. It does the opposite: it boosts them.
  • Defining \(d_j\) as “how often the term appears in total”. It is the number of documents that contain the word.
  • Mixing up the slide’s TF (term frequency, which on slide 17 is the raw count) with row normalisation (count divided by length) without saying which one you mean.

Key terms to use

  • normalisation (adjusting counts so texts compare fairly)
  • raw counts (plain word counts, nothing adjusted)
  • row normalisation (each count divided by text length)
  • document length (total number of words in a text)
  • binary / indicator (1 if the word appears, else 0)
  • term frequency (how often a word is in a text)
  • inverse document frequency (score that is high for rare words)
  • document frequency \(d_j\) (number of documents containing word j)
  • tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more)
  • distinctive vs common words (special to one text vs used everywhere)
  • smoothing (a small tweak, like adding 1, avoiding zero problems)
  • L2 normalisation (rescaling each row so its length is 1)
  • feature selection (keeping only the most useful words)
  • weighting (giving some words more importance than others)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “Under the slide formula, a word in every document gets idf = 0.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Idf (inverse document frequency) is a rarity score for a word: high if few documents use it, low if many do. The slide formula is \(\log(n/d_j)\), where \(n\) is the number of documents and \(d_j\) is how many of them contain the word. If a word is in every document, is its score 0?

    True. Why: If the word is in all \(n\) documents, the formula becomes \(\log(n/n) = \log 1 = 0\). A word that every text uses tells you nothing about any one text, like the word “student” in a pile of student essays. Watch out: scikit-learn (the Python library used in class) adds 1 to the formula, so there the score is not 0. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 17; Interactive 1, cell 24.)

  2. True or false: “Binary representation keeps information on how often a word is used.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Binary representation means each cell in the table is only 1 (the word appears) or 0 (it does not). Does that still record how many times the word was used?

    False. Why: Binary is a tick box: present or absent. Saying “war” once or fifty times both give a 1. The slide says it “Ignores frequency; focuses on term occurrence”. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 19.)

  3. True or false: “Rare terms receive a high idf.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A rare term is a word that only a few documents use. Do such words get a high rarity score (idf)?

    True. Why: Rare words are what set a text apart, like a fingerprint. Fewer documents with the word means a bigger \(n/d_j\), so a bigger log. The slide says “Rare terms: High IDF”. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 18.)

  4. Calculate: a corpus has \(n = 100\) documents; the word “inflation” appears in 10 of them, 4 times in document 7. Using natural log, what is its tf-idf in document 7?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A corpus is your collection of texts, here 100 of them. “Inflation” is in 10 of those texts, and 4 times in text number 7. Tf-idf = the count in this text × the rarity score (idf). “Natural log” is the ln button on a calculator.

    Answer: \(idf = \ln(100/10) = \ln 10 = 2.303\); tf-idf \(= 4 \times 2.303 = 9.21\).

    Why: First the rarity score: 100 texts divided by the 10 that use the word is 10, and ln 10 is 2.303. Then multiply by how often the word is in text 7: 4 × 2.303 = 9.21.

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q2b style): Describe three ways to normalise the DTM and why.

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Name three ways to adjust the word-count table so texts compare fairly, and say why each one helps.

    Model answer: Row normalisation divides each count by the total number of tokens in the document (\(x_i = c_i/m_i\)), so long documents do not get high counts only because they are long. Binary coding sets a cell to 1 if the word appears and 0 otherwise (\(x_{ij} = 1_{c_{ij}>0}\)), which removes the dependence on how often a word is repeated. Tf-idf multiplies the count by \(\log(n/d_j)\), where \(n\) is the number of documents and \(d_j\) the number of documents containing the word. This down-weights words that appear everywhere (weight 0 if in all documents) and up-weights words that are distinctive for a document.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Row normalisation turns counts into shares of the text, so a long text does not win only by being long. Binary records only whether a word is there, not how often. Tf-idf boosts words that are special to one text and shrinks words that are everywhere. A word found in every document ends up with weight 0.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 16–19, 24; GRA4164_Interactive_1_Text_as_data.ipynb cells 21–24, 27; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 5, 11, 12, 15

5. Comparing documents: Euclidean distance vs cosine similarity

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q3(d) asked for a drawing of high vs low cosine similarity; cosine is reused for word embeddings (Lectures 6 and 8)

Start from zero

The problem. You read a news article and the website shows “More articles like this”. How does the computer pick them? Each article is already a row of word counts (Chapter 3), maybe re-weighted with tf-idf (Chapter 4). Now the computer needs a single number that says “how alike are these two rows?” The catch: a long article and a short article on the same topic have very different counts, only because one is longer. We want a measure that looks at the mix of words, not the size of the article. That measure is cosine similarity.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Pick the words. Keep it to two words so you can draw it, such as “good” and “bad”.
  2. Turn each document into an arrow. Draw two axes like a graph: “count of bad” going right, “count of good” going up. A document with good = 2 and bad = 1 becomes an arrow from the corner (0, 0) to the point 1 step right and 2 steps up.
  3. Option one, Euclidean distance: measure with a ruler the gap between the tips of two arrows. Long documents have long arrows, so their tips end up far from short ones.
  4. Option two, cosine similarity: look only at the angle between two arrows. Same direction means the same mix of words, whatever the length.
  5. Compute the cosine. Multiply the matching numbers of the two documents and add them up (the dot product). Divide by the length of each arrow. The result is 1 if the arrows point the same way and 0 if they share no words.

A tiny example by hand. Three made-up reviews (our own), counted on two words, “good” and “bad”.

Document ↓ / Word → good bad
A: “good good bad” 2 1
B: review A written twice 4 2
C: “bad bad good” 1 2

Rows are documents. Columns are words. Each cell is a count. One cell out loud: row B, column “good”. Review A has “good” 2 times, and B is A written twice, so 2 × 2 = 4.

Euclidean distance, A to B. Differences: 4 − 2 = 2 for “good”, 2 − 1 = 1 for “bad”. Square them: 4 and 1. Add: 5. Square root of 5 ≈ 2.24.

Euclidean distance, A to C. Differences: 2 − 1 = 1 and 1 − 2 = −1. Square them: 1 and 1. Add: 2. Square root of 2 ≈ 1.41.

So Euclidean distance says C is closer to A than B is. That feels wrong: B says exactly what A says, only twice.

Cosine, A and B. Dot product: 2 × 4 + 1 × 2 = 8 + 2 = 10. Length of A: square root of (2 × 2 + 1 × 1) = square root of 5 ≈ 2.236. Length of B: square root of (4 × 4 + 2 × 2) = square root of 20 ≈ 4.472. Multiply the lengths: 2.236 × 4.472 ≈ 10. Cosine = 10 ÷ 10 = 1. Same direction, a perfect match.

Cosine, A and C. Dot product: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2 = 4. Both lengths are the square root of 5, and square root of 5 times square root of 5 is 5. Cosine = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8. Similar, but less so.

Cosine gets it right: B is the same review, only longer. The slide-22 example further down shows the same clash with the slide’s own numbers: Euclidean distance says \(d_3\) is closer to \(d_1\) (1.35 against 1.46), while cosine says \(d_2\) is more similar (0.99 against 0.84).

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: ignoring document length, so a long and a short text on the same topic look alike.
  • Good at: finding “the most similar documents” fast, for search and recommendations.
  • Breaks when: two texts share words but make opposite arguments; cosine only sees word overlap, not meaning.
  • Breaks when: shared names, style or time period make texts look alike although the topic differs.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • vector: an ordered list of numbers, such as (2, 1). You can draw it as an arrow.
  • document vector: a document’s row of counts (or tf-idf weights), seen as an arrow. The slide writes it with a little arrow on top, \(\vec{d_1}\).
  • vector space / vector space diagram: the graph where these arrows live, with one axis per word.
  • axis (axes): the two reference lines of a graph, one going right and one going up.
  • origin: the corner point (0, 0) where the axes meet. Every arrow starts there.
  • dimension: one direction in the graph, which here means one word. Two words give a flat 2-D picture; a real vocabulary has thousands of dimensions, which we cannot draw but can still compute.
  • \(d_{1,i}\): the number for word \(i\) in document 1. The small letters below are an address.
  • \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\): “add up over all words, from word 1 to word \(n\)”. Here \(n\) is the number of words, not documents.
  • square / square root: squaring is a number times itself (\(3^2 = 9\)); the square root goes back (\(\sqrt{9} = 3\)).
  • Euclidean distance: the straight-line ruler distance between two arrow tips.
  • angle, \(\theta\) (theta): how far apart two arrows point, measured in degrees. \(\theta\) is the Greek letter used for it.
  • cosine: a calculator button that turns an angle into a number: 0 degrees gives 1, a right angle (90 degrees) gives 0.
  • cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between two document arrows. 1 = same direction, 0 = no shared words.
  • dot product (\(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2}\)): multiply matching numbers and add them up. (2, 1) and (4, 2) give 2 × 4 + 1 × 2 = 10.
  • length / norm (\(\|\vec{d_1}\|\)): how long the arrow is: square each number, add them up, take the square root.
  • orthogonal: at a right angle. For word counts it means the two documents share no words.
  • bounded between −1 and 1: the value can never go below −1 or above 1.
  • proportion / mix: how the words are shared out in a document, such as “twice as much good as bad”.
  • length-invariant: not changed by making the document longer or shorter.
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the table of word counts, one row per document (Chapter 3).
  • tf-idf: counts re-weighted so that rare, telling words count more (Chapter 4).
  • word embeddings: lists of numbers for single words (later lectures), compared with the same cosine.
  • query: the document you start from when you ask “what is most like this one?”
  • cosine_similarity, ravel, argsort: Python tools: the first computes cosines, the second flattens a table into one list, the third sorts and returns the positions in order.
  • index (climate news index): one number per period of time that tracks how much the news talks about a topic.
  • WSJ / The Review of Financial Studies: the Wall Street Journal, a business newspaper; and a top academic journal in finance.

The idea in plain words

Once each document is a row of numbers, you can draw it as an arrow starting at zero. Two documents are similar if their arrows are similar. But “similar” can mean two things:

  • Euclidean distance: how far apart are the two arrow tips? This is affected by length. A long document has a long arrow.
  • Cosine similarity: how small is the angle between the two arrows? This only looks at direction, the mix of words, not how long the document is.

Analogy Two recipes for the same cake, one for 4 people and one for 12. The big recipe uses three times as much of everything. The ingredient lists are far apart in amounts (large Euclidean distance) but point in exactly the same direction (cosine = 1). Cosine asks “same recipe?”, not “same amount?”.

Source: Lecture 2a, slides 20–22.

The exam definition

Slide 20: “Two documents are similar if their vectors are similar” … “BUT: How to measure similarity?” (The slide boxes the Doc2 and Doc3 rows of the DTM to compare.)

Slide 21: take two terms, e.g. “Term a = {good}, and Term b = {bad}”, and draw each document as a vector in a “vector space diagram” using its counts.

Slide 22 gives both measures:

In words: Euclidean distance subtracts the two documents’ counts word by word, squares each difference, adds them up and takes the square root, which gives the ruler distance between the arrow tips.

\[d(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{2} (d_{1,i} - d_{2,i})^2}\]

In words: cosine similarity multiplies the matching counts and adds them up (the dot product), then divides by the length of each arrow, so only the direction of the arrows counts.

\[\cos\theta_{12} = \frac{\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2}}{\left\|\vec{d_1}\right\| \left\|\vec{d_2}\right\|} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{1,i}\, d_{2,i}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{1,i}^2}\ \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{2,i}^2}}\]

“Potential issue: \(d(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2}) > d(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_3})\) simply because \(d_1\) is a longer document and therefore uses all terms more frequently. This issue is avoided by using the Cosine similarity measure (bounded between -1 and 1, where 1 (-1) is perfectly similar and 0 is orthogonal).” (In plain words: the ruler distance can look big only because \(d_1\) is long; cosine avoids this, and it always lands between −1 and 1, where 1 means “same direction” and 0 means “at a right angle”, that is, no shared words.)

Source: Lecture 2a, slides 20–22.

A tiny worked example

The slide-22 example. Each document is counted on two terms. We read each vector as (Term b, Term a), because that matches the slide’s drawing (Term b horizontal, Term a vertical); the slide does not state the order.

Document Term b (horizontal) Term a (vertical)
\(\vec{d_1}\) 1.5 2
\(\vec{d_2}\) 0.75 0.75
\(\vec{d_3}\) 2 0.75

(Rows = documents; columns = the two term counts. Values from slide 22.)

Step 1: Euclidean distances (subtract, square, add, square-root):

  • \(d_1\) vs \(d_2\): \((1.5 - 0.75)^2 + (2 - 0.75)^2 = 0.5625 + 1.5625 = 2.125\), and \(\sqrt{2.125} = 1.458 \approx\) 1.46
  • \(d_1\) vs \(d_3\): \((1.5 - 2)^2 + (2 - 0.75)^2 = 0.25 + 1.5625 = 1.8125\), and \(\sqrt{1.8125} = 1.346 \approx\) 1.35

By Euclidean distance, \(d_3\) looks closer to \(d_1\).

Step 2: lengths of each arrow (the bottom of the cosine formula):

  • \(\|\vec{d_1}\| = \sqrt{1.5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.5\)
  • \(\|\vec{d_2}\| = \sqrt{0.75^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{1.125} = 1.061\)
  • \(\|\vec{d_3}\| = \sqrt{2^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{4.5625} = 2.136\)

Step 3: dot products (multiply matching entries, then add; the top of the formula):

  • \(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2} = 1.5 \times 0.75 + 2 \times 0.75 = 1.125 + 1.5 = 2.625\)
  • \(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_3} = 1.5 \times 2 + 2 \times 0.75 = 3 + 1.5 = 4.5\)

Step 4: divide:

  • \(\cos\theta_{12} = 2.625 / (2.5 \times 1.061) = 2.625 / 2.652 = 0.990 \approx\) 0.99
  • \(\cos\theta_{13} = 4.5 / (2.5 \times 2.136) = 4.5 / 5.340 = 0.843 \approx\) 0.84

By cosine, \(d_2\) is more similar to \(d_1\). The two measures disagree. Cosine is right here: \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) “use the terms \(a\) and \(b\) in roughly the same proportion, while \(d_3\) uses term \(b\) much more frequently” (slide 21). \(d_1\) is only a longer document.

Proof that length does not matter for cosine (our own check): double \(d_2\) to \((1.5, 1.5)\), as if the same document were written twice. Cosine with \(d_1\) stays 0.99. But the Euclidean distance to \(d_1\) changes from 1.46 to 0.50.

Left: Euclidean distance is the dashed line between arrow tips (\(d_1\)–\(d_2\) = 1.46, \(d_1\)–\(d_3\) = 1.35). Right: cosine looks at the angle. The small arc between \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) gives cos = 0.99; the larger shaded angle between \(d_1\) and \(d_3\) gives cos = 0.84. Redrawn from Lecture 2a, slide 22.

Link back to the DTM (slide 20 boxes Doc2 and Doc3). With raw counts from slide 10, Doc2 = (0, 3, 0, 2) and Doc3 = (0, 0, 5, 2). Dot product \(= 2 \times 2 = 4\); lengths \(\sqrt{13} = 3.606\) and \(\sqrt{29} = 5.385\); cosine \(= 4 / 19.416 = 0.206\), so not very similar. If we use the slide-formula tf-idf from Chapter 4 instead, their only shared word “data” gets weight 0, and the cosine becomes 0: no shared distinctive words. (Our own illustration, checked in Python.)

How to draw the answer to 2025 Q3(d)

The question asked for a graph illustrating high vs low cosine similarity. Draw this:

Our own drawing for the exam answer. Vectors used: A = (1, 3), B = (0.7, 1.6), C = (3, 0.3) as (term b, term a). Computed cosines: A–B = 0.996 (angle 5.2°), A–C = 0.409 (angle 65.9°).

Checklist for the hand drawing (from the 2025 evaluation guideline, plus what makes it top-grade): two labelled axes (count of term a, count of term b); every vector starts at the origin; two vectors pointing almost the same way (small angle, high cosine); one vector pointing a very different way (large angle, low cosine); mark the angles θ; write cos θ ≈ 1 and “low”; make one of the similar arrows shorter, to show that length does not matter.

The formula, symbol by symbol

  • \(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2}\) = the two documents as vectors (their rows in the DTM, or their tf-idf rows).
  • \(d_{1,i}\) = the value of term \(i\) in document 1.
  • \(\sum_i d_{1,i}\, d_{2,i}\) = the dot product: multiply matching entries and add them up. It is big when both documents use the same words a lot.
  • \(\|\vec{d_1}\| = \sqrt{\sum_i d_{1,i}^2}\) = the length of the arrow.
  • \(\cos\theta_{12}\) = the cosine of the angle \(\theta\) between the two arrows. Dividing by both lengths removes the effect of document length.
  • \(\sqrt{\sum_i (d_{1,i} - d_{2,i})^2}\) = Euclidean distance: the straight-line distance between the arrow tips.
  • Careful: in the cosine sum, \(n\) is the number of terms (dimensions), which is 2 in the example. It is not the number of documents \(n\) from slide 8. The slide reuses the symbol.

Read aloud: “The cosine similarity of two documents is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths; it is 1 when they point the same way and 0 when they share no terms.”

The slide says cosine is “bounded between -1 and 1”. Counts and tf-idf weights are never negative, so for DTM rows it is in practice between 0 and 1. [Not in course files — general knowledge] In a True/False item, answer by the slide’s wording.

Reading the course code

Practical Day 1, cell 15:

scores = cosine_similarity(tfidf_matrix[query_row], tfidf_matrix).ravel()
scores[query_row] = -1
top = np.argsort(-scores)[:5]
  • Line 1: computes the cosine similarity between one speech (the query, Trump 2018) and every speech in the tf-idf matrix.
  • Line 2: sets the speech’s similarity with itself to −1, so it does not come out as its own best match.
  • Line 3: sorts from highest to lowest and keeps the top 5.

Saved output (rows = the most similar speeches; column = cosine with Trump 2018): Trump_2017 0.516; Obama_2013 0.445; Obama_2014 0.443; Obama_2015 0.438; Obama_2012 0.427. The nearest speeches share speaker and era, so the notebook asks: are we detecting theme, style, era or speaker? Its warning (cell 16): “Cosine similarity measures overlap in the chosen representation. It is not evidence that the speeches make the same argument.”

Real example: “Tf-idf and cosine similarity can be enough!”

Lecture 2a, slide 23 shows Engle, Giglio, Kelly, Lee & Stroebel (2020), “Hedging climate change news”, The Review of Financial Studies (the slide title says “Hedging Climate Risk”). They collect a “climate change vocabulary from a corpus of seventy-four authoritative climate change texts” (biggest words: climate, change, carbon, emissions, greenhouse). They then build a WSJ Climate Change News Index from 1984 to 2017, with peaks at events such as the Kyoto Protocol, the 2009 Copenhagen conference and the Paris Agreement. The method compares each Wall Street Journal article’s tf-idf vector with the tf-idf vector of the climate vocabulary using cosine similarity. [Not in course files — general knowledge] The point of the slide: a published finance paper needed nothing fancier than the tools in this chapter.

How this shows up on the exam 2025 Q3(d) said: “Make a graph illustrating” high vs low cosine similarity (a score for how closely two arrows point the same way). It sat in the word-embeddings block (word embeddings = words turned into lists of numbers), because cosine is also how word vectors are compared in Lectures 6 and 8. Expect True/False items:

  • “Euclidean distance is unaffected by document length” (False). Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between two points, as measured with a ruler.
  • “Cosine similarity of 0 means the documents are orthogonal” (True). Orthogonal means at a right angle (90 degrees).

A small calculation like the slide-22 example is possible. In the reflection question, cosine on tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more) is a good method to “find the most similar documents” (slide 24), for example to group similar survey answers.

What a top-grade answer must include

For the drawing:

  • Labelled axes.
  • Arrows (vectors) that start from the origin (the corner point where both axes are 0).
  • Two arrows with a small angle between them (cosine near 1), and one with a large angle (low cosine).
  • The angles marked.

In words:

  • Cosine measures the angle between document vectors (each document drawn as an arrow of word counts), so it ignores length.
  • Euclidean distance measures the gap between the arrow tips, and it grows with document length (the slide-22 “potential issue”).
  • Give the formula and the range. The slide says −1 to 1: 1 = perfectly similar, 0 = orthogonal (at right angles).
  • Give a course example: the Engle et al. 2020 climate index.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Drawing dots instead of arrows from the origin.
  • Drawing the “similar” pair with a large angle but tips close together. That shows a small Euclidean distance, not a high cosine.
  • Forgetting to label the axes.
  • Saying a longer document is less similar under cosine. Length does not matter for cosine.
  • Saying cosine 0 means “opposite”. 0 means orthogonal: the documents share no words. −1 would be opposite [Not in course files — general knowledge]. Word counts are never negative, so for them cosine cannot go below 0.

Key terms to use

  • vector space (a map where each word is one direction)
  • document vector (a document drawn as an arrow of counts)
  • Euclidean distance (straight-line gap between the arrow tips)
  • cosine similarity (how closely two arrows point the same way)
  • angle θ (theta: the angle between two arrows)
  • dot product (multiply matching numbers, then add them up)
  • vector length / norm (how long the arrow is)
  • length-invariant (not changed by how long a text is)
  • orthogonal (at right angles; no shared words)
  • bounded between −1 and 1 (the score always lies from −1 to 1)
  • tf-idf + cosine (rarity-weighted counts compared by their angle)
  • most similar documents (texts whose arrows point closest together)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “Euclidean distance is unaffected by document length.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Picture each document as an arrow that gets longer as its word counts grow. Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between two arrow tips, as if you measured it with a ruler. Does the gap stay the same no matter how long a document is?

    False. Why: A long document has bigger counts, so its arrow is longer and its tip sits far away, even if it talks about the same things. Think of two people walking in the same direction: one walks 1 km, the other 10 km. Same direction, but far apart. The slide says \(d_1\) is far from \(d_2\) “simply because \(d_1\) is a longer document”. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 22.)

  2. True or false: “Two documents whose word counts are exactly proportional have cosine similarity 1.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Exactly proportional” means one document’s counts are a fixed multiple of the other’s, for example every count doubled. Cosine similarity is a score based on the angle between two arrows: 1 means they point exactly the same way. Do such documents score 1?

    True. Why: Doubling every count makes the arrow longer but keeps its direction, like stretching it. Same direction means zero angle, so cosine is 1. Check with the slide-22 numbers: doubling \(d_2\) leaves its cosine with \(d_1\) at 0.99. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 22 numbers, our own check.)

  3. True or false: “A cosine similarity of 0 means the documents share no terms.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Terms” means words. A cosine of 0 means the two arrows sit at a right angle (orthogonal). Does that mean no word appears in both documents?

    True for count or tf-idf vectors. Why: The cosine formula multiplies the two documents’ counts word by word and adds the results up. Counts are never negative, so the only way to get 0 is when no word appears in both. Think of two shopping lists with nothing in common. The slide says “0 is orthogonal”. (Source: Lecture 2a, slide 22.)

  4. Calculate: \(\vec{x} = (2, 0)\) and \(\vec{y} = (1, 1)\). Cosine?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Two arrows: x goes 2 steps along the first axis and 0 along the second; y goes 1 step along each. Cosine = dot product (multiply matching numbers, then add) divided by the two arrow lengths multiplied together.

    Answer: dot product \(= 2 \times 1 + 0 \times 1 = 2\); lengths \(2\) and \(\sqrt{2} = 1.414\); cosine \(= 2 / 2.828 = 0.707\).

    Why: The dot product is 2 × 1 plus 0 × 1, which is 2. Arrow x has length 2. Arrow y has length \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2} = 1.414\). So the cosine is 2 divided by (2 × 1.414), which is 0.707: fairly similar, but not the same direction.

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences: Why does the course prefer cosine similarity to Euclidean distance for comparing documents?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why does the course compare documents by the angle between their arrows (cosine) rather than by the ruler gap between their tips (Euclidean distance)?

    Model answer: Euclidean distance measures the straight-line gap between the tips of two document vectors, so a long document is far from a short one even if they use words in the same proportions. Cosine similarity measures only the angle between the vectors, by dividing the dot product by both lengths, so document length drops out. In the slide-22 example, Euclidean distance wrongly says \(d_3\) is closer to \(d_1\) (1.35 vs 1.46), while cosine correctly says \(d_2\) is more similar (0.99 vs 0.84). Cosine is 1 for identical direction and 0 for orthogonal (no shared terms).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: The ruler gap punishes long texts, even when they talk about the same things. The angle looks only at direction, meaning the mix of words, so length does not matter. In the slide example, the ruler picks the wrong document as closest and the angle picks the right one.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 20–24; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 12, 15, 16

Part II — Methods built on the bag-of-words

6. The method map: supervised vs unsupervised text methods (L3)

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — you need it to place any method in the right box (and to spot a wrong “learning type” in a True/False statement).

Start from zero

The problem. Picture a small online shop with 10,000 customer reviews. The owner wants to know three things: “Are people happy?”, “What star rating would this new review get?” and “What do people talk about most?” Nobody can read 10,000 reviews by hand, so a computer has to help. But there are many ways a computer can help, and they need different things from you. The big question is: do you already have an answer for each text (like the star rating the customer gave), or do you want the computer to find patterns on its own? This chapter is the map that sorts every method in this part of the course by that one question.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Turn each text into numbers. The computer counts how often each word appears in each text. You get one big table: one row per text (a “document”), one column per word, and each cell is a count. This table is called the document-term matrix.
  2. Ask: do I have an answer for each text? An “answer” is something like the star rating of a review, “spam” or “not spam” for an email, or the political party of the person who gave a speech.
  3. Yes, I have answers → supervised. The computer studies the texts and their answers, learns the link between them, and then guesses the answer for new texts. Text regression (guessing a number, Chapter 8) and Naive Bayes (guessing a category, Chapter 9) live here.
  4. No answers, but I write the rule myself → still called supervised. If you decide the rule in advance (“count the happy words, subtract the angry words”), the course puts it in the supervised box too, because you control exactly what comes out. That is the dictionary/Boolean family (Chapter 7).
  5. No answers and no rule → unsupervised. The computer groups words and texts that look alike. You look at the groups afterwards and give them names. Topic models (LSA and LDA, Chapter 10) live here.

A tiny example by hand. Three short reviews:

  • R1: “great food, tasty food”
  • R2: “bad delivery, wasted money”
  • R3: “great food, late delivery”

The table below has one row per review. The columns show what each branch of the map would do with it.

Review Rule-based (dictionary) score = happy words − angry words Answer key (stars the customer gave), which a supervised method learns from Themes an unsupervised method might find
R1 1 − 0 = +1 5 food
R2 0 − 2 = −2 1 delivery
R3 1 − 0 = +1 4 half food, half delivery

Let’s work out one cell out loud. Our happy list is {good, great} and our angry list is {bad, wasted}. Review R2 says “bad delivery, wasted money”. Happy words: none, so 0. Angry words: “bad” and “wasted”, so 2. Score = 0 − 2 = −2. Nobody learned anything here; we wrote the rule and applied it. Notice R3: “late” is a complaint, but it is not on our angry list, so the rule misses it.

The stars column is the answer key. A supervised method would look at all three rows and learn something like “great goes with high stars, bad and wasted go with low stars”. Then it can guess the stars for a fourth review it has never seen.

The last column needs no answers and no rule. The computer notices that “food” shows up in R1 and R3, and “delivery” shows up in R2 and R3. So it can form two groups of words, one with food and tasty, one with delivery, late and money, and say R3 is a bit of each. We are the ones who name them “food” and “delivery”.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: it tells you which family of methods fits the data you actually have. Have answers → supervised. No answers → unsupervised.
  • Good: it protects you from a favourite exam trap. Dictionaries count as supervised, even though there is no answer column.
  • Limit: the map tells you what kind of method fits, not which single method is best.
  • Limit: real projects often mix branches, for example finding topics first and then using them in a regression (Chapter 10 mentions this).

What the words mean (from zero).

  • NLP (natural language processing): getting computers to work with human language. A spell checker or a translation app is NLP.
  • document: one piece of text we study: one review, one speech, one email, one newspaper article.
  • word count: how many times a word appears in a document. In “great food, tasty food”, the count of “food” is 2.
  • matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
  • document-term matrix (\(C\), DTM): the word-count table. Rows are documents, columns are words, each cell is how often that word appears in that document.
  • \(c_i\): the row of the table that belongs to document number \(i\). The little \(i\) is a “which one” tag: \(c_3\) is the third document’s row.
  • method / algorithm: a recipe a computer follows step by step, like a cooking recipe.
  • outcome (\(y\)): the thing you want to know or guess, such as star rating or party. \(y_i\) is the outcome of document \(i\).
  • observed: we actually have it in our data. The stars a customer gave are observed.
  • explanatory variables (\(x\)): the inputs you use to make the guess. Here, the word counts.
  • label / labelled data / answer key: the correct answer stored next to each text, like “spam” written on an email. Labelled data = texts that come with their answers.
  • supervised: the computer learns from examples that come with answers (or follows a rule you wrote). Like a student who studies past exams together with the correct answers.
  • unsupervised: no answers at all; the computer finds groups on its own. Like sorting a pile of mixed photos into piles that look alike, then naming the piles.
  • semi-supervised / self-supervised: the answers come from the text itself. Hide a word in a sentence and ask the computer to guess it: the hidden word is the answer.
  • training data: the examples the computer learns from, like the practice exams.
  • empirical relationship: a link you see in real data, such as “reviews with ‘great’ tend to get more stars”.
  • linear regression, \(y = \beta x + e\): a straight-line formula. The outcome \(y\) equals a weight \(\beta\) times an input \(x\), plus an error \(e\) for what the line misses. Chapter 8 builds it from zero.
  • \(\beta\) (beta), weight, coefficient: the number that says how much one input matters. If \(\beta = 2\), one more “great” adds 2 to the guess.
  • \(e\) (error): the part the formula gets wrong, the gap between guess and truth.
  • function, \(f()\): a fixed rule that turns an input into an output, like “take the number and add 2”.
  • known functional form: the rule is written down in advance, so for any input you know the output. That is why dictionaries count as “supervised”.
  • latent / latent variable \(v_i\): hidden; something real we cannot see directly, like a writer’s mood or a hidden theme.
  • \(\hat v_i\) (v-hat): a hat on a letter means “our estimate of it”. \(\hat v_i\) is our best guess of the hidden \(v_i\).
  • Boolean search: a search rule built with AND, OR and NOT, like a library search filter.
  • dictionary method: you write lists of words (happy words, angry words) and count hits.
  • sentiment: how positive or negative a text sounds.
  • regression: a method for guessing a number from inputs (Chapter 8).
  • OLS (ordinary least squares): the standard way to draw the best straight line through points (Chapter 8).
  • Lasso: a regression that charges a fee for big weights so that useless words drop out (Chapter 8).
  • classification / classifier / class: sorting things into boxes. The boxes are the classes (“spam”, “not spam”); the method that sorts is a classifier (Chapter 9).
  • Naive Bayes: a classifier that learns how often each word appears in each class, then picks the most likely class (Chapter 9).
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0 = never, 1 = certain, 0.5 = a coin flip.
  • \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\): read the bar “\(\mid\)” as “given”. “The chance of outcome \(y\) given these words.” Example: the chance of 5 stars given the review says “great”.
  • \(p(c_i\mid y_i)\): the reverse: “the chance of these words given the class”. Example: how likely the word “prize” is, given the email is spam.
  • Bayes’ rule: a rule for flipping the second kind of chance into the first (Chapter 9).
  • topic: a group of words that tend to show up together, like {goal, match, team}.
  • topic model: an unsupervised method that finds topics and says how much of each topic is in each document (Chapter 10).
  • \(K\): the number of topics you ask for.
  • LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis): a topic method that uses pure table arithmetic (Chapter 10).
  • LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): a topic method built on chances (Chapter 10).
  • SVD (singular value decomposition): the maths tool LSA uses to split a big table into smaller ones (Chapter 10).
  • word embeddings / neural nets: later methods (Lecture 6) that turn each word into a list of numbers so that similar words get similar lists.
  • word2vec / LLM (large language model): word2vec is a word-embedding method; an LLM is a very large text-predicting model, like the one behind a chatbot. Both learn by guessing hidden words.
  • T/F: a True/False exam question.

The idea in plain words

After Lecture 2 every document is a row of word counts in the document-term matrix \(C\). Lecture 3 asks: what can we do with those rows? The course sorts the answers into a family tree. The first split is simple: do we have an answer key or not?

  • Supervised: we know what we are trying to get out. Either we have observed outcomes \(y\) (GDP growth, “spam / not spam”, the party of a president), or, for dictionaries, we know the exact rule that turns words into a number.
  • Unsupervised: we have no answer key. We let the algorithm find structure (groups of words, groups of documents) in the text by itself.

Analogy Supervised learning is a student with the answer sheet: they study past exams and the correct answers, and learn the link between them. Unsupervised learning is sorting a huge pile of letters into piles with no instructions — you put similar letters together and only afterwards give each pile a name (“bills”, “love letters”, “ads”).

The exam definition

Slide 5 gives the definitions:

  • Supervised: “We know the outcome and the explanatory variables, but need to learn their empirical relationship. Think, e.g., linear regression y = βx + e.” (A straight-line formula: outcome \(y\) = a weight \(\beta\) times the input \(x\), plus an error \(e\). Chapter 8 explains it from zero.)
  • Unsupervised: “We do not know the outcome, but learn relationships in the data (x) directly from the algorithm.”
  • Semi-supervised: “Input (x) and output (y) given by the structure of the training data itself.” (This one returns later with word2vec and LLMs (word2vec = a method that turns words into lists of numbers; LLMs = large language models, the text-predicting models behind chatbots), where the “answer” is simply the next or surrounding word.)

The tree on slide 4 (repeated on slides 6, 13, 21 and 30, each time with one branch in red):

The map table. Rows = the methods in Lecture 3. Columns = which branch, the label the slide writes under the method, and what that label means in plain words.

Method (slide) Branch Slide label In plain words
Boolean / dictionary (slide 6) Supervised \(\hat v_i = f(c_i)\) for known function \(f()\), \(v_i\) treated as latent We write down the rule (word lists, AND/OR) and apply it to each document’s counts to get a score such as sentiment or uncertainty.
Text regression, OLS/Lasso (slide 13) Supervised \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\), \(y_i\) observed Predict an observed outcome from the words.
Naive Bayes (slide 21) Supervised \(p(c_i \mid y_i)\), \(y_i\) observed Learn which words each class produces, then flip it with Bayes’ rule (a rule that turns “chance of these words given the class” into “chance of the class given these words”) to guess the class.
LSA (slide 30) Unsupervised \(f(c_i \mid v_i)\), \(v_i\) latent Find a few hidden factors \(v_i\) that explain the counts; a plain mathematical function, not a probability model.
LDA (slide 30) Unsupervised \(p(c_i \mid v_i)\), \(v_i\) latent Same goal, but as a probability model: hidden topics generate the words.

“Latent” means hidden / never observed. Notice the arrow direction: regression goes from text to outcome (\(y\) given \(c\)), Naive Bayes and topic models go from the class or topic to the text (\(c\) given \(y\) or \(v\)).

Why do dictionaries count as “supervised”? Slide 7: “Although we do not know the outcome, we call these methods supervised because we know the functional form. Thus, if we get some input \(c_i\) to \(f()\), we know what the output will be.” Nothing is learned from the data; the researcher fixes the rule in advance. So “supervised” here means “the researcher is in full control of the mapping”, not “we have labelled training data”.

A tiny worked example

Take one task — “is this customer review positive?” — and solve it with each branch. Rows = method; columns = what you must have in hand and what comes out.

Method What you need What you get
Dictionary A word list (good, great / bad, wasted — slide 8) Score = #positive − #negative per review
Lasso regression 500 reviews with a star score \(y\) A weight \(\beta_j\) for each word (how much that word \(j\) pushes the stars up or down); predicted stars for new reviews
Naive Bayes 500 reviews labelled “good”/“bad” \(P(\text{good}\mid \text{review})\), a class for each new review
LDA / LSA Only the reviews, no labels K topics (“price”, “delivery”, “staff”…) and each review’s mix of them

Only the last row needs no answer key and no hand-written rule; that is what makes it unsupervised. (Illustration made up for this guide; the method labels are from slides 4–30.)

How this shows up on the exam

  • Mostly as True/False statements that put a method in the right or wrong box. Two examples: “Dictionary methods are unsupervised” → False (Source: slide 7). “LDA is an unsupervised method” → True (LDA is the topic model from Chapter 10) (Source: slide 30 and Notebook 2 cell 21).
  • In 2025, T/F (f) said “Large Language Models are estimated using unsupervised learning”. The answer was False. Large Language Models (LLMs) are the text-predicting models behind chatbots. The official guideline gives only “False”. The reason is in the LLM training lecture, slide 4: “Training LLMs is often called self-supervised training”. That means the answers come from the text itself: the model guesses the next word, and the real next word is the answer. It is the same trap as above: the statement puts a method in the wrong learning type.
  • In the reflection question (the open question where you plan your own text study), say which box your method belongs to. Then say why that fits your data: do your texts come with answers (labels) or not? This shows the examiner good judgement.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • One line defining supervised (the computer learns from texts that come with answers) and one line defining unsupervised (no answers; the computer finds groups on its own).
  • The correct box for each method.
  • The reason from slide 7 why dictionaries count as “supervised”: the rule is fixed in advance. The slide calls this a “known functional form” (you already know the formula that turns a text into a score).
  • Which way each model points:
    • text regression guesses the outcome from the words (\(p(y\mid c)\), “the chance of outcome \(y\) given the words \(c\)”);
    • Naive Bayes describes the words from the class (\(p(c\mid y)\), “the chance of these words given the class”);
    • topic models have no outcome at all. They use a hidden variable instead (latent \(v\), for example a document’s mix of topics, which nobody observes).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Calling dictionaries “unsupervised because there is no \(y\)” (no answer column). The course still puts them in the supervised box, because the rule is known.
  • Mixing up text regression (\(p(y_i\mid c_i)\): guess the outcome from the words) with Naive Bayes (\(p(c_i\mid y_i)\): describe the words given the class).
  • Putting LSA (the other topic model from Chapter 10) in the supervised box because its maths looks a bit like regression maths.

Key terms to use

  • supervised (learns from texts with answers, or a fixed rule)
  • unsupervised (no answers; finds groups by itself)
  • semi-supervised (the answers come from the text itself)
  • latent variable \(v_i\) (hidden thing we never observe directly)
  • known functional form \(f()\) (the text-to-score rule is fixed in advance)
  • document-term matrix \(C\) (table: documents as rows, word counts as columns)
  • \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\) (chance of the outcome, given the words)
  • \(p(c_i\mid y_i)\) (chance of the words, given the class)
  • topic model (finds themes in texts without any answers)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Boolean and dictionary methods are called supervised because we observe the outcome \(y\).”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Boolean and dictionary methods are the “count the keywords on my list” methods (Chapter 7). “Supervised” is the box for methods that learn from answers or follow a fixed rule. “Observe the outcome \(y\)” means we have the true answer (like the star rating) in our data. So the statement says: “they are in the supervised box because we have the answers”.

    Answer: False. Why: We do not have the answers. They are in the supervised box for a different reason: the researcher writes the rule (the function \(f()\), the formula from text to score) in advance, so we know exactly what comes out for any text. Think of a recipe you wrote yourself. Nobody taught you with examples, but you know what the cake will be. (Source: slide 7.)

  2. T/F: “Text regression models \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\) while Naive Bayes models \(p(c_i \mid y_i)\).”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: \(p(A\mid B)\) reads “the chance of A, given that we know B”. \(y_i\) is the answer for document number \(i\) (its outcome or class). \(c_i\) is that document’s word counts. So the statement says: text regression asks “given these words, what is the outcome?”, while Naive Bayes asks “given this class, how likely are these words?”

    Answer: True. Why: Text regression goes from words to outcome, like guessing a house’s price from its features. Naive Bayes goes the other way first. It learns which words each class tends to use (football fans say “goal” a lot), then uses Bayes’ rule to flip it round and pick the most likely class. (Source: slides 13 and 21.)

  3. T/F: “LSA is a probabilistic model of how text is generated.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LSA is a topic model (Chapter 10) that finds themes by breaking the big word-count table into smaller tables. A “probabilistic model of how text is generated” is a story, told in chances, of how each word got written, such as “pick a topic, then pick a word from that topic”. Does LSA tell such a story?

    Answer: False. Why: LSA is pure table maths. It summarises the table but gives no chance-based story of how the words came about. That is why the slide writes it with a plain function \(f(c_i\mid v_i)\) and not with a probability \(p\). It is like a map that summarises a city without explaining how the city was built. LDA is the topic model that does tell the story. (Source: slide 30, and slide 43 says it is “not a probabilistic model”.)

  4. Explain (2–5 sentences): “What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised text methods? Give one example of each.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Explain the two boxes of the method map, and name one method from each box.

    Model answer: In supervised methods we know the outcome (or the mapping) and learn or apply the link between the text and that outcome, like a regression \(y=\beta x+e\); e.g. Naive Bayes learns from speeches labelled by party to classify new speeches. In unsupervised methods there is no outcome; the algorithm finds structure in the text itself, e.g. LDA finds topics (clusters of words) and each document’s topic mix. Dictionary methods are also counted as supervised: there is no observed outcome, but the researcher fixes the function \(f()\), so the output for any input is known (L3 slide 7).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Supervised means the computer has answers (or a fixed rule) and learns the link from text to answer. \(y=\beta x+e\) is the straight-line formula: outcome = weight × input + error. Example: Naive Bayes studies speeches marked with the speaker’s party, then guesses the party of new speeches. Unsupervised means there are no answers, so the computer finds groups of words by itself, like LDA finding topics; dictionaries still count as supervised because you write the rule yourself.

Sources: Lecture 3 “Bag-of-words based methods” (Lecture_bow_based_methods.pdf), slides 4–7, 13, 21, 30; Interactive Notebook 2, cell 21.

7. Boolean and dictionary methods: EPU, sentiment dictionaries, and their weaknesses (L3)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q2(c) (5 points, Boolean search + EPU) and 2025 T/F (h) (dictionaries and polysemy).

Start from zero

The problem. Economists wanted to measure how worried people are about what the government will do to the economy: new taxes, budget fights, new rules. There is no thermometer for that kind of worry. But newspapers write about it every day. Three researchers (Baker, Bloom and Davis) had an idea: count how many newspaper articles each month talk about economic policy uncertainty, and track that number over time. A company could do the same with customer emails, for example counting how many mention “refund” or “cancel”. This chapter is about the most basic way to turn text into a number: pick the words, count them, and adjust for size.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Decide what you want to measure. For example, worry about government policy, or how positive a review is.
  2. Write down the words that signal it. For worry: “uncertain”, “uncertainty”. For a happy review: “good”, “great”. This list is your dictionary.
  3. Choose the type of rule. A Boolean rule says which mix of words a document must contain. You join words with AND (both needed), OR (either one is fine) and NOT (must not appear). A dictionary rule counts the hits on each list and combines them, for example happy hits minus unhappy hits.
  4. Run the rule over every document and count. For Boolean: how many documents pass? For a dictionary: what is each document’s score?
  5. Make the counts fair (normalise). A newspaper that prints twice as many articles will get about twice as many hits, even if nobody is more worried. So divide by the total number of articles (or, for a dictionary score, by the number of words).
  6. Rescale so “normal” = 100 (optional). Then a month at 150 means “50% more than a normal month”.

A tiny example by hand. We reuse the chapter’s own example below and go through it slowly.

Which articles count? The table in “A tiny worked example” has one row per made-up article. Its columns ask three yes/no questions and then give the verdict. Take article A1: “Congress fights over the deficit; uncertainty about the economy grows.”

  • Uncertainty word (“uncertain” or “uncertainty”)? Yes: “uncertainty”.
  • Economy word (“economic” or “economy”)? Yes: “economy”.
  • Policy word (congress, deficit, white house, …)? Yes: “congress” and “deficit”.

Three yeses, so A1 counts. Now A2: “Economic uncertainty rises as oil prices jump.” It has an uncertainty word and an economy word, but no policy word. One “no” is enough to fail, because the rule uses AND. So A2 does not count. Of the four articles, A1 and A4 pass: 2 of 4.

Making it fair. The second table has one row per month. Its columns are the steps of the calculation. Month 1 had 4 EPU articles out of 200 articles in total. Share = 4 ÷ 200 = 0.02 (2 in every 100 articles). Month 2: 10 ÷ 250 = 0.04. Month 3: 3 ÷ 100 = 0.03. The average share over the three months is (0.02 + 0.04 + 0.03) ÷ 3 = 0.09 ÷ 3 = 0.03. Month 1’s index = 0.02 ÷ 0.03 × 100 = 66.7. So month 1 was a calm month, about a third below normal.

A dictionary score. Review: “good food but bad service and wasted time”. That is 8 words. Happy list {good, great}: 1 hit (“good”). Unhappy list {bad, wasted}: 2 hits (“bad”, “wasted”). Score = (1 − 2) ÷ 8 = −0.125. Times 1,000 gives −125 per 1,000 words, so the review comes out negative.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: easy to understand, explain and check. You can always see which words gave the score. It is “by far the most used approach in economics and finance” (slide 7).
  • Good: cheap and fast, even on millions of articles.
  • Breaks: it only finds the words you thought of. “Doubt about tax policy” is missed, because “doubt” is not on the list.
  • Breaks: it cannot read context. One word with two meanings (“apple” the fruit or the company), or a “no” in front (“no crisis”), fools a plain count.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Boolean search: a search rule made of words joined by AND, OR and NOT. Like a shop website filter: “shoes AND red AND NOT sandals”.
  • AND: both parts must be present. “uncertainty AND economy” needs both words in the same article.
  • OR: at least one of the parts is enough. “uncertain OR uncertainty” is happy with either.
  • NOT: this part must be absent.
  • dictionary (word list): a hand-made list of words that signal something, like a list of happy words.
  • keyword: a word you search for.
  • hit: one match between the text and your list. “bad” in a review is a hit for the unhappy list.
  • normalise: make numbers fair to compare by dividing by size. 4 bad reviews out of 10 is worse than 4 out of 1,000.
  • share: a part divided by the whole. 4 EPU articles out of 200 = a share of 0.02.
  • average (mean): add the numbers and divide by how many there are. The average of 0.02, 0.04 and 0.03 is 0.03.
  • index: one number that tracks something over time, rescaled so it is easy to read, like a price index.
  • “normalized to mean 100”: rescaled so the average month in the chosen period (1985–2009) equals 100. Then 200 means “twice as much as normal”.
  • series / time series: a list of values in time order, one per month or year.
  • EPU (Economic Policy Uncertainty) index: the Baker, Bloom and Davis measure: the scaled monthly count of newspaper articles that mention uncertainty AND the economy AND policy.
  • policy: what the government decides to do (taxes, rules, budgets, interest rates).
  • latent concept: something real but hidden that we cannot measure directly, like worry or mood.
  • \(f(c_i)\), known function: the fixed rule (our word lists and counting) applied to document \(i\)’s word counts \(c_i\).
  • \(\hat v_i\): the hat means “our estimate”. It is the number our rule gives for the hidden concept in document \(i\).
  • sentiment / tone: how positive or negative a text sounds.
  • per 1,000 words: the score scaled up so it reads like “−125 for every 1,000 words”, which is easier to read than −0.125.
  • \(\#W^{pos}\), \(\#W^{neg}\): “#” means “number of”. The number of positive words and the number of negative words.
  • General Inquirer: a ready-made, general-purpose list of positive and negative words.
  • Loughran and McDonald (2011): a word list made for finance texts.
  • 10-K: the annual report a US listed company must publish.
  • polysemy: one word, several meanings. “Apple” the fruit or the company; “liability” (a bad thing in daily talk, a neutral accounting item in a company report).
  • synonym: different words with the same meaning, like “unsure” and “uncertain”.
  • negation: a “not” or “no” that flips the meaning. “No crisis” is good news, but a plain count sees “crisis”.
  • subjective: depends on the person choosing. Two researchers would pick different word lists.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a bag of loose words, ignoring their order. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look the same.
  • token / tokeniser: a token is one word-piece of a text; the tokeniser is the rule that cuts the text into tokens.
  • re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...): a piece of Python code that pulls out every run of letters as one word.
  • stock returns: how much a share price went up or down, in %.
  • forecast: a prediction about the future, such as next year’s growth.
  • GDP growth: how fast a country’s total production grew, in %. Used as “how well the economy is doing”.
  • quarter: three months. “4 quarters ahead” = one year ahead.
  • \(R^2\) / adjusted \(R^2\): a score from 0 to 1 for how much of the ups and downs in the outcome a model explains. 0 = nothing, 1 = everything. “Adjusted” adds a small charge for using extra inputs. [Not in course files — general knowledge: the exact meaning of “adjusted”.]
  • central bank / Federal Reserve: the bank that sets a country’s interest rates; the Federal Reserve is the US one. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • Financial Stability Report: a report where a central bank says how safe it thinks the financial system is.
  • correlation: how closely two series move together. Near 1 = they rise and fall together; near 0 = no link.
  • baseline index: the starting version you compare your own version with.
  • switch (HANDLE_NEGATION = False): a setting you turn on (True) or off (False) in the code.
  • \(\underbrace{\ \cdots\ }_{U}\) (the curly bracket under the formula): a name tag for a group of words. U, E and P stand for the uncertainty, economy and policy groups.

The idea in plain words

Decide in advance which words matter, then count them and divide by something sensible. That is it. Slide 7: “By far the most used approach in economics and finance. Very simple, just counting and normalizing.”

There are two flavours:

  • Boolean search: a search rule built with AND, OR and NOT. A document either passes the rule or it does not. Then you count how many documents pass.
  • Dictionary: two (or more) word lists, e.g. positive and negative words. You count the hits from each list and combine them, e.g. positive minus negative.

Analogy Boolean search is a library search filter: “show me articles that mention (uncertain OR uncertainty) AND (economy OR economic) AND (Congress OR deficit…)”. A dictionary is a teacher’s marking sheet with a column of “good words” and “bad words”: tick every match and score the essay as ticks in one column minus ticks in the other.

The exam definition

Slide 7: \(v_i\) “represents some latent concept, e.g., the sentiment or political uncertainty, and \(f(c_i)\) is a known function giving an estimate \(\hat v_i\).” (Latent = hidden, something real we cannot see directly. The known function is our fixed counting rule applied to the word counts \(c_i\); the hat on \(\hat v_i\) means “our estimate of”.) (They are “supervised” because \(f\) is known — see Chapter 6.)

Slide 8, side by side:

Dictionary-based technique Boolean-based technique
Step 1 Use general dictionaries (e.g. General Inquirer, a ready-made general-purpose word list) or make your own (e.g. Loughran and McDonald (2011) for finance) Define words of interest, e.g. uncertainty, uncertainties, …
Step 2 List of positive words: good, great, …; list of negative words: bad, wasted, … Use logical operators: AND, OR, NOT
Step 3 Count, normalise and compute, e.g., the difference \(\#W^{pos} - \#W^{neg}\) Search for criteria: “uncertainty” OR “uncertainties”
Step 4 — Count and normalise

The EPU index (Baker, Bloom and Davis 2016) — the course’s Boolean example. From the note under the slide-8 figure:

“Index reflects scaled monthly counts of articles containing ‘uncertain’ or ‘uncertainty’, ‘economic’ or ‘economy’, and one or more policy relevant terms: ‘regulation’, ‘federal reserve’, ‘deficit’, ‘congress’, ‘legislation’, or ‘white house’. The series is normalized to mean 100 from 1985–2009 …” (10 major US newspapers: USA Today, Miami Herald, Chicago Tribune, Washington Post, LA Times, Boston Globe, SF Chronicle, Dallas Morning News, NY Times, Wall Street Journal.) (“Normalized to mean 100” = rescaled so the average month in 1985–2009 equals 100.)

As a Boolean rule, an article counts if:

In words: an article counts only if it has at least one uncertainty word, at least one economy word and at least one policy word.

\[\underbrace{(\text{uncertain OR uncertainty})}_{\text{U}}\ \text{AND}\ \underbrace{(\text{economic OR economy})}_{\text{E}}\ \text{AND}\ \underbrace{(\text{regulation OR federal reserve OR deficit OR congress OR legislation OR white house})}_{\text{P}}\]

All three groups must appear in the same article. The 2025 guideline summarises this as “key words political, economy, and uncertainty and all terms need to occur in a document for a count to happen”. In the exam, write the three groups (Economy, Policy, Uncertainty) and give one or two example words for each.

The EPU chart (slide 8) spikes at Black Monday, Gulf Wars I and II, 9/11, Lehman/TARP, the Euro crisis and the Debt Ceiling Dispute (the highest, about 275).

A tiny worked example

Step 1 — Which articles count? Four made-up articles, all from one month. Rows = articles; columns = whether each word group is present; last column = whether the article counts (needs U AND E AND P).

Article (toy text) U: uncertain/-ty E: economic/economy P: policy term Counts as EPU?
A1 “Congress fights over the deficit; uncertainty about the economy grows.” yes (uncertainty) yes (economy) yes (congress, deficit) yes
A2 “Economic uncertainty rises as oil prices jump.” yes yes no no
A3 “The White House is uncertain about new legislation on stadiums.” yes no yes no
A4 “The Federal Reserve says the economy faces uncertain times.” yes yes yes (federal reserve) yes

So 2 of the 4 articles count. Note A2: it is clearly about economic uncertainty, but with no policy word it is not policy uncertainty. The AND makes the rule strict.

Step 2 — Normalise. Newspapers print different numbers of articles each month, so the raw count is divided by the total number of articles. [Not in course files — general knowledge: Baker et al. scale the count by the total number of articles in the same newspaper and month; the slide only says “scaled monthly counts”.] Then the series is rescaled so that its average over the base period is 100 (the slide’s “normalized to mean 100”). Toy numbers; rows = months, columns = the steps:

Month EPU articles All articles Share Index = share ÷ average share × 100
1 4 200 0.02 0.02 / 0.03 × 100 = 66.7
2 10 250 0.04 133.3
3 3 100 0.03 100.0

Worked by hand for month 1: the average share is \((0.02+0.04+0.03)/3 = 0.03\), so \(0.02/0.03\times100 = 66.7\). Month 2 has the most uncertainty. If we had used raw counts, month 2 (10) would look more than three times as bad as month 3 (3), but in shares it is only \(0.04/0.03 \approx 1.33\) times as high.

A dictionary tone example (from the slides’ own text). Take “Doc1” from slide 32 and the slide-8 word lists (positive: good, great; negative: bad, wasted). Doc1 contains “good”, “great”, “bad” and “wasted”. With the notebook’s tokeniser (re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...), the rule that cuts the text into separate words, treating each run of letters as one word) Doc1 has 74 words. Using the notebook’s tone formula (cell 4/7):

In words: take the happy-word hits minus the unhappy-word hits, divide by the length of the text, and multiply by 1,000 to get a score per 1,000 words.

\[\text{tone} = 1000\times\frac{\#\text{pos} - \#\text{neg}}{\#\text{words}} = 1000\times\frac{2-2}{74} = 0\]

So the text comes out neutral, even though it is quite positive about the course and only worried about “the investment”.

The formula, symbol by symbol

In words: the same tone recipe, written for any document number \(i\).

\[\text{tone}_i = \frac{\#W^{pos}_i - \#W^{neg}_i}{\text{number of words in document } i}\times 1000\]

  • \(\#W^{pos}_i\) = how many words in document \(i\) are on the positive list (slide 8 writes \(\#W^{pos}\)).
  • \(\#W^{neg}_i\) = how many are on the negative list.
  • dividing by the number of words = normalising for length, so a long speech does not look more emotional just because it is long.
  • \(\times 1000\) = “per 1,000 words”, only to make the numbers readable (Notebook 2, cell 7).

Read aloud: “the tone of a document is its positive hits minus its negative hits, per 1,000 words.”

Evidence that this works (slides 8–11). Tetlock et al. (2008): counting positive and negative words in news predicts firms’ stock returns (how much their share prices go up or down). Sharpe et al. (2017): the tone of the Greenbook forecasts (Federal Reserve staff forecasts [Not in course files — general knowledge]) adds to the numeric forecast of GDP growth; 4 quarters ahead (one year ahead), the adjusted \(R^2\) (a 0-to-1 score for how much of the ups and downs in GDP growth the forecast explains; higher is better) rises from 0.25 (forecast only) to 0.36 (with Tonality) and 0.41 (with Trend Tonality) (slide 10). Born et al. (2014): the tone of central-bank Financial Stability Reports moves stock markets.

General vs finance dictionaries. General Inquirer is general-purpose. Loughran and McDonald (2011) built a finance dictionary because, as Notebook 2 (cell 10) says, general dictionaries “misclassify finance text (liability, tax, cost are not negative in a 10-K)”. A 10-K is a firm’s annual report. [Not in course files — general knowledge: a 10-K is the annual report US listed firms file with the SEC.]

Weaknesses (slide 12 + Notebook 2)

Rows = the weakness; columns = what it means and a course example.

Weakness What it means Example
Very subjective Someone chooses the words; another person would choose others Notebook 2 Q1: swap the 5+5 baseline words for your own and see how much the index changes (cell 10)
Need to know what to search for You can only find what you thought of in advance EPU misses an article that says “doubt about tax policy and the outlook”
Polysemy Same word, different meanings in different contexts; a count cannot tell them apart “liability” (negative in daily speech, neutral in a 10-K); “apple” the fruit vs the company (2025 Q3b guideline)
Synonyms Different words, same meaning; missing ones are not counted “unsure”, “doubt” are not in the EPU uncertainty list
Negation Bag-of-words ignores order, so “no crisis” counts as “crisis” see below
One word can be the index A very frequent word dominates the hits Notebook 2 takeaway: “one frequent word (here war) can be the index. Always look at which words produce the hits.”

Negation, worked. Notebook 2’s fix (cell 4) skips a hit when the word before it is one of not, no, never, without, nor. Sentence: “there was no crisis and no war only growth” (9 words; positive list contains growth, negative list contains crisis and war):

  • without negation handling: \(1000\times(1-2)/9 = -111.1\) (sounds bad)
  • with negation handling: “crisis” and “war” both follow “no”, so they are skipped: \(1000\times(1-0)/9 = +111.1\)

The notebook calls this “a crude but common fix”: “not a crisis” would still count as negative, because the word right before “crisis” is “a”.

Reading the course code

POSITIVE = ["prosperity","growth","peace","progress","success"]
NEGATIVE = ["war","crisis","unemployment","debt","inflation"]
HANDLE_NEGATION = False

These lines (Notebook 2, cell 8) are the dictionary: five positive and five negative words, and a switch for the negation fix. The tone function then computes 1000*(pos-neg)/n_words per speech, and the scoreboard shows the correlation with the baseline index (how closely your version moves together with the notebook’s original version) and which words produce the hits. The notebook has no saved outputs; when run, it would show a time series (one value per year, in time order) of State of the Union tone and a list of the words behind most hits (the notebook hints that “war” dominates).

How this shows up on the exam

  • 2025 Q2(c), worth 5 points, asked: “Describe what is meant by a Boolean search-based method in NLP. Use a concrete example discussed in this course.” (Boolean = combining keywords with AND, OR, NOT. NLP = getting computers to work with human language.)
  • 2025 T/F (h) said: “Dictionary-based methods allow you to capture polysemy in text well” → False. Polysemy means one word with several meanings, like “bank” (river bank or money bank). Slide 12 lists it as a problem for dictionaries.
  • In the reflection question (the open question about customer survey texts), a sentiment dictionary (a list of happy words and unhappy words) is an obvious first method. But name the pitfalls: Loughran–McDonald-style domain issues (a word can mean something else in a special field, e.g. “liability” is a normal word in a company report, not bad news), negation (“not good” contains “good”) and subjectivity (the word list depends on the researcher’s own choices).

What a top-grade answer must include

For Q2(c), go through these steps in order:

  1. Start from the documents (or the document-term matrix, the word-count table).
  2. Choose keywords (a dictionary, i.e. your fixed word list).
  3. Combine them with the logical operators AND, OR, NOT.
  4. Count the documents (or words) that match the rule.
  5. Normalise: divide by the number of articles or words, so a month with more news does not look bigger only because there was more news. The EPU index is also rescaled so its average is 100.
  6. Give the EPU example with its three word groups (economy, policy, uncertainty), which must all appear in the same article.

A top answer also adds one weakness: the word choice is subjective, synonyms (different words with the same meaning) are missed, and polysemy (one word, several meanings) confuses it.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Forgetting normalisation. The 2025 guideline says “Think about normalization issues”.
  • Saying an EPU article needs only one of the words. It needs one word from each of the three groups.
  • Inventing your own example when the question asks for an example from the course.
  • Claiming dictionaries handle polysemy (one word, several meanings) or synonyms (several words, one meaning) well.

Key terms to use

  • Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) (words that combine search terms)
  • keyword list / dictionary (the fixed list of words you count)
  • count and normalise (count matches, then divide by the total)
  • Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index (monthly newspaper measure of policy uncertainty)
  • Baker, Bloom and Davis (2016) (the economists who built the EPU index)
  • General Inquirer (an older, general-purpose positive/negative word list)
  • Loughran and McDonald (2011) (word list made for finance reports)
  • tone = positive − negative (happy-word count minus unhappy-word count)
  • polysemy (one word, several meanings)
  • synonyms (different words, same meaning)
  • negation (“not” flips the meaning of a word)
  • subjective (depends on the researcher’s own choices)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Dictionary-based methods allow you to capture polysemy in text well.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Dictionary methods count words from a fixed list. Polysemy means one word has several meanings, like “bank” (river or money). The statement says these methods handle such words well.

    Answer: False. Why: A dictionary only sees the spelling of a word, never its meaning. It counts “bank” the same way in “river bank” and “bank loan”. It is like a metal detector that beeps at bottle caps and coins alike. (Source: slide 12; 2025 T/F h.)

  2. T/F: “An article enters the EPU count if it contains ‘uncertainty’ and ‘economy’, even without a policy term.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The EPU index counts newspaper articles about economic policy uncertainty. The statement says an article is counted if it has an uncertainty word and an economy word, even with no policy word (like “congress” or “deficit”).

    Answer: False. Why: The rule joins the groups with AND, so the article needs one word from each of the three groups: uncertainty, economy and policy. It is like a cake that needs flour, eggs and sugar: two out of three is not the cake. (Source: slide 8 figure note.)

  3. T/F: “Boolean/dictionary methods are by far the most used approach in economics and finance.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Are the “count the keywords” methods the most common way economists and finance researchers study text?

    Answer: True. Why: The slide says so directly. They are popular because they are simple and transparent: anyone can see which words were counted. (Source: slide 7.)

  4. T/F: “General-purpose sentiment dictionaries work well for 10-K reports.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A general-purpose sentiment dictionary is an everyday list of positive and negative words, built for normal text. 10-K reports are the yearly reports that US companies must publish. The statement says the everyday list works well on these reports.

    Answer: False. Why: In company reports, words like liability, tax and cost are normal business words, not bad news. The everyday list still marks them as negative, so the score is wrong. That is why Loughran and McDonald built a special word list for finance. It is like reading a medical test that comes back “positive” as good news, when in medicine it often is not. (Source: Notebook 2 cell 10.)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): “Describe a Boolean search method with a course example.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Explain how a keyword search with AND, OR, NOT works, and use the example from the lectures (the EPU index).

    Model answer: A Boolean method starts from the documents (the document-term matrix), picks keywords of interest and combines them with logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) into a search rule; we then count the documents that satisfy the rule and normalise the count (e.g. by the total number of articles). The course example is the Economic Policy Uncertainty index of Baker et al. (2016): a newspaper article counts if it contains “uncertain” or “uncertainty”, AND “economic” or “economy”, AND at least one policy term such as “congress”, “deficit” or “white house”. The monthly counts from 10 US newspapers are scaled and normalised to mean 100 over 1985–2009, and the index spikes at events like 9/11 and the debt-ceiling dispute. The method is simple and transparent, but subjective: it only finds the words you thought of, and cannot handle synonyms or polysemy.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: You pick some words, join them with AND, OR, NOT into a search rule, count how many articles match, and divide by the total so months can be compared fairly. The EPU index does this with US newspapers: an article counts only if it has an uncertainty word, an economy word and a policy word. The final numbers are scaled so their average is 100, and they jump at big shocks like 9/11. The method is easy to understand, but it only finds the exact words you chose, so it misses other words with the same meaning and is fooled by words with two meanings.

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 6–12 (recipe on the slide-8 figure note); Interactive Notebook 2 cells 4, 7–10, 31; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines, Q2(c) and 1(h).

8. Text regressions and regularisation (Lasso, Ridge, λ, cross-validation) (L3, Interactive 2)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 T/F (e) (“regularization … help overcome the curse of dimensionality” → True) and very likely T/F or short questions on λ and cross-validation.

Start from zero

The problem. An economist asks: do the words a US president uses in the yearly State of the Union speech say anything about how the economy is doing? A shop wants to guess a review’s star rating from its words. An investment fund wants to guess how a share price will move from today’s news. In all three cases you have texts, a number for each text, and you want a recipe that turns words into a good guess of that number. The tool for “guess a number from other numbers” is called a regression. With text it runs into a special problem: there are far more different words than there are texts.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Start with one input. For each speech, count the word “growth”. Also write down that year’s GDP growth (how fast the economy grew, in %). Draw each speech as a dot on a chart: how far right = the count, how high up = the growth.
  2. Draw a straight line through the dots. A line has two numbers. The intercept is where the line starts when the count is 0. The slope (also called the coefficient) is how steep it is: “each extra ‘growth’ adds this much to the guess”.
  3. Score the line. For each dot, measure how far the line misses it. Square each miss (so misses above and below both count as positive, and big misses count extra), then add them up. A smaller total means a better line.
  4. Pick the best line. The line with the smallest total of squared misses wins. That is “ordinary least squares”, or OLS: “least squares” = the smallest total of squared misses.
  5. Now use many words. Instead of one slope, every word gets its own coefficient. The guess = intercept + (count of word 1 × its coefficient) + (count of word 2 × its coefficient) + … for every word.
  6. Here it breaks. We have about 70 speeches but thousands of different words. When there are more coefficients to choose than speeches to check them against, the computer can always find settings that hit every training speech exactly, and in endless different ways. That is memorising, not learning. On a new speech, the guess is bad. This is called overfitting, and the course calls the cause the “curse of dimensionality”.
  7. The fix: charge a fee. Every coefficient that is not zero now costs something. The total to make small becomes “squared misses + fee”.
