The computer only gives a word a big coefficient if that word cuts the misses by more than its fee. This is regularisation (also called penalisation). Lasso and Ridge are two versions of it.
  8. Choose how big the fee is (λ, “lambda”). Fee too small → overfitting again. Fee too big → every coefficient is pushed to zero, and the model guesses the average every time. To choose, hide part of the data, train on the rest, and see how well the model guesses the hidden part. Repeat for several fee sizes and keep the one that guesses the hidden data best. This is cross-validation.
  9. Judge the model only on hidden data. When there are more words than texts, a great score on the training texts proves nothing.

A tiny example by hand.

Part 1: one word, a straight line. Three speeches. In the table, rows are speeches, and the columns are the count of “growth” and that year’s GDP growth. Toy numbers made up for this explanation.

Speech count of “growth” GDP growth (%)
1 1 2
2 2 4
3 3 5

Try line B: “guess = 2 × count”. Speech 1: 2 × 1 = 2, real 2, miss 0. Speech 2: 2 × 2 = 4, real 4, miss 0. Speech 3: 2 × 3 = 6, real 5, miss 1. Squared misses: 0, 0, 1. Total = 1.

Try line C: “guess = 1 + count”. Speech 1: 1 + 1 = 2, miss 0. Speech 2: 1 + 2 = 3, real 4, miss 1. Speech 3: 1 + 3 = 4, real 5, miss 1. Squared misses: 0, 1, 1. Total = 2.

Line B beats line C (1 is smaller than 2). OLS searches all lines and finds the very best one. Here it is about “guess = 0.67 + 1.5 × count”, with a total of about 0.17.

Part 2: many words, and why the line method breaks. Now look at the chapter’s table in “A tiny worked example” below. Rows are 3 speeches; columns are the counts of 4 words, plus the outcome \(y\). So there are 4 coefficients to choose, and only 3 speeches to check them. Take candidate A, coefficients 2, 5, 1, 0. For speech 2 (counts 0, 1, 0, 1): 2 × 0 + 5 × 1 + 1 × 0 + 0 × 1 = 5. The real \(y\) is 5: a perfect hit. Now candidate C, coefficients 0, 3, −1, 2, for speech 3 (counts 0, 0, 1, 1): 0 × 0 + 3 × 0 + (−1) × 1 + 2 × 1 = 1. The real \(y\) is 1: also perfect. Two very different sets of coefficients, both perfect on every speech. The data cannot tell us which one is “true”, so neither means anything.

Part 3: the fee picks a winner. The fee is (number of speeches) × λ × (total size of the coefficients, ignoring minus signs). For candidate A: total size = 2 + 5 + 1 + 0 = 8, so the fee = 3 × λ × 8 = 24λ. Candidate Z sets every coefficient to 0 and always guesses the average, (2 + 5 + 1) ÷ 3 = 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.67. Its misses are 2 − 2.67 = −0.67, 5 − 2.67 = 2.33 and 1 − 2.67 = −1.67. Squared, that is about 0.44, 5.44 and 2.78, a total of about 8.67, and no fee.

  • With λ = 1: A costs 0 + 24 = 24; Z costs 8.67. Z wins.
  • With λ = 0.1: A costs 0 + 2.4 = 2.4; Z still costs 8.67. A wins.

So the size of the fee decides how much the model is allowed to use the words.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: it can use all the words at once and lets the data decide which ones matter.
  • Good: Lasso pushes most coefficients to exactly zero, so you get a short, readable list of the words that matter.
  • Good: cross-validation gives an honest score on texts the model has never seen.
  • Breaks: with few texts (about 70 speeches), even the best model may predict poorly; the honest score can be near zero or below.
  • Breaks: the result depends on the fee λ. A different λ gives a different list of words.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • regression: a method for guessing a number (the outcome) from other numbers (the inputs) by finding the best formula, often a straight line. Example: guessing a house price from its size.
  • text regression: a regression where the inputs are the word counts of each document.
  • outcome (\(y\)): the number we want to guess, such as GDP growth or a star rating. \(y_i\) is the outcome of document \(i\).
  • explanatory variable / regressor / feature (\(x\)): an input used to make the guess. In text regression, each word column is one input.
  • \(x_i = f(c_i)\): the inputs of document \(i\). Either its raw row of word counts, or a changed version of it (like tf-idf weights).
  • intercept (\(\alpha\), alpha): the starting value of the guess when every input is 0.
  • coefficient / slope (\(\beta\), beta): how much the guess changes when an input goes up by one. \(\beta_j\) belongs to word \(j\).
  • prediction / guess (\(\eta_i\), eta): the model’s guess for document \(i\): intercept plus each input times its coefficient.
  • \(x_i'\beta\): short for “multiply each of document \(i\)’s inputs by its coefficient and add them all up”.
  • miss / error / residual: the gap between the real outcome and the guess.
  • squared error: the miss times itself. A miss of 2 becomes 4, a miss of −2 also becomes 4.
  • loss (\(l(\alpha,\beta)\)): the total of how badly the model fits. Here, the total of squared misses.
  • \(\sum\) (sigma): “add up”. \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\) means “add this up for document 1, 2, … up to \(n\)”.
  • \(\min\{\cdot\}\): “choose the numbers that make this as small as possible”.
  • objective: the total you are trying to make as small as possible (here, loss + fee).
  • OLS (ordinary least squares): the standard way of choosing the coefficients: make the total of squared misses as small as possible, with no fee.
  • \(n\) and \(p\): \(n\) = number of documents (rows); \(p\) = number of words (columns).
  • \(n \ll p\): “\(n\) is much smaller than \(p\)”: far fewer documents than words.
  • more unknowns than equations: more numbers to choose (coefficients) than facts to pin them down (documents). Like being asked for two numbers that add to 10: there are endless answers.
  • dimension / high-dimensional: each input column is one “dimension”. Thousands of word columns = high-dimensional.
  • curse of dimensionality: the trouble that comes with too many input columns compared with data rows: perfect but meaningless fits.
  • overfitting: a model that memorises the training examples, including their noise, and so guesses badly on new ones. Like a student who memorises last year’s answers and fails a new exam.
  • regularisation / penalisation: adding a fee for big coefficients, so the model only uses words that really help.
  • penalty: the fee itself.
  • \(\lambda\) (lambda): the fee rate. \(\lambda = 0\) = no fee (plain OLS). Bigger \(\lambda\) = bigger fee, more coefficients pushed to zero.
  • shrinkage: coefficients getting pulled towards zero by the fee.
  • absolute value \(\lvert\beta_j\rvert\): the size of a number ignoring its minus sign. \(\lvert -3\rvert = 3\).
  • Lasso: the version whose fee uses absolute values. It can set coefficients to exactly zero, so it also picks words.
  • Ridge: the version whose fee uses squared coefficients. It shrinks them but keeps every word. [Not in course files — general knowledge, as in the Ridge note below]
  • Elastic net: a mix of Lasso and Ridge.
  • \(\omega_j\) (omega), variable-specific cost: an extra weight on each word’s fee, so words can be charged differently.
  • standard deviation: how much a number varies around its average. Counts that jump around a lot have a big standard deviation.
  • rare feature upweighting: setting each word’s extra weight \(\omega_j\) using its standard deviation (slide 17).
  • conditional expectation \(E[y_i\mid c_i]\): the average outcome you would expect for documents with these word counts, i.e. the best guess of \(y\) given the words.
  • yes/no outcome and logistic loss: when the outcome is yes/no (spam or not), the misses are scored with a different formula, the logistic loss.
  • log: the logarithm, a function that turns multiplying into adding; \(\log(a \times b) = \log a + \log b\). It grows slowly: big numbers become small ones.
  • \(e\) (in \(e^{\eta_i}\)): a fixed number, about 2.718, that appears in growth formulas. \(e^{\eta}\) is \(e\) raised to the power \(\eta\) (for \(\eta = 2\), that is \(e \times e \approx 7.39\)).
  • tf-idf: a word weight that is high for words that are frequent in this document but rare in the other documents.
  • stop words: very common words like “the”, “and”, “of”, usually removed.
  • min_df: “minimum document frequency”: drop words that appear in fewer than this many documents.
  • dimension reduction (PCA, Partial Least Squares): squeezing thousands of word columns into a few summary columns before running the regression. PCA is the same idea as LSA in Chapter 10.
  • non-linear methods (GLMs, regression trees, random forest): methods that allow curves and if-then rules instead of one straight line. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • training set / test set: the part of the data the model learns from, and the hidden part used to check it.
  • cross-validation: choosing λ by repeatedly training on part of the data and checking guesses on the hidden part.
  • fold / 5-fold: the data is cut into 5 equal groups (folds). Train on 4, test on the 5th, and repeat 5 times so every group is tested once.
  • in-sample / out-of-sample: in-sample = measured on the data the model trained on; out-of-sample = measured on data it never saw.
  • held-out data: data kept aside and not used for training.
  • \(R^2\): a score for how much of the ups and downs in the outcome the guesses explain. 1 = perfect; 0 = “no better than always guessing the average”; below 0 = worse than that.
  • cross-validated \(R^2\): the \(R^2\) measured on held-out data only, the honest one.
  • placebo test: a fake test where the outcome is shuffled on purpose, so the words cannot really predict it. If the model still “fits”, the fit is fake.
  • information criteria (AIC, BIC): scores computed on the training data that reward good fit but charge for every extra coefficient. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • pipeline: a chain of steps run in order: first turn text into numbers, then fit the regression.
  • scikit-learn / Ridge(alpha=…): a popular Python toolbox for these methods. Its alpha setting is the fee λ, not the intercept.
  • KFold, shuffle, random_state: the code that cuts the data into folds, mixes up the order first, and fixes the random mixing so you get the same result each time you run it.
  • GDP growth / State of the Union: GDP growth = how fast the economy grew, in %. The State of the Union is the US president’s yearly speech to Congress. [Not in course files — general knowledge]

The idea in plain words

A text regression predicts a number (GDP growth, a review score, a stock return) from the words of documents. The columns of the document-term matrix (the word-count table: rows = documents, columns = words) are the explanatory variables (the inputs used to make the guess).

The problem: there are far more words than documents. Notebook 2 regresses GDP growth on about 70 State of the Union speeches (69 speech–year pairs, 1948–2018), but the speeches contain thousands of different words. With more unknowns (one \(\beta\) per word) than equations (one per speech), ordinary least squares (OLS, the standard “smallest total of squared misses” method) cannot find a single answer. It can fit the training speeches perfectly in endless ways, and none of them means anything. This is the curse of dimensionality (slide 34) or the “\(n \ll p\) problem”.

The fix is regularisation (penalisation): add a cost for big coefficients. The model must now “pay” for each word it uses, so it only keeps words that really help.

Analogy Imagine guessing the price of a house from 70 sales, but you are allowed to use 5,000 features (colour of the door, name of the dog…). With enough features you can explain the 70 prices exactly, yet you will predict the next house badly. Regularisation is a strict budget: every feature you use costs money, so you only keep the few that pay for themselves.

The exam definition

  • Slide 14: text regression estimates \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\) “using observed values for \(y_i\) and \(c_i\). Usually estimated via the conditional expectation \(E[y_i\mid c_i]\).” (That is: the average \(y\) you would expect for a document with these word counts.) It is supervised.
  • Slide 15: “Typically \(n \ll p\), thus we have more explanatory variables than observations of the outcome (more unknowns than equations). Thus, we cannot apply linear regression directly.” One valid approach is to pick a few columns of interest (e.g. the count of “good” for course reviews) and run OLS.
  • Slide 16: or run penalised regressions, “Lasso and friends”. “λ is the penalization term. With λ = 0 we get standard OLS. This is typically not what we do with text data!”
  • Slide 19: “Text regressions are high-dimensional problems. Thus, we need penalization methods or dimension reduction.” Options: the Lasso family (Ridge, Elastic net), dimension reduction (PCA, Partial Least Squares — squeeze the word columns into a few summary columns first), or non-linear methods (GLMs, regression trees, random forest — methods that allow curves and if-then rules instead of one straight line [Not in course files — general knowledge]).

A tiny worked example

Why OLS breaks when \(n < p\). Three speeches (\(n=3\)), four words (\(p=4\)). Rows = speeches; columns = word counts and the outcome \(y\) (GDP growth, %). Toy numbers made up for this guide.

Speech word 1 word 2 word 3 word 4 \(y\)
1 1 0 0 1 2
2 0 1 0 1 5
3 0 0 1 1 1

Model: \(y_i = \beta_1 c_{i1}+\beta_2 c_{i2}+\beta_3 c_{i3}+\beta_4 c_{i4}\). Each row below is a different set of coefficients; every one predicts all three \(y\) values exactly.

Candidate \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3,\beta_4\) Predictions for speeches 1–3 \(\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert\)
A 2, 5, 1, 0 2, 5, 1 8
B 1, 4, 0, 1 2, 5, 1 6
C 0, 3, −1, 2 2, 5, 1 6

Check B by hand for speech 1: \(1\cdot1 + 4\cdot0 + 0\cdot0 + 1\cdot1 = 2\). ✓. There are infinitely many perfect fits, so OLS (\(\lambda=0\)) has no unique answer and the perfect fit tells you nothing.

What λ does. Compare two extreme candidates using the Lasso objective (below; the total to make small = squared misses + fee) with \(n=3\) and all \(\omega_j=1\):

  • Candidate A (perfect fit, intercept \(\alpha=0\)): loss \(=0\), penalty \(=n\lambda\cdot 8 = 24\lambda\).
  • Candidate Z (all \(\beta=0\), \(\alpha\) = average of \(y\) = 8/3 ≈ 2.67): loss \(= (2-2.67)^2+(5-2.67)^2+(1-2.67)^2 = 8.67\), penalty \(=0\).

Rows = value of λ; columns = total objective for each candidate.

λ A: loss + penalty Z: loss + penalty Preferred of these two
0 0 + 0 = 0 8.67 A (OLS: fit at any cost)
0.1 0 + 2.4 = 2.4 8.67 A
1 0 + 24 = 24 8.67 Z (all coefficients zero)

As λ grows, the penalty wins and coefficients are pushed to zero (slide 17: “high values of λ shrink coefficients to zero”). The real Lasso solution lies somewhere between such extremes; the table only shows the direction of the trade-off.

The formula, symbol by symbol

Slide 16 (copy this):

In words: choose the intercept and coefficients that make “how badly we miss” plus “the fee for big coefficients” as small as possible.

\[\min\Big\{\, l(\alpha,\beta) + n\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \omega_j\,|\beta_j| \,\Big\}\]

In words: the miss total is the sum of squared gaps between each real outcome and the model’s guess, and the guess is the starting value plus each word’s value times its coefficient.

\[l(\alpha,\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \eta_i)^2 \quad\text{and}\quad \eta_i = \alpha + x_i'\beta\]

  • \(\min\{\cdot\}\) = choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to make the whole bracket as small as possible.
  • \(l(\alpha,\beta)\) = the loss: how badly the model fits. Here the sum of squared errors, as in OLS.
  • \(y_i\) = the observed outcome for document \(i\) (e.g. GDP growth in the year of speech \(i\)).
  • \(\eta_i = \alpha + x_i'\beta\) = the model’s prediction for document \(i\): an intercept \(\alpha\) plus each word’s value times its coefficient.
  • \(x_i = f(c_i)\) = the features of document \(i\) — its row of the DTM, or a transformation such as tf-idf (word weights that are high for words frequent in this document but rare elsewhere) (slide 16 says “e.g., the identity”).
  • \(\beta_j\) = the coefficient of word \(j\): “The object of interest is β, one for each column in x” (slide 16).
  • \(n\) = number of documents; \(p\) = number of words (columns).
  • \(\lambda\) = the overall penalty: how expensive large coefficients are. \(\lambda=0\) → standard OLS.
  • \(\omega_j\) = a variable-specific cost. In text analysis it is typically scaled by each word’s sample standard deviation (how much that word’s count varies from document to document), called “rare feature upweighting” (slide 17).
  • \(|\beta_j|\) = the size of coefficient \(j\) (absolute value). Using absolute values is what lets Lasso set coefficients exactly to zero.

Read aloud: “Choose the intercept and the word coefficients to minimise the squared prediction errors plus a penalty that is λ times the (weighted) total size of all the coefficients.”

For a yes/no outcome (e.g. spam or not) the slide gives the logistic loss (a different way of scoring the misses; “log” and “\(e\)” are explained in the word list at the top of this chapter) instead: \(l(\alpha,\beta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(\eta_i y_i - \log(1 + e^{\eta_i})\big)\) (slide 17).

Ridge. The slides only name Ridge and Elastic net as members of the “Lasso family” (slide 19) and give no formula. [Not in course files — general knowledge: Ridge uses squared coefficients, \(\sum_j \beta_j^2\), instead of \(|\beta_j|\). It shrinks coefficients towards zero but never exactly to zero, so it keeps all words. Lasso can set some exactly to zero, so it also selects words. Elastic net mixes the two.]

Choosing λ: cross-validation (slide 18)

  • Cross-validation (out-of-sample testing): estimate the model on training data (\(Y^{train}\), \(C^{train}\)) for different λ values; evaluate each on test data (\(Y^{test}\), \(C^{test}\)); keep the λ that predicts the test data best.
  • Information criteria (in-sample): BIC, AIC, etc. (scores computed on the training data that reward good fit but charge for every extra coefficient [Not in course files — general knowledge]).

Notebook 2 (cell 11) uses 5-fold cross-validation: “split the speeches into 5 groups, train on 4, predict the 5th, repeat… \(R^2 = 0\) means ‘no better than predicting the average’.”

In-sample vs cross-validated \(R^2\), and the placebo test. Notebook 2 reports two \(R^2\) values:

In-sample \(R^2\) Cross-validated \(R^2\)
Measured on the speeches the model was trained on speeches the model did not see
With \(p \gg n\) close to 1 almost always (the notebook’s own question says “an R² close to 1”) the honest number; can be near or below 0
What it tells you almost nothing whether the words really predict GDP

The placebo switch (PLACEBO = True) shuffles GDP growth across years, so the words cannot contain information about it. The takeaway (cell 31): “In text regression the in-sample R² is meaningless when p ≫ n — even a scrambled target gets a near-perfect fit. Judge text models on data they have not seen.” So to a vendor showing “R² = 0.95”, your first question is: in-sample or out-of-sample? (cell 14).

Reading the course code

model = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", min_df=MIN_DF),
                      Ridge(alpha=ALPHA))
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
pred = cross_val_predict(model, texts, y, cv=cv)

(Simplified from Notebook 2, cells 12–13.)

  • Line 1–2: build a pipeline (a chain of steps run in order) that turns each speech into tf-idf word weights (dropping English stop words — very common words like “the” and “and” — and words found in fewer than MIN_DF = 5 speeches) and then fits a Ridge regression.
  • Watch the names: scikit-learn’s alpha is the penalty strength — the slide’s λ — not the slide’s intercept α. The notebook says “ALPHA sets how hard it shrinks”; try 0.01 to 100.
  • Line 3: split the data into 5 folds (groups), shuffled.
  • Line 4: for each fold, train on the other 4 and predict this one, giving out-of-sample predictions for every speech; r2_score(y, pred) gives the cross-validated \(R^2\).

No outputs are saved. Running it would print n ≈ 69 speeches, p (thousands of word columns), an in-sample \(R^2\) near 1 for small ALPHA, a much lower cross-validated \(R^2\), and a bar chart of the 8 most positive and 8 most negative word coefficients. The notebook uses Ridge; the slides write the Lasso formula. Both are penalised regressions.

How this shows up on the exam

2025 T/F (e) said: “In text regressions usage of regularization techniques help overcome the curse of dimensionality.” → True. A text regression predicts a number (like GDP growth) from word counts. Regularization means adding a penalty that keeps the word weights small. The curse of dimensionality is the problem of having far more columns (words) than rows (documents), so the model can fit anything.

Likely variants of this question:

  • “With λ = 0 the Lasso equals OLS” → True. λ (the strength of the penalty dial) at 0 means no penalty, so you are back to OLS (ordinary least squares, the plain line-fitting regression).
  • “A high in-sample R² proves the text predicts the outcome” → False. R² (a 0-to-1 score of how well the model fits) measured in-sample (on the same documents the model learned from) proves nothing.
  • “λ is chosen by cross-validation” → True. Cross-validation means testing on documents held back from training.
  • “Text regressions typically have n ≫ p” → False. It is \(n \ll p\): the number of documents (\(n\)) is much smaller than the number of words (\(p\)).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • \(n \ll p\): there are far more word columns than documents. Then OLS (plain line-fitting) fails: there are more unknowns than equations, so it fits the data perfectly but meaninglessly.
  • Penalised regression adds a fee for big weights: \(n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\). In words: take the size of each word’s weight (\(|\beta_j|\)), multiply by that word’s own cost factor (\(\omega_j\)), add them all up, and multiply by λ and by the number of documents \(n\).
  • λ (the strength of the penalty dial) controls shrinkage (how hard the weights are pushed towards zero). λ = 0 gives back OLS.
  • Lasso (one type of penalised regression) sets some weights to exactly zero, so those words drop out.
  • Choose λ by cross-validation on held-out data (documents kept aside during training). Judge the model on out-of-sample \(R^2\) (fit on documents it has not seen), not in-sample \(R^2\).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Writing \(n \gg p\) (more documents than words). It is the other way round.
  • Saying λ = 0 is “maximum penalty”. It is no penalty at all.
  • Confusing the code’s alpha (in the sklearn library, alpha is the penalty dial λ) with the intercept \(\alpha\) on the slides (the starting value of the prediction).
  • Trusting in-sample \(R^2\) (the score on the training documents).
  • Claiming Ridge sets weights to exactly zero. It only shrinks them; Lasso is the one that sets some to zero.

Key terms to use

  • document-term matrix as regressors (word counts used as model inputs)
  • \(n \ll p\) (far fewer documents than words)
  • curse of dimensionality (too many columns, model fits anything)
  • overfitting (memorises training data, fails on new data)
  • penalised / regularised regression (regression with a fee for big weights)
  • Lasso (penalty that can set weights exactly zero)
  • Ridge (penalty that shrinks weights but keeps all)
  • Elastic net (a mix of Lasso and Ridge)
  • penalty λ (dial for how strong the fee is)
  • rare feature upweighting (\(\omega_j\)) (each word gets its own penalty cost)
  • shrinkage (pushing weights towards zero)
  • cross-validation (repeatedly test on held-back documents)
  • train/test split (learn on one part, test on another)
  • out-of-sample \(R^2\) (fit score on unseen documents)
  • placebo test (shuffle the answers; honest score should collapse)
  • dimension reduction (PCA, PLS) (squeeze many word columns into a few)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “In text regressions, regularisation helps overcome the curse of dimensionality.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A text regression predicts a number from word counts. Regularisation means adding a fee for big word weights. The curse of dimensionality is having far more words (columns) than documents (rows). Does the fee help with that problem?

    Answer: True. Why: With thousands of words and only a few dozen documents, the model can bend itself to fit anything. The fee forces it to keep most weights small, so only words that really matter keep a big weight. It is like a packing limit for a trip: you can only bring what you really need. (Source: 2025 T/F e; slides 17, 19, 34.)

  2. T/F: “With λ = 0, the penalised regression on slide 16 becomes standard OLS.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: λ is the strength of the penalty dial. OLS (ordinary least squares) is the plain regression with no penalty. If you turn the dial to 0, do you get plain regression back?

    Answer: True. Why: The fee is λ times the size of the weights. If λ is 0, the fee is always 0, so only the fit counts, and that is exactly OLS. Like a speed camera switched off: it is still there, but it never charges you. (Source: slide 16.)

  3. T/F: “In Lasso, high values of λ make coefficients larger.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Lasso is a regression with a fee for big weights. Coefficients are the word weights. λ is the strength of the fee. The statement says a stronger fee makes the weights bigger.

    Answer: False. Why: A higher fee makes big weights more expensive, so the model shrinks them, and with a high enough λ they become zero. It is like a tax on luggage weight: the higher the tax, the less you pack. (Source: slide 17.)

  4. T/F: “If a Ridge regression of a shuffled (placebo) target on word counts gives an in-sample R² near 1, the words are informative.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Ridge is a regression with a fee for big weights. The target is the number we try to predict (here GDP growth). “Shuffled (placebo)” means we mixed up the target values randomly between years, so the words cannot possibly hold real information about them. In-sample R² near 1 means the model fits the documents it learned from almost perfectly. The statement says this perfect fit proves the words are useful.

    Answer: False. Why: With far more words than documents (p ≫ n), the model can fit almost any target, even a random one. A student given 70 questions with random answers can memorise them and score 100% on those same questions, but that proves memorising, not understanding; the honest test is new questions. Only out-of-sample R² (the score on documents the model has not seen) counts. (Source: Notebook 2 cell 31.)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): “Why do we need regularisation in text regressions, and how is the penalty chosen?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why do we add a fee for big word weights, and how do we decide how strong that fee should be?

    Model answer: In a text regression the regressors are the columns of the document-term matrix, so we usually have far more words than documents (\(n \ll p\)), i.e. more unknowns than equations, and OLS cannot be estimated or fits the training data perfectly but meaninglessly (the curse of dimensionality). Penalised regressions such as Lasso add a cost \(n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\) for large coefficients, which shrinks most of them towards zero (Lasso sets some exactly to zero), so only informative words keep weight; λ = 0 gives back OLS. The penalty λ is chosen by cross-validation: estimate the model on training data for different λ values and pick the one that predicts held-out test data best (or use an information criterion such as AIC/BIC).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: In a text regression every word is an input, so there are far more inputs than documents, and plain regression either breaks or fits the training data perfectly without learning anything real. Lasso and similar methods add a fee for big word weights, so most weights shrink towards zero and only the useful words keep weight; with no fee (λ = 0) you are back to plain regression. To pick the fee, you try several values, train on part of the data, and keep the value that predicts the held-back part best. AIC and BIC are fit scores that charge for every extra weight, and can be used instead.

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 13–20 and 34; Interactive Notebook 2 cells 11–14, 31.

9. Naive Bayes classification (L3, Interactive 2)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 T/F (g) (“Naive Bayes … great for … two continuous variables” → False); the mechanics (Bayes’ rule, “naive”, Laplace smoothing) are a likely T/F or short question.

Start from zero

The problem. Your inbox gets 200 emails a day, and 50 of them are junk (“You won a prize! Click here!”). You want a program that moves the junk to a spam folder before you see it. You have a big pile of old emails that you already marked “spam” or “not spam”. Can the computer learn from that pile and then sort new emails by itself? Naive Bayes is one of the oldest and most basic ways to do this. The same idea can sort political speeches by party, or reviews into good and bad.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Collect labelled examples. Gather old emails that already carry the right label, “spam” or “not spam”. This pile is the training set.
  2. Count how common each label is. If 1 in 4 old emails was spam, then before reading a new email, your starting guess is “1 in 4 chance it is spam”. This starting guess is called the prior.
  3. For each label, count each word. “prize” might be common in spam and rare in normal mail; “meeting” the other way round. Turn these counts into shares: out of all the words in spam emails, what share is “prize”? This share is the likelihood of the word in that label.
  4. Fix the zero problem. If a word never appeared in spam, its share would be 0. One zero wipes out the whole score, because anything times 0 is 0. So pretend every word was seen one extra time in every label. This is Laplace smoothing.
  5. Score a new email for each label. Start from the prior and multiply by the share of each word in the email. “Naive” means we treat every word as separate evidence, as if the words did not affect each other.
  6. Pick the winner. The label with the bigger score wins. To turn the scores into chances that add up to 100%, divide each score by the total of all the scores.
  7. Why “Bayes”. Bayes’ rule is the bit of probability that lets us flip the question. We learned “how likely are these words, if the email is spam?” Bayes’ rule turns that into “how likely is it spam, given these words?”
  8. Test it fairly. Check it on emails that were not in the training pile, and compare with a lazy baseline like “always say not spam”.

A tiny example by hand. This is the chapter’s own example (slides 24 and 26), done slowly.

The situation. Four short texts are already sorted into two groups, a and b. Think of them as two people’s notes:

Text Group
“growth high trump” a
“trump rocket man” a
“trump trump trump” a
“trump inflation norway” b

A new text arrives: “inflation norway high”. Which group does it belong to? Naive Bayes works like a detective with two questions:

  1. How common is each group in general?
  2. How typical are the new text’s words for each group?

Question 1: how common is each group? (the “prior”) 3 of the 4 texts are group a, and 1 of the 4 is group b. So group a starts with 3/4 and group b with 1/4. Before reading a single word, group a looks more likely, because it is more common.

Question 2: how typical is each word for each group? (the “likelihood”) First, count all the words in each group:

  • Group a has 9 words in total (3 texts × 3 words): growth 1, high 1, trump 5, rocket 1, man 1.
  • Group b has 3 words: trump 1, inflation 1, norway 1.

Now take each word of the new text and ask, for each group: what share of this group’s words is this word?

One fix first. Group a never uses “inflation”, so its share would be 0 out of 9. Multiplying by 0 would kill group a’s score because of one missing word. So we pretend every word was seen one extra time (that is the “+1”, called Laplace smoothing). There are 7 different words in total, so each group’s total also goes up by 7: group a’s becomes 9 + 7 = 16, and group b’s becomes 3 + 7 = 10.

New word (rows) Times in group a, +1 Share in a Times in group b, +1 Share in b
inflation 0 + 1 = 1 1/16 1 + 1 = 2 2/10 = 1/5
norway 0 + 1 = 1 1/16 1 + 1 = 2 2/10 = 1/5
high 1 + 1 = 2 2/16 = 1/8 0 + 1 = 1 1/10

Put it together: the score. Score = how common the group is × how typical each word is, all multiplied:

  • Group a: 3/4 × 1/16 × 1/16 × 1/8 = 3/8192 ≈ 0.000366
  • Group b: 1/4 × 1/5 × 1/5 × 1/10 = 1/1000 = 0.001

Both numbers are tiny, because you multiply lots of small fractions. That is normal; only which one is bigger matters. Group b’s score is bigger, so the new text goes to group b.

Turning scores into percentages. Add the two scores: 0.000366 + 0.001 = 0.001366. Each group’s share of that total is its chance: group b = 0.001 ÷ 0.001366 ≈ 73%, and group a ≈ 27%.

The one-sentence intuition. Group a is more common (3 of 4 texts), but “inflation” and “norway” only ever appeared in group b’s text, and that evidence outweighs group a’s head start.

Why “naive”. It scores each word separately and multiplies, as if the words had nothing to do with each other, ignoring order and phrases. That is a simplification, but it works surprisingly well, which is why spam filters have used it for years.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: fast and needs only counting. Despite being so basic, it “works very well for categorizing documents” and is “a good starting point” (slides 22, 29).
  • Good: easy to see which words push a document towards each class.
  • Breaks: it only sorts into categories (spam / not spam). It cannot guess a number like GDP growth (2025 T/F g).
  • Breaks: the “words are independent” idea is false in real text (“New” is often followed by “York”), and a test set that shares people or periods with the training set makes the accuracy look better than it is (see “Evaluation” below).

What the words mean (from zero).

  • classification / classifier: sorting things into boxes; the classifier is the method that does the sorting. Like a post office sorting letters by city.
  • class / category: one of the boxes, such as “spam” or “Democrat”. Written \(v_k\) (class number \(k\)), or \(a\) and \(b\) in the example.
  • categorical vs continuous: categorical = a fixed set of boxes (spam / not spam). Continuous = a number that can take any value (2.37% growth).
  • label / labelled data: the correct class written next to each training document.
  • training set / test set: the training set is the labelled pile the model learns from. The test set is a separate pile kept aside to check how well it sorts.
  • probability / chance, \(P(\cdot)\): a number from 0 to 1 for how likely something is. \(P(\text{rain}) = 0.3\) = 30% chance of rain.
  • \(P(A\mid B)\): “the chance of A, given B”. \(P(\text{umbrella}\mid\text{rain})\) = how likely you carry an umbrella when it rains.
  • document \(d\): the text we want to sort.
  • prior, \(P(v_k)\): how common a class is before you read the document. If 3 of 4 emails are class a, the prior for a is 3/4.
  • likelihood, \(P(c_{ij}\mid v_k)\): how likely a word is to show up in a class. “prize” has a high likelihood in spam.
  • posterior, \(P(v\mid d)\): the updated chance of a class after reading the document. Prior + evidence → posterior.
  • \(P(d)\): the overall chance of seeing this document. It is the same for every class, so it can be dropped when comparing.
  • Bayes’ rule: the rule that flips “chance of words given class” into “chance of class given words”: posterior = likelihood × prior ÷ \(P(d)\).
  • \(\propto\) (“proportional to”): “equal up to a common scaling”. We skip dividing by the same number for every class, because it does not change the winner.
  • \(\arg\max\): “the choice that gives the biggest value”. If a scores 0.000366 and b scores 0.001, the argmax is b.
  • MAP, \(v_{map}\) (maximum a posteriori): the class with the highest posterior chance, the winner.
  • naive / independence / conditional independence: treating each word as separate evidence, as if knowing one word tells you nothing about the next once you know the class.
  • bag-of-words assumption: a document is a loose bag of words; order does not matter.
  • \(\prod\) (capital pi): “multiply all of these together”, like \(\sum\) means “add all of these”.
  • \(c_{ij}\): the count of word \(j\) in document \(i\).
  • token: one word occurrence. “trump trump trump” is 3 tokens of 1 word.
  • vocabulary, \(p\): the list of different words seen in training. In the example, \(p = 7\).
  • Multinomial Naive Bayes: the version of Naive Bayes that works with word counts.
  • Laplace smoothing (+1 / +p): add 1 to every word’s count in every class, and add the vocabulary size \(p\) to the bottom, so no chance is ever exactly zero.
  • normalise: divide each score by the total so the chances add up to 1.
  • estimate, hat (\(\hat P\)): a value worked out from the data. \(\hat P(a)\) = our estimated prior for class a.
  • inference: drawing a conclusion from the data.
  • odds: how many times more likely one thing is than another. In the notebook’s quote, how much more a word belongs to one party than the other.
  • Support Vector Machines, logistic regression, neural networks: other, more complex classifiers, named on the slides but not taught here.
  • accuracy: the share of test documents sorted into the right class. 70 right out of 100 = 70%.
  • majority-class baseline: the lazy rule “always guess the biggest class”. A real model must beat it.
  • data leakage: when information from the test set sneaks into training, so the test score looks better than it should.
  • random split vs grouped split (GroupShuffleSplit): a random split picks test documents at random. A grouped split holds out whole groups (for example, all speeches by some presidents).
  • random seed: the starting number for the computer’s random choices. Same seed = same split; new seed = new split.
  • log / log probability: the logarithm, a function that turns multiplying into adding. The difference of two logs compares how many times bigger one chance is than the other.
  • CountVectorizer, fit, MultinomialNB, feature_log_prob_: Python tools that count words, learn from training data, run Naive Bayes, and store the log chance of each word in each class.
  • stop words / min_df: very common words (“the”, “and”) that are removed / drop words seen in fewer than this many documents.

The idea in plain words

Naive Bayes sorts documents into categories (spam / not spam, Democrat / Republican, good / bad review). It learns from labelled examples how often each word shows up in each category. For a new document it asks: “If this document came from category A, how likely are these exact words? And from category B?” It combines that with how common each category is, and picks the category with the highest score.

Notebook 2 (cell 15) puts it nicely: “Naive Bayes learns, for each party, the odds of every word, and lets the words vote.” (Odds here = how much more often a word shows up for one party than for the other.)

Analogy A doctor guessing between a cold and the flu. They know how common each illness is right now (the prior) and how often each symptom appears with each illness (the likelihoods). For a patient with a fever and aching muscles, they multiply “how common the illness is” by “how typical each symptom is for it” and choose the larger. “Naive” means the doctor treats every symptom as independent evidence, even though fever and aches often come together.

The exam definition

Slide 22:

  • The outcome is categorical (“good versus bad, spam versus not spam, etc.”). Regression (e.g. OLS) “works best for continuous outcome variables” (numbers that can take any value, like 2.37% growth); for categorical outcomes (a fixed set of boxes, like spam / not spam) “it is more common and better to apply classification methods”.
  • “It is called ‘Naive’ because it operates under the bag-of-words assumption and assumes that the words in a document are independent.”
  • “It is called ‘Bayes’ because it applies the Bayes rule to make inference.” (Inference = drawing a conclusion from the data; here, deciding the class.)
  • Despite its simplicity it “works very well for categorizing documents” and has a long history in NLP. Slide 29: it “is usually regarded as a good starting point”. Other classifiers: Support Vector Machines, logistic regression, neural networks (other, more complex sorting methods; named, not taught here).

Slide 27 summary: we know the classes \(V^{train}\) and observe \(C^{train}\) (the known labels and the word-count table of the training documents); we learn \(p(c^{train}\mid v^{train})\); “Via Bayes rule we can use this to predict \(p(v^{test}\mid c^{test})\).” So Naive Bayes models \(p(c_i\mid y_i)\) — the reverse of text regression’s \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\) (Chapter 6).

The formula, symbol by symbol

The derivation on slide 25, line by line:

In words: the chance of class \(v\) after reading document \(d\) equals how likely the document is under that class, times how common the class is, divided by how likely the document is overall.

\[P(v\mid d) = \frac{P(d\mid v)P(v)}{P(d)} \qquad\text{(Bayes' rule: posterior = likelihood × prior / data)}\]

In words: the predicted class is the one with the largest of these chances.

\[v_{map} = \arg\max \frac{P(d\mid v)P(v)}{P(d)} \qquad\text{(pick the most probable class)}\]

In words: treat the document as its list of word counts, and drop the bottom part \(P(d)\) because it is the same for every class.

\[v_{k,map} = \arg\max P(c_{i1},\dots,c_{ip}\mid v_k)P(v_k) \qquad\text{(document = its words; } P(d) \text{ dropped)}\]

In words: the chance of seeing all the words together is taken to be the chance of each word on its own, multiplied together.

\[P(c_{i1},\dots,c_{ip}\mid v_k) = P(c_{i1}\mid v_k)\times\dots\times P(c_{ip}\mid v_k) \qquad\text{(the "naive" independence step)}\]

In words: for each class, multiply how common the class is by the chance of each word in that class, and pick the class with the largest result.

\[v_{k,nb} = \arg\max P(v_k)\,\prod_j P(c_{ij}\mid v_k) \qquad\text{(Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier)}\]

  • \(v_k\) = class \(k\) (e.g. \(a\) or \(b\)). \(d\) = the document.
  • \(P(v_k)\) = the prior: how common class \(k\) is before reading the document.
  • \(P(c_{ij}\mid v_k)\) = the likelihood of word \(j\) in class \(k\).
  • \(\arg\max\) = “the class that gives the largest value”.
  • \(P(d)\) is dropped because it is the same for every class, so it does not change which class wins.
  • \(\prod\) = multiply over all words in the document (the slide writes a capital \(\Pi\)).

Estimation is “simple counting” (slide 25):

In words: the prior of a class is the share of training documents that belong to it.

\[\hat P(v_k) = \frac{doccount(V = v_k)}{n} = \frac{n_k}{n}\]

In words: the chance of word \(j\) in class \(k\) is how often it appears in that class (plus 1), divided by the total number of words in that class (plus the vocabulary size).

\[\hat P(c_{\cdot j}\mid v_k) = \frac{count(c_{\cdot j}, v_k) + 1}{\sum count(c, v_k) + p}\]

  • \(n_k\) = number of training documents in class \(k\); \(n\) = all training documents.
  • \(count(c_{\cdot j}, v_k)\) = how many times word \(j\) appears in all class-\(k\) documents together.
  • \(\sum count(c, v_k)\) = total number of words (tokens) in class-\(k\) documents.
  • \(p\) = vocabulary size (number of different words).
  • \(+1\) and \(+p\) = Laplace smoothing “to avoid zeros”: pretend every word was seen once more in every class.

Read aloud: “Pick the class whose share of training documents, times the smoothed frequency of each of the document’s words in that class, is largest.”

A tiny worked example (slides 24 and 26)

The data (slide 24). Rows = documents; columns = the words and the class.

Doc Words Class
1 (train) growth high trump a
2 (train) trump rocket man a
3 (train) trump trump trump a
4 (train) trump inflation norway b
5 (test) inflation norway high ?

Step 1 — Priors. 3 of 4 training documents are class a: \(\hat P(a)=3/4\), \(\hat P(b)=1/4\).

Step 2 — Counts. Class a has 9 word tokens (trump 5, growth 1, high 1, rocket 1, man 1). Class b has 3 tokens (trump, inflation, norway). The vocabulary has \(p=7\) words (growth, high, trump, rocket, man, inflation, norway).

Step 3 — Smoothed likelihoods for the test words. Rows = the words in document 5; columns = the two classes. Each cell is (count + 1) / (tokens in class + 7).

Word Class a Class b
inflation (0+1)/(9+7) = 1/16 (1+1)/(3+7) = 1/5
norway (0+1)/(9+7) = 1/16 (1+1)/(3+7) = 1/5
high (1+1)/(9+7) = 1/8 (0+1)/(3+7) = 1/10

Step 4 — Multiply prior × likelihoods.

In words: class a’s score is its prior 3/4 times the chances of “inflation”, “norway” and “high” in class a.

\[\hat P(a\mid d5) \propto \tfrac34\cdot\tfrac1{16}\cdot\tfrac1{16}\cdot\tfrac18 = \tfrac{3}{8192} \approx 0.000366\]

In words: the same for class b: its prior 1/4 times the chances of the three words in class b.

\[\hat P(b\mid d5) \propto \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac1{10} = \tfrac{1}{1000} = 0.001\]

Step 5 — Normalise so the two add to 1 (slide: “a/(a+b)”):

In words: divide each score by the sum of both scores, so the two chances add up to 1.

\[\hat P(a\mid d5) = \frac{0.000366}{0.000366+0.001} \approx 0.27, \qquad \hat P(b\mid d5) \approx 0.73\]

Document 5 is classified as b. Class b’s score is about 2.7 times class a’s.

Note on the slide. Slide 26 prints the step-4 numbers as ≈ 0.00004 and ≈ 0.0001. These are about 10 times too small (the exact values are 0.000366 and 0.001). Because both are off by the same factor, the ratio, the normalised 0.27 / 0.73 and the class “b” are all correct. In the exam, write the correct values (0.000366 and 0.001) or just the fractions.

Why b wins. “trump” is the typical class-a word, but document 5 has no “trump”. Its words “inflation” and “norway” were seen only in the class-b document, and that outweighs the 3/4 prior for class a.

Why smoothing matters. Without the +1/+p, \(P(\text{inflation}\mid a) = 0/9 = 0\), so class a’s product is 0. Also \(P(\text{high}\mid b) = 0/3 = 0\), so class b’s product is 0 too. Both classes score zero and we cannot decide. One unseen word wipes out all other evidence; smoothing prevents that.

Evaluation: how good is the classifier? (Notebook 2, Q3)

  • Accuracy vs a baseline. Notebook 2 compares accuracy on test speeches with the majority-class baseline, “always guessing the bigger party”. 70% accuracy is not impressive if 65% of the test speeches belong to one party anyway (illustrative numbers).
  • How you split decides what accuracy means.
Split What goes into the test set Problem
"random" a random quarter of the speeches the same president appears in training and test, so the model can recognise the president and era (names, events) rather than the party — information leaks from train to test
"by_president" (GroupShuffleSplit) a random quarter of the presidents every test speech is by a president the model never saw — an honest test of party

Takeaway (cell 31): “How you choose the test data decides what the accuracy means. A random split rewards a Naive Bayes model that recognises presidents and eras; holding out whole presidents reveals how little of that is party.” Also “one split proves little”, so cell 19 repeats the experiment over 20 random seeds (a seed is the starting number for the random split; a new seed gives a new split). The business version: a complaint-email flagger trained on a random split of last year’s mail may fail on next year’s mail (cell 20).

Reading the course code

vec = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english", min_df=5, token_pattern=r"[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z]+")
Xtr = vec.fit_transform(train.rawtext)
nb  = MultinomialNB().fit(Xtr, train.party)
acc = nb.score(vec.transform(test.rawtext), test.party)
tilt = nb.feature_log_prob_[0] - nb.feature_log_prob_[1]

(Simplified from Notebook 2, cell 17.)

  • Line 1: a counter that turns text into word counts, drops English stop words and keeps only words found in at least 5 speeches.
  • Line 2: learn the vocabulary on the training speeches only and build their DTM.
  • Line 3: fit Multinomial Naive Bayes: this does the counting (priors and smoothed likelihoods) shown above. Scikit-learn’s default smoothing is the same add-one (Laplace) idea. [Not in course files — general knowledge: MultinomialNB has a smoothing parameter alpha that defaults to 1.]
  • Line 4: accuracy = share of test speeches given the right party.
  • Line 5: for each word, log P(word | party 0) − log P(word | party 1) (log = logarithm; a difference of logs compares how many times bigger one chance is than the other): positive = “more Democratic”, negative = “more Republican”. The notebook lists the top 12 of each. For the toy data, the “tilt” of “trump” towards a is \(\log(3/8) - \log(1/5) \approx 0.63\) (P(trump | a) = (5+1)/(9+7) = 3/8, P(trump | b) = (1+1)/(3+7) = 1/5).

There are no saved outputs. When run, it would print test accuracy next to the majority-class baseline, the test presidents and the most party-typical words. With a random split, the notebook hints these are often names and events.

How this shows up on the exam

  • 2025 T/F (g) said: “The Naive Bayes Classifier is great for capturing the relationship between two continuous variables.” → False. Naive Bayes is a classifier for a categorical outcome (an answer that is one of a few groups, like “spam / not spam” or “party a / party b”), and it works on word counts. Continuous variables are numbers that can take any value, like height or GDP growth (slide 22).

  • Likely variants:

    • why it is called “naive” and why “Bayes”;
    • what Laplace smoothing (adding 1 to every word count) does;
    • regression (guessing a number) vs classification (guessing a group);
    • a short posterior calculation (working out the chance of each class for a new document) like slide 26;
    • the evaluation trap: a random split vs a grouped split (keeping all speeches by one person on the same side of the train/test line).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The outcome is categorical (a group label, not a number).
  • From labelled training data (documents that come with their correct class), learn the chance of the words given the class (\(p(c\mid v)\)). Then flip it with Bayes’ rule to get the chance of the class given the words (\(p(v\mid c)\)).
  • “Naive” = the bag-of-words assumption (word order is ignored) plus the assumption that words are independent given the class (each word is treated as if it tells you nothing about the other words).
  • The prior (how common each class is before reading the document) is \(n_k/n\): the number of training documents in class \(k\) divided by all training documents.
  • The likelihood is the smoothed share of that word among all words in the class.
  • Laplace smoothing adds 1 to each word count (top of the fraction) and \(p\), the number of different words in the vocabulary, to the bottom. This avoids zero chances.
  • Choose the class with the highest posterior (the chance of the class after reading the document).
  • Evaluate on held-out data (documents the model did not learn from) and compare with a baseline (a dumb rule such as always guessing the biggest class). Hold out whole groups (e.g. all speeches by one president) to avoid leakage (test information sneaking into training).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Using Naive Bayes for continuous outcomes (numbers like GDP growth).
  • Saying “naive because it is simple”. It is naive because of the independence assumption (words treated as unrelated given the class).
  • Forgetting smoothing, or adding 1 to the bottom of the fraction instead of \(p\) (the number of different words).
  • Forgetting the prior (how common each class is).
  • Stopping at the raw products (before dividing by their total) without saying which class wins.
  • Reporting accuracy from a random split as proof that the model learned “party”. It may have only learned names and events of each president.

Key terms to use

  • classification (guessing which group a document belongs to)
  • categorical outcome (answer is a group, not a number)
  • Bayes’ rule (formula that flips “words given class” round)
  • prior (how common each class is beforehand)
  • likelihood (how typical these words are for a class)
  • posterior (chance of a class after reading the words)
  • maximum a posteriori (argmax) (pick the class with the highest posterior)
  • conditional independence (words treated as unrelated within a class)
  • bag-of-words assumption (word order is ignored; only counts matter)
  • Multinomial Naive Bayes (the word-count version of Naive Bayes)
  • Laplace smoothing (add 1 so no chance is zero)
  • training/test data (learn on one part, check on another)
  • accuracy (share of documents classified correctly)
  • majority-class baseline (always guess the most common class)
  • data leakage (test information sneaking into training)
  • grouped split (keep each group wholly in train or test)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “The Naive Bayes classifier is great for capturing the relationship between two continuous variables.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Naive Bayes is a method that sorts documents into groups. Continuous variables are numbers that can take any value, like height and weight. The statement says Naive Bayes is good at linking two such numbers.

    Answer: False. Why: Naive Bayes is built to pick a group (a categorical outcome, like “spam” or “not spam”), using word counts. Linking two numbers is a job for regression. It is like using a letter-sorting machine to measure parcels: wrong tool. (Source: slide 22; 2025 T/F g.)

  2. T/F: “Naive Bayes is called naive because it assumes the words in a document are independent (bag-of-words).”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Independent” means each word is treated as if it tells you nothing about the other words in the document. Bag-of-words means we ignore word order and only count words, as if the words were shaken up in a bag. Is that the reason for the name “naive”?

    Answer: True. Why: In real text, words clearly depend on each other (“New” is often followed by “York”). Pretending they do not is a naive (overly simple) assumption, hence the name. It still works well in practice. (Source: slide 22.)

  3. T/F: “Laplace smoothing adds 1 to every word count so that unseen words do not give zero probability.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: If a word never appeared in a class’s training documents, its chance for that class would be 0. Because Naive Bayes multiplies all word chances together, one 0 makes the whole result 0. The statement says Laplace smoothing fixes this by adding 1 to every count.

    Answer: True. Why: Adding 1 to every count means no word ever has a chance of exactly 0. To keep the shares adding up properly, you also add \(p\) (the number of different words in the vocabulary) to the bottom of each fraction. Think of it as giving every word one free “starter” sighting, so one missing word cannot veto all the other evidence. (Source: slide 25; +1 in numerator, +p in denominator.)

  4. Calculation: “Using the slide-24 training data, classify a new document containing only ‘trump’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Use the small four-document example from the worked example above. Class a has 3 of the 4 training documents and 9 words in total, 5 of them “trump”. Class b has 1 document with 3 words, 1 of them “trump”. There are 7 different words overall. Which class does a new document that says only “trump” belong to?

    Answer: a: \(\tfrac34\times\tfrac{5+1}{9+7} = \tfrac34\times\tfrac38 = 0.281\); b: \(\tfrac14\times\tfrac{1+1}{3+7} = \tfrac14\times\tfrac15 = 0.05\). Normalised: a ≈ 0.85, b ≈ 0.15 → class a.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: For each class, multiply how common the class is (the prior: 3/4 or 1/4) by the smoothed chance of “trump” in that class (count + 1, divided by the class’s word total + 7). Class a scores 0.281 and class b scores 0.05. Dividing each by their sum gives chances of about 85% for a and 15% for b, so the document goes to class a. That makes sense: “trump” is the typical class-a word, and class a is also the more common class.

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): “How does Naive Bayes classify a document, and why is it called ‘naive’ and ‘Bayes’?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Walk through the steps Naive Bayes uses to put a document in a group, and explain both parts of its name.

    Model answer: From labelled training documents, Naive Bayes estimates the prior share of each class (\(n_k/n\)) and, for each class, the probability of each word (its smoothed frequency among all words in that class, with +1/+p Laplace smoothing so unseen words do not give zero). For a new document it multiplies the class prior by the probabilities of all the document’s words and picks the class with the largest result. It is “Bayes” because it uses Bayes’ rule to turn \(p(\text{words}\mid\text{class})\) into \(p(\text{class}\mid\text{words})\), and “naive” because it uses the bag-of-words assumption that words are independent given the class. It is for categorical outcomes (spam/not spam), not continuous ones.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: First it learns from documents that already have their correct group: how common each group is, and how often each word shows up in each group (with 1 added to every count so nothing is zero). For a new document, it multiplies the group’s share by the chances of all the document’s words, and picks the group with the biggest result. “Bayes” is the rule that flips “how likely are these words in this group?” into “how likely is this group, given these words?”. “Naive” is the simplifying belief that words do not depend on each other; and it sorts into groups, it does not predict numbers.

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 21–29; Interactive Notebook 2 cells 15–20, 31.

10. Topic models: LSA via SVD and LDA (L3, Interactive 2, Practical day 1)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q2(d) (5 points: what topic models are, two methods, intuition and difference); slide 43’s “LSA is not probabilistic” is a natural T/F.

Start from zero

The problem. A newspaper archive holds 50,000 articles, and nobody has tagged them by subject. A central-bank researcher has years of meeting notes and wants to know what the members talk about, and how that changes over time. A company has 5,000 open answers to a customer survey. In each case you want the computer to sort the pile into themes that nobody named in advance, and to say how much of each theme is in each text. Nobody gives the computer a list of themes or any answers. That is what a topic model does.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Make the word-count table. Rows are documents, columns are words, and each cell is how often that word appears in that document.
  2. Notice that some words travel together. “goal” and “match” often show up in the same articles; so do “stock” and “market”. A group of words that tend to appear together is a topic.
  3. Notice that one text can mix themes. A news story about a car factory hit by a volcano is part “cars”, part “natural disasters”.
  4. Choose how many themes you want. This number is called \(K\). The computer does not know the “right” number; you pick it.
  5. Way 1, LSA: pure table arithmetic. A maths tool called SVD splits the big table into three smaller tables. One says how much of each theme each document has. One says how important each theme is. One says how strongly each word belongs to each theme. Keep only the \(K\) most important themes and throw the rest away as noise.
  6. Way 2, LDA: a story about how texts are written. Imagine every article was written like this. The writer first picks a mix of themes (“80% finance, 20% football”). Then, for each word, the writer picks a theme from that mix, and then picks a word from that theme’s word list. The computer works backwards: which themes, and which mix per article, would best explain the word counts we actually see?
  7. Name the themes yourself. Look at each theme’s top words and give it a name (“finance”, “football”). The computer never names them.
  8. Check stability. LDA starts from a random guess. Run it again with a different random start. Themes that come back both times deserve more trust.

A tiny example by hand. We reuse the chapter’s own two examples and go through them slowly.

LSA. Look at the table in “A tiny worked example (LSA)” below. Rows are 4 documents; columns are counts of 4 words. Documents d1 and d2 talk about stock and market (finance). Documents d3 and d4 talk about goal and match (football). d4 also has one stray “market”. SVD turns this into two smaller tables, \(F\) and \(L\), each with 2 columns (we keep \(K = 2\) components).

  • In \(F\) (rows = documents), look at column “comp. 2”: d1 = 2.485 and d2 = 2.389 are positive, while d3 = −2.560 and d4 = −2.100 are negative. So component 2 splits finance documents from football documents.
  • In \(L\) (rows = words), column “comp. 2”: stock = 0.536 and market = 0.439 are positive, goal = −0.520 and match = −0.500 are negative. The same split, now for words.

Now rebuild one cell of the original table out loud: d1’s count of “stock”. Multiply d1’s row in \(F\) by stock’s row in \(L\), number by number, and add: 2.504 × 0.456 = 1.142, and 2.485 × 0.536 = 1.332. Total: 1.142 + 1.332 = 2.474, about 2.47. The real count was 3. It is close but not exact, because we threw away the two smallest components. That gap is the “noise” we dropped.

LDA. Look at the table in “A tiny worked example (LDA mixing)”. Rows are 2 topics; columns are 4 words; each cell is the chance that the topic picks that word, so each row adds up to 1. A document that is 80% finance and 20% football mixes the two rows. For “goal”: 0.8 × 0.05 + 0.2 × 0.50 = 0.04 + 0.10 = 0.14. So in this document we expect about 14 words in every 100 to be “goal”.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: no labels and no word lists are needed. It finds themes on its own.
  • Good: it shrinks thousands of word columns into a few theme columns, which you can then use as inputs in a regression (Chapter 8).
  • Breaks: you must choose \(K\) yourself, and the names of the themes are your own interpretation.
  • Breaks: LDA can give different themes with a different random start (seed). LSA’s numbers can be negative, so they cannot be read as shares.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • topic: a group of words that tend to appear together, like {goal, match, team}.
  • topic model: an unsupervised method that finds topics and says how much of each topic is in each document.
  • cluster: a group of things that are alike.
  • mixture (of topics): a document made of several topics in different amounts, like a smoothie that is 70% strawberry and 30% banana.
  • latent: hidden; we never see the topics directly, only the words.
  • unsupervised: no answers or labels are given; the method finds the structure itself.
  • parsimonious: using as few pieces as possible to explain a lot.
  • document-term matrix (DTM, \(C\)): the word-count table, rows = documents, columns = words.
  • matrix: a table of numbers. Its size is written “rows × columns”: \(n\times p\) = \(n\) rows and \(p\) columns.
  • sparse / dense: a sparse table is mostly zeros (most words do not appear in most documents). A dense table has few zeros.
  • dimension / dimension reduction: each column is a dimension. Dimension reduction = summarising many columns with a few.
  • \(K\), and \(K \ll p\): \(K\) is the number of topics (components) kept; “\(\ll\)” means “much smaller than”. 6 topics instead of 10,000 words.
  • component / factor: one hidden theme found by the method.
  • factors \(F\): a table with one row per document saying how much of each component it has (\(n\times K\)).
  • loadings \(L\): a table with one row per word saying how strongly it belongs to each component (\(p\times K\)).
  • LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis): the topic method that applies SVD (or PCA) to the word-count table.
  • PCA (Principal Components Analysis): a standard method that finds the few directions in which the data vary the most. For text, it gives the same result as SVD.
  • SVD (Singular Value Decomposition): a maths tool that rewrites any table as three tables multiplied together: \(U\) (documents), \(S\) (importance) and \(V'\) (words).
  • singular values (\(s\)): the importance numbers on the diagonal of \(S\), largest first.
  • diagonal matrix: a table that is all zeros except on the line from top-left to bottom-right.
  • orthogonal / unitary matrix: a table whose columns point in completely separate directions, so they share no information.
  • \(U'\), \(V'\) (the prime): the table flipped, so rows become columns.
  • identity matrix \(I\): the “do-nothing” table, with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing, like multiplying a number by 1.
  • truncation: keeping only the first \(K\) components and dropping the rest.
  • rank-2 approximation: the table rebuilt using only the 2 kept components; close to, but not the same as, the original.
  • variance / variance explained (\(\lambda_l\)): variance = how much numbers spread out around their average. Variance explained = how much of that spread a component accounts for. (This \(\lambda\) is not the fee \(\lambda\) from Chapter 8.)
  • centred columns: each column with its own average subtracted, so it averages zero.
  • LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): the probabilistic topic model.
  • probabilistic model: a model where every number is a chance between 0 and 1, and the chances in a group add up to 1.
  • generative model / generative story: a model that tells a step-by-step story of how the text could have been produced.
  • non-parametric (as used on slide 43): here, it does not assume any probability model with settings to estimate.
  • distribution / probability vector: a list of chances that add up to 1, like (0.50, 0.40, 0.05, 0.05) for four words.
  • \(\theta_l\) (theta), \(\Theta\): topic \(l\)’s list of word chances; \(\Theta\) is all topics stacked together.
  • \(v_{il}\), topic weights, \(V\): the share of document \(i\) that is topic \(l\); each document’s shares add up to 1.
  • \(\mathbf q_i\): document \(i\)’s blended list of word chances.
  • \(m_i\): the length of document \(i\) (its total number of words).
  • \(\sim\): “is drawn at random from”.
  • multinomial distribution (\(MN\)): the chances of getting each possible set of counts when you make several draws, like drawing coloured balls from an urn several times.
  • with replacement: each ball goes back into the urn after it is drawn.
  • factorial (\(6!\)): multiply down to 1: \(6! = 6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1 = 720\).
  • categorical distribution: one single draw from several possible outcomes, like picking one word.
  • Dirichlet distribution / Dirichlet prior: a way of drawing a random list of shares that add up to 1. As a prior, it is LDA’s starting assumption about which topic mixes (and word lists) are likely.
  • prior: what you assume before seeing the data.
  • \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (in LDA): the two Dirichlet settings. Low \(\alpha\) → each document has few main topics. Low \(\beta\) → each topic has few main words. (This \(\beta\) is not the regression coefficient of Chapter 8.)
  • sparsity (in LDA): most chances are near zero, and only a few are big.
  • Beta distribution: the two-outcome version of the Dirichlet: a random share between 0 and 1.
  • conjugate prior: a prior that fits the multinomial so neatly that the maths stays easy.
  • Bayesian estimation: combining a prior with the data to get updated beliefs.
  • variational Bayes / Gibbs sampling: two computer methods that start from a guess and improve it step by step, many times. [Not in course files — general knowledge: the “start from a guess and improve” description]
  • iterative: repeated round after round.
  • random seed: the starting number for the computer’s random guess. Same seed = same result; a new seed can give different topics.
  • cosine similarity: a score of how alike two lists of numbers are; 1 = identical pattern.
  • marginal likelihood / out-of-sample testing: how probable held-out texts are under the fitted model; higher = the model explains new texts better. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • plate diagram: a box-and-arrow picture of the LDA story.
  • \(\varphi_k\) (phi), \(\theta_m\): the plate diagram’s names for the topic-word list and the document-topic mix.
  • stem (e.g. “vehicl”): a word cut to its root, so “vehicle” and “vehicles” both become “vehicl”.
  • second-stage regression: a regression that uses the topic shares as its inputs.
  • polysemy / synonyms: one word with several meanings / several words with one meaning.
  • tf-idf: a word weight, high for words that are frequent here but rare elsewhere. LDA needs plain counts instead.
  • Gensim / LdaModel / passes: a Python toolbox for topic models / its LDA tool / how many times it goes through all the texts.
  • filter_extremes, min_df, max_df: settings that drop words that are too rare or too common.
  • components_: where scikit-learn stores each topic’s word weights.
  • FOMC: the US central bank’s committee that sets interest rates. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • dynamic / supervised / correlated topic models: extensions of LDA named on slide 59.

The idea in plain words

A topic model answers “what is this text about?” without anyone labelling anything (slide 31: “in a parsimonious (unsupervised) manner”; parsimonious = using as few pieces as possible).

Two ideas carry the whole chapter:

  1. A topic is a cluster of words that tend to appear together. E.g. {motor, toyota, nissan, vehicl, car, auto…} (slide 55). (“vehicl” is a stem: words cut to their root, so “vehicle” and “vehicles” both become “vehicl”.)
  2. A document is a mixture of topics. The Nissan/volcano news article on slides 54–55 is part “Motor”, part “Natural disasters” and part “Outlook”.

Mathematically: the huge, sparse (mostly zeros) \(n\times p\) (\(n\) documents in rows, \(p\) words in columns) document-term matrix \(C\) is explained by a much smaller set of \(K\) common factors (\(K \ll p\)). Slide 33 names the two pieces: F (how much of each topic each document has, \(n\times K\)) and L (how much each topic weights each word, \(p\times K\)).

Analogy Think of a smoothie bar. Each smoothie (document) is a mix of a few base fruits (topics) — 70% strawberry, 30% banana. Each fruit has its own taste profile over many flavour notes (words). Tasting only the smoothies, a topic model works out what the base fruits must be and each smoothie’s recipe.

Why bother (slide 34)? Because \(K \ll p\): (1) easier interpretation — look at 6 topics, not 10,000 words; (2) noise reduction — \(C\) is large and sparse (many zeros), \(F\) is small and dense (few zeros); (3) might capture polysemy and synonyms; (4) avoids the curse of dimensionality when the text is used in a second-stage regression (a regression that uses the topic shares as its inputs; Chapter 8).

The exam definition

  • LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis): “Simply Principal Components Analysis (PCA) applied to text”, i.e. to \(C\) (PCA = a standard method that finds the few directions in which the data vary the most). It finds “\(K \ll p\) common latent components that explain as much of the variation in \(C\) as possible” (variation = how much the counts differ from document to document), computed by PCA or the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) — “Same results, but differences in implementation” (slide 35).
  • LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): a probabilistic topic model in which “Topics are distributions of words” and “Documents are distributions of topics”, so it is “seen as a more plausible generative model for text” (slide 45) (generative model = a model that tells a story of how the text could have been produced). It “combines the factor model assumption for multinomial data with a Dirichlet prior” (slide 53; Blei et al. 2003) (multinomial data = counts of how often each word was drawn; Dirichlet prior = a starting assumption about which mixes of shares are likely — see the word list above).
  • Key contrast (slide 43): “LSA is not a probabilistic model (non-parametric), and not seen as a plausible generative model for text!” (Non-parametric here: it does not assume a probability model with settings to estimate; it is pure table arithmetic.)
  • 2025 guideline for Q2(d): “In NLP topics are basically clusters of words. Articles/documents are assumed to consist of different topics, with different weights. SVD for matrix decomp and LDA for probabilities.”

Part 1 — LSA via SVD

The formula, symbol by symbol (slides 36–37).

In words: any word-count table can be rebuilt exactly as three tables multiplied together: one for documents, one for how important each component is, and one for words.

\[\underbrace{C}_{n\times p} = \underbrace{U}_{n\times n}\ \underbrace{S}_{n\times p}\ \underbrace{V'}_{p\times p}\]

  • \(C\) = the document-term matrix (\(n\) documents in rows, \(p\) words in columns).
  • \(U\) = a “unitary matrix (orthogonal, \(UU' = I\))”: one row per document. (Orthogonal = its columns point in completely separate directions. \(U'\) is \(U\) flipped so rows become columns, and \(I\) is the “do-nothing” table with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.)
  • \(S\) = “a diagonal matrix of singular values \(s_i\)”: numbers on the diagonal, largest first, saying how important each component is.
  • \(V'\) = another unitary matrix: one column per word.

Read aloud: “any document-term matrix can be written exactly as a document matrix times a diagonal importance matrix times a word matrix.”

Truncation — keep only the \(K\) most important components (slide 37):

In words: keep only the \(K\) biggest components, so the three tables become much smaller and rebuild the original table approximately.

\[\underbrace{C}_{n\times p} \approx \underbrace{U}_{n\times K}\ \underbrace{S}_{K\times K}\ \underbrace{V'}_{K\times p}\]

  • Factors \(F = U_{1:K}S_{1:K}\) (\(n\times K\)): “the prevalence of the common components in each document”. Similar documents have similar factor rows.
  • Loadings \(L = V_{1:K}\) (\(p\times K\)): “the importance of each factor for each word”. Similar words have similar loading rows (slide 38).
  • The columns of \(F\) are orthogonal (unrelated to each other). The first component captures the most variance (spread of the numbers around their average), the second the next most, and so on. The variance explained by component \(l\) is \(\lambda_l = s_l^2/(n-1)\), which falls as \(l\) rises (slide 38). (Slide 44 shows PCA and SVD give the same factors: \(F = XV = US\).)

A tiny worked example (LSA). Four documents, four words. Rows = documents; columns = word counts. Toy data made up for this guide; computed with numpy’s SVD.

Doc stock market goal match
d1 3 2 0 0
d2 2 3 0 0
d3 0 0 3 2
d4 0 1 2 3

The singular values are \(s = (5.285,\ 4.780,\ 1.273,\ 0.778)\). The first two components explain \((5.285^2+4.780^2)/\sum s_l^2 \approx 96\%\) of the total, so \(K=2\) is a natural choice. (In slide terms, \(\lambda_l = s_l^2/(n-1) = 9.31,\ 7.62,\ 0.54,\ 0.20\); strictly, “variance” needs centred columns (each column with its average subtracted) as in slide 44, but the ranking idea is the same.)

Factors \(F\) (rows = documents, columns = components 1 and 2) and loadings \(L\) (rows = words, columns = components):

\(F\) comp. 1 comp. 2
d1 2.504 2.485
d2 2.616 2.389
d3 2.411 −2.560
d4 3.000 −2.100
\(L\) comp. 1 comp. 2
stock 0.456 0.536
market 0.568 0.439
goal 0.474 −0.520
match 0.495 −0.500

How to read it: component 1 is roughly “how many words in total” (all positive). Component 2 is the finance vs football contrast: d1, d2, stock and market are positive; d3, d4, goal and match are negative. Documents on the same subject have similar rows of \(F\); words on the same subject have similar rows of \(L\).

Hand check of one cell. The rank-2 approximation (the table rebuilt from only the 2 kept components) of d1’s “stock” count is row d1 of \(F\) times row “stock” of \(L\): \(2.504\times0.456 + 2.485\times0.536 = 1.142 + 1.332 = 2.474 \approx 2.47\) (true count 3). Note also: the entries of \(F\) and \(L\) are unrestricted — negative values appear and rows do not sum to 1. That is a key difference from LDA. (SVD software may flip the sign of a whole component; here component 1 was flipped to be positive, which changes nothing.)

Synonyms and polysemy in LSA (slide 42). Synonyms “might load heavily on the same topic”: good = [10 1 …] and fine = [10 1 …] in \(L\). A polysemous word has “associations with multiple topics”: check = [5 5 …].

Part 2 — LDA, the probabilistic topic model

The generative story (slide 52). LDA imagines each document was written like this:

  1. “Pick the overall theme of an article by randomly giving it a distribution over topics.”
  2. For each word:
    • 2.1 “From the topic distribution chosen in 1., randomly pick one topic”;
    • 2.2 “Given that topic, randomly choose a word from this topic.”

Repeating step 2 gives one document made of several topics with different weights; repeating 1 and 2 gives a corpus. Estimation runs this story backwards: “Assign words to topics and assign topics to documents such that the fit of the Document-term matrix becomes as good as possible” (slide 48).

The formula, symbol by symbol (slide 47).

In words: each document’s word counts are drawn at random from one list of word chances, made by blending the topics’ word lists using the document’s own topic shares.

\[\mathbf{c}_i \sim MN(\mathbf{q}_i, m_i), \qquad \mathbf{q}_i = v_{i1}\boldsymbol\theta_1 + v_{i2}\boldsymbol\theta_2 + \dots v_{ik}\boldsymbol\theta_k = \mathbf{v}_i\boldsymbol\Theta\]

  • \(\mathbf{c}_i\) = the word counts of document \(i\) (its DTM row).
  • \(MN(\cdot)\) = the multinomial distribution: \(m_i\) independent draws of a word from the vocabulary, with probabilities \(\mathbf{q}_i\).
  • \(m_i = \sum_j c_{ij}\) = document length.
  • \(\mathbf{q}_i\) = document \(i\)’s probability of each word.
  • \(v_{il}\) = share of document \(i\) devoted to topic \(l\); \(\sum_{l} v_{il} = 1\) (topic weights).
  • \(\boldsymbol\theta_l\) = topic \(l\): a probability vector (a list of chances that add up to 1) over all \(p\) words; \(\sum_{j} \theta_{lj} = 1\).

Read aloud: “each document’s words are drawn from a blend of the topics’ word distributions, blended with that document’s topic weights.” Slide 47: “a probabilistic topic model is just a factor model for multinomial data!” The topic weights \(V\) play the role of LSA’s factors \(F\), and the topics \(\Theta'\) (all topic word-lists side by side, one column per topic) play the role of LSA’s loadings \(L\), “but, here, the matrix entries are probabilities”: each row of \(V\) sums to one and each column of \(\Theta'\) sums to one (slide 48).

A tiny worked example (LDA mixing). Two topics over the same four words (toy numbers). Rows = topics; columns = word probabilities (each row sums to 1).
