Topic stock market goal match
\(\theta_1\) finance 0.50 0.40 0.05 0.05
\(\theta_2\) football 0.05 0.05 0.50 0.40

A document that is 80% finance, 20% football (\(\mathbf v_i = (0.8, 0.2)\)) has word probabilities \(\mathbf q_i = 0.8\,\theta_1 + 0.2\,\theta_2\):

stock market goal match
\(\mathbf q_i\) 0.41 0.33 0.14 0.12

By hand for “stock”: \(0.8\times0.50 + 0.2\times0.05 = 0.40 + 0.01 = 0.41\). The four numbers sum to 1, as probabilities must.

The multinomial building block (slide 46). Urn example: 8 “true”, 3 “false”, 9 “maybe” balls; draw 6 with replacement (each ball goes back after it is drawn). \(P(2\text{ true}, 1\text{ false}, 3\text{ maybe}) = \frac{6!}{2!\,1!\,3!}(8/20)^2(3/20)^1(9/20)^3 = 60\times0.16\times0.15\times0.091125 \approx 0.131\). (The “!” is a factorial: \(6! = 720\), \(2! = 2\), \(3! = 6\), so \(\frac{6!}{2!\,1!\,3!} = 720/12 = 60\) is the number of different orders in which those balls can come out.) (The slide’s formula is missing the “=” sign and uses commas where products are meant; write it with products.) Slide 58: with \(k>2\) outcomes and \(n=1\) trial (one single draw, like picking one word) it is the categorical distribution, “the one we typically use in NLP”.

Dirichlet priors and sparsity (slide 57). LDA puts a Dirichlet prior (a way of drawing random lists of shares that add up to 1, used as the starting assumption) on the topic weights and on the topics. The motivation is sparsity: “Small number of high probability topics in each document, and small number of words with high probability in each topic.”

  • \(Dir(\alpha)\) = prior on \(v_i\) (the document’s topic weights): “lower values of α will give fewer topics a high probability in each document”.
  • \(Dir(\beta)\) = prior on \(\theta_l\) (the topics): “lower values of β will give fewer words higher probability in the topic distributions”.
  • Benchmarks (this β is LDA’s topic setting, not the regression coefficient of Chapter 8): “β = 0.01 and α = 50/k”; the lecturer has used “β = 200/N and α = 50/k” (N is not defined on the slide).

Illustration (numpy draws from a 3-topic Dirichlet, seed 1; general illustration, not from the slides): with α = 0.1 the draws were (0.00, 1.00, 0.00), (0.06, 0.00, 0.94), (0.99, 0.00, 0.00) — each document dominated by one topic. With α = 10 they were (0.29, 0.29, 0.43), (0.21, 0.36, 0.44), (0.18, 0.49, 0.33) — even mixtures.

The Dirichlet is the multivariate (many-outcome) version of the Beta distribution (a random share between 0 and 1 for two outcomes) and the “conjugate prior” of the multinomial (it fits the multinomial so neatly that the maths stays easy), which makes Bayesian estimation (combining a prior with the data) convenient (slide 58). Estimation: variational Bayes (Blei et al. 2003) or Gibbs sampling (Griffiths and Steyvers 2004) (slide 53) — two step-by-step computer methods that start from a guess and improve it many times [Not in course files — general knowledge: this description of the two methods]. LDA is popular because it classifies text “in much the same manner as humans would do” (Chang et al. 2009).

Notation warning: the plate diagram (a box-and-arrow picture of the LDA story) on slide 56 calls the document–topic distribution \(\theta_m\) and the topic–word distribution \(\varphi_k\). Slides 47 and 57 call them \(v_i\) and \(\theta_l\). In the exam, use the slide-47 notation and say what each symbol means.

Practical issues: choosing K and seed instability

  • How many topics? “Ad-hoc or based in out-of-sample testing (marginal likelihood)! For LSA one can look at the variance explained (λ)” (slide 59). (Ad hoc = chosen by judgement; out-of-sample testing = checking how well the model explains texts it did not see.)
  • Seed instability (Notebook 2, Q4). LDA “starts from a random guess (SEED) and improves it”. The notebook fits LDA twice with different seeds and matches each topic from run 1 to its most similar topic in run 2 by the cosine similarity of their word weights (a score of how alike two lists of numbers are; 1 = identical). Takeaway: “LDA topics depend on the seed and on K. Topics that reappear across runs deserve more trust than those that do not.” Before using topics as data (as Hansen et al. 2018 do to study FOMC deliberation, slide 60; FOMC = the US central bank’s interest-rate committee [Not in course files — general knowledge]), show that results do not hinge on one lucky seed.
  • Practical day 1 (Gensim LDA on State of the Union speeches; Gensim is a Python toolbox for topic models, and passes is how many times it goes through all the speeches). LdaModel(corpus=corpus, id2word=dictionary, num_topics=6, passes=5, random_state=42) on 72 speeches × 6,241 terms (after filter_extremes(no_below=3, no_above=0.8), Gensim’s version of min_df/max_df). Saved output: readable themes such as Cold War/Europe (soviet, europe…), budget (spending, deficit, taxes…) and Iraq/terror (weapons, saddam, hussein…). Most speeches got topic shares near 0 or 1 (e.g. Truman_1946–1949 ≈ 1.000 on one topic), so the mixtures were very “peaky” and tracked era vocabulary (“tonight” shows up in 4 topics). Quotable lines: “We supply word counts, not the TF-IDF matrix. We choose the number of topics; the model does not discover a uniquely correct number”; “Names are your interpretations; they are not labels supplied by LDA”; “A fixed seed makes one run reproducible; it does not establish that the topics are stable.” Topic numbers can also change between seeds, so compare words and documents, not “Topic 1”.
  • Extensions: dynamic, supervised and correlated topic models (slide 59).

Reading the course code

vec = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_df=MAX_DF, min_df=5)
X = vec.fit_transform(texts)
run_a = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=N_TOPICS, random_state=SEED).fit(X)
run_b = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=N_TOPICS, random_state=SEED+1).fit(X)
match = cosine_similarity(run_a.components_, run_b.components_).max(axis=1)

(Simplified from Notebook 2, cells 22–23.)

  • Line 1: count words, dropping stop words, words in more than MAX_DF = 90% of speeches (too common) and words in fewer than 5 speeches. LDA uses raw counts, not tf-idf (practical day 1: “We supply word counts, not the TF-IDF matrix”), which fits its multinomial model of counts.
  • Line 2: build the DTM for post-1945 speeches.
  • Lines 3–4: fit LDA with K = N_TOPICS (default 6) topics, twice, with two different random seeds.
  • Line 5: components_ holds each topic’s word weights (one row per topic). For each run-A topic, find the best-matching run-B topic by cosine similarity.

No outputs are saved. When run, it would show a best-match score per topic plus the average, and a table of the top 8 words per topic. The notebook asks whether the topics with a match below about 0.8 are the hard-to-name ones (cell 24).

Comparison table: SVD/LSA vs LDA

Rows = feature; columns = the two methods.

Feature LSA (via SVD/PCA) LDA
What it is Matrix decomposition: PCA applied to the DTM (slide 35) Probabilistic generative model: factor model for multinomial data + Dirichlet prior (slides 47, 53)
Slide label \(f(c_i\mid v_i)\) — a function \(p(c_i\mid v_i)\) — a probability model
Document side Factors \(F = U_{1:K}S_{1:K}\) (\(n\times K\)), any real numbers Topic weights \(V\) (\(n\times K\)), probabilities, each row sums to 1
Word side Loadings \(L = V_{1:K}\) (\(p\times K\)), any real numbers Topics \(\Theta'\) (\(p\times K\)), probabilities, each column sums to 1
Topics are Orthogonal components, ordered by variance explained Distributions over words; all words in all topics with different probability
Generative story? No — “not a probabilistic model … not seen as a plausible generative model for text” (slide 43) Yes — pick topic mix, then for each word pick topic, then word (slide 52)
Sparsity control None built in Dirichlet α (topics per document) and β (words per topic)
Estimation SVD — exact, one answer Variational Bayes or Gibbs sampling — iterative, starts from a random seed, so results can change with the seed
Choosing K Variance explained \(\lambda_l = s_l^2/(n-1)\) Ad hoc or out-of-sample marginal likelihood
Synonyms / polysemy Synonyms load on the same component; a polysemous word loads on several (slide 42) Same idea: a word can have high probability in several topics
Shared ground Both are unsupervised; both explain the \(n\times p\) DTM with \(K \ll p\) latent factors; both treat a topic as a cluster of words and a document as a mix of topics ← same

How this shows up on the exam

  • 2025 Q2(d), worth 5 points, asked: “what is meant by topic models? Mention at least two methods for estimating topics and the underlying intuition and difference/similarity of these methods.”

  • Likely True/False statements:

    • “LSA is a probabilistic generative model” → False. LSA is table maths with no chance-based story of how words get written (slide 43).
    • “In LDA each document’s topic weights sum to one” → True. Each document’s topic mix is a set of shares, like 70% sport + 30% money (slide 48).
    • “Lower α in LDA gives each document fewer dominant topics” → True. α is the dial for how spread out a document’s topics are (slide 57).
    • “LDA always gives the same topics regardless of the random seed” → False. The random seed is the starting point of the computer’s random guessing; a different start can give different topics (Notebook 2).

  • In the reflection question (the open question about customer survey answers), LDA is a strong method for “what do customers talk about”. Name two pitfalls: choosing K (the number of topics, which you must pick yourself) and seed instability (topics can change from run to run).

What a top-grade answer must include

For Q2(d), cover these four parts:

  1. The idea. Topics are clusters of words that tend to appear together. Each document is a mix of topics with different weights. It is unsupervised (no answers needed). It summarises the big word-count table (\(n\times p\) DTM: \(n\) documents by \(p\) words) with a small number of topics (\(K \ll p\), far fewer topics than words).
  2. LSA. It runs SVD/PCA (a standard way to break a table into a few main patterns) on the DTM: \(C \approx U_K S_K V_K'\), i.e. the table is roughly rebuilt from \(K\) patterns. This gives factors \(F\) (a documents × topics table) and loadings \(L\) (a words × topics table). The values can be any number, even negative, and there are no probabilities.
  3. LDA. It is probabilistic. A topic is a set of chances over words; a document is a set of chances over topics (so the rows/columns add up to 1). It tells a story of how each word is generated. Dirichlet priors (settings that push the model towards few topics per document and few main words per topic) give sparsity.
  4. One clear sentence on how they differ and how they are alike: “Both decompose the DTM into document–topic and topic–word parts; LSA does it as a matrix factorisation, LDA as a probability model.”

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Naming the methods without the intuition: topics = clusters of words, documents = mixtures of topics.
  • Calling LSA probabilistic.
  • Saying LDA needs labelled data (texts with answers). It does not; it is unsupervised.
  • Mixing up α (the document–topic dial: how many topics per document) and β (the topic–word dial: how many main words per topic).
  • Forgetting that \(K\) (the number of topics) must be chosen by you, and that LDA results depend on the seed (the random starting point).
  • Feeding tf-idf (re-weighted word scores) into LDA. LDA models plain word counts.

Key terms to use

  • topic model (finds themes in texts without answers)
  • latent topics (hidden themes, never observed directly)
  • unsupervised (no answers or labels needed)
  • dimension reduction (\(K \ll p\)) (summarise many words with few topics)
  • Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) (topic model built on table maths)
  • PCA (finds the few main patterns in a table)
  • Singular Value Decomposition \(C = USV'\) (splits the table into three simpler tables)
  • truncation (keep only the \(K\) biggest patterns)
  • factors \(F\) (each document’s score on each topic)
  • loadings \(L\) (each word’s weight in each topic)
  • variance explained (how much of the table a pattern captures)
  • Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (topic model built on chances)
  • generative model (a story of how the words were written)
  • multinomial distribution (chances for drawing one item from many)
  • topic weights \(v_i\) (document \(i\)’s mix of topics)
  • topic–word distribution \(\theta_l\) (chances of each word in topic \(l\))
  • Dirichlet prior α and β (dials for how concentrated the mixes are)
  • sparsity (only a few topics or words dominate)
  • Gibbs sampling (step-by-step random guessing that estimates LDA)
  • number of topics \(K\) (how many topics you ask for)
  • random seed (the starting point of the random guessing)
  • polysemy (one word, several meanings)
  • synonyms (different words, same meaning)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “LSA is not a probabilistic model and is not seen as a plausible generative model for text.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LSA is a topic model that breaks the word-count table into smaller tables. A “probabilistic model” works with chances. A “plausible generative model” is a believable story of how each word in a text came to be written. The statement says LSA is neither of these.

    Answer: True. Why: LSA is pure table maths. Its numbers can be any value, even negative, so they cannot be chances, and they tell no story of how words were written. It is like a summary of a book’s word list, not a story of how the author wrote it. (Source: slide 43.)

  2. T/F: “In LDA, each row of the document–topic matrix sums to one.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LDA is the chance-based topic model. The document–topic matrix is a table with one row per document and one column per topic, showing how much of each topic is in each document. The statement says the numbers in each row add up to 1.

    Answer: True. Why: Each row is a document’s topic mix written as shares, like a pie chart: 0.7 sport + 0.3 money = 1. The slices of one pie always make a whole pie. (Source: slide 48.)

  3. T/F: “In LDA, a higher α gives each document fewer high-probability topics.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: α is a dial in LDA that controls how spread out each document’s topic mix is. “Fewer high-probability topics” means each document is mostly about one or two topics. The statement says turning α up makes documents more focused.

    Answer: False. Why: It is the other way round. A lower α gives more sparsity: each document is dominated by a few topics. A higher α spreads each document over many topics. Think of α as how much a cook mixes the ingredients: low α gives a dish with one or two main flavours, high α gives a stew of everything. (Source: slide 57.)

  4. T/F: “Running LDA twice with different random seeds always gives exactly the same topics.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LDA finds topics by guessing randomly and improving step by step. The random seed is the starting point of that random guessing. The statement says changing the starting point never changes the topics.

    Answer: False. Why: Different starting points can lead to different topics, and so can a different number of topics (K). Like two people sorting the same pile of photos: they may end up with slightly different piles. So trust the topics that show up again and again across runs. (Source: Notebook 2 cells 21, 31.)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): “What is a topic model? Describe two methods and how they differ.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Say what topic models do, then explain LSA and LDA and the difference between them.

    Model answer: A topic model is an unsupervised method that explains what texts are about: topics are clusters of words that tend to occur together, and each document is a mixture of topics with different weights, so the large \(n\times p\) document-term matrix is summarised by \(K \ll p\) latent factors. LSA applies the singular value decomposition \(C = USV'\) to the DTM and keeps the \(K\) largest components, giving document factors \(F = U_KS_K\) and word loadings \(L = V_K\); it is a pure matrix decomposition, with unrestricted values and no probabilistic story. LDA is a probabilistic generative model: each document draws a distribution over topics, and each word is drawn by first picking a topic and then a word from that topic’s word distribution, with Dirichlet priors encouraging sparsity. So both decompose the DTM into document–topic and topic–word parts, but in LDA these are probabilities (rows/columns sum to one), which makes it a more plausible model of how text is generated.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: A topic model finds themes without any answers: a topic is a group of words that often appear together, and each document is a blend of a few topics. LSA does this with table maths: it breaks the big word-count table into a few main patterns and keeps the biggest ones, giving a score for each document and a weight for each word. LDA instead tells a chance-based story: each document has a topic mix, and every word is written by first picking a topic, then picking a word from that topic. Both end up with “documents → topics” and “topics → words”, but only LDA’s numbers are real shares that add up to one.

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 30–59; Interactive Notebook 2 cells 21–24, 31; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 16–22 (LDA section, from the Part A notes); 2025 exam evaluation guideline Q2(d).

Part III — Learning from prediction: n-grams, neural networks and word embeddings

11. Language models from counting: n-grams, bigram probabilities, smoothing, sampling, temperature, loss and perplexity

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — not asked in 2025, but taught in 2026 and perfect material for True/False and a small calculation.

Start from zero

The problem. You type “see you” on your phone, and the keyboard offers “tomorrow” or “soon”. Nobody wrote a rule for every sentence, so how does it know? Earlier in the course, text was turned into a table of word counts: one row per document, one column per word, and each cell says how often that word shows up. That table throws away the order of the words, so it can’t tell you what comes next. This chapter builds the smallest possible machine that guesses the next letter, using nothing but counting. The big chatbots run on the same “guess the next piece” idea, only much bigger.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Collect a pile of example text. In the course, that’s a long list of first names.
  2. Go through it and write down every pair of neighbouring letters: “e then m”, “m then m”, and so on. Also mark where each name starts and ends, so the machine learns which letters like to begin or finish a name.
  3. Count how often each pair shows up. Put the counts in a grid: one row for “the letter I’m on”, one column for “the letter that came next”.
  4. Turn each row into chances. Divide every count in a row by that row’s total. Now each row says: “after this letter, here’s how likely each next letter is”.
  5. Fix the zeros. A pair you never saw gets a chance of zero, which is too harsh. So pretend you saw every pair one extra time. This is called smoothing.
  6. To write a new name: start at “start”, roll a loaded dice that follows that row’s chances, write down the letter you get, jump to that letter’s row, and roll again. Stop when you roll “end”. A “temperature” knob makes the dice more cautious or more adventurous.
  7. To grade the machine: walk through real names, and at each step look at the chance it gave to the letter that really came next. Squash all of that into one “wrongness” score, the loss. From the loss you get perplexity: roughly how many letters the machine was torn between at each step. Lower is better.

A tiny example by hand. Our whole corpus is the word “hello” written twice: “hello hello”. (This is the chapter’s own example, done slowly.)

Step A: list the pairs. One “hello”, with a start mark in front and an end mark behind, gives six neighbour pairs: start→h, h→e, e→l, l→l, l→o, o→end. We have two copies, so we see each pair 2 times.

Step B: the count grid. Rows = the letter you’re on. Columns = the letter that came next. Each cell = how many times that happened. The last column adds up the row.

On ↓ / Next → h e l o <end> Row total
<start> 2 0 0 0 0 2
h 0 2 0 0 0 2
e 0 0 2 0 0 2
l 0 0 2 2 0 4
o 0 0 0 0 2 2

Let’s work out one cell out loud: row l, column o. “l then o” happened once in each “hello”, so 2 times. The l row’s total is 4, because l is followed by something four times (twice by another l, twice by o). So the chance of o after l is 2 out of 4 = 0.5. The chance of l after l is also 2/4 = 0.5. After h, e came 2 times out of 2, so its chance is 2/2 = 1: certain.

Step C: write a new word. Start→h is certain, h→e is certain, e→l is certain. At l, it’s a coin flip: half the time o, half the time another l. So the machine might write “helo” (chance 0.5), “hello” (0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25) or “helllo” (0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125). It only remembers one letter back, so it can’t keep track of how many l’s it has already written. It even rates “helo” as more likely than “hello”.

Step D: smoothing. “q after h” never happened, so its chance is 0 out of 2 = 0. Smoothing adds a pretend count of 1 to every cell. In the course’s full grid there are 28 possible characters, so the h row gains 28 pretend counts and its total grows from 2 to 30. Now q after h = (0 + 1)/30 ≈ 0.033, and e after h = (2 + 1)/30 = 0.10.

Step E: grade it. Score the word “hello” with the unsmoothed grid. The chances of each real next letter are 1, 1, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 1. Multiplied together: 0.25. Now take the log of each one: the log of 1 is 0, and the log of 0.5 is about −0.693. Add them up: −0.693 + −0.693 = −1.386. Divide by the 6 steps and drop the minus sign: loss = 1.386 / 6 = 0.231. Perplexity = \(e^{0.231}\) ≈ 1.26. So the machine is torn between about 1.26 letters per step: nearly sure every time. A machine that guesses blindly among 27 characters has perplexity 27.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: easy to build and easy to understand. You can check every number by hand.
  • Good: it already beats blind guessing by a lot (perplexity 11.6 against 27 on the names).
  • Breaks: it only looks one letter back, so it happily writes “helllo”. Looking further back makes the grid explode: with 27 characters, two letters of memory already needs 27 × 27 = 729 rows [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Breaks: a pair it never saw gets chance zero, and that makes the loss endless, unless you smooth.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • language model: a machine that guesses what comes next in a text. Your phone’s autocomplete is a small one.
  • token: one small piece of text the model works with. It can be a letter, a word, or a piece of a word.
  • character / character-level: a character is a single letter or symbol. A character-level model guesses one letter at a time instead of one word at a time.
  • sub-word token: a piece of a word, such as “play” and “ing” in “playing”. Big chatbots use about 100,000 such pieces.
  • vocabulary: the full list of tokens the model knows. Here: 26 letters plus start and end.
  • next-token prediction: guessing the next piece of text from the pieces before it, like finishing a friend’s sentence.
  • LLM (large language model): a very big next-token guesser, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a bag of loose words. You count each word and ignore the order. That’s what gives the word-count table (rows = documents, columns = words).
  • corpus / dataset: the pile of example text you learn from. In the course: 32,033 first names.
  • training: the learning step, where the model looks at examples and sets its numbers. For this model, training means counting.
  • probability (chance): a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0 = never, 1 = certain, 0.5 = half the time, like heads on a coin.
  • conditional probability: a chance worked out once you already know something. “The chance of e, given that we saw h a moment ago.” The bar “|” in \(P(e \mid h)\) is read “given”.
  • n-gram: a run of n tokens in a row. An n-gram model guesses the next token from the n − 1 tokens before it.
  • bigram: two neighbouring tokens, like “h then e”. A bigram model looks back one token.
  • trigram: three neighbouring tokens. A trigram model looks back two tokens.
  • start and end markers (<start>, <end>, <S>, <E>, .): pretend characters put before and after each word, so the model learns which letters begin and end names.
  • matrix / count matrix: a grid of numbers with rows and columns. The count matrix N has one row per current letter, one column per next letter, and each cell counts how often that pair appeared.
  • row total / normalise: add up a row, then divide every cell by that total, so the row adds up to 1. “Renormalise” means doing it again after the numbers changed.
  • probability distribution: a list of chances for every possible outcome that adds up to 1. Like a weather forecast: 70% dry, 20% rain, 10% snow.
  • smoothing / add-one (Laplace) smoothing: pretending you saw every pair one extra time, so nothing gets a chance of exactly zero. Like giving every new restaurant one free review so it isn’t marked “impossible”.
  • sampling: picking the next letter at random, weighted by the chances, like rolling a loaded dice.
  • deterministic: always giving the same answer for the same starting point. The opposite of random.
  • greedy decoding: always picking the most likely next letter, never rolling the dice.
  • temperature (T): a knob that reshapes the chances before you roll. Below 1 = cautious, the favourite wins more often. Above 1 = adventurous, rare letters get more of a chance.
  • proportional to (∝): “goes up and down together with”. In the temperature formula: work out the powers first, then rescale so they add up to 1.
  • power / exponent: how many times you multiply a number by itself. \(0.5^2 = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). A power of 1/2 means the square root.
  • e: a fixed number, about 2.718, that shows up all over maths. \(e^{x}\) means “e to the power x”.
  • log (logarithm), ln: the reverse of a power. ln asks “e to what power gives this number?” So ln 1 = 0 and ln 0.5 ≈ −0.693. The log of a number below 1 is negative. \(\log_2\) asks the same question with 2 instead of e.
  • likelihood: the chance the model gave to the real text, found by multiplying the chances of each real next letter. For “hello” in our example: 0.25.
  • log-likelihood (ℓ): the sum of the logs of those chances. Adding logs carries the same information as multiplying the chances, but avoids super-tiny numbers.
  • negative log-likelihood: the log-likelihood with its sign flipped, so it becomes a positive “surprise” score. Lower = less surprised.
  • loss / loss function: one number that says how wrong the model is. Here it’s the average negative log-likelihood per step. Training tries to make it small.
  • minimise / maximise: make as small as possible / make as large as possible.
  • −∞ (minus infinity): “endlessly negative”. The log of 0 is −∞, so a single zero chance makes the loss endless.
  • sum (Σ): the sign for “add all of these up”.
  • perplexity: e to the power of the loss. Roughly “how many letters the model is torn between at each step”. 27 = clueless, 1 = always sure.
  • uniform guessing (baseline): giving each of the 27 characters the same chance, 1/27. It’s the “knows nothing” yardstick you compare against.
  • context / context length: the text the model looks at before it guesses. A bigram’s context is 1 letter; the MLP’s is 5 letters.
  • neural network: a machine of many adjustable number-dials that learns from examples (next chapter).
  • MLP: short for “multi-layer perceptron” [Not in course files — general knowledge]: a neural network with at least one hidden middle layer (next chapter).
  • self-supervised: learning where the text gives its own answers. The right next letter is already sitting in the text, so no human has to label anything.
  • notebook / Python / PyTorch (torch): a notebook is a document that mixes code and text; Python is the programming language; PyTorch is a Python toolkit for building this kind of model.
  • torch.multinomial: the PyTorch command that rolls the loaded dice: it draws random picks according to the chances you give it.

The idea in plain words

Until Lecture 4, the course treated every word in a text as if it had nothing to do with its neighbours (the bag-of-words idea: count each word, ignore the order). Real language does not work like that. After “thank” comes “you” far more often than “banana”.

A language model is a machine that guesses what comes next. The smallest possible one does this by counting: look at a lot of text, count how often each letter follows each other letter, and turn those counts into probabilities. To write new text, start at the beginning, pick a next letter at random using those probabilities, then pick the next one, and so on.

The lecture’s big message: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are, “at their core, next-token predictors trained on trillions of tokens. Today we build the smallest possible one” (slide 2). In plain words: these chatbots are machines that guess the next small piece of text, after reading an enormous amount of text.

Analogy Think of the autocomplete on your phone. After you type “see you”, it offers “tomorrow” or “soon” because it has seen those follow “see you” many times. A bigram model is a very simple autocomplete that only looks at the one letter you just typed.

Source: L4 slides 2–3; Part 1 notebook cell 0.

The exam definition

  • Next-token prediction: “predicting the next word or token in a sequence given the previous tokens.” Models such as GPT are trained this way (L4 slide 2).
  • n-gram model: “predicts the next token by calculating the most likely token based on the previous \(n-1\) tokens” (slide 2). So a bigram (\(n = 2\)) looks back one token; a trigram looks back two.
  • Bigram: “two consecutive characters that appear together in a text” (slide 4). The course model is a bigram character-level language model: tokens are single letters (slide 3).
  • Tokens vs characters: “Real LLMs use sub-word tokens (a vocabulary of ∼100k pieces). We use single characters (26 letters + start/end) so the whole model fits on one screen” (slide 3). (Sub-word tokens are pieces of words; real chatbots work with those, the course model works with single letters.)
  • Start and end markers count as characters too. “hello” gives the bigrams h→e, e→l, l→l, l→o, plus <start>→h and o→<end> = 6 bigrams (slide 4).
  • Smoothing: unseen bigrams get probability zero. “We fix this with smoothing (add a ‘fake’ count of 1 to every bigram)” = add-one (Laplace) smoothing (slide 6; notebook cell 27).
  • Temperature: “the ‘creativity’ setting in LLM interfaces” (slide 7). It reshapes the probabilities before sampling (notebook cell 38).
  • Loss: the average negative log-likelihood per character transition (notebook cell 41). (In plain words: how surprised the model was by each real next letter, averaged over all steps.)
  • Perplexity \(= e^{\text{Loss}}\): “roughly how many characters the model is ‘choosing between’ at each step” (slide 9).

Source: L4 slides 2–9; Part 1 cells 27, 38, 41–42.

A tiny worked example

Step 1 — the “hello hello” corpus (L4 slide 6). Treat it as two words, each with a start and an end marker. Counting every bigram (my count with python, matching the slide):

Bigram (previous → next) Count
<start> → h 2
h → e 2
e → l 2
l → l 2
l → o 2
o → <end> 2

How often each letter appears as the first letter of a bigram: h = 2, e = 2, l = 4, o = 2.

Now the slide’s calculation:

In words: the chance that e comes next after h is the number of times “h then e” appeared, divided by the number of times h appeared as a first letter.

\[P(e \mid h) = \frac{\text{count}(h, e)}{\text{count}(h)} = \frac{2}{2} = 1.0\]

“Whenever ‘h’ appears, it is always followed by ‘e’” (slide 6). Two more by hand: \(P(l \mid l) = 2/4 = 0.5\) and \(P(o \mid l) = 2/4 = 0.5\). The letter l is followed by another l half the time and by o half the time.

And the problem case from the slide: \(P(q \mid h) = 0/2 = 0\). “Unseen bigrams get probability zero.”

Step 2 — add-one smoothing on the same corpus. Add 1 to every cell of the count table. In the course notebook the table is 28 × 28 (26 letters + start + end, cell 22), so the row for h gets 28 extra fake counts. My illustration (computed in python, not on a slide):

  • \(P(e \mid h) = (2 + 1)/(2 + 28) = 3/30 = 0.10\)
  • \(P(q \mid h) = (0 + 1)/(2 + 28) = 1/30 \approx 0.033\) — no longer zero.

Notice how much smoothing changes things when the corpus is tiny. On 32,033 names the counts are large, so the fake 1s matter much less.

Step 3 — the names dataset (Part 1 notebook). names.txt holds 32,033 lowercase first names (emma, olivia, ava, …, zzyzx), only the letters a–z, 2 to 15 letters long. For “emma” the notebook prints the bigrams <S> e, e m, m m, m a, a <E> — 5 bigrams (cell 12). All counts go into a 28 × 28 count matrix N: rows = the current character (<S>, a, …, z), columns = the next character (a, …, z, <E>) (cells 20, 22). Each row is divided by its row total to give the probability matrix P. The notebook’s one written-out result: the most likely first letter is a, with \(P(\langle S \rangle \to a) = 0.14\) (cell 30).

Step 4 — loss and perplexity by hand. Score the word “hello” with the model trained on “hello hello” (my illustration, computed in python). The chain of probabilities is

Transition <start>→h h→e e→l l→l l→o o→<end>
Probability 1 1 1 0.5 0.5 1
  • Likelihood = product = \(1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 1 = 0.25\).
  • Log-likelihood \(\ell = \ln 0.25 = -1.386\).
  • Number of transitions \(n = 6\), so Loss \(= -\ell/n = 1.386/6 = 0.231\).
  • Perplexity \(= e^{0.231} = 1.26\). The model is almost never unsure: it only hesitates after l.

Step 5 — the uniform baseline (notebook cell 42, slide 9). A model that guesses each of 27 characters with equal probability \(1/27\) gives every transition loss \(-\ln(1/27) = \ln 27 = 3.2958 \approx 3.30\) (checked in python). Perplexity \(= e^{3.30} = 27\): it is “choosing between” all 27 characters.

Step 6 — the comparison table (L4 slide 9; Part 2 cell 33). Rows = models; columns = how much previous text each model sees, its loss, and its perplexity.

Model Context (letters looked back) Loss Perplexity
Uniform guessing none 3.30 27
Count-based bigram (Part 1) 1 character 2.45 11.6
Neural network bigram (Part 2) 1 character 2.46 11.7
MLP (Part 3) 5 characters 2.22 9.2

Check (python): \(e^{2.45} = 11.59\), \(e^{2.46} = 11.70\), \(e^{2.22} = 9.21\). All match. How to read it: counting and the neural net learn the same thing (2.45 vs 2.46). The real gain comes from more context (MLP, 5 letters: 2.22). “The neural network learns the same thing as counting, but it scales: we can give it more context without the table exploding” (slide 9).

Source: L4 slides 4, 6, 9; Part 1 cells 12, 20–22, 27, 30, 42; Part 2 cell 33.

The formula, symbol by symbol

1. Bigram probability (L4 slide 5)

In words: to get the chance of a next letter, count how often that pair appeared, and divide by how often the first letter appeared at the start of any pair.

\[P(c_n \mid c_{n-1}) = \frac{\text{count}(c_{n-1}, c_n)}{\text{count}(c_{n-1})}\]

  • \(c_n\) = the next character, the one we want to predict.
  • \(c_{n-1}\) = the character just before it.
  • \(P(c_n \mid c_{n-1})\) = the probability of \(c_n\) given that we just saw \(c_{n-1}\) (the bar “\(\mid\)” reads “given”).
  • \(\text{count}(c_{n-1}, c_n)\) = “the number of times the pair of characters \((c_{n-1}, c_n)\) appears in the training corpus.”
  • \(\text{count}(c_{n-1})\) = “the total number of times the character \(c_{n-1}\) appears as the first character of any bigram.”

Read aloud: “The chance that \(c_n\) comes next, given \(c_{n-1}\), is how often the pair appeared, divided by how often \(c_{n-1}\) appeared as a first letter.”

2. Temperature (Part 1 cell 38)

In words: raise every chance to the power “one divided by the temperature”, then rescale the results so they add up to 1 again.

\[P_T(c) \propto P(c)^{1/T}\]

  • \(P(c)\) = the model’s probability for character \(c\).
  • \(T\) = temperature. \(\propto\) = “proportional to”: after raising to the power \(1/T\), divide by the total so the numbers sum to 1 again.
  • \(T < 1\): sharper, the likely characters dominate (safer, more repetitive). \(T = 1\): the model as estimated. \(T > 1\): flatter, rare characters more likely (more random). \(T \to 0\): always pick the top character (greedy decoding).

Example (my illustration, python): start with \(P = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\). With \(T = 0.5\) it becomes \((0.66, 0.24, 0.11)\), sharper. With \(T = 2\) it becomes \((0.42, 0.32, 0.26)\), flatter.

3. Log-likelihood and loss (Part 1 cell 41)

In words: add up the logs of the chances the model gave to every real next letter in every word (that total is ℓ), then divide by the number of steps and flip the sign to get the loss.

\[\ell \;=\; \sum_{w\in D}\;\sum_{t=0}^{T_w} \log P(c_{t+1}\mid c_t) \qquad\qquad \text{Loss function} = -\frac{\ell}{n}\]

  • \(D\) = the dataset; \(w\) = one word in it.
  • \(t\) = position inside the word; \(T_w\) = the last transition in word \(w\) (here \(T\) is a length, not the temperature).
  • \(\log P(c_{t+1}\mid c_t)\) = log of the probability the model gave to the letter that really came next.
  • \(\ell\) = the sum of all these logs = the log-likelihood.
  • \(n\) = the total number of character transitions.

Read aloud: “Add up the log-probabilities of every real next letter, divide by how many there were, and flip the sign.” Logs are used because they turn a product into a sum and avoid tiny numbers that a computer rounds to zero (cell 41). The minus sign makes it something to minimise (“we want to maximize the log likelihood but minimize the loss”).

4. Perplexity (Part 1 cell 42; L4 slide 9)

In words: take e (about 2.718) to the power of the loss; the answer is roughly how many letters the model is torn between at each step.

\[\text{Perplexity} = e^{\text{Loss}}\]

Read aloud: “Perplexity is e to the power of the loss; it says roughly how many characters the model is choosing between at each step.” Lower is better.

Source: L4 slides 5, 9; Part 1 cells 38, 41–42.

Reading the course code

Turning counts into probabilities with smoothing (Part 1, cell 27):

P = (N+1).float()            # Add-one (Laplace) smoothing
P /= P.sum(1, keepdim=True)
  • Line 1 adds a fake count of 1 to every cell of the 28 × 28 count matrix N, so no bigram is ever 0.
  • Line 2 divides every row by its row total. Each row now sums to 1: it is the probability distribution of the next letter.

Sampling instead of always choosing the top letter (cells 30–37): torch.multinomial(P[0], 10, replacement=True) (the PyTorch “loaded dice” command) draws 10 first letters at random, in proportion to their probabilities. “We don’t want our model to be deterministic.” Temperature in code (cell 39): P_T = P ** (1 / T), then rows are renormalised.

The loss loop (cell 43) adds torch.log(P[ix1, ix2]) over all transitions, then computes -log_likelihood/n and torch.exp(...) for perplexity. The notebook has no saved outputs; slide 9 reports the result: loss ≈ 2.45, perplexity ≈ 11.6. Cell 45 shows that without smoothing the made-up name “jq” gets log-likelihood \(-\infty\), because \(\log(0) = -\infty\) (cell 44).

Exam boxes

How this shows up on the exam This topic was not asked in 2025. But it is in the 2026 slides, so we expect it as True/False or short questions (our prediction, see _exam_prep_work/exam_blueprint.md). The topics: bigram chances (the chance of the next letter given the one before), smoothing (adding pretend counts so nothing is zero), softmax (turning scores into chances), loss and perplexity (how wrong the model is), and temperature (the cautious/adventurous knob).

Typical True/False traps:

  • “A bigram conditions on the previous two tokens.” False. “Conditions on” means “looks at before guessing”, and a bigram looks back only one piece.
  • “The n-gram model treats tokens as independent.” False. Independent would mean each piece has nothing to do with the one before. The whole point is that it uses the one before.
  • “Higher temperature makes output more predictable.” False. Turning the knob up makes it more random, not less.

You might also get a small sum, like the chance of e after h (\(P(e \mid h)\)) = 2/2. The topic also links to 2025-style questions on tokens vs words, and “are LLMs (big chatbots) supervised or unsupervised?”. The answer there: next-letter guessing is self-supervised. The text holds its own answers, so no human labels anything.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The formula, naming both counts: how often the pair appeared, and how often the first letter appeared at the start of any pair.
  • The “hello hello” example.
  • Why smoothing is needed: a pair never seen gets chance 0. The log of 0 is minus infinity (\(\log 0 = -\infty\)), so the loss becomes endless.
  • Loss = the average negative log-likelihood (the average “surprise” at each real next letter).
  • Perplexity = e to the power of the loss (\(e^{\text{Loss}}\)), compared with blind guessing among 27 characters, which gives 27.
  • The lesson of the comparison table: the neural network does as well as counting, no better, but it can grow to look further back without the table exploding.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying a bigram uses the two previous pieces. It uses one.
  • Forgetting the start and end pairs (start→h and o→end).
  • Dividing by the total number of pairs in the whole text. The right number to divide by is how often the first letter appeared at the start of a pair (\(\text{count}(c_{n-1})\)).
  • Saying the neural network bigram is “much better”. Its loss is 2.46 against 2.45 for counting: the same.
  • Getting temperature backwards. Above 1 = more random, below 1 = more cautious.
  • Forgetting the minus sign in the loss. Without it, the loss would be negative and you’d want it big, which is the wrong way round.

Key terms to use

  • next-token prediction (guessing the next piece of text)
  • n-gram (guess from the previous n − 1 pieces)
  • bigram (two neighbouring pieces; looks back one)
  • conditional probability (a chance, given something already known)
  • character-level vs sub-word tokens (single letters vs pieces of words)
  • add-one (Laplace) smoothing (pretend every pair appeared once more)
  • sampling (picking the next letter by weighted dice)
  • temperature (knob: cautious below 1, adventurous above)
  • greedy decoding (always pick the most likely letter)
  • likelihood (chances of the real letters, multiplied together)
  • log-likelihood (the logs of those chances, added up)
  • negative log-likelihood (loss) (average surprise score; lower is better)
  • perplexity (roughly how many letters it’s torn between)
  • context length (how much earlier text it sees)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “A bigram model predicts the next character from the previous two characters.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A bigram model is the letter-guesser from this chapter. A character is one letter or symbol. Does it look back two letters before guessing the next one?

    False. Why: “Bi” means two, but the two are the letter you’re on plus the one you’re guessing. So it looks back only one letter. In general, an n-gram looks back n − 1 pieces. It’s like a friend who only remembers the last word you said. (Source: L4 slide 2.)

  2. T/F: “Without smoothing, a single unseen bigram can make the loss infinite.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Smoothing means adding a pretend count of 1 to every pair. An unseen bigram is a letter pair that never showed up in the training text. The loss is the “how wrong” score. Can one never-seen pair make that score endless?

    True. Why: A never-seen pair gets chance 0. The loss uses the log of each chance, and the log of 0 is minus infinity (\(\log 0 = -\infty\)). One endless number makes the whole average endless. It’s like a judge who gives a score of “impossible”: one such vote wrecks the whole total. (Source: Part 1 cell 44.)

  3. T/F: “Setting the temperature above 1 makes rare characters more likely.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Temperature is the knob that reshapes the chances before the model rolls its dice. Rare characters are letters that normally get a small chance. If you turn the knob above 1, do those letters get picked more often?

    True. Why: Above 1, the chances get flatter: the favourite loses some of its lead and the underdogs gain. Think of turning up a DJ’s “surprise me” setting: less-played songs come on more often. (Source: Part 1 cell 38.)

  4. T/F: “A model with loss 3.30 on 27 characters is doing better than random guessing.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The loss is the “how wrong” score, lower is better. The model chooses among 27 characters (26 letters plus an end mark). Is a score of 3.30 better than picking letters blindly?

    False. Why: Blind guessing, giving each of the 27 characters the same chance, gives a loss of exactly ln 27 ≈ 3.30 (perplexity 27). So 3.30 is blind guessing, not better. It’s like scoring 25% on a test with four answer options per question: that’s what you’d get by guessing with your eyes closed. (Source: L4 slide 9.)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): What does perplexity measure, and what do the course’s numbers show?

    Model answer: Perplexity is \(e^{\text{Loss}}\), where the loss is the average negative log-likelihood of the true next character. It can be read as how many characters the model is “choosing between” at each step, so lower is better. Uniform guessing over 27 characters gives perplexity 27, the count-based bigram 11.6, the neural network bigram 11.7, and the MLP with 5 characters of context 9.2. So counting and the simple neural net learn the same thing, and the gain comes from giving the model more context (L4 slide 9).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Perplexity tells you roughly how many letters the model is torn between at each step, so smaller is better. Blind guessing is torn between all 27. Counting letter pairs brings that down to about 12, and the simple neural network gets the same. The model that looks back five letters does best, at about 9, so looking further back is what really helps.

Sources: Lecture 4 “Introducing next token prediction” (Larsen), slides 2–9; notebook Predict_the_next_token_part1.ipynb (cells 0–45); dataset names.txt.

12. Neural network basics you need: one-hot vectors, weights, softmax, loss, gradient descent, backpropagation

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — the one-hot vector was 2025 Q3(c); softmax, loss and training words come back in the transformer and LLM questions.

Start from zero

The problem. The counting machine from Chapter 11 works, but only with one letter of memory. If you want it to look further back, the count grid grows out of control. And many jobs aren’t about counting at all: spotting spam, or guessing the next word from the last ten words. We want a machine that learns a pattern from examples, without anyone writing the rules for it. A neural network is that machine. It matters in this course because word2vec (next chapter) and the big chatbots are built from exactly these parts.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Picture a machine of many small dials that get nudged after every wrong guess. Numbers go in at one end and numbers come out at the other. Each dial (a weight) decides how much one input counts.
  2. Words and letters aren’t numbers, so first turn each one into a row of 0s with a single 1 in its own slot (a one-hot vector). With the three-word list cat, dog, car, “dog” becomes 0, 1, 0.
  3. Inside the machine, small units called neurons each take their inputs, multiply each one by its dial, add it all up, and add a baseline nudge (the bias). Then they pass the result through a squashing rule (the activation function).
  4. Neurons are stacked in layers. The outputs of one layer are the inputs of the next. The middle layers are called “hidden”: they find useful in-between patterns on their own.
  5. The last layer gives one raw score for each possible answer. Softmax turns these scores into chances that are all positive and add up to 1.
  6. Compare the guess with the truth. If the right answer got a small chance, the loss (the “how wrong were you” score) is big.
  7. For every dial at once, work out which way to turn it to make the loss a little smaller. That calculation is backpropagation.
  8. Turn every dial a small step in that better direction. That’s gradient descent. The size of the step is the learning rate.
  9. Repeat with many examples, many times. One full pass through all the examples is an epoch. At first the dials are random and the guesses are bad. After thousands of nudges, the guesses get good.

A tiny example by hand. Five small steps, each with every number shown. Parts 2 to 5 reuse the chapter’s own worked example below, slowed down.

Part 1: one neuron. Say the input is 2, the dial (weight) is 0.5, and the bias is 1. The weighted sum is 1 + 0.5 × 2 = 2. Now squash it with the sigmoid rule: 1 / (1 + \(e^{-2}\)) = 1 / (1 + 0.135) = 1 / 1.135 ≈ 0.88. The output, 0.88, sits between 0 and 1, so you can read it as a chance. (My own numbers.)

Part 2: a one-hot vector picks out a row. In the chapter’s grid W below, the rows are the words (cat, dog, car) and the columns are the two numbers each word owns. Multiply dog’s one-hot vector (0, 1, 0) by W, one column at a time. First column: 0 × 0.9 + 1 × 0.8 + 0 × 0.1 = 0.8. Second column: 0 × 0.2 + 1 × 0.3 + 0 × 0.9 = 0.3. The answer is (0.8, 0.3), which is dog’s row. The zeros wipe out the other rows.

Part 3: softmax. The network gives three raw scores for three possible next characters: 2, 1 and 0. Softmax first takes e to the power of each score: \(e^2\) = 7.389, \(e^1\) = 2.718, \(e^0\) = 1. Their total is 11.107. Then it divides each one by the total: 7.389 / 11.107 = 0.665, then 2.718 / 11.107 = 0.245, then 1 / 11.107 = 0.090. These add up to 1.000. In the chapter’s softmax table below, the columns are the three characters and the rows are the steps of this calculation.

Part 4: the loss. Say the true next character was character 1, which got the chance 0.665. The loss for this example is −ln 0.665 = 0.41. Compare: if the model had given the truth 0.9, the loss would be −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.11. If it had given only 0.1, the loss would be −ln 0.1 ≈ 2.30. Confident and right means a small loss. Giving the truth a low chance means a big loss.

Part 5: one nudge. Take one dial set to 2.0. Backpropagation says its gradient is 0.5: turning this dial up would push the loss up. So we turn it down. With a learning rate of 1, the new value is 2.0 − 1 × 0.5 = 1.5. Then repeat for every dial, for every example, many times.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: it learns the pattern from examples on its own. Nobody has to write rules or hand-pick the inputs.
  • Good: it grows gracefully. Giving it more context doesn’t blow up a table: the MLP with 5 letters of memory reaches loss 2.22, against 2.45 for counting.
  • Breaks: with the same information, it’s no smarter than counting (2.46 vs 2.45 for the one-letter version).
  • Breaks: it needs lots of data and computing power, and it can memorise its training examples instead of learning the general pattern (overfitting). GPUs help with the computing; dropout and regularisation help against overfitting.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • neural network: a machine of many small adjustable dials that turns input numbers into output numbers and learns by nudging the dials after each wrong guess.
  • weight (w, W): one dial. It says how much one input counts. A big weight is like turning up the volume on that input.
  • bias (b): a baseline nudge added on top, whatever the inputs are. Like a shop that adds a fixed delivery fee to every order.
  • parameters: all the weights and biases together: everything the network learns.
  • input / output: the numbers you feed in / the numbers that come out.
  • neuron / neural unit / node: one small calculator inside the network. It adds up its weighted inputs plus the bias, then squashes the result.
  • weighted sum (z): multiply each input by its weight and add it all up. Like a course grade: exam × 0.6 + project × 0.4.
  • activation function (f): the squashing rule a neuron applies to its weighted sum, so the output stays in a useful range.
  • sigmoid (σ): an activation function that squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. Sigmoid of 0 is 0.5; big numbers get close to 1.
  • tanh: a squashing rule like sigmoid, but its outputs run from −1 to 1. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • softmax: turns a list of raw scores into chances that are all positive and add up to 1. The biggest score gets the biggest chance.
  • logits / scores: the raw numbers a network gives before softmax. They can be any size, even negative.
  • e, exponentiate: e is a fixed number, about 2.718. To exponentiate a score z means to work out \(e^{z}\), which is always positive.
  • vector: a list of numbers in a row, like (0.8, 0.3). Its length is how many numbers it holds.
  • matrix: a grid of numbers with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
  • matrix multiplication (@, \(xW\)): a way to combine a list with a grid: for each column, multiply the list’s numbers by the column’s numbers one by one and add up.
  • size notation (\(K \times p\), \(27 \times 27\)): “rows × columns”. A 3 × 2 grid has 3 rows and 2 columns.
  • “stored on its side” (transposed): the same grid with rows and columns swapped.
  • one-hot vector: a list as long as the vocabulary, all 0s except one 1 in the word’s own slot. Like a row of light switches with only one turned on.
  • selection vector: another name for a one-hot vector when it’s used to pick one row (or column) out of a grid.
  • vocabulary (p): the list of all words (or characters) the model knows.
  • embedding: a short list of learned numbers that stands for a word or letter (next chapter). In the MLP, each character gets 10 such numbers.
  • layer: a group of neurons that work side by side. The outputs of one layer feed the next.
  • input layer: where the numbers enter. It does no calculation, so it usually isn’t counted.
  • hidden layer: a layer between input and output. “Hidden” because you never see its numbers directly.
  • output layer: the last layer. It gives the final scores.
  • two-layer network: one hidden layer plus the output layer (the input layer isn’t counted).
  • fully connected: every neuron in one layer is linked to every neuron in the next.
  • feed-forward: numbers flow one way only, from input to output, with no loops back.
  • deep learning: using networks with many hidden layers.
  • feature / latent feature: a feature is a useful piece of information about the input (“does the word end in -ing?”). Latent = hidden: patterns the network finds on its own, which nobody named.
  • logistic regression: a classic method that turns a weighted sum into a chance with sigmoid (or softmax for many classes). A network with a softmax output works the same way in its last layer.
  • cost function / loss (\(\hat{y}\) vs \(y\)): one number that measures how far the guess \(\hat{y}\) (“y-hat”) is from the truth \(y\). Training tries to make it small.
  • negative log-likelihood / cross-entropy: the loss used here: minus the log of the chance the model gave to the right answer, averaged. A low chance for the truth gives a big loss.
  • log, ln: the reverse of a power: ln asks “e to what power gives this number?” ln 1 = 0; ln of a number below 1 is negative.
  • gradient: for each dial, how much the loss changes if you turn that dial up a tiny bit. It points “uphill”.
  • gradient descent: turning every dial a small step against its gradient, so you walk downhill to a lower loss. Like walking down a foggy hill by always stepping where the ground slopes down.
  • learning rate (lr): how big each step is. Too small = slow. Too big = you overshoot.
  • backpropagation: the method that works out the gradient for every dial at once, by tracing the error backwards from the output through each layer.
  • stochastic gradient descent (SGD): gradient descent that uses a small random handful of examples for each step, instead of all of them. Faster, slightly noisier. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • mini-batch: that small handful of examples, here 32 at a time.
  • epoch: one full pass through all the training examples.
  • overfitting: memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern, like learning last year’s exam answers by heart without understanding them.
  • dropout: during training, switching off some random neurons each time, so the network can’t lean on any single one. It helps against overfitting. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • regularisation: any trick that keeps the network from overfitting, for example by keeping the weights small. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • GPU: a graphics chip. It can do thousands of small multiplications at the same time, which is exactly what networks need. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • train / dev / test split, validation loss: keep most examples to learn from (train) and hold some back to check the model (dev and test). Validation loss is the loss on held-back examples the model didn’t learn from.
  • perplexity: e to the power of the loss: roughly how many options the model is torn between (Chapter 11).
  • MLP: a neural network with at least one hidden layer. The course’s Part 3 model.
  • PyTorch, .backward(), .grad: PyTorch is a Python toolkit for neural networks. .backward() runs backpropagation, and .grad holds the resulting gradient for each dial.

The idea in plain words

A neural network is a big adjustable formula. You give it numbers in, it gives numbers out. Inside are many weights, small dials. At first the dials are random, so the guesses are bad. You show it an example, measure how wrong it was (the loss), work out which way to turn each dial to be a bit less wrong (backpropagation gives the direction, gradient descent turns the dials), and repeat thousands of times.

Two practical problems need solving first:

  1. Computers do not understand letters or words. So each one becomes a one-hot vector: a long row of 0s with a single 1 in that word’s slot.
  2. The raw outputs are any numbers (like 2.0, 1.0, −3.5). We want probabilities. Softmax turns them into positive numbers that add up to 1.

Analogy Tuning an old radio in the dark. You turn the knob a little, listen whether the noise got better or worse, and turn it further in the better direction. The loss is the noise; gradient descent is the “turn a little in the better direction” rule; backpropagation is working out, for each of thousands of knobs at once, which direction is “better”.

Source: L6 slides 15–19; Part 2 notebook cells 0, 12–21.

The exam definition

  • One-hot vector: a vector as long as the vocabulary (\(p\) entries), all zeros except a single 1 at the position of the word. “Computers do not understand words, so for each observation t, the target and context words are turned into one-hot-vectors” (L6 slide 21). Multiplying a one-hot vector by a weight matrix just selects one row or column: “\(x_t\) just serves as a selection vector” (L6 slide 22). (In plain words: the one-hot vector only picks something out of the grid; it doesn’t change it.)
  • Neural unit: \(z = b + wx\), “where \(w\) are weights and \(b\) bias terms”; its output is given by an activation function \(a = f(z)\), e.g. sigmoid or softmax (L6 slide 17).
  • Layers: input layer (not counted), hidden layer(s), output layer. A network with one hidden layer is a “two-layer (feed-forward) Neural Network”. “Fully connected” = every node is linked to every node in the next layer. “Deep Learning: Add more hidden layers.” Each hidden layer represents “(latent) features of the input” (L6 slide 16), meaning hidden patterns in the input that the network finds by itself.
  • Logistic-regression link: a softmax-output network “is just like logistic regression … a deep Neural Network is like layer after layer of logistic regression classifiers”, and the earlier layers “induce the feature representations themselves” instead of us hand-making features (L6 slide 18). (“Induce the feature representations” = work out by themselves which useful summaries of the input to build.)
  • Cost function: a measure of the distance between prediction \(\hat{y}\) (read “y-hat”: the network’s guess) and truth \(y\) that we minimise (L6 slide 19). In the bigram notebooks it is the negative log-likelihood (Part 2 cell 19).
  • Training (“classical way”): make a prediction with the current weights and compute the cost; “Use Gradient descent and backpropagation to update the parameters”; “Redo the ‘experiment’” (L6 slide 19).
  • Why NNs got popular: “Stochastic gradient descent”, “Various dropout and regularization techniques to, e.g., improve the learning (rate) and avoid overfitting”, “GPU computing” (L6 slide 19). (Overfitting = memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern; GPUs = graphics chips that do many small sums at once.)

Source: L6 slides 16–19, 21–22; Part 2 cell 19.

A tiny worked example

One-hot × W = picking a row. Take a toy vocabulary of three words: cat, dog, car. Their one-hot vectors (rows = the word, columns = the vocabulary slot):

Word slot “cat” slot “dog” slot “car”
cat 1 0 0
dog 0 1 0
car 0 0 1

Now a weight matrix \(W\) with one row per word and two columns (my made-up numbers):

In words: this is a grid of six made-up dial values: one row of two numbers for each of the three words.

\[W = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \quad\begin{matrix}\leftarrow \text{cat}\\ \leftarrow \text{dog}\\ \leftarrow \text{car}\end{matrix}\]

Multiply the one-hot vector for “dog” by \(W\), by hand:

In words: multiply each 0 or 1 of dog’s one-hot vector by the matching number in a column of W and add up, once per column; only dog’s row survives.

\[(0,\;1,\;0)\,W = \big(0{\times}0.9 + 1{\times}0.8 + 0{\times}0.1,\;\; 0{\times}0.2 + 1{\times}0.3 + 0{\times}0.9\big) = (0.8,\;0.3)\]

That is exactly the “dog” row of \(W\) (checked in python). Every 0 wipes out a row; the single 1 keeps one row. This is what the Part 2 notebook comment says: “for one-hot input this simply picks out row x of W” (cell 13). Lecture 6 writes the same thing the other way round, \(W^1 x_t\) with \(W^1\) of size \(K \times p\), so there the one-hot vector picks out a column (slide 22). Same idea, the matrix is just stored on its side. In an exam answer about word2vec, use the slide-22 version (column of \(W^1\)).

Softmax on three numbers. Suppose the network outputs the scores (called logits) \(z = (2, 1, 0)\) for three possible next characters. Softmax:

Character 1 Character 2 Character 3 Sum
Score \(z\) 2 1 0
\(e^{z}\) 7.389 2.718 1.000 11.107
Softmax \(= e^{z}/\text{sum}\) 0.665 0.245 0.090 1.000

By hand for character 1: \(7.389 / 11.107 = 0.665\) (all values checked in python). The biggest score gets the biggest probability, every probability is positive, and they sum to 1.

Loss and one gradient-descent step. If the true next character was character 1, the loss for this example is \(-\ln 0.665 = 0.41\) (python). A gradient-descent step moves every weight a little against its gradient: with a weight of 2.0, gradient 0.5 and learning rate 1, the new weight is \(2.0 - 1 \times 0.5 = 1.5\) (my illustration). Part 2 does exactly this with W.data -= lr * W.grad (cell 21).

The course’s network (Part 2 notebook). “A single linear layer (a 27×27 weight matrix, no hidden layer) followed by a softmax” (cell 0; L4 slide 8). 27 inputs (one per character, with . standing for both start and end), 27 outputs, \(27 \times 27 = 729\) weights, “the same size as the count table from part 1”. From the first name “emma” it builds 5 training examples: inputs ., e, m, m, a and targets e, m, m, a, . (cells 6–8). After training it reaches loss 2.46 vs 2.45 for counting (cell 33): “exp(W) normalized row-wise is close to the count table P”.

Note on a source inconsistency: the Part 2 subtitle says “neural network with one hidden layer”, but the text, the code and L4 slide 8 say no hidden layer. Write “no hidden layer” in the exam.

Part 3 (MLP) adds depth. Each of the 27 characters gets a learned 10-number embedding (matrix C, 27 × 10). Five previous characters → 50 numbers → a hidden layer of 300 units with tanh (a squashing rule) → 27 output scores → softmax/cross-entropy. Trained on mini-batches (small groups) of 32 examples for 200,000 steps, with an 80/10/10 train/dev/test split (80% of the names to learn from, 10% and 10% held back for checking). Validation loss 2.22, perplexity 9.2 (cells 5, 7, 10, 16). Total weights (my count, not printed in the file): \(270 + 15{,}000 + 300 + 8{,}100 + 27 = 23{,}697\).

Source: Part 2 cells 0, 6–13, 19–21, 33; Part 3 cells 5, 7, 10, 16; L6 slide 22.

The formula, symbol by symbol

Inside one neuron (L6 slide 17):

In words: a neuron adds a baseline to its weighted inputs to get a raw score z, then an activation function turns z into the output; sigmoid squeezes it between 0 and 1, and softmax turns a list of scores into chances that add up to 1.

\[z = b + wx, \qquad a = f(z), \qquad a = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad a = \text{softmax}(z) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum e^{z_j}}\]

  • \(x\) = the inputs; \(w\) = the weights (how much each input counts); \(b\) = the bias (a baseline shift).
  • \(z\) = the weighted sum, a raw score.
  • \(f\) = the activation function that turns \(z\) into the neuron’s output \(a\).
  • \(\sigma\) (sigmoid) squeezes any number into (0, 1), e.g. \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\).
  • softmax: exponentiate each score \(z_j\) and divide by the sum of all of them. (The slide uses the same letter \(j\) above and below the line; it means “this score, divided by the sum over all scores”. You may write \(\sum_k e^{z_k}\) in the denominator to be clear.)

Read aloud: “Each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and pushes it through an activation function.”

A two-layer network with softmax output (L6 slide 18):

In words: layer 1 weights the inputs, adds biases and squashes the result with sigmoid; layer 2 weights those results into scores; softmax turns the scores into chances.

\[h^1 = \sigma(W^1 h^0 + b^1), \qquad h^2 = W^2 h^1 + b^2, \qquad y = \text{softmax}(h^2)\]

  • \(h^0 = x\) = the input vector.
  • \(W^1, b^1\) = weights and biases of layer 1; \(h^1\) = the hidden layer’s outputs (“activations”).
  • \(W^2, b^2\) = weights and biases of layer 2; \(h^2\) = the output scores.
  • \(W^l\) is a \(j^l \times k^{l-1}\) matrix (a grid with one row per neuron in this layer and one column per output of the layer before) linking the \(j\) neurons of layer \(l\) to the \(k\) activations of layer \(l-1\).
  • \(y\) = the output: a probability for each class.

Read aloud: “Weight the inputs, squash them into hidden features, weight those features into scores, and turn the scores into probabilities with softmax.”

Source: L6 slides 17–18.

Reading the course code

The whole forward pass, loss and one training step in Part 2 (cells 13, 19–21):

H = xs_onehot @ W                                          # picks out row x of W
output = torch.exp(H) / torch.exp(H).sum(1, keepdim=True)  # softmax
loss = -output[torch.arange(len(ys)), ys].log().mean()     # negative log-likelihood
loss.backward()                                            # backpropagation
W.data -= lr * W.grad                                      # gradient descent step
  • Line 1: multiply the one-hot inputs by the weights. Because each input is one-hot, this just looks up a row of W (the logits).
  • Line 2: softmax. Exponentiate and divide by the row sum, so each row is a probability distribution over the 27 next characters.
  • Line 3: for each example, take the probability given to the true next character, take its log, average, and flip the sign. Same loss as Part 1’s \(-\ell/n\).
  • Line 4: backpropagation. PyTorch works out how the loss would change if each weight moved a little (the gradient).
  • Line 5: move every weight a small step against its gradient. Repeat (cells 27–28 run 10 steps with learning rate 1, then 1,000 steps with learning rate 15).

No outputs are saved; the summary table (cell 33) gives the final loss ≈ 2.46.

Exam boxes

How this shows up on the exam In 2025, Q3(c) (2.5 points) asked what a one-hot vector is (a row of 0s with a single 1 in the word’s slot) and how word2vec (the word-map method of Chapter 13) uses it in its first layer. The model answer is in Chapter 13.

Expect True/False items such as:

  • “A softmax output layer makes a neural network like logistic regression.” True (L6 slide 18). Logistic regression is a classic method that turns a weighted sum into a chance; a network ending in softmax does the same in its last layer.
  • “The input layer is counted as a layer.” False (slide 16). The input layer only passes numbers in, so it isn’t counted.
  • “The neural network bigram has a hidden layer.” False. The course’s letter-pair network has no middle layer.

The training words also come back in the transformer chapter: gradient descent (turning the dials downhill), backpropagation (working out which way to turn each dial), cross-entropy (the “how wrong” score) and epoch (one full pass through the examples).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For one-hot: “vector of length \(p\) (vocabulary size), all zeros except a 1 at the word’s index”. In words: a list as long as the word list, all 0s except a 1 in the word’s own slot. Plus: “multiplying it by a weight matrix selects one row/column = that word’s vector (a selection vector)”. In words: multiplying it by the grid of dials picks out only that word’s own row or column.
  • For softmax: it “turns scores into positive probabilities that sum to 1”.
  • For training: “minimise a cost function; backpropagation computes gradients; gradient descent updates weights; repeat”. In words: make the “how wrong” score small; backpropagation works out which way to turn each dial; gradient descent turns them a small step; do it again and again.
  • For why networks got popular: SGD (learning from small random handfuls of examples), dropout and regularisation (tricks against memorising), and GPUs (graphics chips that do many sums at once).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying a one-hot vector “counts how often a word appears”. That describes a row of the word-count table (the document-term matrix). A one-hot vector only marks which word it is.
  • Saying softmax picks the single biggest value. It gives a chance to every option, a whole list of chances that adds up to 1.
  • Mixing up backpropagation and gradient descent. Backpropagation works out the directions (the gradients). Gradient descent uses them to turn the dials.
  • Saying neural networks are popular because they are “new”. Slide 14 says they have a “long history”. Slide 19 says the rise in popularity is “partly due to newer developments”: SGD, dropout/regularisation and GPUs.

Key terms to use

  • one-hot vector (all 0s, one 1 for the word)
  • selection vector (one-hot used to pick one row)
  • weights (dials saying how much each input counts)
  • bias (a fixed baseline nudge added on)
  • neural unit (one small calculator inside the network)
  • activation function (the squashing rule after the sum)
  • sigmoid (squeezes any number between 0 and 1)
  • softmax (turns scores into chances adding to 1)
  • logits (raw scores before softmax)
  • hidden layer (middle layer you never see directly)
  • fully connected (every unit linked to every next unit)
  • feed-forward (numbers flow one way, no loops)
  • deep learning (networks with many hidden layers)
  • cost/loss function (one “how wrong” score to shrink)
  • negative log-likelihood (minus log of the truth’s chance)
  • gradient descent (turn dials a step downhill)
  • learning rate (how big each step is)
  • backpropagation (works out which way each dial goes)
  • stochastic gradient descent (steps using small random handfuls of examples)
  • dropout (randomly switching off units while training)
  • regularisation (tricks that stop memorising)
  • GPU (chip doing thousands of sums at once)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Multiplying a one-hot vector by a weight matrix returns the sum of all rows of the matrix.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A one-hot vector is a list of 0s with a single 1 in one word’s slot. A weight matrix is a grid of dials with one row per word. When you multiply the two, do you get all the rows added together?

    False. Why: Every 0 wipes out its row, and the single 1 keeps one row. So you get only that one row (or column), the one where the 1 sits. It’s like a row of light switches with only one on: only that one lamp lights up. (Source: Part 2 cell 13; L6 slide 22.)

  2. T/F: “A deep neural network can be seen as layer after layer of logistic regression classifiers.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A deep neural network is one with many middle layers. Logistic regression is a classic method that adds up weighted inputs and squeezes the result into a chance. A classifier is something that sorts items into groups. Is a deep network like many of these stacked on top of each other?

    True. Why: Each layer does a weighted sum and then a squashing step, which is what logistic regression does. Stack them, and each layer feeds the next, like a relay of small judges each passing their verdict on. (Source: L6 slide 18.)

  3. T/F: “The input layer is counted when we call a network with one hidden layer a two-layer network.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The input layer is where the numbers come in. A hidden layer is a middle layer. A network with one middle layer is called “two-layer”. Is the input layer one of those two?

    False. Why: The input layer does no calculation, so it usually isn’t counted. The two layers are the hidden layer and the output layer. It’s like a front door: you don’t count it as a room of the house. (Source: L6 slide 16, “The input layer is usually not counted”.)

  4. T/F: “Softmax outputs always sum to 1.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Softmax is the step that turns a list of raw scores into chances. Do those chances always add up to exactly 1?

    True. Why: Softmax makes each score positive (e to the power of the score), then divides each one by the total of all of them. Anything divided by its own total adds up to 1, like slices of one pizza always making one whole pizza. (Source: L6 slide 17; Part 2 cell 14.)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): How is a neural network trained, and why did neural networks become popular?

    Model answer: With the current weights the network makes a prediction, and a cost function (e.g. negative log-likelihood) measures how far it is from the truth. Backpropagation computes how the cost changes with each weight, and gradient descent moves every weight a small step in the direction that lowers the cost. This is repeated many times over the data. Neural networks became popular partly thanks to stochastic gradient descent, dropout and regularisation (better learning, less overfitting), and GPU computing (L6 slide 19).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: The network makes a guess with its current dials, and a score says how wrong the guess was. Backpropagation works out which way each dial should turn, and gradient descent turns them all a small step that way. You repeat this many times. They took off thanks to faster learning tricks, tricks against memorising the examples, and graphics chips that do many sums at once.

Sources: Lecture 4 slide 8; Lecture 6 “Neural Networks and Word Embeddings” (Thorsrud) slides 15–19, 21–22; notebooks Predict_the_next_token_part2_nn.ipynb (cells 0–33) and Predict_the_next_token_part3_mpl.ipynb (cells 5–16).

13. Word embeddings: distributional hypothesis, co-occurrence, PMI/PPMI, SVD on PMI, word2vec, vector arithmetic, static vs contextual

Exam priority: ★★★ High — a whole 15-point block in 2025: Q3(a) assumption + PMI matrix, Q3(b) word2vec vs BERT, Q3(c) one-hot in word2vec, Q3(d) cosine drawing, plus a True/False item on SVD on PMI.

Start from zero

The problem. You’d like a search for “automobile” to also find pages that only say “car”. But think back to the word-count table: one row per document, one column per word, each cell a count. In that table, “car” and “automobile” are two separate columns with nothing linking them. The computer has no idea they mean the same thing. We want it to learn which words are close in meaning, without anyone writing a dictionary for it. Word embeddings do exactly that. Researchers then use them to measure things like “how much do the news link recession with credit?” month by month.

How it works, step by step.

  1. The goal: give each word a spot on a map, so similar words sit close together. A spot is a short list of numbers, like map coordinates. A paper map uses 2 numbers; embeddings use maybe 100 or 300.
  2. The clue: words with similar meanings keep similar company. “Apricot” and “pineapple” both turn up near “sugar” and “pinch”. So we learn the map from which words appear near each other.
  3. Choose a window, for example 4 words to the left and right of each word. Words inside the window count as “appearing together”.
  4. Way 1, counting. Build a big table with one row per word and one column per neighbour word. Each cell says how often the two appeared together. This is the co-occurrence matrix.
  5. Re-weight the table with PMI. For each pair, compare how often they really met with how often they’d meet by pure chance, given how common each word is on its own. Pairs that meet more than chance score above 0. Then set any negative score to 0 (this version is called PPMI).
  6. The table is huge and mostly zeros. SVD squeezes it: it keeps only the few strongest patterns and hands each word a short list of numbers, say 300. That list is the word’s spot on the map.
  7. Way 2, predicting (word2vec). Play a guessing game. Show a small neural network one word and ask it to guess which words appear nearby (Skipgram). Or show it the neighbours and ask for the middle word (CBOW). Every wrong guess nudges the dials. After training, each word’s own set of dials is its spot on the map.
  8. To compare two words, draw an arrow from the centre of the map to each word’s spot, and measure the angle between the two arrows (cosine similarity). A small angle means similar meaning.

A tiny example by hand. Our corpus is three sentences:

  1. “the cat drinks milk”
  2. “the dog drinks water”
  3. “the car needs fuel”

Rule: two words “appear together” if they’re in the same sentence. (So the window is the whole sentence, like in the course notebook.) We skip “the”, because it’s in every sentence and tells us nothing.
