The co-occurrence table. Rows = the words we want spots for (target words). Columns = the neighbour words (context words). Each cell = the number of sentences where both words appear.

Target ↓ / Context → drinks milk water needs fuel
cat 1 1 0 0 0
dog 1 0 1 0 0
car 0 0 0 1 1

One cell out loud: row dog, column drinks. “Dog” is only in sentence 2, and “drinks” is also in sentence 2. They’re together once, so the cell is 1. Another: row cat, column water. “Cat” is only in sentence 1 and “water” only in sentence 2. They never meet, so the cell is 0.

Each row is already a rough spot on a map, with 5 numbers: cat = (1, 1, 0, 0, 0), dog = (1, 0, 1, 0, 0), car = (0, 0, 0, 1, 1).

Cosine similarity, cat vs dog.

  • Dot product: multiply the numbers in matching positions and add: 1 × 1 + 1 × 0 + 0 × 1 + 0 × 0 + 0 × 0 = 1.
  • Length of each arrow: square each number, add, take the square root. Cat: √(1 + 1) = √2 ≈ 1.414. Dog: also √2 ≈ 1.414.
  • Cosine = dot product ÷ (length × length) = 1 ÷ (1.414 × 1.414) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.

Cat vs car: the dot product is 1 × 0 + 1 × 0 + 0 × 0 + 0 × 1 + 0 × 1 = 0, so the cosine is 0. So cat is halfway similar to dog (they share “drinks”) and not at all like car. With millions of sentences, this kind of sharing is what pulls related words together.

PMI by hand, slowly, with the chapter’s slide-12 table (Table 1 below: rows = target words, columns = context words, cells = counts). Look at apricot and pinch.

  • The whole table holds 19 co-occurrences. Apricot is part of 2 of them. Pinch is part of 2. Apricot-with-pinch happens 1 time.
  • Real share of apricot-with-pinch: 1/19 ≈ 0.053.
  • Share you’d expect by pure chance: apricot’s share times pinch’s share, (2/19) × (2/19) = 4/361 ≈ 0.011. Think of two people who each visit a café rarely: by luck alone, they’d hardly ever be there at the same time.
  • How many times more than chance: (1/19) ÷ (4/361) = 361/76 = 4.75.
  • Take log base 2. Doubling 1 twice gives 4, so the answer is a bit over 2: \(\log_2 4.75\) = 2.25.

PMI = 2.25, well above 0: apricot and pinch meet far more often than luck would explain.

The guessing game (word2vec), in one line. From sentence 1, Skipgram makes the training pairs (cat, drinks) and (cat, milk): shown “cat”, the network should give “drinks” and “milk” high chances.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: it learns “similar meaning” from raw text alone, with no dictionary. The spots are short lists, so comparing words is quick.
  • Good: directions on the map can carry meaning: King − Man + Woman lands near Queen.
  • Breaks: every word gets one spot, whatever the sentence. “Bank” the river and “bank” the money share a single spot (static embeddings). Newer models like BERT fix this.
  • Breaks: it needs a lot of text. On a small corpus the word arithmetic can fail, and PMI over-rewards rare pairs like apricot–pinch.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • bag-of-words / document-term matrix (C): the word-count table: one row per document, one column per word, each cell a count. Word order is thrown away.
  • word embedding: a word’s spot on the meaning map: a short list of numbers. Similar words get nearby spots.
  • “embedding is location”: the slides’ slogan: an embedding is a position in space.
  • vector: a list of numbers, like (0.4, 0.9). You can draw it as an arrow from the centre of a map to that point.
  • vector space: the “map” where all these arrows live.
  • dimension: how many numbers each vector has. 2 dimensions = a flat map; 300 dimensions = a map you can’t draw but a computer can handle.
  • dense vs sparse: dense = most numbers are not zero; sparse = almost everything is zero, like a huge spreadsheet with a few filled cells.
  • distributional hypothesis: the idea that words used in similar surroundings have similar meanings. “You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth 1957).
  • target word / context word: the target is the word we’re looking at; context words are its neighbours in the window.
  • window (b): how far left and right we look for neighbours. b = 4 means 4 words on each side.
  • co-occurrence: two words appearing near each other.
  • co-occurrence matrix (Co): a word-by-word table counting how often each pair appears together. Rows = target words, columns = context words.
  • \(p \times p\): “p rows by p columns”, where p is the number of words in the vocabulary. Words × words, not documents × words.
  • vocabulary (p): the list of all distinct words the model knows.
  • probability (chance): a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is.
  • joint probability (\(p_{ij}\)) / skipgram probability: the share of all pairs that are this exact pair. Information-with-data: 6/19 = 0.32.
  • unigram probability (\(p_i\), \(p_j\)): how common one word is on its own, as a share of the total. Information: 11/19 = 0.58.
  • PMI (pointwise mutual information): the log of “how often two words really appear together” ÷ “how often they would by pure chance”. Above 0 = they attract; below 0 = they avoid each other.
  • PPMI (positive PMI): PMI with every negative number replaced by 0.
  • log, \(\log_2\), ln: the reverse of a power. \(\log_2 8 = 3\) because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. ln does the same with the number e (about 2.718). The log of a number above 1 is positive, below 1 negative.
  • max(…, 0): “take whichever is bigger, the number or 0”. It turns negatives into 0.
  • sum (Σ): “add all of these up”.
  • add-one smoothing: add 1 to every count, so rare pairs don’t get extreme scores and zeros disappear.
  • SVD (singular value decomposition): a maths tool that breaks a big table into three smaller tables (U, S, V′) that multiply back to it. Like summarising a long survey by its few main themes.
  • truncated SVD: keeping only the K strongest themes and throwing the rest away, so each word ends up with K numbers.
  • U, S, V′, factors, loadings: the three pieces of SVD. Each word’s row of U is its embedding. “Factors” (US) and “loadings” (V′) are the slides’ names for these pieces.
  • K: the number of dimensions you keep, for example 100 or 300.
  • LSA: the earlier course method that runs SVD on the document-term matrix C. Here the same tool runs on the PMI matrix M.
  • tf-idf: the earlier re-weighting of the word-count table that turns down words appearing in almost every document. PMI plays a similar role here.
  • stop words: very common words like “the” and “and” that are usually removed.
  • binary: only 0 or 1: “is the word there or not”, not “how many times”.
  • cosine similarity: a score from −1 to 1 for how closely two arrows point the same way. With plain counts (never negative) it stays between 0 and 1. Small angle → close to 1 → similar. It ignores how long the arrows are.
  • dot product: multiply two vectors’ numbers in matching positions and add up. Big when the arrows point the same way and are long.
  • length / norm (\(\lVert a \rVert\)): how long an arrow is: square each number, add, take the square root.
  • angle: how far apart two arrows point. 0° = same direction; 90° = unrelated.
  • nearest neighbours (most_similar): the words whose spots are closest to a given word.
  • vector arithmetic: adding and subtracting word vectors number by number, as in King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen.
  • neural network: a machine of many small dials that learns by nudging them after each wrong guess (Chapter 12).
  • shallow / two-layered / feed-forward: a small network with one hidden layer, where numbers flow one way from input to output.
  • word2vec: a small neural network that learns word embeddings by playing the “guess the neighbours” game (Mikolov et al. 2013).
  • CBOW (continuous bag of words): the word2vec version that guesses the middle word from its neighbours. Like a fill-in-the-blank exercise. (The long name is [Not in course files — general knowledge].)
  • Skipgram: the opposite version: from the middle word, guess the neighbours.
  • supervised / unsupervised / self-supervised: supervised = a human gives the right answers; unsupervised = no answers at all; self-supervised = the text itself provides the answers (the real neighbours).
  • one-hot vector / selection vector: a list as long as the vocabulary, all 0s except a single 1 at the word’s slot. Multiplying it by a grid picks out that word’s column.
  • target embedding matrix (\(W^1\)): the grid of dials holding one column per word. After training, those columns are the embeddings.
  • context embedding matrix (\(W^2\)): the second grid, used to score every word as a possible neighbour.
  • hidden layer (\(h^1\)): the middle step of the network. In word2vec it’s the chosen word’s embedding.
  • softmax: turns a list of scores into chances that are all positive and add up to 1.
  • sigmoid: squeezes any number into a chance between 0 and 1.
  • logistic regression: a classic method that turns a score into a yes/no chance with the sigmoid.
  • epoch: one full pass through all the training data.
  • negative sampling: a shortcut for word2vec. Instead of scoring every word in the vocabulary, mix each real pair with 2–5 fake pairs made of random words, and train the network to tell real from fake.
  • α = 0.75: a power applied to word counts when picking the fake words. It gives rarer words a slightly better chance of being picked [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • static vs contextual (context-specific) embeddings: static = one fixed spot per word in every sentence (word2vec); contextual = the spot changes with the sentence (BERT).
  • BERT / transformer: newer, bigger language models (2017/2018) that give each word a spot depending on its sentence.
  • pre-trained embeddings: embeddings someone already learned from a huge amount of text, which you can reuse instead of training on your own small corpus.
  • gensim: the Python package the notebook uses to train word2vec.
  • min_df: a setting that drops words appearing in too few sentences.
  • GloVe, Doc2vec, Word Mover’s Distance: alternatives on the slides: GloVe is another way to learn word embeddings; Doc2vec gives whole documents embeddings; Word Mover’s Distance compares documents using word embeddings [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • LDA: the topic-model method from an earlier course chapter; the slides call Doc2vec an alternative to it.

The idea in plain words

In bag-of-words, “car” and “automobile” are just two unrelated columns. The computer has no idea they mean the same thing. Word embeddings fix this by giving every word a location: a short list of numbers, like map coordinates. Words with similar meaning get nearby locations.

How do we find the locations without a dictionary? By looking at which words a word hangs out with. “Apricot” and “pineapple” both appear near “sugar” and “pinch”. “Digital” and “information” both appear near “computer” and “data”. So apricot ends up near pineapple, and digital near information.

There are two ways to turn “who hangs out with whom” into locations:

  1. Counting: build a big word-by-word table of co-occurrences, re-weight it with PMI, then shrink it with SVD.
  2. Predicting: train a small neural network (word2vec) to guess a word’s neighbours. The weights it learns are the locations.

Analogy You can guess a lot about a stranger from their friends. If someone always hangs around climbers, buys chalk and talks about ropes, they are probably a climber, even if nobody tells you. Word embeddings guess a word’s meaning from the words it keeps company with.

Source: L6 slides 4–9; Interactive 3 cell 0.

The exam definition

  • The underlying assumption (distributional hypothesis): Firth (1957): “You shall know a word by the company it keeps!” Words that occur in similar contexts have similar meanings (L6 slide 9). The slides quote Firth but do not use the phrase “distributional hypothesis”; it is the standard name for this idea [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Embedding is location: “word embedding methods build on vector space representations” (each word stored as a list of numbers, a point on a map), “focus on co-occurrence”, “across space or time” (slide 4). “Words that share some type of meaning are close to each other in the (large) vector space” (slide 6).
  • Why move beyond bag-of-words: BoW + document-term matrix (the word-count table: rows = documents, columns = words) “does not (in general) take into account context”; “word embeddings and word embedding models do” (slide 4).
  • Unsupervised / self-supervised: in the course map, word embeddings sit under “Unsupervised/Self-supervised”, estimated by SVD or neural networks (slide 3). Skipgram “makes the problem self-supervised” (no human labels needed), since real text decides which words occur together (slide 20).
  • Co-occurrence matrix: “the fraction of times word \(w_i\) and \(w_j\) appear within, say \(b\) words of each other”; a \(p \times p\) matrix, rows = words, columns = context words (slide 11).
  • PMI (pointwise mutual information): “words that appear a lot together relative to individually get a high score” (slide 10).
  • PPMI: PMI with negatives set to 0, because negative values are “strange” (slide 11).
  • SVD on PMI: the PMI matrix “is large and sparse” (huge and mostly zeros) like the document-term matrix, so “use the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), but now not on C, but on M!” Use the truncated U matrix (U cut down to its first K columns, so each word keeps K numbers) as the word vectors (slide 13).
  • word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013, a “game changer”): “a shallow two-layered feed-forward Neural Network taking words from a vocabulary as input and embeds them as vectors into a lower dimensional space”. In plain words: a small one-way network that turns each word into a short list of numbers. Two versions: CBOW, “predict a term based on surrounding terms”, and Skipgram, “predict surrounding terms based on a term” (slide 14).
  • Static vs contextual: “Word2vec-style word embeddings are not context dependent in the sense that a word will have the same embedding irrespective of the sentence it is used in”; “newer language models [BERT, transformers, 2017/2018] have context specific embeddings” (slide 27).

Source: L6 slides 3–4, 6, 9–11, 13–14, 20, 27.

A tiny worked example

A. Building co-occurrence counts (L6 slide 10). Take each highlighted centre word and look \(b = 4\) words to the left and right. “Working with text as data is so fun that we can’t stop.” Within 4 words of “data” are “text” and “fun”, so those cells get a 1. The slide’s partial matrix (rows = target words, columns = context words, cells = how often they occur within the window):

Target ↓ / Context → text fun economics stuff bore great
data 1 1 0 0 0 0
cool 0 0 1 1 0 0
after 0 0 0 0 0 1

B. The full PMI example (L6 slide 12). Four target words, five context words. Every number below was recomputed in python and matches the slide.

Table 1 — raw co-occurrence counts Co. Rows = target words, columns = context words, cells = number of times they co-occur. Row and column totals added by me.

Co computer data pinch result sugar Row total
apricot 0 0 1 0 1 2
pineapple 0 0 1 0 1 2
digital 2 1 0 1 0 4
information 1 6 0 4 0 11
Column total 3 7 2 5 2 19

Table 2 — joint probabilities \(p_{ij}\) = cell ÷ 19, with the row shares \(p_i\) and column shares \(p_j\) (as on the slide, 2 decimals).

\(p_{ij}\) computer data pinch result sugar \(p_i\)
apricot 0.00 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.05 0.11
pineapple 0.00 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.05 0.11
digital 0.11 0.05 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.21
information 0.05 0.32 0.00 0.21 0.00 0.58
\(p_j\) 0.16 0.37 0.11 0.26 0.11

The slide’s own examples: \(p(\text{information}, \text{data}) = 6/19 = 0.32\); \(p(\text{information}) = 11/19 = 0.58\); \(p(\text{data}) = 7/19 = 0.37\).

Table 3 — PPMI \(\tilde{M}_{ij}\). Rows = target words, columns = context words, cells = PPMI score. Blank = the pair never co-occurs (Co = 0), so the log is undefined and PPMI treats it as 0.

\(\tilde{M}_{ij}\) computer data pinch result sugar
apricot 2.25 2.25
pineapple 2.25 2.25
digital 1.66 0.00 0.00
information 0.00 0.57 0.47

One cell by hand: information–data.

In words: divide how often information and data really appeared together by how often they would by chance, then take log base 2.

\[\text{PMI} = \log_2\!\left(\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i\,p_j}\right) = \log_2\!\left(\frac{6/19}{(11/19)(7/19)}\right) = \log_2\!\left(\frac{0.316}{0.213}\right) = \log_2(1.48) = 0.57\]

In words: if “information” and “data” were unrelated, they would share a window \(0.58 \times 0.37 = 0.213\) of the time. They actually do so \(0.316\) of the time, about 1.48 times more than chance. \(\log_2 1.48 = 0.57\), positive, so PPMI keeps it.

A second cell: apricot–pinch. \(\frac{1/19}{(2/19)(2/19)} = 4.75\), and \(\log_2 4.75 = 2.25\). Apricot appears only twice, yet it gets the highest score in the table. That is the slide’s warning: “Rare events, e.g. apricot in context of pinch, get high weight.” The fix suggested on slide 11 is add-one smoothing on Co.

Where the 0.00s come from (my python check). Three pairs co-occur less than chance, so their raw PMI is negative: digital–data −0.56, digital–result −0.07, information–computer −0.80. PPMI = max(PMI, 0) clips them to 0.00.

C. From the big PMI matrix to short word vectors (slide 13). With a real vocabulary of, say, \(p\) = 20,000 words, \(M\) is 20,000 × 20,000 = 400 million cells. Most pairs never appear together, so most cells are 0. Even in the tiny slide example, 10 of the 20 cells are empty. So \(M\) is large and sparse: lots of storage, little information per number, just like the document-term matrix. Truncated SVD keeps only \(K\) dimensions (\(M \approx U S V'\)). Each word’s row of \(U\) (with \(K\) numbers, e.g. 100 or 300) becomes its embedding. Compare words with cosine similarity.

D. King − Man + Woman (L6 slides 5–8). The slide’s toy vocabulary of four words in 2-D: Queen (0.4, 0.9), King (0.5, 0.7), Woman (0.4, 0.3), Man (0.5, 0.1).

By hand (checked in python):

In words: subtract Man’s two coordinates from King’s, one at a time.

\[\text{King} - \text{Man} = (0.5 - 0.5,\; 0.7 - 0.1) = (0.0,\; 0.6)\]

In words: add Woman’s coordinates to that result, one at a time; you land exactly on Queen’s spot.

\[(0.0,\; 0.6) + \text{Woman} = (0.0 + 0.4,\; 0.6 + 0.3) = (0.4,\; 0.9) = \text{Queen}\]

King − Man is a “royalty” direction. Add it to Woman and you land on Queen. On real data the result is not exactly Queen but has “high cosine similarity with Queen” (slide 13). In the toy example the cosine similarity of the result with Queen is exactly 1.

E. word2vec’s first layer with a one-hot vector (slides 21–22; 2025 Q3c). Vocabulary of 3 words (cat, dog, car), embedding size \(K = 2\). The target embedding matrix \(W^1\) is \(K \times p = 2 \times 3\), one column per word (my made-up numbers):

In words: \(W^1\) holds one column of two numbers per word, and multiplying it by dog’s one-hot vector pulls out dog’s column.

\[W^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad x_{\text{dog}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad h^1 = W^1 x_{\text{dog}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 \\ 0.3 \end{pmatrix}\]

The one-hot vector selects the “dog” column. That column is dog’s embedding. With these numbers cat (0.9, 0.2) and dog (0.8, 0.3) point almost the same way (cosine 0.99), while cat and car (0.1, 0.9) do not (cosine 0.32): similar words, similar embeddings (python check).

Source: L6 slides 5–8, 10–13, 21–22.

The formula, symbol by symbol

1. PMI (slide 10, informal) and the formal set (slide 11).

In words: PMI compares how often two words appear together with how often they would if they had nothing to do with each other, and takes the log.

\[\text{PMI}(word_1, word_2) = \log\left(\frac{P(word_1, word_2)}{P(word_1)P(word_2)}\right)\]

In words: count the pairs inside the window; divide a cell by the grand total to get its share; add up a row (or a column) and divide by the grand total to get how common each word is on its own.

\[Co_{i,j} = \#pair(i, j \mid b), \qquad p_{i,j} = \frac{Co_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}, \qquad p_i = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}, \quad p_j = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}\]

In words: M is PMI with log base 2; the version with the wavy line on top keeps the score if it’s positive and puts 0 otherwise.

\[M_{i,j} = \log_2\left(\frac{p_{i,j}}{p_i p_j}\right), \qquad \tilde{M}_{i,j} = \max\left(\log_2\left(\frac{p_{i,j}}{p_i p_j}\right), 0\right)\]

  • \(p\) = number of words in the vocabulary, so the matrix is \(p \times p\).
  • \(i\) = row = the target word; \(j\) = column = the context word \(c_j\).
  • \(b\) = window size (how many words either side count as “together”).
  • \(Co_{i,j}\) = count of times \(i\) and \(j\) appear within \(b\) words of each other.
  • \(p_{i,j}\) = that count divided by the grand total: the joint probability (“skipgram probability”).
  • \(p_i\), \(p_j\) = row and column shares: how common each word is on its own (“unigram probability”).
  • \(p_i p_j\) = how often they would meet if they were unrelated.
  • \(M_{i,j}\) = PMI; \(\tilde{M}_{i,j}\) = PPMI, negatives replaced by 0.

Read aloud: “PMI is the log of how often two words actually appear together, divided by how often they would appear together by pure chance.” Above 0 = they attract; below 0 = they avoid each other.

Inconsistency to know: slide 10 writes plain “log”, slide 11 uses \(\log_2\), and the Interactive 3 code uses the natural log. In the exam, write the slide-11 \(\log_2\) version (the slide-12 numbers use it). Changing the log base only rescales the scores and never changes the sign [Not in course files — general knowledge].

2. Truncated SVD on M (slide 13).

In words: the big p-by-p PMI table is approximated by three slimmer tables multiplied together, keeping only K patterns.

\[\underbrace{M}_{p\times p} \approx \underbrace{U}_{p\times K}\;\underbrace{S}_{K\times K}\;\underbrace{V'}_{K\times p}\]

  • \(M\) = the PMI matrix; \(K\) = number of dimensions kept (much smaller than \(p\)).
  • \(U\) = one row per word, \(K\) numbers each = the word embeddings (the convention); \(US\) = “Factors”, \(V'\) = “Loadings” (the slide’s names for these pieces).

Read aloud: “Approximate the huge word-by-word PMI table by three thin matrices, and use each word’s row of U as its short, dense vector.” This is the same tool as LSA (the earlier method that runs SVD on the word-count table) on the document-term matrix C, now applied to M.

3. word2vec layers (slides 21–22).

In words: the one-hot vector picks the word’s column out of \(W^1\) (its embedding), \(W^2\) turns that into a score for every word in the vocabulary, and softmax turns the scores into chances of being a neighbour.

\[\underbrace{h^1_t}_{K\times 1} = \underbrace{W^1}_{K\times p}\;\underbrace{x_t}_{p\times 1}, \qquad \underbrace{h^2_t}_{p\times 1} = \underbrace{W^2}_{p\times K}\;\underbrace{h^1_t}_{K\times 1}, \qquad \underbrace{y_t}_{p\times 1} = \text{softmax}(h^2_t)\]

  • \(t\) = one row of the training data (one target–context pair); \(x_t\) = one-hot vector of the target word, “a selection vector”.
  • \(W^1\) = target embedding matrix (“our ultimate goal”); \(h^1_t\) = the selected word’s embedding.
  • \(W^2\) = context embedding matrix; \(h^2_t\) = a score for every word in the vocabulary.
  • \(y_t\) = probability of each word being a context word.
  • No activation on the hidden layer and no bias terms (slide 21). Typical \(K = 300\); train over the data many times (each pass = one epoch) (slide 22).

4. Negative sampling (slides 23–25). The softmax over all \(p\) words is “computationally expensive since p is large”. So add fake pairs with outcome 0, typically 2–5 negatives per real pair, drawn with \(P_\alpha(w) = \frac{count(w)^\alpha}{\sum count(w')^\alpha}\), \(\alpha = 0.75\). Similarity = the dot product \(\vec{w}^{\,t} \cdot \vec{w}^{\,c}\) (“the un-normalized cosine”: a cosine without dividing by the two arrow lengths), turned into a probability by the sigmoid, which is a logistic regression:

In words: the first part turns the dot product of two word vectors into the chance that the pair is real; the second part is the score training pushes up, which is high when the real pair gets a high chance and the fake pair a low one.

\[P(true \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\vec{w}^{\,t} \cdot \vec{w}^{\,c}}}, \qquad L(\theta) = \log\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\right) + \log\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{nx}}\right)\]

  • \(x\) = dot product of the target with a real context word; \(nx\) = dot product with a negative (random) word.
  • Maximise \(L\): make real pairs’ dot products big and negative pairs’ dot products small.

Example (python): a real pair with dot product 2 gets \(P(true) = 1/(1+e^{-2}) = 0.88\).

5. Cosine similarity (slide 29). \(\cos = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert\,\lVert b \rVert}\), the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Small angle → close to 1 → similar; it depends on direction, not length (slide 30). The 2025 Q3(d) drawing task is covered in the cosine-similarity chapter.

Source: L6 slides 10–13, 21–25, 29–30.

Reading the course code

The count-based recipe in Interactive 3 (cell 4), “sentence-word matrix -> co-occurrence -> (PMI) -> SVD”:

X = vec.fit_transform(sentences)                  # rows: sentences, columns: words (binary)
C = (X.T @ X).toarray().astype(float)             # C[i, j]: sentences with word i AND j
expected = np.outer(freq, freq) / X.shape[0]      # co-occurrence if words were random
M = np.clip(np.log(C / expected), 0, None)        # PMI, keep only positive surprise = PPMI
vectors = TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_dims).fit_transform(M)

(Lines lightly shortened from the notebook.)

  • Line 1: a binary sentence-by-word matrix (stop words removed, rare words dropped with min_df).
  • Line 2: co-occurrence = how many sentences contain both words. The window here is the whole sentence, not ±b words as on the slides.
  • Line 3: the count you would expect by chance (same idea as \(p_i p_j\)).
  • Line 4: log of observed ÷ expected = PMI, then clip negatives to 0 = PPMI.
  • Line 5: truncated SVD keeps n_dims numbers per word: the embeddings. cosine_similarity then finds nearest neighbours.

word2vec in gensim (the Python package the notebook uses; cells 16, 18): Word2Vec(..., vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=10) and w2v.wv.most_similar(positive=["king","woman"], negative=["man"]). The notebook does not set sg, so gensim uses CBOW by default [Not in course files — general knowledge]. No outputs are saved, so the notebook does not show the answers; the takeaways say:

  • PMI does for embeddings what tf-idf (the re-weighting that turns down words found in almost every document) did for documents: it removes the “frequent word” noise. Raw counts make common words everybody’s neighbour.
  • You need enough SVD dimensions to hold the structure.
  • Meaning drifts: “union meant the Constitution in 1850 and the Soviet Union in 1980” (222 State of the Union speeches, 1791–2018).
  • “Word arithmetic works only for relations the corpus actually contains.” On a small corpus, king − man + woman may fail. That is a point for using pre-trained embeddings vs training on your own small business corpus.

Course examples and applications

  • Kozlowski et al. (2019), “The geometry of culture” (slide 28): word embeddings trained on US text for each decade of the 20th century. They measure the cosine similarity between a “class” dimension and five cultural dimensions (beautiful–ugly, educated–uneducated, employed–unemployed, graceful–awkward, fine–coarse). Roughly read from the chart: aesthetic and manners dimensions (graceful, fine) fall, while education and employment rise. The meaning of class shifts over time.
  • Labonne & Thorsrud (2023), “Risky news and credit market sentiment” (slides 29–30): define concepts as sums of word vectors, \(gr_t = recession_t + risk_t\) and \(fc_t = credit_t + leverage_t + funding_t\), then compute each month \(RNI_t = \frac{gr_t \cdot fc_t}{\lVert gr_t \rVert \, \lVert fc_t \rVert}\). A small angle (vectors pointing the same way) = high RNI; a near right angle = low RNI.
  • Kapfhammer, Larsen & Thorsrud (2020) (slide 31): a “transition risk for Norway” index built with word embeddings, moving with climate-policy events (EU ETS, Paris agreement).
  • Levy et al. (2015) (slide 26): “Neural Network-based methods might not outperform the simple SVD.” Counting + SVD can match word2vec.
  • Alternatives (slide 26): GloVe; Doc2vec (documents, “an alternative to LDA”); Word Mover’s Distance.

Exam boxes

How this shows up on the exam In 2025 this was a whole block worth 15 points:

    1. “What is the underlying assumption … and the PMI matrix?” (5 points). The assumption is the idea that words keeping similar company mean similar things. The PMI matrix is the table scoring how much more often two words meet than by chance.
  • (b) word2vec vs BERT, in two sentences at most (2.5 points). word2vec gives each word one fixed map spot; BERT gives a new spot in each sentence.
  • (c) What a one-hot vector is (all 0s with one 1 in the word’s slot) and how word2vec’s first layer uses it (2.5 points).
  • (d) Draw two arrows with high cosine similarity (small angle between them) and two with low cosine similarity (big angle) (5 points).

The 2025 True/False block also had an item on SVD on the PMI matrix (squeezing that big table down to a few numbers per word). Yes, that is a course method for making word embeddings (slides 3, 9, 13).

Likely new questions: CBOW vs Skipgram (guess the middle word from its neighbours, or the neighbours from the middle word), negative sampling (training against a few random fake neighbours), PPMI and rare words, King − Man + Woman (word arithmetic), a small PMI sum, and an example of how researchers use embeddings.

What a top-grade answer must include

Q3(a) model answer (5 pts): “Word embeddings rest on the distributional hypothesis, ‘You shall know a word by the company it keeps’ (Firth 1957): words used in similar contexts have similar meanings, so meaning can be learned from co-occurrence. The PMI matrix is a \(p \times p\) matrix (\(p\) = vocabulary size) with words in rows and context words in columns. Each cell is \(\log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p_j}\): how much more often word \(i\) appears within \(b\) words of word \(j\) than it would by chance. Negative values are set to 0 (PPMI). The matrix is large and sparse, so we apply truncated SVD and use the rows of \(U\) as dense, \(K\)-dimensional word embeddings.”

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The big idea is that words keeping similar company have similar meanings, so you can learn meaning by seeing which words appear near each other. The PMI table has one row and one column per word (\(p\) is the number of words in the word list). Each cell compares how often two words really meet nearby with how often they’d meet by luck; the formula \(\log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p_j}\) is that comparison, and \(b\) is how many words either side count as “nearby”. Negative scores are set to 0, and the huge, mostly-empty table is then squeezed with SVD so each word ends up with a short list of \(K\) numbers: its spot on the map.

Q3(b) model answer (max two sentences): “word2vec gives each word one fixed (static) embedding whatever the sentence, so ‘apple’ the fruit and ‘Apple’ the computer company share the same vector. BERT produces context-specific embeddings, so ‘apple’ gets a different vector in ‘I ate an apple’ than in ‘Apple released a new laptop’.” (The apple example is the one in the 2025 evaluation guideline. “Bank” as river bank vs money bank works the same way [Not in course files — general knowledge].)

What this answer is saying, in plain words: word2vec hands each word one map spot that never changes, so “apple” the fruit and “Apple” the company get the same spot. BERT works out a fresh spot for the word each time, based on the sentence around it.

Q3(c) model answer (2.5 pts): “A one-hot vector is a \(p \times 1\) vector of zeros with a single 1 at the word’s position in the vocabulary. In word2vec the target word enters as a one-hot vector \(x_t\). The first layer computes \(h^1_t = W^1 x_t\) with no activation and no bias, so \(x_t\) just selects the column of \(W^1\) belonging to that word: a ‘selection vector’. That column is the word’s \(K\)-dimensional embedding, and \(W^1\) (the target embedding matrix) is what word2vec learns.”

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A one-hot vector is a list as long as the word list, all 0s except a 1 in the word’s slot. word2vec feeds the word in this way. Multiplying it by the first grid of dials (\(W^1\)), with no squashing and no extra nudge, picks out that word’s own column. That column, \(K\) numbers long, is the word’s spot on the map, and learning that grid is the whole point of word2vec.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying Skipgram guesses the word from its neighbours (its context). That is CBOW. Skipgram goes the other way: it guesses the neighbours from the word.
  • Saying PMI favours common words. It over-rewards rare ones: a rare pair that meets once or twice can get a huge score.
  • Calling the PMI table \(n \times p\) (documents × words, like the word-count table). It is \(p \times p\): words in the rows and words in the columns.
  • Saying word2vec gives a word different spots in different sentences. It gives one fixed spot.
  • Writing three sentences when the question says “max two”.
  • Saying the neural-network maps always beat the counting-plus-SVD maps. Levy et al. (2015) found they might not.
  • Calling word embeddings supervised (learned from human-made labels). They are self-supervised or unsupervised: the text supplies its own answers.

Key terms to use

  • distributional hypothesis (similar company means similar meaning)
  • Firth (1957) (“know a word by its company”)
  • embedding is location (a word’s meaning = its map spot)
  • co-occurrence (two words appearing near each other)
  • window size \(b\) (how many words either side count)
  • \(p \times p\) matrix (words in rows, words in columns)
  • PMI (how much more than chance two words meet)
  • PPMI (PMI with negative scores set to 0)
  • add-one smoothing (add a pretend 1 to every count)
  • large and sparse (huge table, mostly zeros)
  • truncated SVD (squeeze the table to K strongest patterns)
  • matrix \(U\) (SVD output; its rows are word vectors)
  • dense vectors (short lists with few zeros)
  • cosine similarity (angle between two word arrows)
  • word2vec (neural network that learns map spots by guessing)
  • CBOW (guess the middle word from neighbours)
  • Skipgram (guess the neighbours from the middle word)
  • self-supervised (the text supplies its own answers)
  • one-hot / selection vector (all 0s, one 1; picks a column)
  • target embedding matrix \(W^1\) (grid holding each word’s map spot)
  • context embedding matrix \(W^2\) (grid scoring words as possible neighbours)
  • \(K = 300\) (each word gets 300 numbers)
  • negative sampling (train against a few random fake neighbours)
  • static vs contextual (context-specific) embeddings (one fixed spot vs a new spot per sentence)
  • BERT (model giving context-specific spots)
  • transformer (the network design behind BERT and chatbots)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Word embeddings can be obtained by applying SVD to a PMI matrix.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Word embeddings are each word’s short list of numbers, its spot on the meaning map. The PMI matrix is the big words-by-words table that scores how much more often two words meet than by chance. SVD is a way to squeeze a big table down to its few strongest patterns. Can you get the word spots by squeezing that table?

    True. Why: That is one of the two course methods (the other is word2vec). The table is huge and mostly zeros; squeezing it keeps the main patterns and gives each word a short list of numbers. It’s like summing up a long survey with a few key scores per person. (Source: L6 slide 13, “Use the SVD … not on C, but on M!”.)

  2. T/F: “Skipgram predicts a word from its surrounding words.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Skipgram is one of word2vec’s two guessing games. Surrounding words are the neighbours within the window. Does Skipgram guess the middle word from its neighbours?

    False. Why: That’s the other game, CBOW. Skipgram goes the other way: it sees the middle word and guesses its neighbours. Think of CBOW as a fill-in-the-blank exercise, and Skipgram as “here’s a word, which words would you expect around it?”. (Source: L6 slide 14.)

  3. T/F: “PMI gives rare word pairs low weight, so add-one smoothing is not needed.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: PMI scores how much more often two words meet than by luck. Weight means how much a pair counts. Add-one smoothing means adding a pretend 1 to every count. Does PMI give rare pairs small scores, so no fix is needed?

    False. Why: It’s the opposite: PMI gives rare pairs big scores. “Apricot” appears only twice, yet apricot–pinch gets the top score in the table, 2.25. One lucky meeting looks hugely “more than chance”. It’s like a café regular you’ve seen once with a stranger: one sighting and you’d wrongly guess they’re best friends. Adding a pretend 1 to every count calms that down. (Source: L6 slides 11–12, “PMI gives rare words high weight”.)

  4. T/F: “In word2vec, the word ‘bank’ gets the same embedding in ‘river bank’ and ‘bank loan’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: An embedding is the word’s spot on the meaning map. “Bank” means a riverside in one phrase and a money business in the other. Does word2vec give it one spot for both?

    True. Why: word2vec hands each word one fixed spot, whatever sentence it’s in. It’s like a phone contact list with only one entry for two different people named “Sam”. Models such as BERT fix this by giving a new spot in each sentence. (Source: L6 slide 27.)

  5. Calculate: With the slide-12 counts, compute PMI(digital, computer).

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Use the chapter’s small count table (slide 12, 19 counts in total) to work out how much more often “digital” and “computer” meet than they would by luck.

    Answer: \(p_{ij} = 2/19\), \(p_i = 4/19\), \(p_j = 3/19\); ratio \(= \frac{2/19}{(4/19)(3/19)} = 38/12 = 3.17\); \(\log_2 3.17 = 1.66\) (matches the slide).

    Why: The pair met 2 times out of 19 (that’s \(p_{ij}\)). “Digital” makes up 4 of the 19 counts (\(p_i\)) and “computer” 3 of the 19 (\(p_j\)). By luck you’d expect them to meet (4/19) × (3/19) of the time. They really met about 3.17 times as often as that. The log base 2 asks “2 to what power gives 3.17?”, and the answer is 1.66. Above 0 means “more than luck”. (Source: L6 slide 12.)

  6. Explain (2–5 sentences): Why does negative sampling make word2vec practical?

    Model answer: In plain word2vec the softmax output must be computed over the whole vocabulary for every training pair, which is expensive because \(p\) is large. Negative sampling instead adds a few (2–5) random “negative” word pairs with outcome 0 for every real pair, drawn by word frequency raised to 0.75. The model then only has to tell real context words from these fakes, a logistic-regression (sigmoid) task on the dot product of the two word vectors. It pushes real pairs’ vectors together and negative pairs’ vectors apart (L6 slides 23–25).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Without the trick, word2vec must score every word in the whole word list for each example, which is very slow because the list is huge. With the trick, each real neighbour pair is matched with 2 to 5 random fake pairs, and the model only has to say “real or fake?”. It’s a yes/no question, like spotting the one real photo among a few fakes, instead of ranking every photo in the world. Real pairs get pulled closer on the map, and fake pairs get pushed apart.

Sources: Lecture 6 “Neural Networks and Word Embeddings” (Thorsrud), slides 2–14, 20–31; notebook GRA4164_Interactive_3_Embeddings_and_llms.ipynb (cells 0–27).

Part IV — Large Language Models and the Transformer

14. What a Large Language Model is

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 T/F (b) and (f) came straight from this lecture, and it is the base for all of Block 4.

Start from zero

The problem. You type “What is the capital of Norway?” into ChatGPT. A second later it writes “The capital of Norway is Oslo.” Nobody wrote that answer in advance, and the program is not looking it up in an atlas. So how can a computer write a fresh, sensible answer to almost any question? The answer is a Large Language Model: a program that has read a huge amount of text and learned which pieces of text tend to come next. This chapter explains what that program is, how it is trained, and what it can and cannot “remember”.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Collect text. The builders gather an enormous pile of text: books, websites, code and more.
  2. Cut it into pieces. A tool called a tokenizer cuts the text into small pieces called tokens (whole words or bits of words). Each piece gets an ID number, because computers can only work with numbers.
  3. Start with a blank brain. The model is a giant set of adjustable numbers, called weights or parameters. Picture billions of tiny volume knobs. At the start they are set at random, so the model’s guesses are rubbish.
  4. Play “guess the next piece” (pre-training). The model reads a stretch of text, hides the next token, and guesses it. Then it checks the real token. The knobs get nudged a tiny bit so the right answer becomes a little more likely next time. This repeats billions of times. The text itself supplies the right answers, so no person has to mark anything. That is why it is called self-supervised.
  5. Teach it to be a helpful assistant (post-training). People write example questions with good answers, and the model learns from them (supervised fine-tuning). Then it is rewarded for answers people prefer, or for answers that can be checked, like code that passes a test.
  6. Freeze the knobs and answer (inference). When you use the model, the knobs no longer move. Your question goes in as tokens. The model gives every possible next token a chance (a probability), picks one, adds it to the text, and goes round again. It stops when the answer is complete.
  7. Everything it “sees” sits in one window. Your question, the chat so far, any uploaded files and the answer being written all sit in the context window. Anything outside that window is not seen. Uploading a file changes what is in the window. Only more training changes the knobs.

A tiny example by hand. Let’s reuse the chapter’s own example (Lecture 7, slide 7) and go slowly.

  1. You type three words: “This course is”.
  2. The tokenizer turns them into three ID numbers: 17, 42 and 9. (The slide says these numbers are made up for illustration.)
  3. The model looks at those three IDs and gives a chance to every token it knows. Two tokens get most of it: “useful” gets 50% and “practical” gets 30%. All the other tokens share the remaining 20%. Check: 50 + 30 + 20 = 100, so all the chance is handed out.
  4. One token is picked. Say it picks “useful”, the most likely one. (Real systems often draw at random, weighted by these chances, so “practical” would sometimes win. [Not in course files — general knowledge])
  5. The text is now “This course is useful”, four tokens long. It goes back in at step 1, and the model guesses the fifth token.

The same sentence shows how training works. Suppose the training text really says “This course is useful”. The model sees “This course is”, makes its guess, and gives “useful” 50%. The real next word is “useful”, so the knobs are nudged to make “useful” a bit more likely next time. Nobody had to label anything: the sentence held its own answer.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: writing, summarising, translating and answering common questions, because it has seen so much text of that kind.
  • Breaks: it writes what sounds likely, not what has been checked. So it can invent facts and references with total confidence (hallucination, see Chapter 17).
  • Breaks: it does not learn from your chat. Once something falls outside the context window, the model has no memory of it.
  • Breaks: it never sees letters or digits one by one, only tokens, so spelling and arithmetic can go wrong (see Chapter 15).

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (Large Language Model): a very big computer program that predicts the next piece of text, over and over, to write answers. ChatGPT is a product built on one [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Model: a set of numbers plus rules that turns an input into an output. Like a recipe that turns ingredients into a dish.
  • Parameter / weight: one adjustable number inside the model, like one volume knob. Big LLMs have billions of them. “Parameters” and “weights” mean the same thing here.
  • Training: adjusting the weights by showing the model lots of examples, the way practising scales slowly trains your fingers.
  • Pre-training: the first and biggest training stage: guessing the next token across a huge pile of text.
  • Self-supervised learning: learning where the right answers come for free from the data itself. Covering the next word in a book and checking it is self-supervised.
  • Supervised learning: learning from examples where a person has written the right answer, like emails already marked “spam” or “not spam”.
  • Unsupervised learning: finding patterns with no right answers at all, like sorting customers into groups nobody named in advance.
  • Continued pre-training / mid-training: extra rounds of next-token practice on chosen text, such as long documents or legal texts, to strengthen one skill.
  • Post-training: all the training steps after pre-training that turn a text-guesser into a helpful assistant.
  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) / fine-tuning: extra training on examples of a question plus a good answer written by people. Like a new employee studying model answers. Fine-tuning changes the weights.
  • Preference optimization: training the model to give answers people like better, by showing it pairs of answers and which one was preferred.
  • Reinforcement learning (RL): learning from rewards, like a dog getting a treat for sitting. The model gets a “reward” for good answers.
  • Reward / verifiable result: a score for an answer. A verifiable result is one a computer can check, like “did the code pass its tests?”.
  • Token: a small piece of text the model reads: a word, part of a word, a space or a punctuation mark. “strawberry” is three tokens (Chapter 15).
  • Token ID: the number a token gets in the model’s list. “This” might be number 17.
  • Tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens and swaps each one for its ID number.
  • Vocabulary: the fixed list of all tokens the model knows, like the full box of LEGO pieces.
  • Probability: a chance between 0% and 100%. “50% useful” means the model rates “useful” as a coin-flip likely next token.
  • Transformer: the design (blueprint) that almost all modern LLMs are built on. Chapter 16 explains how it works.
  • Inference / answer time: using a finished model to produce answers, with its weights frozen. Like a chef cooking from a recipe they already know.
  • Inference software: the program that runs the model on a computer and produces the answer.
  • Context: all the text the model can see while answering right now: your question, earlier messages, uploaded files.
  • Context window: the maximum amount of text (counted in tokens) the model can see at once, like the size of a desk where papers must fit.
  • System instructions: hidden instructions the app gives the model before your question, like “You are a polite helper”.
  • Deep neural network: a model built from many layers of simple number-crunching units stacked on top of each other. “Deep” means many layers.
  • Layer / hidden layer: one stage of number-crunching. A hidden layer is any layer between the input and the output, which you do not see directly.
  • Representation: the model’s internal list of numbers that summarises what a piece of text means, like a fingerprint of the meaning.
  • Transformer block: one repeated unit of the Transformer. LLMs stack many of them (Chapter 16).
  • Mixture-of-experts (MoE): a model split into many “expert” parts, where only a few experts work on each token. Like a hospital where each patient sees two specialists, not all 200 doctors.
  • Quantization: storing each weight with fewer digits so the model takes less memory. Like rounding 3.14159 to 3.1.
  • Precision: how many digits a number is stored with. Lower precision = shorter numbers = less memory.
  • Memory (computer memory): the space a computer has to hold numbers while it works.
  • Reasoning at answer time: the model “thinks out loud” with extra hidden text before its final answer. It can help on hard tasks but takes longer.
  • Latency: waiting time before the answer arrives.
  • Open weights: a model whose weights you can download and run yourself. You do not necessarily get its training data or recipe.
  • License: the legal terms saying what you may do with something, like the rules on a rental contract.
  • Hugging Face: a website where people share models and datasets for free, often called the AI community’s open-source hub.
  • Ollama: a free program for downloading and running LLMs on your own computer; the slide shows its model library [Not in course files — general knowledge: what the program does].
  • Retrieval: searching a collection (say, company reports) and fetching the relevant pieces.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first search for relevant text, then paste it into the context so the model can use it. Like handing a student the right page before the question. It changes the context, not the weights.
  • Tools: outside programs the model can ask to run, like a calculator, a web search or a database.
  • Agent: a setup where the model repeats a loop of deciding, using tools and checking, until a task is done, within set permissions.
  • Chat application: using the model through a website or app, like the ChatGPT site.
  • API (application programming interface) / API integration: a doorway that lets your own program send text to the model and get answers back, with no chat window.
  • Local deployment: running the model on your own computer or company servers instead of someone else’s.
  • Memorization: the model storing exact bits of its training text (including mistakes) and repeating them later.
  • Notebook: a file that mixes short pieces of code with their saved results, used in the course’s exercises.

The idea in plain words

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a very big guessing machine. You give it some text. It guesses the next small piece of text. It adds that piece to the text and guesses again. It repeats this until the answer is finished.

That is all it does, even in 2026. The lecture says it plainly: “The basic mechanism is unchanged: a Transformer predicting the next token” (slide 6). (Transformer = the model’s design, explained in Chapter 16; token = a small piece of text, explained in Chapter 15.) What has changed is the size, the training recipes and the software built around the model.

How does it learn to guess well? It reads a huge amount of text. At each spot it hides the next piece, guesses it, checks the real answer, and adjusts itself a tiny bit. The “answers” are just the text itself. Nobody has to label anything by hand. That is why this is called self-supervised learning.

Analogy Think of a student who learns a language by covering the next word in millions of books with a finger, guessing it, then lifting the finger to check. No teacher marks the answers; the book itself is the answer key. After years of this, the student’s “gut feeling” (the weights) is very good at guessing. When you later ask the student a question, they do not keep learning; they just use that gut feeling. Handing them a document to read is like putting a sheet on their desk (context). Sending them on a training course changes their gut feeling (weights).

The exam definition

What an LLM is (slide 4):

  • “A learned set of parameters (weights), used with a tokenizer and inference software to generate language.” (In plain words: the model is a big pile of learned numbers; the tokenizer cuts text into pieces, and the inference software is the program that runs those numbers to write text.)
  • “Most generative LLMs use the Transformer architecture and predict the next token: a word, word fragment, or other symbol.”
  • “Pre-training learns patterns from large datasets; it can also memorize examples and errors.”
  • “Post-training develops instruction following, tool use, and reasoning capabilities.” (Post-training = the training steps after pre-training that turn a text-guesser into a helpful assistant.)

Self-supervised pre-training (slide 7): “the next token in the training text is the target; future tokens are hidden from the prediction.” So the targets come from the text, not from humans. This is why the 2025 statement “Large Language Models are estimated using unsupervised learning” was marked False. The course word is self-supervised: there is a correct answer (the real next token), it just comes for free from the text.

The training pipeline (slide 9) — “common ingredients, not a fixed pipeline”: (Read this list as the usual order of training stages, from first to last.)

  1. Pre-training: “Learn to predict tokens from large collections of text, code, and, for some models, other media.”
  2. Continued pre-training / mid-training (when used): “Add targeted data, for example long documents, domain material, or tool interactions.”
  3. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): “Learn from examples of instructions and desired responses.” (This step is supervised: humans write the example answers.)
  4. Preference optimization / reinforcement learning: “Improve responses using preferences or rewards, including verifiable results such as passing code tests.” (The model is rewarded for answers people prefer, or for answers a computer can check.)

Training vs answering (slide 10): training changes the weights; answering uses fixed weights. The key line: “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.” Slide 20 repeats it for retrieval: “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights. Neither guarantees accuracy.”

The context window (slide 30): one window, measured in tokens, holds the system instructions, conversation history, uploaded or retrieved documents, tool results and the answer being generated. Size: “from a few thousand to about one million tokens, depending on the model”. “Everything the model uses at answer time must fit in the window; nothing else is ‘remembered’ unless the application re-inserts it.” Longer contexts cost more and are slower, and a big window “does not guarantee that every detail is used reliably”.

Other terms the slides define:

  • Deep neural network (slide 8): layers of connected units; “Hidden layers learn representations of the input” (hidden layers = the in-between stages; representations = internal number-summaries of the text); LLMs stack many Transformer blocks.
  • Mixture-of-experts, MoE (slide 12): “only a subset of the parameters is activated for each token.” (Only a few “expert” parts of the model work on each token.)
  • Quantization (slide 14): “stores weights at lower precision, reducing memory needs.” (Each number is kept with fewer digits, like rounding 3.14159 to 3.1.)
  • Reasoning at answer time (slide 11): extra computation before the final answer can help hard tasks “but increases latency and resource use” (latency = waiting time), and “A longer answer or a persuasive explanation does not guarantee correctness.”
  • Open weights (slide 25): “downloadable model parameters; permissions depend on the license.” They “do not necessarily include training data or the full training recipe.” The slide shows the Hugging Face model hub (“The AI community building the future.”) and the Ollama model library. The course outline calls Huggingface “the AI community’s open-source hub for Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing”. So the 2025 statement “HuggingFace is a open source hub for Natural Language Processing” was True. (Notebook 4 also downloads its model from Hugging Face.)
  • RAG, tools, agents (slide 20): (RAG = retrieval-augmented generation: search for relevant text first, then give it to the model.) “RAG: add retrieved evidence to context.” “Tools: run operations outside the model.” “Agents: repeat decisions and tool calls, with permissions and stopping conditions.”

A tiny worked example

Example 1 — the generation loop (slide 7, illustrative numbers from the slide).

Step What happens Slide 7 example
1 Text goes in “This course is”
2 Tokenizer turns it into token IDs 17, 42, 9
3 Model turns IDs into numbers and computes next-token probabilities useful 50%, practical 30%, other tokens 20%
4 One token is selected and appended “This course is useful”
5 Go back to step 1 with the longer text —

Rows = the steps of one loop; columns = what happens and the slide’s example. Check: 50% + 30% + 20% = 100%, so the probabilities cover all tokens. The slide says the IDs and percentages are “illustrative”.

Example 2 — how much of an MoE model works per token (slide 13). DeepSeek-V4-Flash has 284 billion parameters in total and uses about 13 billion per token, pre-trained on more than 32 trillion tokens.

  • Share used per token = 13 / 284 = 0.0458, so about 4.6%.
  • So for each token, roughly 95% of the model sits idle. That is the point of MoE: a huge model that is cheaper to run per token.

Example 3 — context or weights? (slides 10, 20).

Action (rows) Changes the context? Changes the weights?
Upload a PDF to a chat Yes No
RAG: search company reports and paste excerpts in Yes No
Fine-tune on 5,000 labelled support tickets No Yes
Chat with the model for an hour Yes (history is in the window) No (weights are fixed at answer time)

Columns = which part of the system the action changes.

Business-use frameworks (useful for the Block 5 reflection):

  • Four ways to use an LLM (slide 16): chat application (a website or app), API integration (your own program sends text to the model), agent (the model loops through tasks using tools), local deployment (the model runs on your own machine). “The mode determines the cost structure, where data goes, and who is accountable for errors.”
  • A good use case (slide 18): Clear Task, Available Context, Verifiable Results, Manageable Errors, Business Value.
  • Risk grid (slide 19): rows = “Consequences of an error” (lower/higher); columns = “Difficulty of checking the output” (easier/harder).
Consequences of an error ↓ / Difficulty of checking → Easier to check Harder to check
Higher Extract invoice fields for payment — “Validate against original records” Authorize unusual payments — “Require human approval”
Lower Draft marketing copy — “Check before publishing” Summarize feedback — “Ambiguous responses: inspect examples”

Reading the course code

No code in Lecture 7 itself. Notebook 4 (GRA4164_Interactive_4_A_real_LLM_on_your_laptop.ipynb) downloads a small open-weight model from Hugging Face and runs it locally: a live example of “local deployment” and “open weights” (slides 16, 25).

How this shows up on the exam The 2025 exam had two true/false (T/F) items on this chapter. T/F (f) said “Large Language Models are estimated using unsupervised learning” → False. The right word is “self-supervised” (the text supplies its own answers) (slide 7). T/F (b) said “HuggingFace is a open source hub for Natural Language Processing” → True (course outline; slide 25). Hugging Face is a free website where people share AI models. Likely new T/F items:

  • “RAG updates the model’s weights” → False (slide 20). RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: the system looks up documents and pastes the useful bits into what the model reads) changes only what the model reads, not what it has learned.
  • “An LLM updates its weights during each conversation” → False (slide 10). The weights (the huge set of numbers the model learned in training) stay fixed while you chat.
  • “In an MoE model all parameters are used for every token” → False (slide 12). An MoE (mixture-of-experts) model is split into many “expert” parts, and only a few of them work on each token (small piece of text).
  • “Open weights always include the training data” → False (slide 25). Open weights means you can download the learned numbers, not the texts the model learned from.
  • “Bigger is always better” → False (slide 12).

In Block 5 of the exam (the business-case part) you can use slides 16, 18 and 19 to explain where an LLM fits in a business case.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • When you describe how an LLM is trained, use the words “next token” (the next small piece of text) and “self-supervised”. Also say why it is self-supervised: the target (the right answer) is the next token of the text itself, so no human has to label anything.
  • Give the training steps in order: pre-training (reading huge amounts of text and guessing the next token) → (mid-training, an extra in-between round) → SFT (supervised fine-tuning: learning from example questions with answers written by people) → preference optimization/RL (reinforcement learning: rewarding the answers people like better). Name SFT as the supervised step.
  • Explain context vs weights in one sentence, quoting slide 10. Context is what the model reads right now (your prompt and any pasted documents). Weights are what it learned in training.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Calling pre-training “unsupervised”. This was the 2025 trap. The right word is “self-supervised”.
  • Saying the model “learns from your chat” or “remembers you”. The weights are fixed; only the context (what it is reading right now) changes.
  • Saying RAG or uploading documents “retrains” the model. It only gives the model more to read.
  • Thinking one token = one word. A long word can be split into several tokens (see Chapter 15).
  • Claiming a bigger model or a longer answer is automatically more correct (slides 11, 12).

Key terms to use

  • next-token prediction (guessing the next piece of text)
  • parameters, also called weights (the numbers the model learned)
  • Transformer (the model design behind all LLMs)
  • self-supervised pre-training (learning from raw text, no human labels)
  • supervised fine-tuning, SFT (learning from human-written example answers)
  • preference optimization / reinforcement learning (rewarding answers people like better)
  • context vs weights (what it reads now vs what it learned)
  • inference with fixed weights (using the model without changing it)
  • context window, counted in tokens (how much text it reads at once)
  • mixture-of-experts, MoE (only a few expert parts work per token)
  • quantization (storing the numbers more roughly to save memory)
  • open weights (learned numbers anyone can download)
  • Hugging Face hub (free website for sharing AI models)
  • RAG (look up documents, paste them into the prompt)
  • tools (outside programs the model can call, like search)
  • agents (models that plan and carry out steps themselves)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Estimated” here means trained: how the model learns its numbers. “Unsupervised learning” means learning with no right answers at all, only hunting for patterns. So: does an LLM learn with no right answers to check against?

    Answer: False. Why: There is a right answer at every step: the next token (small piece of text) in the book. The model covers it up, guesses, then checks. Because the text supplies its own answers, this is called self-supervised, not unsupervised. Think of a puzzle book with the answers printed at the back: no teacher is needed, but there are still answers to check. (Source: slide 7; 2025 T/F f.)

  2. T/F: “HuggingFace is an open-source hub for NLP.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Open-source” means free for anyone to use and share. A “hub” is a central meeting place, here a website. “NLP” (Natural Language Processing) means getting computers to work with human language. So: is Hugging Face a free, shared website for language AI?

    Answer: True. Why: Hugging Face works like an app store for AI models where most things are free. People upload models, and others download them. The course’s Notebook 4 downloads a small model from there. (Source: course outline; Hugging Face model hub on slide 25; 2025 T/F b.)

  3. T/F: “Giving an LLM a company handbook through RAG changes its weights.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means the system searches documents, such as a handbook, and pastes the useful bits into what the model reads. “Weights” are the numbers the model learned in training, its long-term memory. So: does handing it a handbook change its long-term memory?

    Answer: False. Why: RAG is like an open-book exam. The student looks things up in the handbook during the exam, but their brain is not changed by it. Take the book away and that knowledge is gone. Changing the weights needs extra training, called fine-tuning. The slide puts it as “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights”. (Source: slide 20.)

  4. T/F: “In a mixture-of-experts model only part of the parameters is used for each token.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model is built from many smaller “expert” parts. Parameters are the learned numbers. A token is a small piece of text. So: for each piece of text, does only some of the model do the work?

    Answer: True. Why: Think of a hospital with many specialists. A patient with a broken arm sees the bone doctor, not every doctor in the building. In the same way, each token is sent to only a few experts. DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses about 13 billion of its 284 billion numbers for each token. (Source: slide 12; DeepSeek figures on slide 13.)

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences: Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised, and which training step is supervised?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why do we say the model “marks its own homework” when it first learns? And which later step uses answers written by people?

    Model answer: In pre-training the model reads large amounts of text and, at each position, predicts the next token; the true next token in the text is the target, and future tokens are hidden from the prediction (Lecture 7, slide 7). Because the labels come from the text itself, no one has to label data by hand, so it is called self-supervised rather than supervised or unsupervised. The supervised step comes later: in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) the model learns from examples of instructions paired with desired responses written by people (slide 9).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: First, the model reads a huge amount of text and keeps guessing the next piece. The real next piece in the text is the right answer, so nobody has to write answers by hand; that is why it is called self-supervised. Later, people write example questions with good answers, and the model learns from those. That later step (SFT) is the supervised one.

Sources: Lecture 7 “Introducing Large Language Models” (Vegard H. Larsen, Lecture_llm_intro.pdf), slides 4–20, 25, 29–30; course outline GRA4164_2026.pdf; 2025 exam with evaluation guidelines (GRA4164_2025-11-27_kl_14_EG.pdf).

15. Tokens and tokenization

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(c) (5 points) and T/F (c) asked exactly this.

Start from zero

The problem. A computer cannot read letters. It needs numbers. The first idea is to give every word its own number: “cat” = 1, “dog” = 2, and so on. But what number do you give a word the computer has never seen, like a brand-new product name, a typo like “teh”, or a long Norwegian compound word? You would need millions of numbers and still miss words. The other extreme, one number per letter, makes every sentence very long and slow to process. Tokens are the clever middle way, and this chapter shows how they are built.

How it works, step by step. This is how the most common method, byte-pair encoding (BPE), builds its list of pieces.

  1. Gather example text. Take a big pile of text to learn from.
  2. Start tiny. Cut every word into single letters. Add a small “end of word” marker so you know where each word stops.
  3. Count neighbours. Count how often each pair of side-by-side pieces appears. For example, how often “l” is followed by “o”.
  4. Glue the winner. Take the pair that appears most often and glue it into one new piece, everywhere it appears. Add that new piece to your list of known pieces (the vocabulary).
  5. Repeat. Go back to step 3 with the glued text. Keep going until your list has the size you want. The GPT-4o tokenizer in the course notebook has about 200,000 pieces.
  6. Use the list on new text. To cut up a new sentence, start from its letters and repeat the same glue steps, in the same order. Common words end up as one piece. Rare words end up as a few familiar pieces.
  7. Swap pieces for numbers. Every piece in the list has an ID number. The model only ever receives these numbers.

A tiny example by hand. We reuse the chapter’s own mini text of four words: low, lower, newest, widest.

  1. Cut into letters. low becomes l, o, w, end-marker: 4 pieces. lower gives 6, newest gives 7 and widest gives 7. Total: 4 + 6 + 7 + 7 = 24 pieces.
  2. Starting list. The different letters used are d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w: that is 10. Add the end-marker and the list has 11 pieces.
  3. Count pairs. “l then o” appears in low and in lower: 2 times. Several other pairs also appear 2 times, so there is a tie, and the code takes the first one it met, “l o”.
  4. Glue “l o” into “lo”. It happens in 2 words, and each glue turns 2 pieces into 1. So the text shrinks from 24 to 22 pieces, and the list grows from 11 to 12.
  5. Glue “lo w” into “low”. Again in 2 words: 22 becomes 20 pieces, and the list grows to 13.
  6. Keep going. Four more glue steps (e+s, es+t, est+end-marker, low+end-marker) bring the text down to 13 pieces and the list up to 17. The table further down in this chapter shows every step.
  7. Try a new word. The word lowest was never in the text. Run the same six glue steps, in the same order, on its 7 starting pieces (l, o, w, e, s, t, end-marker). Glue steps 1 and 2 (l+o, lo+w) make “low”. Glue steps 3 to 5 (e+s, es+t, est+end-marker) make “est” with the end-marker. Glue step 6 (low+end-marker) does not apply, because “low” is not at the end of this word. Result: two known pieces, low and est</w>, instead of “unknown word”.

A real tokenizer at work (from the notebook): “strawberry” is one word but three tokens, st | raw | berry. A five-word English sentence costs 6 tokens, while the same sentence in Norwegian costs 8.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: handling new or rare words, because they can always be built from smaller known pieces.
  • Good at: keeping all the text. You can glue the tokens back together and get the exact original.
  • Breaks: the model never sees single letters or digits, so it is weak at spelling, counting letters (“how many r’s in strawberry?”) and arithmetic.
  • Breaks: some languages need more tokens for the same meaning (Norwegian 8 vs English 6). That costs more money and fills the context window faster.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Token: a small piece of text the model reads: a word, part of a word, a space, a punctuation mark or a chunk of digits. “strawberry” = st | raw | berry, three tokens.
  • Tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens and gives each one its ID number.
  • Tokenization: the act of cutting text into tokens.
  • Vocabulary: the fixed list of all tokens a tokenizer knows, like the full box of LEGO pieces you are allowed to build with.
  • Token ID: the number a token has in the vocabulary list, like a product’s barcode.
  • Vocabulary size: how many pieces are in the list. GPT-4o’s tokenizer has 200,019.
  • Subword: a piece smaller than a whole word, like “berry” in “strawberry”.
  • Byte-pair encoding (BPE): the method that builds a vocabulary by gluing the most frequent pair of neighbouring pieces again and again.
  • Byte: the basic unit a computer stores text in; one simple letter like “a” is one byte. BPE got its name from gluing pairs of these [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Pair frequency: how many times two pieces appear side by side in the text.
  • Merge: gluing two neighbouring pieces into one new piece, like snapping two LEGO bricks together for good.
  • End-of-word marker (</w>): a small tag stuck on the last piece of a word, so “est” at the end of a word is kept apart from “est” in the middle.
  • Corpus: the collection of text you learn from. Here: the four words low, lower, newest, widest.
  • Symbol: one piece in the text at a given moment, either a single letter or an already-glued chunk.
  • Sequence / sequence length: a sequence is the text as a row of tokens; its length is how many tokens are in the row.
  • Vocabulary size vs sequence length (the trade-off): a bigger list means fewer, longer pieces per sentence, but a bigger list to store. A smaller list means more pieces per sentence.
  • Rare / unknown word: a word that hardly ever, or never, appeared in the training text.
  • Generalization: doing well on new things you have not seen before, like the new word “lowest”.
  • Multilingual: working in many languages.
  • Compute: the amount of computer work needed, which costs time, money and electricity.
  • Context window: the maximum number of tokens a model can see at once (Chapter 14).
  • Price per token: LLM providers charge by the number of tokens you send and receive, so more tokens = higher bill.
  • Vector: a list of numbers, like [0.2, -1.3, 0.7]. Every token ID is turned into one of these before the model works with it.
  • Bag-of-words (Lecture 2): an older method that counts how often each word appears in a text and ignores word order. There, a “token” meant a whole word.
  • Stemming: chopping words down to a rough root by fixed rules, like “running” → “run”. It can produce non-words like “easili”.
  • Affix: a bit added to the start or end of a word, like “-ing”, “-ed” or “-s”.
  • Porter stemmer: one well-known set of stemming rules.
  • Root: the core of a word, like “run” in “running”.
  • tiktoken: a free Python tool for using OpenAI’s tokenizers [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Encoding (o200k_base): the name of one specific learned vocabulary plus its glue rules; this one is used by GPT-4o.
  • Encode / decode: encode = turn text into token IDs; decode = turn token IDs back into text.
  • GPT-4o: one of OpenAI’s LLMs [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Python / code / notebook cell: Python is a programming language; a notebook cell is one small block of code with its saved output.
  • Counter.most_common: a Python command that lists items from most to least frequent.
  • LLM: Large Language Model, the next-token-guessing program from Chapter 14.

The idea in plain words

An LLM does not read words. It reads tokens: small chunks of text. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a space, a punctuation mark or a chunk of digits. Each token has an ID number in a fixed list (the vocabulary). The model only ever sees these ID numbers.

Why not just use whole words? Because there are too many words, new words appear all the time, and many languages glue words together. Why not single letters? Because then every sentence becomes very long and slow to process. Tokens sit in the middle: common words get one token, rare words get built from a few familiar pieces.

Analogy Think of LEGO. If you only had one brick per possible object (a “castle brick”, a “car brick”), you would need millions of bricks and could not build anything new. If you only had the tiniest 1×1 bricks, every model would take forever to build. LEGO sells a fixed set of common pieces in between, and you can build almost anything from them. A tokenizer’s vocabulary is that fixed box of useful pieces.

The exam definition

  • “A tokenizer splits text into pieces and maps them to vocabulary IDs. Tokens can include spaces, punctuation, or word fragments.” (Lecture 7, slide 29)
  • “Token counts depend on language and formatting; one word need not equal one token.” (slide 29). “tokens are not the same as words” (slide 13).
  • “Token counts matter in practice: prices, context limits, and speed are all measured in tokens.” (slide 29)
  • “Subword methods such as byte-pair encoding (BPE) balance vocabulary size against sequence length.” (slide 29) (In plain words: BPE keeps the list of pieces a manageable size while keeping sentences from getting too many pieces long.)
  • Lecture 9, slide 4: “We do not input words per se, but tokens.” This is the basis for 2025 T/F (c) “The input to a Large Language Model is actually not words, but tokens” → True.
  • 2025 evaluation guideline for Q4(c): tokenization is “the process of breaking down raw text … into smaller, more manageable pieces called tokens”; it “defines what type of units of text that is turned into (computable) vectors” (vectors = lists of numbers the computer can calculate with); tokens give “better handling [of] rare words, makes compute more efficient and improves generalization, makes multilingual modelling easier.”

Contrast with Lecture 2 (bag-of-words). In Lecture 2a, slide 7, tokenization meant “Split text into individual words (tokens) using text.split()” (a Python command that cuts text at the spaces), e.g. “hello world” → {“hello”, “world”}. There a token is simply a word cut out at the spaces. In LLMs a token is a learned subword piece. Same word “token”, two different meanings: say which one you mean.

Contrast with stemming (notebook cells 1–3). Stemming cuts words down to a root by fixed rules (“stripping affixes (e.g., -ing, -ed, -s)”), and the result “may not necessarily be a valid word”. The Porter stemmer’s saved output: running → run, runs → run, but runner → runner, ran → ran, easily → easili, fairly → fairli. Stemming throws information away to shrink the vocabulary for bag-of-words. BPE tokenization keeps all the text: you can glue the tokens back together and get the exact original.

A tiny worked example

Part A — BPE step by step (notebook cells 15–16). The steps (cell 15): (1) Initialization: start with single characters; (2) Counting pair frequencies: count every pair of neighbouring symbols; (3) Merging pairs: merge the most frequent pair into one new token; (4) Updating the vocabulary: replace that pair everywhere in the text; (5) Iteration: repeat until the target vocabulary size is reached.

Corpus (the example text we learn from): low, lower, newest, widest. Each word is split into letters plus an end-of-word marker </w>:

l o w </w> | l o w e r </w> | n e w e s t </w> | w i d e s t </w> → 24 symbols in total (4 + 6 + 7 + 7). The starting vocabulary is the 10 distinct letters (d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w) plus </w> = 11 symbols.

Count the pairs by hand (step 1). Rows = adjacent pairs; column = how often they appear across all four words:

Pair Count Where
l o 2 low, lower
o w 2 low, lower
w e 2 lower, newest
e s 2 newest, widest
s t 2 newest, widest
