t </w> 2 newest, widest
every other pair (w </w>, e r, r </w>, n e, e w, w i, i d, d e) 1 each —

Six pairs tie at 2. The code takes the first one it met, l o (our reading of Counter.most_common, the Python command that ranks items by count; the notebook does not say this). The saved output of the six merges:

Merge Pair merged Corpus after the merge Total symbols
1 l + o lo w </w> | lo w e r </w> | n e w e s t </w> | w i d e s t </w> 22
2 lo + w low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w e s t </w> | w i d e s t </w> 20
3 e + s low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w es t </w> | w i d es t </w> 18
4 es + t low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w est </w> | w i d est </w> 16
5 est + </w> low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w est</w> | w i d est</w> 14
6 low + </w> low</w> | low e r </w> | n e w est</w> | w i d est</w> 13

Rows = merge steps; columns = the pair merged, the corpus afterwards, and the symbol count (computed by us; each merge that hits 2 words removes 2 symbols, the last one hits 1 word). What happened: the frequent piece low and the common ending est (est</w> = “est at the end of a word”) became single tokens. The text got shorter (24 → 13 symbols), and the vocabulary grew by one entry per merge (11 → 17). That is the “vocabulary size versus sequence length” trade-off in action.

Why this helps with rare words (our illustration, using the same six merges): a new word lowest that was never in the corpus is still tokenized as low | est</w> — two meaningful known pieces instead of “unknown word”.

(The notebook’s text in cell 15 describes a possible end result ['low', 'er', 'new', 'est', 'wide']; that is an illustration of where more merges would lead, not the output of the six coded merges.)

Part B — a real tokenizer (notebook cell 18, saved output). tiktoken (a Python tokenizer tool) with the GPT-4o-family encoding o200k_base (the name of its learned list of pieces), vocabulary size 200,019:

Input text (rows) Number of tokens Tokens
The market fell sharply yesterday. 6 The | market | fell | sharply | yesterday | .
Markedet falt kraftig i går. 8 Marked | et | falt | kraft | ig | i | går | .
12345.67 + 89.01 9 123 | 45 | . | 67 | + | (space) | 89 | . | 01
strawberry 3 st | raw | berry

What to see:

  • English vs Norwegian: the same sentence (5 words + full stop) costs 6 tokens in English and 8 in Norwegian. 8 / 6 = 1.33, so 33% more tokens for the same meaning. More tokens means a higher price, more of the context window used, and a harder job for the model (notebook cell 0: “Tokenization is language-dependent”).
  • strawberry = st | raw | berry: the model never sees the letters, which is why LLMs “struggle to spell a word” (cell 0) and miscount the r’s.
  • Numbers are chopped into arbitrary chunks (123 | 45), which is why LLMs are “bad at simple arithmetic” (cell 0).
  • Leading spaces are part of the tokens (” market”), and a space can be its own token.

Reading the course code

pairs[(a, b)] += 1                         # count every neighbouring pair
(a, b), _ = pairs.most_common(1)[0]        # pick the most frequent pair
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")  # load GPT-4o's real tokenizer
toks = enc.encode(s)                       # text -> list of token IDs
" | ".join(enc.decode([t]) for t in toks)  # show each token as text
  • Line 1 (cell 16): loops over every word and adds 1 for each pair of neighbouring symbols. This is BPE step 2, “Counting Pair Frequencies”.
  • Line 2: takes the single most common pair. This is the pair that gets merged (step 3).
  • Line 3 (cell 18): loads the vocabulary of a real model, about 200,000 learned pieces (“real models train millions of merges on terabytes of text”, cell 17).
  • Line 4: turns the sentence into a list of ID numbers, which is what the model actually receives.
  • Line 5: turns each ID back into its text piece so we can see the split; len(toks) gives the token counts in the table above.

How this shows up on the exam 2025 Q4(c) asked: “Describe in general terms what a token is, how it differs from words, and why we might want to use them” (5 points). 2025 T/F (c) said: “The input to a Large Language Model is actually not words, but tokens” → True. A token is a small piece of text, such as a whole word or part of a word. New versions you might see:

  • “one token always equals one word” → False.
  • “BPE merges the least frequent pair” → False. BPE (byte-pair encoding, the method that builds the list of tokens) merges the most frequent pair.
  • “the same sentence costs the same number of tokens in every language” → False.
  • a short “explain how BPE works” question.

What a top-grade answer must include

  1. What a token is: a small unit of text (a word, a word piece, a punctuation mark, or a space). Each token gets an ID number, and that ID is turned into a vector (a list of numbers the model can calculate with).
  2. How it differs from a word: one word can be several tokens (strawberry = st|raw|berry; Markedet = Marked|et). So token counts and word counts differ, and the gap changes from language to language.
  3. Why we use tokens: rare and new words can be built from known pieces. The vocabulary (the fixed list of all tokens) stays a manageable size, and texts do not turn into very long chains of pieces. BPE “balance[s] vocabulary size against sequence length” (sequence length = how many tokens a text becomes). So computing is efficient, it generalises (copes with words it never saw), and it handles many languages.

Bonus: one sentence on BPE: find the pair of neighbouring pieces that appears most often, glue it into one new piece, and repeat.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Defining a token as “a word”. That is the Lecture 2 bag-of-words meaning (text treated as counts of whole words), not the LLM meaning.
  • Giving only the “what” and forgetting the “why”.
  • Confusing tokenization with stemming. Stemming chops words down to a root (so “easily” becomes “easili”) and loses information. Tokenization keeps the full text; it only cuts it into pieces.
  • Saying BPE uses a dictionary written by hand. It is learned from data, by counting which pairs of pieces sit together most often.
  • Saying tokens are always smaller than words. Common words are one token.

Key terms to use

  • token (a small piece of text)
  • tokenizer (the tool that cuts text into tokens)
  • vocabulary / token IDs (the fixed token list and their numbers)
  • subword (a piece smaller than a whole word)
  • byte-pair encoding, BPE (builds tokens by merging frequent pairs)
  • most frequent pair (the two neighbours seen together most)
  • merge (glue two pieces into one new token)
  • vocabulary size vs sequence length (bigger token list, shorter token chains)
  • rare/unknown words (built from smaller pieces it already knows)
  • multilingual (works across many languages)
  • context window and price measured in tokens (limits and costs count tokens, not words)
  • tiktoken / o200k_base (OpenAI’s tokenizer tool and one of its vocabularies)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “The input to a Large Language Model is actually not words, but tokens.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A Large Language Model (LLM) is the “brain” behind a chatbot like ChatGPT. The “input” is what you feed in. A token is a small piece of text: a word, part of a word, a space or a punctuation mark. So: does the model read pieces rather than whole words?

    Answer: True. Why: Before the model sees your text, a tokenizer cuts it into pieces and gives each piece an ID number. The model only ever sees those pieces. It is like LEGO: the model never gets a finished castle, only a box of standard bricks. (Source: Lecture 9 slide 4; Lecture 7 slide 29; 2025 T/F c.)

  2. T/F: “In BPE, each step merges the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: BPE (byte-pair encoding) is the method that builds a tokenizer’s list of pieces. “Adjacent symbols” means two pieces sitting next to each other, like “t” and “h”. “Merge” means glue them into one new piece, “th”. So: at each step, does BPE glue together the pair that shows up most often?

    Answer: True. Why: BPE starts with single letters. It counts which neighbouring pair appears most often in the training text, glues that pair into one piece, and repeats. It is like noticing you type “th” all the time and making one key for it. Watch the wording: most often, not least often. (Source: notebook cell 15, step 3; cell 16 code.)

  3. T/F: “A Norwegian sentence and its English translation use the same number of tokens.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Take one sentence with the same meaning in two languages. Are both cut into the same number of pieces?

    Answer: False. Why: A tokenizer’s pieces fit some languages better than others. In the course notebook, the Norwegian sentence needed 8 tokens and its English translation needed 6. Since limits and prices are counted in tokens, the same message can cost more in one language than another. The slide says: “Token counts depend on language”. (Source: notebook cell 18; slide 29.)

  4. T/F: “Stemming and BPE tokenization both keep all the information in the original text.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Stemming is an older trick that chops words down to a rough root, so “easily” becomes “easili”. BPE tokenization cuts text into pieces. “Keep all the information” means you could rebuild the exact original text afterwards. So: can you get the exact text back from both?

    Answer: False. Why: Stemming throws parts away, so you cannot get the original word back. BPE only cuts: glue the pieces back together and you have the exact text again. Think of cutting a photo into puzzle pieces (BPE) versus trimming its edges off (stemming). Only one of the two keeps everything, so the statement is false. (Source: notebook cell 2.)

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q4c): What is a token, how does it differ from a word, and why use tokens?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: What is the small piece of text an LLM reads? Why is it not always a whole word? And why do LLMs use these pieces at all?

    Model answer: A token is the unit of text an LLM actually reads: the tokenizer splits text into pieces such as whole words, word fragments, spaces or punctuation, and maps each to an ID that is turned into a vector (Lecture 7, slide 29). A token is not the same as a word: a common word may be one token, but “strawberry” becomes st|raw|berry, and a Norwegian sentence needs 8 tokens where its English translation needs 6 (tokenizer notebook). We use subword tokens, for example from byte-pair encoding, because they balance vocabulary size against sequence length: rare or new words can be built from known pieces, the vocabulary stays fixed and manageable, compute is more efficient, and the same scheme works across many languages.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: A token is a piece of text that the model turns into a number, and then into a list of numbers. Some words are one token, others get split into several, and different languages need different numbers of tokens. Using pieces lets the model handle any word, even a brand-new one, with one fixed list of pieces. It also keeps texts short enough to process quickly.

Sources: Lecture 7 Lecture_llm_intro.pdf slides 13 and 29; notebook llm_tokenizers.ipynb cells 0–18 (saved outputs); Lecture 9 Lecture_llm_inputoutput.pdf slide 4; Lecture 2a Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf slide 7; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines Q4(c).

16. Attention and the Transformer

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(b) and Q4(d) (10 points) plus T/F (a) and (i) (4 points).

Start from zero

The problem. Read two sentences: “We sat on the river bank” and “I put my salary in the bank.” Same word, two very different meanings. Older methods gave “bank” one fixed list of numbers, the same in both sentences, so the computer could not tell the two apart. Or take “The dog chased the cat because it was hungry.” To understand “it”, you have to look back at “dog” and “cat” and decide which one fits. So a model needs a way for every word to look at the words around it and update its own meaning. That way is called self-attention, and it is the heart of the Transformer, the design behind every modern LLM.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Turn each token into numbers. Each token gets a list of numbers (its embedding) from a big lookup table. At this point “bank” has the same list in every sentence.
  2. Add the position. The model will look at all words at the same time, so it has no built-in sense of order. A “position pattern” (positional encoding) is added to each word’s list, a bit like stamping a seat number on each word.
  3. Make three versions of every word: query, key and value. Think of a library. You walk in with a question: that is your query. Every book has a label on its spine: that is its key. Inside every book are its contents: that is its value. You check how well each label matches your question, and you read more from the books that match best. In the model, each word’s list of numbers is multiplied by three learned tables to give its query, key and value.
  4. Score the matches. For the word being updated, compare its query with every word’s key. The comparison is a dot product: multiply the matching numbers and add them up. A bigger score means a better match.
  5. Shrink the scores. Divide every score by the square root of the key’s length. This keeps the scores from getting too large.
  6. Hide the future (only in causal models). A model that writes text left to right must not peek at words that come later. So the scores for later words are set to “minus infinity”, which turns into a weight of zero in the next step.
  7. Turn scores into shares (softmax). Softmax turns a row of scores into shares that are all positive and add up to 1. It is like splitting 100% of your attention between the words.
  8. Mix the contents. Multiply each word’s value by its share and add them all up. The result is a new list of numbers for the word that now carries its context. “bank” next to “river” now looks different from “bank” next to “salary”.
  9. Do it several times side by side (multi-head). Several “heads” repeat steps 3 to 8 at the same time, each with its own three tables. Each head is free to pick up a different kind of link between words. Their results are glued together and shrunk back to the original size.
  10. Finish the block, then stack. A small extra network (feed-forward) works on each word. “Add the input back” shortcuts (residual connections) and a tidy-up step (layer normalization) are added. That is one Transformer block. Real models stack many blocks, so meanings get richer layer by layer.

A tiny example by hand. We reuse the chapter’s own made-up example, “the river bank”, and follow only the word “bank”, slowly. In the first table further down, each row is one word, and the columns are that word’s query, key and value. Every list has two numbers. Read a value’s first number as “money-ness” and its second as “nature-ness”.

  1. The lists. “bank” asks with query [1, 1]. The keys (spine labels) are: “the” = [0, 1], “river” = [2, 1], “bank” = [1, 0].
  2. Match “bank” with each word (dot product). With “the”: 1×0 + 1×1 = 1. With “river”: 1×2 + 1×1 = 3. With itself: 1×1 + 1×0 = 1. So “river” is the best match.
  3. Shrink. Each list has 2 numbers, and the square root of 2 is about 1.414. So 1 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 0.707 and 3 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 2.121. The scores are now 0.707, 2.121 and 0.707.
  4. Hide the future. “bank” is the last word, so all three words come before it or are itself. Nothing is hidden in this row. (For “the”, the first word, the later words are hidden, so “the” can only look at itself.)
  5. Softmax. Raise the number e (about 2.718) to the power of each score: about 2.028, 8.342 and 2.028. Add them: 12.398. Divide each by 12.398: 0.164, 0.673 and 0.164. So “bank” gives about 16% of its attention to “the”, 67% to “river” and 16% to itself. (These add to 1.001 only because of rounding.)
  6. Mix the values. The values are “the” = [0.5, 0.5], “river” = [0, 2], “bank” = [2, 1]. Take 0.164 of [0.5, 0.5] = [0.082, 0.082]. Take 0.673 of [0, 2] = [0, 1.346]. Take 0.164 of [2, 1] = [0.328, 0.164]. Add the first numbers: 0.082 + 0 + 0.328 = 0.410. Add the second numbers: 0.082 + 1.346 + 0.164 = 1.592.
  7. Read the result. “bank” started with value [2, 1], more money than nature. After attention it is about [0.41, 1.59], more nature than money. Looking at “river” pulled its meaning towards the riverside.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good at: linking words that are far apart. Every word can look straight at every other allowed word, so “it” can find “animal” even many words back.
  • Good at: speed in training. All words are handled at the same time (in parallel), not one after another, so training is much more efficient.
  • Breaks: long texts get expensive. Every word compares itself with every other word, so doubling the text gives about four times as many comparisons [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Breaks: on its own, attention ignores word order. Without positional encoding, “The cat chased the dog” and “The dog chased the cat” would look the same to it.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Embedding / word embedding: a list of numbers that stands for a word, so the computer can calculate with it. Words with similar meanings get similar lists.
  • Vector: a list of numbers, like [2, 1]. An embedding is a vector.
  • Dimension: one slot in a vector. In [2, 1], the first dimension is 2 and the second is 1.
  • word2vec: an older method that learns one fixed vector per word, whatever sentence it is in.
  • Contextual (context-specific) embedding: a word’s vector after it has looked at its neighbours, so “bank” by a river and “bank” with money get different vectors.
  • Transformer: the model design built from attention layers that all modern LLMs use.
  • Layer / block: one stage of processing. A Transformer block is one full round of attention plus the extra steps; models stack many of them.
  • Attention / self-attention: the step where each word looks at the other words in the same text and mixes in information from the relevant ones. “Self” because the words look at their own sentence.
  • Query: the word’s question, “what am I looking for?”. The question you bring to the library.
  • Key: each word’s label, “what do I offer?”. The label on a book’s spine.
  • Value: each word’s actual content that gets passed on. The text inside the book.
  • Database / information retrieval analogy: the course’s picture of attention as looking things up: match a question to labels, then fetch the contents.
  • Dot product: multiply two lists number by number and add up the results. [1, 1] with [2, 1] gives 1×2 + 1×1 = 3. Bigger means a better match.
  • Compatibility score: the course’s name for the match score from the dot product.
  • Scaling / \(\sqrt{d_k}\): dividing the scores by the square root of the key length, to keep them from getting too big.
  • Square root: the number that, times itself, gives the original. The square root of 9 is 3; of 2 it is about 1.414.
  • \(d\), \(d_k\), \(d_v\): lengths of lists. \(d\) = length of a word’s embedding (typically 512); \(d_k\) = length of each query and key; \(d_v\) = length of each value (both typically 64).
  • \(d_{model}\): another name for \(d\), the length of the word embeddings.
  • Softmax: a rule that turns any row of scores into positive shares that add up to 1. Bigger scores get bigger shares.
  • e / exponential: e is a fixed number, about 2.718. Softmax raises e to the power of each score, which makes every result positive.
  • Attention weight (\(\alpha_{ij}\)): the share of attention word \(i\) gives to word \(j\). In the example, “bank” gives “river” 0.673.
  • Weighted sum / weighted average: adding things up after multiplying each by its share, like a course grade where the exam counts 60% and the project 40%.
  • Causal attention: each word may look only at itself and earlier words, never later ones. Used by models that write text left to right.
  • Bidirectional attention: each word may look at all words, before and after it.
  • Mask / masking: hiding some words from the comparison, here the future words, by setting their scores to minus infinity.
  • Minus infinity (\(-\infty\)): a “smaller than any number” value. After softmax it becomes a share of exactly 0.
  • Matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns.
  • Score matrix / diagonal: the table of all match scores, one row per looking word and one column per looked-at word. The diagonal is the line from top left to bottom right where each word meets itself; “above the diagonal” means later words.
  • Weight matrix (\(W^Q, W^K, W^V, W^O\)): a learned table of numbers that turns one list into another, like a recipe that turns a word’s embedding into its query.
  • Learned: set by training, not written by hand.
  • Parameters: all the learned numbers in the model, including these weight matrices.
  • Multi-head attention / head: running several attention steps side by side; each one is a “head” with its own tables and can notice a different kind of link.
  • Concatenate: glue lists end to end. Gluing [1, 2] and [3, 4] gives [1, 2, 3, 4].
  • Projection: multiplying by one more learned table (\(W^O\)) to bring the glued list back to its original length.
  • Residual connection: adding a step’s input back onto its output, a shortcut so useful information is not lost on the way through many layers.
  • Layer normalization (Layer Norm): rescaling the numbers in each word’s list to a standard range, so training stays steady [Not in course files — general knowledge: what the rescaling does; the slide says it “makes training … easier”].
  • Feed-forward network (FFN): a small extra calculation applied to each word on its own after attention.
  • Linear / non-linearity: a linear step only multiplies and adds, so it can only bend things in straight-line ways. A non-linearity lets the model capture curved, more complex patterns.
  • Deep neural network: a model made of many stacked layers of simple calculations.
  • Feature / representation: a piece of information the model has worked out about a word, stored as numbers.
  • Positional encoding / positional embedding: a list of numbers that says “this is word number 1, 2, 3…”, added to each word’s embedding so the model knows word order.
  • Absolute vs relative position: absolute = “this is word 5”; relative = “this word is 2 places after that one”.
  • Sinusoidal / sine / cosine: sine and cosine are smooth wave patterns that go up and down between −1 and 1. Sinusoidal encoding fills the position list with such waves of different speeds.
  • Composite embedding: word vector plus position vector added together.
  • One-hot: a list that is all zeros except a single 1 that marks which token it is, like ticking one box on a long form.
  • Embedding matrix (\(E\)): the big lookup table with one row (one embedding) for each token in the vocabulary.
  • \(N\) and \(|V|\): \(N\) = how many tokens are in the text; \(|V|\) = how many tokens are in the vocabulary.
  • Encoder / decoder: two halves of the original Transformer. The encoder reads and understands the input; the decoder writes output one token at a time, using causal attention [Not in course files — general knowledge: the encoder’s role; Lecture 9 slide 17 names the decoder’s causal self-attention layer].
  • Cross-attention: attention where the words being written look at the words of another text, for example the sentence being translated [Not in course files — general knowledge: the translation example].
  • GPT-style / BERT-style models: GPT-style models write text and use causal attention; BERT-style models read and understand text and use bidirectional attention [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Long-range dependency: a link between words far apart, like “it” pointing back to “animal” many words earlier.
  • Syntactic / semantic: syntactic = about grammar (who does what to whom); semantic = about meaning.
  • Parallel processing: doing many calculations at the same time instead of one after another.
  • GPU: a computer chip that does thousands of simple sums at once, which suits parallel attention [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Training efficiency: how much learning you get for a given amount of computer time.
  • Interpretability: being able to see why the model did something. Attention weights show which words a word looked at.
  • Robustness: still working well when the input changes a little.
  • Prediction: the model’s guess, here the guess of the next token.

The idea in plain words

Older word embeddings (word2vec, an older method that learns one list of numbers per word) give each word one fixed vector (one fixed list of numbers), whatever the sentence. But words change meaning with context. Lecture 8 uses “bank” (slides 7–8):

  • “I walked along the pond, and noticed that one of the trees along the bank had fallen into the water…” → here “bank” should sit close to “water”.
  • “Hoping on a high return, the bank had issued a lot of credit to the investor” → here “bank” should sit close to “credit”.

Self-attention fixes this. For every word, the model looks at the other words in the sentence, decides how relevant each one is, and mixes their information into a new, context-specific vector. After attention, “bank” in the river sentence and “bank” in the money sentence have different vectors (slide 20: “In Transformers, the word embeddings are context specific”).

The Transformer stacks many such layers, so the representation gets “richer and richer” (slide 9). Slide 9’s example: in “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired”, the word “it” attends most strongly to “animal”.

Analogy Imagine a meeting where each person (word) wants to update their own notes. Each person has a question they want answered (Query), a name tag saying what they know about (Key), and the actual notes they can share (Value). You compare your question with everyone’s name tag. The better the match, the more of that person’s notes you copy into your own. “Bank” asks “what kind of place am I?”, sees that “water” and “pond” have matching name tags, and copies mostly their “nature” notes.

The exam definition

Query, Key, Value — the database analogy (slide 12):

  • Query: “the current item you are looking to find more information about … the representation of a specific word for which the model is trying to determine its contextual relevance”.
  • Key: “the searchable items in the database … what the query is matched against to find relevant information”.
  • Value: “the actual information you want to retrieve … the content that is retrieved if their corresponding key matches the query”.

The three steps (slide 14): (1) Compatibility score: dot product of the query with each key (multiply matching numbers and add them up); higher = more relevant. (2) Weight calculation: softmax (a rule that turns scores into shares) turns the scores into weights that are non-negative and sum to 1. (3) Multiply the weights with the value vectors and sum them: “a new representation of the word that incorporates contextual information”.

Why self-attention is powerful (slide 15): it captures syntactic and semantic relations “without being limited by the sequence’s distance”; handles long-range dependencies (links between words far apart); “Allows for processing data in parallell, rather than sequentially. Implies significant improvements in training efficiency”; and the attention weights give some interpretability (you can look at them to see which words a word paid attention to).

Causal vs bidirectional (slide 11): in “a) A causal self-attention layer” each word sees only itself and earlier words. In “b) A bidirectional self-attention layer” each word sees all words, before and after. The output vectors have “equal size as x_i, but potentially different numerical values” (each new list has the same length as the word’s original list, but different numbers in it). So the 2025 statement “you can have two types of attention; causal- and bidirectional-attention” → True. (GPT-style next-token models use causal attention; BERT-style models use bidirectional attention [Not in course files — general knowledge]; Lecture 9 slide 17 does name the decoder’s “Causal Self-Attention Layer”.)

Left: causal — a1 uses only x1, a2 uses x1 and x2, a3 uses all three. Right: bidirectional — every output uses every input (after Lecture 8, slide 11).

Masking out the future (slide 16): “Remember, it is all about prediction. But, if we know the future, it is easy to predict it. Thus, when traning, Transformers use masking.” Every score above the diagonal of the score matrix (the table of match scores; above the diagonal = words that come later) is set to \(-\infty\) (minus infinity). Since \(e^{-\infty} = 0\), those words get zero weight after the softmax [Not in course files — general knowledge: the \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) step; the slide shows only the −∞ matrix].

Multi-head attention (slide 17): several attention “heads” run side by side, each with its own \(W^Q_c, W^K_c, W^V_c\). Their outputs are concatenated (\(N \times hd_v\)) (glued side by side; \(h\) = the number of heads) and projected back to size \(d\) with \(W^O\) (multiplied by one more learned table to shrink them to the original length). Why: it “Increases the model’s representation capacity. E.g., capturing a richer array of relationships within the data, such as different types of syntactic or semantic connections in a sentence” and “Improves learning dynamics and ensures robustness to input variations”. With the typical sizes on slide 13 (\(d = 512\), \(d_v = 64\)), 8 heads give \(8 \times 64 = 512 = d\) (our calculation). The heads work in parallel, and slide 15 stresses parallel processing as a source of training efficiency. So the 2025 statement “Multi-head attention mechanisms makes estimation of Large Language Models slower and less efficient” → False.

The Transformer block (slides 18–19): MultiHead Attention → add the input back (residual connection) → Layer Normalize (rescale the numbers to a steady range) → Feedforward (a small extra calculation on each word) → residual connection → Layer Normalize.

  • Residual connection: “Makes training the Deep Neural Network easier”; “Enabling feature reuse and avoiding that important features are lost”.
  • Layer Norm: “Makes training the Deep Neural Network easier”.
  • Feedforward: “Adds non-linearity to the mix (self-attention is linear operations)” (linear = only multiplying and adding; non-linearity lets the model capture more complex, curved patterns); “Enables richer feature representations”.

In words: first let each word look at all the words (multi-head attention), then add the original input back, then tidy the numbers with layer normalization.

\[T^1 = \text{MultiHeadAttention}(x_i, [x_1, \ldots, x_N]) \quad T^2 = T_1 + X \quad T^3 = \text{LayerNorm}(T^2)\]

In words: next run each word through the small feed-forward network, add its input back again, and tidy once more; the result \(H\) is what this block hands to the next block.

\[T^4 = \text{FFN}(T^3) \quad T^5 = T^4 + T^3 \quad H = \text{LayerNorm}(T^5)\]

(The slide writes \(T_1\) with a subscript in line 2; it is the same \(T^1\). \(X\) = the input embeddings.)

Positional encoding (Lecture 9, slides 5–8). The input to the first block is token embeddings (a one-hot matrix \(N \times |V|\) times the embedding matrix \(E\), \(|V| \times d\), gives an \(N \times d\) matrix; slide 5). (In plain words: each of the \(N\) tokens picks out its own row from the big lookup table \(E\), so you get one embedding row per token.) “But, to this input matrix we also add so-called positional embeddings.” Why (slide 7):

  • “The Transformer’s self-attention mechanism processes all words in the input sequence simultaneously, but does not automatically understand the position or order of words in a sentence.”
  • “E.g., ‘The cat chased the dog’ and ‘The dog chased the cat’ have the same words but entirely different meanings due to the order of those words.”
  • “By adding these positional embeddings to the word embeddings, the Transformer can maintain information about the sequence order of the input data.”

The position vector is added (⊕) to the word vector: “X = Composite Embeddings (word + position)” (slide 6, example “Janet will back the bill”). There are absolute (“this is word 5”) and relative (“2 words after that one”) types; the “Original Transformer work used so-called sinusoidal function” (slide 7). In Lecture 8 positional encoding appears only as a label in the architecture diagram on slide 3.

A tiny worked example

Our own illustration (made-up numbers, not from the slides). Sentence: “the river bank”. Three tokens, \(d_k = 2\). Normally \(q_i = x_i W^Q\) etc.; here we just pick the query, key and value vectors directly. Read the value dimensions as (money-ish, nature-ish).

Token (rows) Query \(q\) Key \(k\) Value \(v\)
the [1, 0] [0, 1] [0.5, 0.5]
river [0, 1] [2, 1] [0, 2]
bank [1, 1] [1, 0] [2, 1]

Columns = the three vectors each token gets. Note “bank”’s own value [2, 1] leans “money”.

Step 1 — scores \(q_i \cdot k_j\). Rows = the word doing the looking (query); columns = the word being looked at (key).

k(the) k(river) k(bank)
q(the) 0 2 1
q(river) 1 1 0
q(bank) 1 3 1

By hand for the bank row: \(q_{bank}\cdot k_{river} = 1\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 1 = 3\); \(q_{bank}\cdot k_{the} = 1\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1 = 1\); \(q_{bank}\cdot k_{bank} = 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 0 = 1\).

Step 2 — divide by \(\sqrt{d_k} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\), and apply the causal mask (everything above the diagonal becomes \(-\infty\)):

k(the) k(river) k(bank)
q(the) 0 \(-\infty\) \(-\infty\)
q(river) 0.707 0.707 \(-\infty\)
q(bank) 0.707 2.121 0.707

Step 3 — softmax along each row. Bank row by hand: \(e^{0.707} = 2.028\), \(e^{2.121} = 8.342\), \(e^{0.707} = 2.028\); sum = 12.398. Weights: 2.028/12.398 = 0.164, 8.342/12.398 = 0.673, 0.164 (they add to 1; 1.001 here only from rounding).

Attention weights \(\alpha_{ij}\) the river bank
the 1 0 0
river 0.5 0.5 0
bank 0.164 0.673 0.164

“the” can only see itself, so its weight is 1. “river” splits evenly between “the” and itself. “bank” pays most attention to “river”.

Step 4 — weighted sum of values for “bank”: \(0.164 \times [0.5, 0.5] + 0.673 \times [0, 2] + 0.164 \times [2, 1] \approx [0.41, 1.59]\).

“bank” started with value [2, 1] (money-ish). Its new contextual vector is about [0.41, 1.59]: it has moved strongly towards “nature” because it attended to “river”. That is the slide-8 picture of “bank” moving towards “water”, done with numbers. (All numbers checked in Python.)

Positional encoding, tiny example (our illustration, formula from Lecture 9 slide 8). With \(d_{model} = 4\), position \(pos = 1\): dimensions 0 and 1 use \(1/10000^{0} = 1\), giving \(\sin(1) = 0.841\) and \(\cos(1) = 0.540\); dimensions 2 and 3 use \(1/10000^{2/4} = 0.01\), giving \(\sin(0.01) = 0.010\) and \(\cos(0.01) = 1.000\). So \(PE_1 = [0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000]\). Position 2 gives \([0.909, -0.416, 0.020, 1.000]\). Each position gets its own pattern, and it is added to the token’s word vector, element by element.

The formula, symbol by symbol

Lecture 8, slide 13 (copied exactly):

In words: each word’s embedding is multiplied by three learned tables to give its query (question), key (label) and value (contents).

\[q_i = x_i W^Q \qquad k_i = x_i W^K \qquad v_i = x_i W^V\]

In words: the match score between word \(i\) and word \(j\) is the dot product of \(i\)’s query and \(j\)’s key, divided by the square root of the key length.

\[\text{score}(x_i, x_j) = \frac{q_i \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}\]

In words: softmax turns word \(i\)’s row of scores into attention shares that are positive and add up to 1.

\[\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}(\text{score}(x_i, x_j))\]

In words: word \(i\)’s new vector is the sum of the values of itself and the earlier words, each multiplied by its attention share.

\[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i = \sum_{j \le i} \alpha_{ij}\, v_j\]

  • \(x_i\) = the embedding of word (token) \(i\), a row of \(d\) numbers (slide 10).
  • \(W^Q, W^K, W^V\) = learned weight matrices that turn \(x_i\) into a query, key and value. \(W^Q, W^K\) are \(d \times d_k\); \(W^V\) is \(d \times d_v\). “Typical sizes are \(d = 512\) and \(d_k = d_v = 64\).”
  • \(q_i\) = word \(i\)’s query (“what am I looking for?”); \(k_j\) = word \(j\)’s key (“what do I offer?”); \(v_j\) = word \(j\)’s value (“my content”).
  • \(q_i \cdot k_j\) = dot product: multiply matching entries and add. Large = good match.
  • \(\sqrt{d_k}\) = square root of the key length; dividing by it scales the scores down (the “Scale” box in slide 3’s diagram).
  • softmax = turns a row of scores into positive weights that sum to 1 (taken over \(j\) for each \(i\)).
  • \(\alpha_{ij}\) = how much word \(i\) attends to word \(j\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i\) (bold) = the new, context-aware vector for word \(i\).
  • \(j \le i\) = only the word itself and earlier words: this is the causal version. For bidirectional attention the sum runs over all \(j\).

Read aloud: “For each word, compare its query with the key of every allowed word, scale by the square root of \(d_k\), turn the scores into weights with softmax, and take the weighted average of those words’ values.”

Matrix form: the Transformer lecture shows it only as a block chart (slide 3: MatMul → Scale → Mask (opt.) → SoftMax → MatMul), but Lecture 9 slide 18 writes it for cross-attention (attention where one text looks at another text) as \(\text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK'}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\). Either form is fine in the exam; the per-word form above is the one Lecture 8 uses.

Sinusoidal positional encoding (Lecture 9, slide 8, copied exactly):

In words: the even-numbered slots of a position’s vector are filled with a sine wave value that depends on the position and on the slot.

\[PE_{(pos,2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right) \quad \text{even positions}\]

In words: the odd-numbered slots are filled the same way, but with a cosine wave instead.

\[PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right) \quad \text{odd positions}\]

  • \(pos\) = the token’s position in the sequence (1st, 2nd, …).
  • \(i\) = which dimension of the vector we are filling; \(2i\) = even dimensions get a sine, \(2i+1\) = odd dimensions get a cosine. (The slide labels these “even/odd positions”, but they are even/odd dimensions of the embedding. Write “dimensions” in the exam.)
  • \(d_{model}\) = the length of the word embeddings. Read aloud: “Fill the position vector with sine and cosine waves of different speeds, so every position gets a unique pattern.” Slide 8’s advantages: uniqueness (each position has its own vector), relative positions (“the sum of two sinusoids is another sinusoid”, so the model can tell how far apart words are), scalability (works for sequences longer than those seen in training).

How this shows up on the exam

  • 2025 Q4(d) asked: “Describe in intuitive terms the motivation for the self-attention layer within the Transformer block”. In plain words: why does the model need self-attention (the step where each word looks at the other words)? The marking guide wants three things. First, Q, K, V named (Query, Key, Value: what a word is looking for, the label each word shows, and the information each word hands over). Second, the information-retrieval (database search) analogy. Third, the idea that “one token [attends] to earlier/later tokens with varying weights” (each piece pays more attention to some words than to others).
  • 2025 Q4(b) asked: “Why do we typically add positional information to the embeddings entering a Large Language Model?” Embeddings are the lists of numbers that stand for each token. The guide’s answer: self-attention “does not necessarily identify the ordering of the terms. Yet, the ordering is crucial for the meaning”.
  • 2025 T/F (a), on causal and bidirectional attention → True. Causal means each word only looks at earlier words; bidirectional means it looks both ways.
  • 2025 T/F (i), multi-head makes LLMs “slower and less efficient” → False.
  • Possible new items: “masking hides earlier words” → False, it hides future words. “The feed-forward layer adds non-linearity” → True (it lets the model capture curved, more complex patterns, not only straight-line ones). “Positional vectors are concatenated” (stuck on the end) → False, they are added.

What a top-grade answer must include

For self-attention:

  • The problem: a word’s meaning depends on context (e.g. “bank” by a river vs a bank for money), and the helpful words can be far apart.
  • Q, K, V with the database analogy: the Query is your search, the Keys are labels on the files, the Values are what is inside the files.
  • The steps: dot-product scores (a match score between a Query and each Key) → softmax weights (scores turned into shares that add up to 1) → weighted sum of values (mix the Values using those shares).
  • The result is a context-specific embedding (a new list of numbers for the word that fits this sentence).
  • Bonus: all words are handled at the same time (parallel processing), and far-apart words can still link up (long-range dependencies) (slide 15).

For positional encoding:

  • Attention processes all tokens at once, so it is blind to word order.
  • Order changes meaning: “The cat chased the dog” vs “The dog chased the cat”.
  • A position vector (a list of numbers standing for “1st place”, “2nd place” and so on; built from sine waves, called sinusoidal, in the original Transformer) is added to each token embedding.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Explaining attention without naming Query, Key and Value. The 2025 marking guide asks for them.
  • Saying causal masking hides past words. It hides future words.
  • Saying multi-head attention is slower, or that self-attention reads one word at a time. It works on all words in parallel.
  • Saying positional encoding is needed “because words have different meanings”. That is attention’s job. Positional encoding is about order.
  • Saying word2vec-style vectors (older word number lists) already depend on context. They do not: each word gets one fixed list, whatever the sentence (slide 20).

Key terms to use

  • contextual (context-specific) embeddings (word numbers that change with the sentence)
  • self-attention (each word looks at the other words)
  • query, key, value (what I seek, my label, what I share)
  • dot product (multiply-and-add score of how well two lists match)
  • compatibility score (how well a Query matches a Key)
  • scaling by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) (dividing scores by the square root of key length)
  • softmax weights (scores turned into shares adding to 1)
  • weighted sum of values (mixing the Values using those shares)
  • causal vs bidirectional (look back only vs look both ways)
  • masking the future, \(-\infty\) (giving later words a minus-infinity score, so zero weight)
  • multi-head attention, with parallel heads and more representation capacity (several attention steps side by side)
  • residual connection (adding a step’s input back onto its output)
  • layer normalization (rescaling numbers to a steady range)
  • feed-forward, adds non-linearity (small extra network for curved patterns)
  • positional encoding/embedding, added to token embeddings (position numbers added to each word’s numbers)
  • sinusoidal (built from sine and cosine waves)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “In the Transformer’s self-attention mechanism, you can have two types of attention; causal- and bidirectional-attention.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The Transformer is the design behind LLMs. Self-attention is the step where each word looks at the other words to work out its meaning. Causal attention: each word may only look at the words before it. Bidirectional attention: each word may look both backwards and forwards. So: do both kinds exist?

    Answer: True. Why: Think of reading a mystery novel. A model that writes text word by word must read like a first-time reader: no peeking at later pages, because they are not written yet. That is causal. A model that only needs to understand a finished text can read the whole page in both directions. That is bidirectional. (Source: Lecture 8, slide 11; 2025 T/F a.)

  2. T/F: “Multi-head attention makes estimation of LLMs slower and less efficient.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Multi-head” means doing the attention step several times side by side; each copy is called a “head” and can look for a different kind of link between words. “Estimation” means training. So: does having several heads make training slow and wasteful?

    Answer: False. Why: The heads work at the same time (in parallel), not one after another. Think of four friends each searching one room for lost keys, all at once: it is not slower than one person, and you cover more ground. The extra heads give the model more ways to spot patterns (more “representation capacity”). (Source: slides 15, 17; 2025 T/F i.)

  3. T/F: “In causal attention, the scores for future words are set to −∞ before the softmax.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Each word gives every other word a score for how useful it is. Softmax is the step that turns scores into shares that add up to 1 (like 70%, 20%, 10%). −∞ means minus infinity, lower than any number. So: before turning scores into shares, are later words given the lowest possible score?

    Answer: True. Why: After softmax, a score of minus infinity becomes a share of exactly zero. So future words get zero attention. It is like blacking out the rest of the sentence with a marker so the word cannot peek ahead. (Source: slide 16.)

  4. T/F: “Positional embeddings are added to the word embeddings.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A word embedding is a list of numbers that stands for a word. A positional embedding is a list of numbers that stands for a place in the sentence (1st, 2nd, 3rd and so on). “Added” means you add the two lists number by number, giving one list. So: is the place information added on top of the word information?

    Answer: True. Why: Attention on its own cannot tell word order, but order matters (“the cat chased the dog” vs “the dog chased the cat”). So each word’s numbers get its position’s numbers added on top, like stamping a seat number onto each ticket. The list stays the same length; nothing is stuck on the end. (Source: Lecture 9, slides 5–6, “word + position”.)

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q4d): What is the motivation for the self-attention layer?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Motivation” means the reason it exists. So: why does an LLM need a step where the words look at each other?

    Model answer: A word’s meaning depends on its context: “bank” means something different next to “water” than next to “credit”, and the helpful words can be far away in the sentence (Lecture 8, slides 7–9). Self-attention lets each token build a new, context-specific embedding by looking at the other tokens with different weights. It works like retrieving from a database: each token’s Query is compared with every token’s Key by a dot product, softmax turns these scores into weights that sum to one, and the new representation is the weighted sum of the Values. Because all tokens are processed in parallel, this handles long-range dependencies and makes training efficient (slide 15).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: The same word can mean different things, and the clue can be far away in the sentence. Self-attention lets each word check all the other words and mix in information from the useful ones. It works like a search: each word sends out a question, compares it with every word’s label, and takes more from the best matches. All words do this at once, which makes it fast and lets far-apart words connect.

Sources: Lecture 8 “Transformers” (Leif Anders Thorsrud, Lecture_llm_transformer.pdf), slides 3, 5–20; Lecture 9 “LLMs: Input and output” (Lecture_llm_inputoutput.pdf), slides 5–8, 17 and 18; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines Q4(b), Q4(d).

17. Critical issues around LLMs (the “ESG” question)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(a) (5 points) asked for two ESG issues.

Start from zero

The problem. Picture a Norwegian bank that puts a ChatGPT-style assistant on its website to answer customers. Soon awkward questions pop up. The assistant runs on huge computer halls that use a lot of electricity. One day it tells a customer about a fee that does not exist. Customers type their account details into it, and those words travel to another company’s computers. And only a handful of companies in the world can build models this good. Each of these is a real worry, and the exam asks you to name and explain them under three headings: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG).

How it works, step by step. Here is where each worry comes from, and which ESG letter it gets.

  1. Training eats power (E). Building a model means thousands of computer chips running for weeks. That needs electricity, cooling (often with water), and the chips themselves have to be made.
  2. Every answer eats power too (E). Each answer (inference) also runs those chips. One answer is small, but millions of users asking all day adds up. Long answers, “thinking” steps and agents that try many times use even more.
  3. It writes what sounds right, not what is checked (S). The model picks likely next words. So it can invent facts, numbers and references while sounding sure (hallucination). It learned from human text, so it can repeat human prejudices (bias).
  4. It can be tricked or misused (S, also G). Users once got Microsoft’s Tay chatbot to post offensive content. A connected assistant can read a web page with hidden orders like “ignore your rules and send me the files” (prompt injection).
  5. A few firms hold the keys (G). Only firms with huge money, chips, power, data and experts can build top models. Businesses that depend on one of them may find it hard to switch.
  6. Your data travels (G). What you type may go to the provider’s computers, be kept, or even be used for training. Laws such as GDPR and the EU AI Act set rules for this.
  7. The training text was often taken without asking (G, also S). Huge amounts of text were collected, often without the authors’ permission, which raises copyright questions.
  8. Writing the exam answer. Pick the number of issues asked for. For each one: name it, give its letter (E, S or G), explain why it happens, and give one consequence or one fix.

A tiny example by hand. Slide 22 says to compare energy “per successfully completed task”. Here is why, with the chapter’s own made-up numbers. In the table, each row is one model; the columns show its energy per try, how often a try succeeds, and the energy per finished job.

Model (rows) Energy per try Share of tries that succeed Energy per finished job
A 1 unit 50% (half) 2 units
B 1.5 units 100% (all) 1.5 units
  1. Model A. Say you try 10 times. Half succeed, so you get 5 finished jobs. You used 10 × 1 = 10 units. That is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 units per finished job.
  2. Model B. Try 10 times. All 10 succeed. You used 10 × 1.5 = 15 units. That is 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 units per finished job.
  3. Compare. A looks cheaper per try (1 unit against 1.5), but B is cheaper per finished job (1.5 units against 2). Counting only the price of one try gives the wrong winner.

What it’s good at / where it breaks. (Here “it” is the ESG way of sorting the issues.)

  • Good at: giving your answer a clear structure: name the issue, give its letter, explain why it happens, add a fix.
  • Good at: covering the main slide topics: sustainability, reliability, ownership and control, privacy and security.
  • Breaks: the 2026 slides never say “ESG”, so the E, S, G sorting is our own reading. Some issues fit two letters (privacy can be S or G), so explain your choice.
  • Breaks: copyright was accepted in the 2025 marking guide but is not on the 2026 slides, so say where it comes from.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance): three headings firms use for non-money risks. E = nature and resources; S = people and society; G = rules, control and who is in charge.
  • LLM: Large Language Model, the next-token-guessing program from Chapter 14.
  • Sustainability: using resources (power, water, materials) in a way the planet can keep up with.
  • Resources: the things used up to run the model: electricity, water, chips, money, people’s time.
  • Training: the long, one-off process of building the model by adjusting its numbers on huge amounts of text.
  • Inference / repeated inference: using the finished model to answer. “Repeated” because it happens again for every question from every user.
  • Chip / GPU: the computer parts that do the model’s sums. GPUs are chips that do many sums at once [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Data centre: a big building full of computers that run services like LLMs [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Cooling / water use: computers get hot; cooling them often uses water.
  • Carbon footprint: the amount of greenhouse gas released because of something, for example from making the electricity it uses.
  • Hardware / workload / electricity supply: hardware = the physical computers; workload = how much work they are given; electricity supply = where the power comes from (wind and water power vs coal).
  • Reasoning (at answer time): the model writing hidden “thinking” text before the final answer, which uses more computing.
  • Long context: giving the model a lot of text to read at once, which costs more computing.
  • Agent / agent steps: a setup where the model repeats a loop of deciding and using tools until a job is done. Each loop round is a step.
  • Efficient model: a model that does the same job with less computing.
  • Per successfully completed task: measuring cost per finished job, counting the failed tries and the human checks too.
  • Retries: asking again because the first answer was not good enough.
  • Rebound effect: when something gets cheaper, people use it much more, so total use can still go up [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Ownership and control: who owns the models and the computers they run on, and who decides who may use them.
  • Infrastructure: the basic equipment everything runs on: chips, data centres, cloud services, power lines.
  • Frontier model / frontier training: the newest, most powerful models, and the very costly process of training them.
  • Capital: money for investment.
  • Barriers to entry: things that make it hard for new firms to join a market, like needing billions of kroner before you can start.
  • Monopoly: one firm controlling a whole market.
  • Concentration: a few firms holding most of the market at some level, such as chips or cloud hosting.
  • Cloud hosting: renting computing power in someone else’s data centre over the internet.
  • Distribution: how the model reaches users, for example through apps or built into office software.
  • Dependency / vendor lock-in: relying so much on one supplier that switching is hard or costly, like a phone that only works with one charger.
  • Switching provider / exporting data: moving to another company, and taking your own data with you.
  • Open weights: a model whose learned numbers you can download and run yourself. You do not necessarily get its training data.
  • Licence: the legal terms saying what you may do with something.
  • Training data / training recipe: the text the model learned from, and the full step-by-step method used to train it.
  • Reliability: whether answers are correct, backed by evidence and fit for the task.
  • Hallucination: the model inventing facts, numbers, quotes or references that are not true, while sounding confident.
  • Bias: a systematic slant in the answers, for example treating some groups unfairly, learned from the training text.
  • Sensitivity (to wording): getting a different answer when you ask the same thing in slightly different words.
  • Evidence / sources: the documents or facts that back up an answer.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first search for relevant text, then give it to the model to use in its answer. The found sources still need checking.
  • Benchmark: a standard test used to score and compare models, like a school exam for AI.
  • Verification: checking an answer against something trustworthy before you rely on it.
  • Responsibility / harm: who answers for damage the model’s output causes, such as abuse, misleading claims or unfair treatment.
  • Overly agreeable output: the model telling users what they want to hear instead of what is true.
  • Tay chatbot (2016): a Microsoft chatbot on Twitter that users quickly taught to post offensive messages; it was taken down [Not in course files — general knowledge: the details].
  • Prompt injection: hidden instructions placed in a document or web page that try to take over an assistant that reads it.
  • Connected assistant / tool permissions: an assistant that can use outside tools (email, files, payments); permissions say which tools it may use.
  • Consequential action: an action with real effects, like sending money or deleting files.
  • Privacy: keeping personal information about people safe and under their control.
  • Security: protecting systems from attack or misuse.
  • Personal data: any information about an identifiable person, like a name, address or account number.
  • Confidential information: business secrets or private material that should not be shared.
  • Retention / processing location: how long the provider keeps what you send, and in which country its computers handle it.
  • Authorized: officially allowed. An assistant should only see records the user is allowed to see.
  • GDPR: the EU’s main law protecting personal data. It applies to personal data in prompts and answers.
  • EU AI Act: the EU’s law setting rules for AI systems, including duties for firms that provide general-purpose AI models.
  • General-purpose AI model provider: a firm that offers a model usable for many tasks, like an LLM maker.
  • High-risk uses: uses where mistakes can seriously hurt people, such as hiring or credit decisions; stricter rules apply [Not in course files — general knowledge: the examples].
  • Copyright: the legal right of authors to control copies of their work.
  • Memorization: the model storing exact bits of its training text and repeating them later.
  • Mitigation: a step that reduces a risk, like human checks before payments.

The idea in plain words

LLMs are useful, but they come with real costs and risks. The course groups them into four questions (slide 21): what resources do they use, who controls them, can we trust what they say, and where does our data go?

The 2025 exam called these “Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) issues”. The 2026 slides do not use the word “ESG”, so you have to sort the slide topics into E, S and G yourself. That is easy once you see the mapping below.

Analogy Think of a new factory in town. E: it uses lots of electricity and water. S: its products are mostly great but sometimes faulty, and a faulty product can hurt people. G: one or two owners control it, it holds customers’ personal data, and the government has rules about what it may do. An LLM raises the same three kinds of worries.

The exam definition

The four headline issues (slide 21, exact):

  • “Sustainability: What resources do training and repeated inference consume?” (inference = using the model to answer)
  • “Ownership and Control: Who controls the models, infrastructure, and access?”
  • “Reliability: Are outputs accurate, supported by evidence, and appropriate for the task?”
  • “Privacy and Security: Where does data go, and what can a connected system do with it?”

Sustainability (slide 22): “Both training and inference consume electricity; cooling, water use, and chip production also matter.” The footprint “varies with model size, hardware, workload, and the electricity supply.” “Reasoning, long contexts, and repeated agent steps can increase computation per task. Efficient models can reduce it.” “Compare resources per successfully completed task; include retries and human checking.” “No universal carbon cost per prompt.” Discussion: “If each request becomes cheaper, what happens when usage grows?” (Cheaper use can lead to much more use, so total resource use can still rise: the rebound effect [Not in course files — general knowledge].)

Responsibility (slide 23): “Harm can come from biased, abusive, misleading, or overly agreeable outputs.” Historical example: Microsoft’s Tay chatbot, 2016 (users got it to post offensive content [Not in course files — general knowledge]). “Prompt injection: malicious instructions in a document or website try to redirect a connected assistant.” (A connected assistant is one that can use tools such as email or files.) Remedy: “Restrict tool permissions, review consequential actions, and keep records of what happened.”

Dangerous monopoly? (slide 24): frontier training (building the newest, most powerful models) needs “substantial capital, chips, power, data, and expertise. These create barriers to entry.” (Barriers to entry = things that make it hard for new firms to compete.) But “the market is not a single monopoly”; concentration can occur at “chips, cloud hosting, models, and distribution” (a few firms can dominate any of these levels). “Open weights and smaller models broaden access, but do not remove infrastructure costs or dependencies.” Business question: “Can you switch provider, export your data, or run an alternative model?”

Open models (slide 25): open weights = “downloadable model parameters; permissions depend on the license”; they “do not necessarily include training data or the full training recipe.”

Can we trust the output? (slide 26): “Hallucinations: Models can invent facts, numbers, quotations, and references, even when they sound confident.” “Bias and sensitivity: Outputs can reflect training biases and change with wording or context.” Sources from search/RAG must be checked; use a calculator or code for arithmetic; benchmark scores (results on standard AI tests) “alone do not establish business reliability”. “Best Practice: Decide how an answer will be checked before relying on it.”

Privacy (slide 27): prompts and uploads “may contain personal or confidential information. Use approved services and minimize what you share.” Retention, training use and processing location (how long your data is kept, whether it trains future models, and where it is handled) “depend on the product and contract; verify them.” Retrieval and agents “should only access records the user is authorized to see.” “Regulation: GDPR applies to personal data in prompts and outputs. The EU AI Act’s obligations for general-purpose AI model providers have applied since August 2025; rules for high-risk uses were postponed in 2026 to 2027–2028.”

Copyright / training data used without permission. The 2025 evaluation guideline for Q4(a) accepted: “electricity/energy consumption and carbon footprint, large data needed - often used without permission/copy right issues. Other answers might also be ok, but need to be well grounded.” Copyright is not on the 2026 slides. It is still a safe answer because the 2025 guideline accepts it. The closest 2026 slide point is that pre-training “can also memorize examples and errors” (slide 4; slide 12 also lists “memorization”).

A tiny worked example

Mapping the slides onto E, S and G. The course gives the issues; the E/S/G sorting is our reading (the slides do not use “ESG”).

ESG letter (rows) Course issue Slide One concrete point to write
E Environmental Sustainability 21, 22 Electricity for training and inference; cooling, water, chip production; more reasoning/agent steps = more compute
S Social Reliability (hallucination, bias) 21, 26 Invented facts and references said with confidence; outputs reflect training biases
S Social Responsibility (abuse, Tay, prompt injection) 23 Tay 2016; biased, abusive or “overly agreeable” outputs
G Governance Ownership and control / dangerous monopoly 21, 24, 25 Barriers to entry; concentration in chips, cloud, models; lock-in; open weights only partly help
G Governance Privacy and security, regulation 21, 27 Personal data in prompts → GDPR; EU AI Act; agents’ access rights; prompt injection as a security risk
G (also S) Copyright / training data without permission 2025 guideline only Large training sets often used without permission

Columns = the course’s name for the issue, where it is in Lecture 7, and a point you can write. Privacy and prompt injection can be argued as S (harm to people) or G (rules, control, security). Either works if you explain it.

Worked numbers on “per successfully completed task” (our illustration, made-up numbers). Model A uses 1 unit of energy per request but succeeds only half the time, so a task needs on average 2 tries: 1 / 0.5 = 2 units per completed task. Model B uses 1.5 units per request and succeeds 100% of the time: 1.5 / 1 = 1.5 units per completed task. The “cheaper” request is the more expensive way to finish the job. This is exactly why slide 22 says to compare “per successfully completed task; include retries”.

Model answer (2025 Q4a: “Discuss shortly two of these”)

Issue 1 — Environmental: energy and carbon footprint. Both training and using (inference) an LLM consume a lot of electricity, and cooling, water use and chip production add to the footprint (Lecture 7, slide 22). The footprint depends on model size, hardware, workload and how clean the electricity is, and reasoning, long contexts and repeated agent steps raise the computation per task. A firm should therefore compare resource use per successfully completed task, including retries and human checks, and choose an efficient or smaller model where it is good enough. Also, as requests get cheaper, total use may grow, so the overall footprint can still rise.

Issue 2 — Social: reliability (hallucination and bias). LLMs can invent facts, numbers, quotations and references while sounding confident, and their outputs can reflect biases in the training data and change with the wording of the prompt (slide 26). This can mislead customers or decision makers and treat groups unfairly; the Tay chatbot in 2016 showed how quickly a system can produce abusive content (slide 23). The mitigation is to decide how an answer will be checked before relying on it: check sources, use code or a calculator for numbers, and keep human review for consequential decisions.

Alternative second issue — Governance: copyright and data use (accepted by the 2025 guideline, not on the 2026 slides). LLMs need very large training datasets, and these are often collected without the permission of the authors, which raises copyright and consent questions. Because pre-training can also memorise examples (slide 4), a model may reproduce protected or personal text in its output.

How this shows up on the exam 2025 Q4(a) (5 points) asked: “We discussed several Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) issues related to Large Language Models in this course. Discuss shortly two of these.” ESG means three kinds of worries: harm to the environment (E), to people and society (S), and questions of who controls and regulates things (G, governance). Expect the same question, a variant (“discuss one governance issue”), or T/F items such as:

  • “Only training, not inference, consumes energy” → False (slide 22). Inference means using the model after training, for example each time someone asks it a question.
  • “Open weights always include the training data” → False (slide 25). Open weights means you can download the model’s learned numbers.
  • “GDPR applies to personal data in prompts” → True (slide 27). GDPR is the EU’s privacy law; a prompt is what you type into the model.
  • “the LLM market is a single monopoly” → False (slide 24). A monopoly means one company controls the whole market.

It also feeds the Block 5 reflection: when you propose an LLM for survey text, name a pitfall (a risk) such as hallucination (the model making things up) or privacy.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • Exactly the number of issues asked (two).
  • Each issue named and labelled E, S or G.
  • The mechanism for each, meaning why it happens. Examples: computers need power both for training and for inference (every use); models predict text that sounds right, not facts that were checked; a few firms own the chips and the models; prompts carry personal data.
  • One consequence or mitigation for each (what goes wrong, or how to reduce it).
  • Energy/carbon is the safest first choice, because the 2025 marking guide names it. For the second, pick copyright (also in the 2025 guide) or any well-grounded issue from the slides (reliability, ownership and control, privacy).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Listing four issues in one line each with no explanation. “Discuss” means explain.
  • Saying only training costs energy. Using the model costs energy too.
  • Writing vague “ESG” issues (“AI is dangerous”) with no mechanism (no why).
  • Stating copyright is on the 2026 slides. It is not. Say it is a well-known issue that was accepted in the 2025 marking.
  • Confusing hallucination (inventing content) with bias (a systematic slant: leaning the same way again and again).

Key terms to use

  • sustainability (not using up what the future needs)
  • electricity for training and inference (power for learning and for every use)
  • cooling, water, chip production (hidden resource costs behind the computers)
  • resources per successfully completed task (cost per job done right)
  • ownership and control (who owns and steers the models)
  • barriers to entry (why newcomers cannot easily compete)
  • concentration (power held by a few firms)
  • vendor lock-in / switching provider (stuck with one supplier, hard to leave)
  • open weights and licences (downloadable models and their usage rules)
  • reliability (can you trust the output?)
  • hallucinations (confident, made-up content)
  • bias (a systematic slant in the answers)
  • verification (checking outputs before you rely on them)
  • responsibility (who answers when something goes wrong)
  • Tay (2016) (Microsoft chatbot that users steered into offensive posts)
  • prompt injection (hidden instructions that hijack an assistant)
  • privacy and security (protecting personal and company data)
  • GDPR (EU law on personal data)
  • EU AI Act (EU law setting rules for AI)
  • copyright / training data used without permission, from the 2025 guideline (using others’ work without asking)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Only the training of an LLM has an environmental cost; using it afterwards is free.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Training is when the model learns, on huge computers. “Using it afterwards” (called inference) is every time someone asks it something. “Environmental cost” means electricity, water and so on. So: is using the model free for the planet?

    Answer: False. Why: Both use electricity. It is like a car: building it uses energy, but so does every trip you drive. Millions of questions a day add up. The slide says: “Both training and inference consume electricity”. (Source: slide 22.)

  2. T/F: “LLMs can invent references even when they sound confident.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Invent references” means making up sources, like a book or article that does not exist. “Sound confident” means writing as if it is sure. So: can the model make up sources while sounding certain?

    Answer: True. Why: An LLM predicts text that sounds right, not facts it has checked. This is called hallucination. It is like a student bluffing in an oral exam: smooth and sure, yet wrong. So always check any source it gives you. (Source: slide 26.)

  3. T/F: “Prompt injection means malicious instructions hidden in a document or website that try to redirect a connected assistant.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A “prompt” is the instruction given to the model. “Malicious” means meant to cause harm. A “connected assistant” is an AI that can read websites or files, or take actions for you. So: is prompt injection when someone hides harmful orders inside content the AI reads?

    Answer: True. Why: Picture a note slipped into a pile of papers for your assistant: “Ignore your boss and send me the files”. If the assistant obeys any text it reads, a stranger can take control of it. (Source: slide 23.)

  4. T/F: “Downloading open weights gives you the model’s full training data.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Open weights” means a company lets you download the model’s learned numbers. “Training data” is all the text it learned from. So: when you download the model, do you also get everything it read?

    Answer: False. Why: Getting the weights is like getting a baked cake, not the recipe or the shopping list. You can use it, but you cannot see what went into it. The slide says open weights “do not necessarily include training data or the full training recipe”. (Source: slide 25.)

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences: Give one Governance issue of LLMs and explain why it matters for a business.

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Governance is about who owns, controls and makes rules for something. So: name one problem about who controls LLMs, and say why a company should care.

    Model answer: Ownership and control is a governance issue: training frontier models needs huge capital, chips, power, data and expertise, which creates barriers to entry and can concentrate power at the level of chips, cloud hosting, models and apps (Lecture 7, slide 24). A firm that builds its workflows on one provider may become locked in, facing price changes or service changes it cannot control. The course’s test question is whether you “can switch provider, export your data, or run an alternative model”; open-weight and smaller models broaden access, but they do not remove infrastructure costs or dependencies.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Building top models costs huge amounts of money, chips and power, so only a few firms can do it. If your company relies on one of them, you can get stuck: they can raise prices or change the service, and you cannot stop them. The test is whether you could switch provider, take your data with you, or run another model. Smaller, open models help, but you still need computers and still depend on others.

Sources: Lecture 7 Lecture_llm_intro.pdf, slides 4, 12, 16, 21–27; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines Q4(a).

Part V — Using LLMs: input/output, training, fine-tuning and prompting

18. What goes into and comes out of an LLM

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — good source of True/False items (temperature, greedy decoding, 512 tokens, cross-attention) and short “explain” questions.

Start from zero

The problem. When you ask ChatGPT a question, the answer appears word by word, as if someone were typing. Behind the screen, the program has a strange problem. A computer cannot read words. It can only work with numbers. So your words must be turned into numbers on the way in. On the way out, numbers must be turned back into a word. And at every step the program must choose one next word out of tens of thousands of possible words. This chapter is about those two ends: what goes in, what comes out, and how one word gets picked.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Cut the text into pieces. The pieces are called tokens. A token is often a whole word (“cat”). Sometimes it is a piece of a word, or a punctuation mark.
  2. Look up each piece in a big table. The table gives every token its own fixed list of numbers, a bit like a secret code. That list is the token’s embedding.
  3. Add “where am I?” numbers. A second list of numbers says where the token sits in the sentence (1st, 2nd, 3rd …). It is added on top of the first list. Now each token carries both “which word” and “where”.
  4. Let the words talk to each other. The lists pass through many layers. In each layer, every token “looks at” the other tokens and updates its numbers. (This is attention, chapter 16.)
  5. Score every possible next word. Take the numbers of the very last token. Compare them with every token in the vocabulary. Each candidate gets a raw score. A high score means “fits well here”.
  6. Turn scores into chances. A step called softmax turns the raw scores into probabilities. They are all positive and add up to 100%.
  7. Pick one word. Either always take the top one (greedy), or roll a weighted dice (sampling). A dial called temperature decides how lopsided the dice is.
  8. Add it and go again. The chosen word is stuck onto the end of the text, and the whole thing runs again for the next word. This repeats until the answer is done.

A tiny example by hand. The text so far is “So long and thanks for”. Imagine the model has only 3 candidate next words: “all”, “the” and “fish”. Their raw scores are 2, 1 and 0. (These are the same made-up scores as in Part 3 of the worked example further down.)

Turning scores into probabilities (softmax, temperature 1).

  1. Make every score positive by raising the number \(e\) (about 2.718) to the power of the score. “all”: \(e^2 = 7.389\). “the”: \(e^1 = 2.718\). “fish”: \(e^0 = 1\).
  2. Add them up: 7.389 + 2.718 + 1 = 11.107.
  3. Divide each one by the total. “all”: 7.389 / 11.107 = 0.665. “the”: 2.718 / 11.107 = 0.245. “fish”: 1 / 11.107 = 0.090.
  4. Check: 0.665 + 0.245 + 0.090 = 1.000. So “all” gets 66.5%, “the” 24.5% and “fish” 9%.

Picking a word. With greedy decoding the model always writes “all”, because it has the highest probability. With sampling, it rolls a weighted dice. Out of 1,000 rolls you would expect about 665 “all”, 245 “the” and 90 “fish”.

Turning the temperature dial. Temperature is a number we divide the scores by before softmax.

  • Cautious (temperature 0.5). Dividing by 0.5 doubles the scores to 4, 2 and 0. Then \(e^4 = 54.598\), \(e^2 = 7.389\), \(e^0 = 1\). The total is 62.987. “all” now gets 54.598 / 62.987 = 0.867, so 86.7%. The favourite wins even more often.
  • Adventurous (temperature 2). Dividing by 2 halves the scores to 1, 0.5 and 0. Then \(e^1 = 2.718\), \(e^{0.5} = 1.649\), \(e^0 = 1\). The total is 5.367. “all” now gets 2.718 / 5.367 = 0.506, so about 50.6%. “fish” rises to 1 / 5.367 = 0.186, almost 1 in 5.

So a low temperature makes the model play safe. A high temperature makes it take risks.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: one simple loop (score, pick, add, repeat) can write long answers, one token at a time.
  • Good: one dial, temperature, lets you choose between “same answer every time” and “varied, creative answers”.
  • Breaks: the input has a size limit. Text that is too long gets cut off without warning, or causes an error.
  • Breaks: greedy picking gives dull, repetitive text. High temperature gives surprising words, and at very high values, nonsense.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that has learned from huge amounts of text to predict what text comes next. Like a phone’s autocomplete, but far bigger.
  • token: one small piece of text the model reads, often a word, sometimes part of a word or a comma. “Unhappy” might be two tokens: “un” + “happy”.
