  • vocabulary (\(|V|\)): the full list of tokens the model knows. \(|V|\) means “how many tokens are on the list”. Like the full list of words in a dictionary.
  • vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order, such as (0.1, 0.2). Like a row of measurements for one person: height, weight.
  • matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns. A spreadsheet full of numbers.
  • dimension (\(d\)): how many numbers are in each list. A list of 2 numbers has \(d = 2\).
  • embedding: the list of numbers that stands for one token. Like a postcode that stands for a street.
  • embedding matrix (\(\mathbf{E}\)): the big lookup table with one row of numbers per token in the vocabulary. Like a phone book: name in, number out.
  • one-hot vector (one-hot row): a row of zeros with a single 1 that marks which token it is. Like a row of light switches with only one switched on.
  • positional embedding: a second list of numbers that tells the model where a token sits in the sentence. Like a seat number at a cinema.
  • sinusoidal: built from smooth wave shapes (sine and cosine waves). Here, a recipe for making the seat-number lists.
  • Transformer layer: one processing stage inside the model where tokens exchange information. Like one round of discussion in a group, repeated many times.
  • attention / self-attention: the step where each token looks at the other tokens and decides which ones matter for it. Like reading “it” and glancing back to see what “it” refers to.
  • causal self-attention: attention where a token may only look at itself and earlier tokens, never later ones. Like reading a book with the next pages glued shut.
  • bidirectional: each token may look both backwards and forwards in the text. Like reading the whole page before deciding what a word means.
  • cross-attention: attention where the part that writes the output looks at the part that read the input. Like a translator glancing back at the original sentence while writing the translation.
  • query, key, value (Q, K, V): three lists made from each token for attention. The query is “what am I looking for?”, the key is “what do I offer?”, the value is “here is my content”. Like a library search: your question, the book labels, the books themselves.
  • scaled dot-product attention (\(d_k\)): the attention formula: compare queries with keys by multiplying, divide by the square root of \(d_k\) (the length of each key) so the numbers don’t get too big, then softmax.
  • dot product: multiply two lists number by number and add up the results. (1, 0.5) and (1.0, 0.0) give 1×1.0 + 0.5×0.0 = 1.0. A quick “how well do these two match?” score.
  • hidden state (\(h^L_N\)): the list of numbers the model holds for a token after a layer. \(h^L_N\) is the one for the last token (\(N\)) after the last layer (\(L\)). Like the model’s final “summary note” about the text so far.
  • context window / maximum length: the most tokens the model can read at once. Like the size of a desk: only so many pages fit.
  • truncation: cutting off the part of the text that doesn’t fit. Like a photocopier that drops the last page of a too-long document.
  • computer memory: the working space a computer uses while it calculates. Attention needs a lot of it for long texts.
  • BERT: a well-known model family that reads text in both directions and is used to understand text (for example, to judge if a review is positive).
  • GPT: a well-known model family that reads left to right and is used to write text, one token at a time. ChatGPT belongs to this family.
  • [CLS] token: a special token put at the start of the text in BERT. Its final numbers are used as a summary of the whole text.
  • masked words: words hidden in a sentence that the model must guess, like a fill-in-the-blanks exercise.
  • pre-training: the first, huge training stage where the model learns from masses of ordinary text (chapter 19).
  • logit (\(u\)): the raw score a model gives each possible next token, before it is turned into a probability. Can be any number, even negative. Like a judge’s raw marks before they are converted to percentages.
  • softmax: the step that turns raw scores into probabilities: raise \(e\) to each score, then divide by the total. The results are all positive and add up to 1.
  • \(e\) / exponentiate: \(e\) is a fixed number, about 2.718. “Exponentiate” means raise \(e\) to a power, such as \(e^2 = 7.389\). It turns any score into a positive number, and bigger scores into much bigger numbers.
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0.665 means 66.5%, about two times in three.
  • probability distribution (\(y\)): the full set of probabilities for all options, adding up to 1. Like a weather forecast: 70% sun, 20% cloud, 10% rain.
  • language modelling head (LM head): the final part of the model that turns the last token’s numbers into one score per vocabulary token. Like the “results board” at the end of a quiz.
  • transpose (\(E'\) or \(\mathbf{E}^T\)): the same table turned on its side, so rows become columns.
  • unembedding layer: the slides’ name for using \(\mathbf{E}\) turned on its side at the output, to go from numbers back to token scores.
  • weight / parameter: one adjustable number inside the model, set during training. Think of a dial. Big models have billions of them.
  • weight tying: using the same table \(\mathbf{E}\) both to read tokens in and to score tokens out. One phone book used in both directions.
  • training: the process that sets all the dials so the model predicts well (chapter 19).
  • decoding (choosing a word): the rule for picking one token from the probabilities. (Careful: the word “decoding” also has a second meaning, see decoder below.)
  • greedy decoding: always pick the token with the highest probability. Like always ordering the most popular dish on the menu.
  • random sampling: pick a token at random, but weighted by its probability. Like drawing a ball from a bag with 665 red, 245 blue and 90 green balls.
  • top-k sampling: keep only the \(k\) most likely tokens, throw the rest away, then sample among those. With \(k = 2\), only the top two are allowed.
  • re-normalise: rescale the kept probabilities so they add up to 1 again. If 0.665 and 0.245 are kept, divide each by their sum 0.910.
  • top-p (nucleus) sampling: keep the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least \(p\), then sample. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • temperature (\(\tau\)): a number the scores are divided by before softmax. Low = cautious and predictable; high = adventurous and varied. Like a “boldness” dial.
  • deterministic: gives exactly the same result every time for the same input. A calculator is deterministic; a dice is not.
  • autoregressive: each new token is added to the input and used to predict the next one. Like writing a story where each sentence builds on what you wrote before. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • encoder: the part of a model that reads the whole input and turns it into meaning-filled number lists, one per word.
  • decoder: the part of a model that writes the output one token at a time, using what it has written so far.
  • encoding (in the encoder–decoder sense): turning the input into those meaning-filled number lists.
  • encoder–decoder model: a model with both parts: one reads, one writes. The original Transformer was built like this for translation.
  • translation: turning a sentence in one language into another, e.g. English to Norwegian.
  • sentiment classification: sorting a text by feeling, such as positive or negative.
  • extraction: pulling a specific fact out of a text, such as the amount on an invoice.
  • notebook / cell: a notebook is a document that mixes code and text and runs in a web browser. A cell is one box of code or text in it. Like a recipe book where each step can be “cooked” by pressing a button.
  • model.generate, do_sample, max_new_tokens: code commands from the notebook. generate asks the model to write text; do_sample says whether to roll the dice; max_new_tokens caps how many tokens it may write.
  • AutoModelForCausalLM: the code command that loads a left-to-right, next-token (GPT-type) model.
  • T/F: a True/False exam question.

The idea in plain words

An LLM is a machine that reads a piece of text and guesses the next token. It does this in three steps:

  1. Turn tokens into numbers. Each token (a word or a piece of a word) gets a row of numbers from a big lookup table. A second row of numbers that says where the token stands in the sentence is added on top.
  2. Mix the numbers through many Transformer layers. This is where attention happens (see chapter 16).
  3. Turn numbers back into a guess. The last layer gives a score to every token in the vocabulary. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Then the model picks one token, adds it to the text, and starts again.

How it picks that token is called decoding. You can always take the top token (greedy), roll a weighted dice (random sampling), roll the dice only among the top few (top-k), or make the dice fairer or more lopsided first (temperature).

Analogy Think of a very well-read friend playing “finish my sentence”. First they look up what each word means in their head (the lookup table). Then they think about how the words relate (the Transformer layers). Finally they have a gut feeling for every possible next word: “all” feels very likely, “fish” not very likely. Temperature is how adventurous the friend is feeling. On a cautious day (low temperature) they almost always say the obvious word. On a wild day (high temperature) they often say something surprising.

The exam definition

Input (slides 4–6). “The input in the first block must be word embeddings, not words!” More precisely, “We do not input words per se, but tokens.” Let \(|V|\) be the size of the vocabulary and \(d\) the length of each embedding. The sentence of \(N\) tokens is written as an \(N \times |V|\) matrix of one-hot rows (each row is all zeros except a single 1 that marks which token it is). Multiplying it by the embedding matrix \(\mathbf{E}\) (\(|V| \times d\)) “is just selecting … the elements in \(\mathbf{E}\) that correspond to the sequence”. Then “to this input matrix we also add so-called positional embeddings”. The word embedding and the position embedding are added, not placed side by side. Why positions are needed, and the sinusoidal formula (a recipe built from wave shapes), are covered in chapter 16.

Maximum length (slide 9). How long the input can be “really depends on the exact model”. The original BERT takes 512 tokens. The GPT series takes “some thousand tokens”. The limit comes mainly from computer memory (self-attention is expensive). If the input is too long, it “might be truncated automatically”, which can change your output, or it “might throw an error”. (Newer models have a context window from “a few thousand to about one million tokens”, Lecture 7 slide 30. The notebook model’s window is 32,768 tokens, Notebook 4 cell 22.)

Output (slides 10–12). “The output is typically a prediction: the likelihood of the next word in the sequence.” The language modelling head (the final part of the model that turns numbers into next-word scores) takes the final-layer output of the last token only, \(h^L_N\), and predicts the token at position \(N+1\).

In words: take the last token’s final list of numbers, score it against every token in the vocabulary (that gives \(u\)), then turn those scores into probabilities (that gives \(y\)).

\[u = h^L_N\,E' \qquad y = \mathrm{softmax}(u)\]

\(u\) are the logits (one raw score per vocabulary token). \(E'\) is the transpose of the embedding matrix (the same table turned on its side). Slide 11 writes \(\mathbf{E}^T\) and calls it the “unembedding layer”; it is the same thing. Weight tying: “E is used to form the input and to re-shape the output. And, E can be learned during training!” (In plain terms: one table does both jobs, and its numbers are set during training.)

Decoding (slide 13). From the probability vector \(y\), how do we choose one word?

  • Random sampling “works bad because low probability words are chosen too often”.
  • Greedy decoding (always take the most likely word) “produces text that is generic and often quite repetitive”.
  • Top-k sampling: “Throw away words that are not among top-k, re-normalize output probabilities (rescale them so they add up to 1 again), and do random sampling. Down-side: k is fixed, but the shape of the probability distribution shifts in different contexts.”
  • Temperature sampling: \(y = \mathrm{softmax}(u/\tau)\), then random sampling. “τ < 1 sharpens the probability distribution. τ > 1 flattens the probability distribution.”
  • Top-p is listed on the agenda (slide 3) but no slide explains it. [Not in course files — general knowledge] Top-p (“nucleus”) sampling keeps the smallest group of top words whose probabilities add up to at least \(p\), re-normalises, and samples. So the number of kept words changes with the context, which fixes top-k’s downside.

The chosen token is added to the input and the model runs again: “So long and thanks for” → “all” → “all the” … (slide 15). [Not in course files — general knowledge] This loop is called autoregressive generation.

Encoding and decoding (slides 16–18).

  • Encoding = “representing the input sequence … into new word representations that capture the sequence meaning and the contextual relationship between the words”. The encoder outputs one vector per input word.
  • Decoding = generating “an output sequence, one element at a time, based on the encoded representations of the input sequence as well as what it has generated so far”.
  • The lecture “mostly described a decoder structure”. The original Transformer was an encoder–decoder model for translation: “I am a dog” → “Jeg er en hund”.
  • The decoder block has a causal self-attention layer (each word may only look at earlier words) and a cross-attention layer (the writing part looks at the reading part’s output). In cross-attention the queries come from the decoder, and the keys and values come from the encoder (slide 18). The \(W\)’s are tables of dials learned in training, and \(H\) stands for the number lists coming out of a layer.

In words: the questions (Q) are made from what the decoder has written so far, while the keys (K) and the contents (V) are made from the encoder’s reading of the input sentence.

\[Q = W^Q H^{dec(i-1)} \quad K = W^K H^{enc} \quad V = W^V H^{enc}\]

In words: compare each question with every key, shrink the scores by dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\), turn them into weights with softmax, and use those weights to blend the values.

\[\mathrm{CrossAttention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK'}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

The queries stand for “the decoder’s current state” (what it has written so far). The keys pick out which parts of the input are relevant. The values supply the content. The formula is the same scaled dot-product attention as in chapter 16; only the source of Q versus K, V differs.

BERT-type vs GPT-type models. The slides never put these side by side, so here is what they do say, combined.

Rows = a feature; columns = the two model families.

Feature BERT-type GPT-type
Which part of the Transformer Encoder: “Bidirectional Transformer Encoder” (L9b slide 22) Decoder: the structure “mostly described” in L9a (slide 16)
Attention Bidirectional: each word sees all words (L8 slide 11, chapter 16) Causal: each word sees only itself and earlier words (L8 slide 11)
Pre-training task Predict “masked words” (L9b slide 4) Predict “the next word” (L9b slide 4)
Typical use Understanding a text: sentiment classification with a head on the [CLS] token (L9b slide 22); extracting embeddings (L9b slide 23) Generating text token by token (L9a slides 13–15)
Max length named in slides Original BERT: 512 tokens (L9a slide 9) “Some thousand tokens” (L9a slide 9)

[Not in course files — general knowledge] The slides list “next word (or masked words)” and “causal vs bidirectional” without saying which model uses which. Matching BERT to masked words plus bidirectional attention, and GPT to next word plus causal attention, is standard knowledge. The notebook’s model is loaded with AutoModelForCausalLM (the code command that loads a next-word model), which makes it a GPT-type (decoder-only, next-token) model.

A tiny worked example

Part 1: the input lookup (slide 5). Take a made-up vocabulary of \(|V| = 4\) tokens and embeddings of length \(d = 2\).

Rows = vocabulary tokens; columns = the two embedding numbers (the matrix \(\mathbf{E}\), \(4 \times 2\)).

Token dim 1 dim 2
the 0.1 0.2
cat 1.0 0.0
sat 0.0 1.0
mat 0.9 0.1

The input “the cat sat” (\(N = 3\)) as one-hot rows. Rows = position in the sentence; columns = vocabulary tokens.

Position the cat sat mat
1 (“the”) 1 0 0 0
2 (“cat”) 0 1 0 0
3 (“sat”) 0 0 1 0

By hand, row 2 times \(\mathbf{E}\): \(0\times(0.1, 0.2) + 1\times(1.0, 0.0) + 0\times(0.0, 1.0) + 0\times(0.9, 0.1) = (1.0, 0.0)\). That is exactly the “cat” row. So the \(3\times4\) one-hot matrix times the \(4\times2\) matrix \(\mathbf{E}\) gives a \(3\times2\) input: (0.1, 0.2), (1.0, 0.0), (0.0, 1.0). A one-hot row is just a pointer that says “fetch this row”. Next, the position embeddings are added (chapter 16).

Part 2: the output head with weight tying (slides 11–12). Suppose the last layer’s output for the last token is \(h^L_N = (1, 0.5)\). The head multiplies by \(E'\), which means taking the dot product of \(h\) with each token’s row. By hand for “cat”: \(1\times1.0 + 0.5\times0.0 = 1.0\). For “mat”: \(1\times0.9 + 0.5\times0.1 = 0.95\). All four logits are \(u = (0.2, 1.0, 0.5, 0.95)\). Softmax gives \(y = (0.149, 0.333, 0.202, 0.316)\) for (the, cat, sat, mat). These add up to 1. The same \(\mathbf{E}\) was used going in and coming out, which is weight tying.

Part 3: temperature (slide 13). Say the next-word candidates after “So long and thanks for” have made-up logits all = 2, the = 1, fish = 0. We apply \(\mathrm{softmax}(u/\tau)\).

Rows = candidate word; columns = temperature τ; each cell = probability (rounded to 3 decimals, so a column may add to 0.999).

Word (logit) τ = 0.5 (sharper) τ = 1 (unchanged) τ = 2 (flatter)
all (2) 0.867 0.665 0.506
the (1) 0.117 0.245 0.307
fish (0) 0.016 0.090 0.186

By hand for τ = 0.5 and “all”: divide the logits by 0.5 to get (4, 2, 0). Exponentiate: \(e^4 = 54.598\), \(e^2 = 7.389\), \(e^0 = 1\). The sum is 62.987, so P(all) = 54.598 / 62.987 = 0.867.

What the table shows:

  • Low τ makes the favourite more dominant. “Fish” almost never gets picked (1.6%).
  • High τ evens things out. “Fish” now gets picked almost 1 time in 5.
  • Greedy decoding picks “all” every time. In Notebook 4, “temperature 0 = always pick the top token” (cell 3). The code switches to greedy for T = 0, because dividing by zero is not possible [Not in course files — general knowledge: the notebook gives no reason].
  • Top-k with k = 2 at τ = 1 drops “fish” and re-normalises the rest: all = 0.665/0.910 = 0.731, the = 0.269.
  • [Not in course files — general knowledge] Top-p with p = 0.9 would keep “all” and “the” too, because 0.665 + 0.245 = 0.910 ≥ 0.9.

The formula, symbol by symbol

In words: score the last token against every vocabulary token, divide the scores by the temperature, and turn the result into probabilities.

\[y = \mathrm{softmax}(u/\tau), \qquad u = h^L_N E'\]

  • \(h^L_N\) = the output vector of the last Transformer layer (\(L\)) for the last token (\(N\)). Its size is \(1 \times d\).
  • \(E'\) = the embedding matrix turned on its side, \(d \times |V|\). This is the same matrix used for the input (weight tying).
  • \(u\) = the logits: one raw score per token in the vocabulary, size \(1 \times |V|\).
  • \(\tau\) = temperature. Dividing by a small τ stretches the gaps between scores. Dividing by a large τ shrinks them.
  • softmax = exponentiate each score and divide by the total, so all values are positive and add up to 1.
  • \(y\) = the probability of each vocabulary token being the next one.

Read aloud: “Take the last token’s final vector, score it against every token’s embedding, divide the scores by the temperature, and turn them into probabilities that add up to one.”

Reading the course code

Notebook 4, cell 3 (the chat() helper), key lines in simplified form:

if temperature == 0:
    out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens)
else:
    out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=True, temperature=temperature,
                         top_p=1.0, top_k=0, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens)
  • The first line checks whether the temperature is 0.
  • do_sample=False means “do not roll the dice, always take the top token”. This is greedy decoding.
  • Otherwise, do_sample=True with the chosen temperature gives temperature sampling.
  • top_p=1.0, top_k=0 turn top-p and top-k off, so only temperature shapes the dice (“pure temperature sampling”).
  • max_new_tokens caps how many tokens are generated.

The notebook has no saved output. When run, T = 0 gives the identical answer every time, and higher T gives more varied answers (see chapter 21).

How this shows up on the exam Mostly as True/False statements. These are the likely ones, with the answer and the reason in plain words:

  • “Higher temperature makes the output more deterministic” → FALSE. Temperature (τ, the dial for how adventurous the word choice is) above 1 flattens the chances, so the output gets more random. “Deterministic” means “the same answer every time” (slide 13).
  • “Greedy decoding always picks the most likely word” → TRUE. Greedy decoding (always taking the top-scoring next word) does exactly that.
  • “The original BERT can take inputs of 512 tokens” → TRUE. BERT (an early Google model built to read text) can take up to 512 tokens (words or word pieces) at once (slide 9).
  • “In cross-attention, queries come from the encoder” → FALSE. Cross-attention is the step where the writing part looks back at the input. The queries (the “what am I looking for?” signals) come from the decoder (the writing part), not the encoder (the reading part) (slide 18).
  • “Word and position embeddings are concatenated” → FALSE. A word’s numbers and the numbers for its place in the sentence are added together, not glued end to end (“concatenated”).

The 2025 exam’s T/F (c), on tokens vs words, and Q4(c), “token vs word, why tokens”, both came from slide 4. A short question could ask you to compare decoding strategies (rules for picking the next word). Or it could ask why temperature 0 suits extraction tasks (pulling one exact fact, like an amount, out of a text).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For decoding (how the model picks the next word): name at least two strategies, each with its downside, from slide 13. Random sampling (draw a word according to its chances) → too many unlikely words slip in. Greedy (always take the top word) → generic and repetitive text. Top-k (keep only the k most likely words, then draw) → k stays fixed whatever the situation. Temperature → τ < 1 sharpens the chances (safer picks), τ > 1 flattens them (wilder picks).
  • For the output, write: “a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token, from the last token’s final hidden state via \(u = h^L_N E'\) and softmax”. In plain words: the model gives a chance to every token it knows (its vocabulary). It starts from its final inner summary of the last token (\(h^L_N\)) and multiplies it by the embedding table turned on its side (\(E'\)). That gives raw scores (\(u\)). Softmax (a formula that turns scores into chances adding up to 1) then turns the scores into chances.
  • For encoder vs decoder: the encoder (reading part) gives a context-aware list of numbers for every input word. The decoder (writing part) produces one token at a time. In cross-attention, Q (the queries) comes from the decoder, and K and V (the keys and values) come from the encoder.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying “high temperature = more focused”. It is the opposite: high temperature means more random.
  • Saying the input is words. It is tokens (words or word pieces, like “play” + “ing”) (slide 4).
  • Forgetting that top-k re-normalises before sampling. After keeping the top k words, it rescales their chances so they add up to 1 again.
  • Claiming the head (the last layer, which turns numbers into next-word scores) uses all \(N\) hidden states (the model’s inner summaries, one per token). It uses only the last one, \(h^L_N\).
  • Mixing up which side supplies Q (the queries) in cross-attention. It is the decoder.
  • Presenting top-p (another rule for picking words) as defined in the slides. It is not explained there.

Key terms to use

  • token (a word or a piece of a word)
  • one-hot vector (row of zeros with one 1 marking a token)
  • embedding matrix \(\mathbf{E}\) (table with one row of numbers per token)
  • positional embedding, added (numbers marking each token’s place, added on)
  • context window / maximum sequence length (most tokens the model reads at once)
  • truncation (cutting off text beyond that limit)
  • language modelling head (last layer giving a score per token)
  • logits (raw scores before they become chances)
  • softmax over the vocabulary (turns scores into chances summing to 1)
  • weight tying (same table E used at input and output)
  • greedy decoding (always pick the most likely next token)
  • random sampling (draw the next token by its chances)
  • top-k (draw only from the k likeliest tokens)
  • temperature τ (dial: low = predictable, high = adventurous)
  • encoder (the part that reads the input)
  • decoder (the part that writes, one token at a time)
  • causal self-attention (each token looks only at earlier tokens)
  • cross-attention (decoder looks back at the encoder’s notes)
  • bidirectional, BERT-type (reads the words on both sides)
  • [CLS] token (special first token that summarises the text)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Setting τ > 1 makes the next-word distribution sharper.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: τ (the Greek letter tau) is the temperature, a dial for how adventurous the model is when it picks the next word. The “next-word distribution” is the list of chances the model gives every possible next word, and “sharper” means the top word gets even more of the chance. So: does turning the dial above 1 make the model more predictable?

    False. Why: τ above 1 flattens the chances. The top word loses some of its lead and unlikely words catch up, so the output gets more surprising. τ below 1 does the opposite and sharpens. Think of a friend finishing your sentence: on a cautious day (low τ) they say the obvious word; on a wild day (high τ) they often surprise you. (Source: L9a slide 13)

  2. T/F: “Multiplying a one-hot row by the embedding matrix E simply selects one row of E.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A one-hot row is a long row of zeros with a single 1 that marks which token it is. The embedding matrix E is a big table with one row of numbers for each token. Does multiplying the two pick out that token’s row of numbers?

    True. Why: every 0 wipes out its row of the table, and the single 1 keeps exactly one row. It is like a wall of lockers where you hold only one key: only one locker opens. The slide says the one-hot rows select “the elements in E that correspond to the sequence”. (Source: L9a slide 5)

  3. T/F: “Weight tying means the same matrix E is used to build the input and to produce the output scores.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: At the start, the model uses table E to turn tokens into numbers. At the end, it must turn numbers back into a score for every token. Is “weight tying” the name for reusing the same table for both jobs?

    True. Why: that is exactly the definition. It is like using one English–French dictionary to translate both ways, instead of buying two. (Source: L9a slide 11)

  4. T/F: “In the decoder’s cross-attention layer, the keys and values come from the encoder.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Some models have an encoder (a part that reads the input) and a decoder (a part that writes the output). Cross-attention is the step where the decoder looks back at the input. It uses queries (“what am I looking for?”), keys (labels on the encoder’s notes) and values (the content of those notes). Do the keys and values come from the encoder?

    True. Why: the decoder brings the question (the queries). The encoder supplies the notes being searched (the keys) and what they say (the values). Picture a writer searching a library: the writer brings the question, and the library supplies the labels on the shelves and the books. (Source: L9a slide 18)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): Why might a company set temperature to 0 when extracting invoice amounts, but not when writing campaign slogans?

    Model answer: The model’s next-token probabilities are reshaped by \(\mathrm{softmax}(u/\tau)\). A low τ sharpens them, and at 0 the model always takes the top token (greedy), so the same input gives the same output. That predictability is what you want when one correct answer exists and another program reads the result. For slogans you want variety, so a higher τ flattens the distribution and lets less obvious words through. The cost is a higher risk of nonsense (Notebook 4 cells 13 and 28).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Temperature 0 means the model always picks its top word, so the same invoice always gives the same amount. That is good when there is one right answer and a computer will read it. For slogans you want fresh ideas, so you turn the temperature up. The price is that the model may now and then write nonsense.

Sources: Lecture 9a LLMs: Input and output (Lecture_llm_inputoutput.pdf), slides 3–18; Lecture 9b Training and fine tuning, slides 4 and 22; Interactive Notebook 4, cells 2–3.

19. How LLMs are trained

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — 2025 T/F (f) “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning” (answer: FALSE); training terms make easy True/False items.

Start from zero

The problem. Picture a brand-new LLM as a machine with billions of little dials, all set at random. Ask it to finish “So long and thanks for” and it writes gibberish. To get something like ChatGPT, every one of those dials has to be set to a good position. Nobody could ever do that by hand. Training is the automatic way of setting the dials, using enormous piles of ordinary text from books and websites. This chapter explains how that works and what the key words mean.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Grab a sentence from the pile of text, for example “So long and thanks for all the fish”.
  2. Hide the next word. Show the model only “So long and thanks for”.
  3. Let the model guess. It gives a probability to every word it knows, such as 30% for “all”.
  4. Reveal the true word (“all”) and look at how much probability the model gave it.
  5. Measure how wrong it was with one number, called the loss. Lots of probability on the true word gives a small loss. Little probability gives a big loss.
  6. Work out which way to turn each dial to make the loss a bit smaller. The clever bookkeeping that does this for all dials at once is called backpropagation.
  7. Nudge every dial a tiny bit in that direction. How big the nudge is, is set by the learning rate. This “nudge downhill” rule is called gradient descent.
  8. Work in small handfuls. Each nudge uses a small random handful of sentences (a mini-batch). One full trip through all the text is one epoch.
  9. Repeat billions of times. Slowly the guesses get better and better.
  10. Freeze the dials. When training stops, the dials stay put. When you later chat with the model, it is not learning from you.

Notice that no human wrote an answer key. The text itself holds the right answer every time. That is why this is called self-supervised.

A tiny example by hand.

Part A: how wrong was the guess? The model sees “So long and thanks for” and gives the true next word “all” a probability of 0.3. The loss is “minus the natural log of 0.3”. The natural log (written ln) is a button on any calculator. For a number between 0 and 1 it gives a negative answer: \(\ln(0.3) = -1.204\). The minus sign flips it to a positive penalty: 1.204. If the model had been more confident and given “all” 0.9, the penalty would be \(-\ln(0.9) = 0.105\), much smaller. If it gave “all” a probability of 1, the penalty would be 0. (These are the same numbers as in the table further down.)

Part B: one nudge of one dial. Real models have billions of dials. Imagine a toy model with only one dial, called \(v\). Its loss is \(v \times v\), so the best position is \(v = 0\), where the loss is 0.

  1. Start at \(v = 2\). The loss is 2 × 2 = 4.
  2. The slope here is 2 × 2 = 4. A positive slope means “turning the dial up makes the loss worse”, so we turn it down.
  3. Pick a learning rate of 0.1. The nudge is 0.1 × 4 = 0.4.
  4. New dial position: 2 − 0.4 = 1.6. New loss: 1.6 × 1.6 = 2.56. Smaller than 4, so the step helped.
  5. Next step: the slope is 2 × 1.6 = 3.2, the nudge is 0.1 × 3.2 = 0.32, and \(v\) becomes 1.28.

Now try a learning rate that is too big, 0.9. The nudge is 0.9 × 4 = 3.6, so \(v\) jumps from 2 to 2 − 3.6 = −1.6. It has leapt right over the best spot (0) to the other side. That is why the learning rate matters. (Same numbers as the table in Part 3 of the worked example below.)

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: no one has to label anything, so the model can learn from trillions of words of ordinary text.
  • Good: the same recipe (guess, measure, nudge, repeat) works for any kind of text.
  • Breaks: it is hugely expensive. It needs mountains of data and huge computers, which is why most people never train a model from scratch.
  • Breaks: a bad learning rate makes training crawl or bounce around, and the “landscape” of the loss has many hills and valleys where it can get stuck.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • training: the process of setting the model’s dials so it predicts well. Like practising piano until your fingers know the piece.
  • weight / parameter: one adjustable number (one dial) inside the model. Big LLMs have billions of them.
  • B / T (as in 0.34B, 1.6T): B = billion (a thousand million), T = trillion (a thousand billion). Counts of parameters or of tokens.
  • token: one small piece of text, often a word or part of a word (chapter 18).
  • vocabulary: the full list of tokens the model knows.
  • target: the right answer the model’s guess is compared with. Here, the true next word.
  • label / labelled data: a right answer written down by a person, such as “positive” next to a review. Labelled data = examples that come with such answers.
  • supervised learning: learning from examples that come with the right answer. Like a student doing exercises with an answer key.
  • unsupervised learning: finding patterns in data with no right answers at all. Like sorting a pile of photos into groups without being told what the groups are.
  • self-supervised learning: there is a right answer, but it comes from the data itself, not from a person. Like covering the next word in a book with your thumb and then checking.
  • topic model / LDA: a method from earlier in the course that groups documents into themes without any answer key. A classic unsupervised method.
  • pre-training: the first, giant training stage on ordinary text, before any special task.
  • next-token prediction: guessing which token comes next. The main pre-training task for GPT-type models.
  • masked words: words hidden inside a sentence that the model must fill in. The pre-training task for BERT-type models.
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is. 0.3 means 30%.
  • probability vector (\(\hat y_t\)): the model’s full list of probabilities, one per vocabulary token, at position \(t\). The little hat means “the model’s guess”.
  • loss: one number that says how wrong the model was. Smaller is better. Like the number of points you lost on a test.
  • cross-entropy loss (\(L_{CE}\)): the loss used for LLMs: minus the log of the probability given to the true next word.
  • log / natural log (ln): a calculator function. For numbers between 0 and 1 it gives a negative number, and the closer to 0, the more negative. ln(1) = 0.
  • negative log probability: the log of a probability with a minus sign in front, so the result is a positive penalty.
  • average loss over a sequence: add up the losses at every position and divide by how many there are.
  • function: a rule that turns an input into an output. “Square the number” is a function: 2 goes in, 4 comes out.
  • optimum / minimum: the best point. For a loss, the lowest point, like the bottom of a valley.
  • slope / derivative: how much the output changes when you change the input a tiny bit. Like how steep a hill is where you stand.
  • partial derivative (\(\partial\)): the slope with respect to one input while all the others are held still. \(\partial e/\partial b\) = “how much \(e\) changes if only \(b\) changes”.
  • gradient (\(\nabla L\)): the full list of slopes, one for every dial. It points uphill, so you step the opposite way.
  • gradient descent: repeatedly take a small step downhill on the loss. Like walking down a foggy mountain by always stepping where the ground slopes down.
  • learning rate (\(\eta\), “eta”): how big each downhill step is. Too big and you overshoot; too small and it takes forever.
  • learning-rate decay (\(\eta_k\)): making the steps smaller as training goes on (\(k\) = step number). Like slowing down as you get close to a parking spot.
  • backpropagation: the method that works out every dial’s slope in one backward sweep, starting from the loss. Like tracing blame backwards through a chain of people after a mistake.
  • chain rule: to get the slope through a chain of steps, multiply the slopes of the steps. If A doubles B and B triples C, then A changes C six-fold.
  • reverse-mode vs forward-mode differentiation: two ways of applying the chain rule. Reverse mode starts at the output and goes backwards, giving all slopes in one go. Forward mode starts at one input and gives only that one slope.
  • computational graph / node / edge: a diagram of a calculation. Each circle (node) is one value, and each arrow (edge) shows which value feeds which. The numbers on the arrows are the local slopes.
  • epoch: one complete pass through all the training data. Like reading the whole textbook once.
  • batch / mini-batch: a small group of examples used for one nudge. Like tasting a spoonful of soup instead of the whole pot.
  • online training: nudging after every single example (a mini-batch of size one). Very noisy.
  • SGD (stochastic gradient descent): gradient descent where each step uses a random mini-batch. “Stochastic” means “random”.
  • noise: random wobble in the steps, because each mini-batch is a bit different.
  • convergence: settling down at (or near) the lowest point.
  • generalisation: doing well on new examples, not only the ones trained on.
  • over-fitting: memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern. Like learning test answers by heart without understanding.
  • regularisation: anything that discourages over-fitting.
  • tuning parameter: a setting you choose yourself (like the mini-batch size), rather than one the model learns.
  • adaptive optimisers (AdaGrad, AdaDelta, RMSProp, Adam): improved versions of gradient descent that adjust the step size automatically for each dial. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • non-convex: a loss landscape with many hills and valleys, not one simple bowl. You might end up in a valley that isn’t the deepest one.
  • parameter initialisation: the starting positions of the dials before training begins.
  • vanishing / exploding gradients: slopes that shrink to almost nothing, or blow up to huge numbers, as they are passed backwards through many layers. Either way, the dials stop learning sensibly. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • saturation / dead neurons: parts of the network that get stuck and stop reacting to their input, so they stop learning. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • layer normalization: rescaling the numbers inside each layer so they stay in a sensible range. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • shuffling: mixing the order of the training examples after each epoch, like shuffling flashcards.
  • teacher forcing: during training, always show the model the true earlier words, not its own earlier guesses. Like a teacher correcting each word before you write the next one.
  • time step: one position in the sequence, one word after another.
  • continued pre-training / mid-training: extra rounds of pre-training, often on more specific text, before the task-training steps.
  • SFT (supervised fine-tuning): further training on examples of instructions paired with good answers.
  • preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: further training where the model is rewarded for answers that people (or a scoring system) prefer. Like a dog getting treats for good behaviour.
  • fine-tuning: extra training of an already-trained model on a specific task (chapter 20).
  • fixed weights at answer time: once training is done, the dials do not move while you use the model.
  • frontier model: one of the biggest, most advanced models of its time.
  • Transformer, BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3, Switch Transformer, DeepSeek-V4-Flash: names of specific models, used on the slides to show how fast model size grew.
  • \(\theta\) (“theta”) and \(\hat g\): on slide 16, \(\theta\) is the list of all dials and \(\hat g\) is the slope estimated from one mini-batch.

The idea in plain words

Training means setting the model’s billions of numbers (weights) so it predicts the next word well. The trick is that no human has to label anything. Take any sentence from the internet, hide the next word, ask the model to guess, then reveal the true word. If the model gave the true word a low probability, it is penalised and its weights are nudged so it does a bit better next time. Repeat this over trillions of words.

The penalty is called the loss (cross-entropy). The nudging rule is gradient descent: walk downhill on the loss. The way to work out which direction is downhill for every weight at once is backpropagation. To save time, each nudge looks at only a small random batch of examples (mini-batch SGD, short for stochastic gradient descent, where “stochastic” means “random”).

Analogy It is like learning a language from a pile of books with a sticky note covering the next word. You guess, lift the note, and see how wrong you were. Nobody wrote an answer key; the book itself is the answer key. That is why it is called self-supervised: there is a correct answer every time, but it comes from the text, not from a human labeller.

The exam definition

Self-supervised training (L9b slide 4, the key slide): > “Training LLMs is often called self-supervised training. Why? We use the actual text and train the model to predict the next word (or masked words). I.e., no need for manually creating training data.”

Lecture 7 slide 7 says the same: “Self-supervised pre-training: the next token in the training text is the target; future tokens are hidden from the prediction.”

Why “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning” is FALSE (2025 T/F f).

  • In unsupervised learning there is no target to compare against. Topic models (LDA, the theme-finding method from earlier in the course) just find structure in the data.
  • In LLM training there is a target at every position: the true next word. The loss measures how far the prediction is from that target. The course writes it as cross-entropy against the correct next word, \(L_{CE} = -\log \hat y_t[w_{t+1}]\) (slide 4).
  • So it works like supervised learning, except the labels come from the text itself. The course’s word for this is self-supervised.
  • The word “unsupervised” does not appear in any of the four LLM lecture decks (Lectures 7, 8, 9a, 9b).
  • [Not in course files — general knowledge] Some older textbooks loosely call language-model pre-training “unsupervised” because no human labels are needed. That is exactly the trap. In this course, write self-supervised.
  • Fine-tuning for a task is supervised. Fine-tuning for sentiment “requires supervised training and training data already classified” (L9b slide 22). Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) “learn[s] from examples of instructions and desired responses” (L7 slide 9).

The training pipeline (L7 slide 9).

  1. Pre-training: “learn to predict tokens from large collections of text, code, and, for some models, other media”. This step is self-supervised.
  2. Continued pre-training / mid-training, when used.
  3. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). This step is supervised.
  4. Preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: “improve responses using preferences or rewards” (the model is rewarded for answers that are preferred).

“Recipes differ across models.” The result is a set of updated weights. At answer time those weights are fixed (L7 slide 10).

Loss (L9b slides 4–5). The cross-entropy loss is “the negative log probability the model assigns to the next word in the training sequence”. The loss for a whole sequence is “the average cross-entropy loss over the entire sequence”. The weights are adjusted to minimise it “via gradient descent”.

Gradient descent (slides 7–9). It is “a general method to find the optimum (or minimum) of a function”. The update rule is \(v \to v' = v - \eta \nabla L\) (new dial setting = old setting minus a small step against the slope). Here η is the learning rate, which “affects the degree of updating”.

Backpropagation (slides 7, 13). It “is a ML term for reverse-mode differentiation, which in turn is just one way of applying the multivariate chain rule” (the rule that you multiply slopes along a chain of steps). “Reverse-mode gives derivative of output with respect to every node! Forward-mode gives derivative of output with respect to a single input.” (A derivative is a slope; a node is one value in the calculation diagram.) With millions of weights and one loss, reverse mode is far faster.

More terms (slides 6, 15–18).

  • Epoch: “a complete pass through the entire training dataset”.
  • Mini-batch: “small subset of the training dataset selected to perform a single update”. If its size equals the full sample, you are doing standard gradient descent. If its size is one, it is “online training (with a lot of noise)”, meaning one nudge after every single example. The size is a tuning parameter.
  • Teacher forcing: “give the model the correct history sequence to predict the next word rather than feeding the model its best case from the previous … time step”. In plain terms: during training, the model always sees the true earlier words, not its own earlier guesses.
  • SGD is the standard method for large networks because it is “more efficient and scalable”, gives “(potentially) faster convergence” (reaching the bottom sooner), and “introduces noise … that might help in terms of generalization (prevent over-fitting)” (doing well on new data instead of memorising the training data).
  • Beyond SGD (slide 17): gradually decrease the learning rate (\(\eta_k\) depends on step \(k\)), or use adaptive optimisers (methods that adjust the step size on their own): AdaGrad, AdaDelta, RMSProp, Adam.
  • Optimisation issues (slide 18): the loss is non-convex (many hills and valleys). Further issues: parameter initialisation (the dials’ starting values); vanishing and exploding gradients (slopes that shrink to nothing or blow up); saturation and dead neurons (parts of the network that stop reacting) (“layer normalization helps”); and shuffling the data after each epoch, which acts as a form of regularisation (a guard against memorising). See the word list above for these terms.

Training is “not for all” (slide 19). Model size grew about 10× a year. The slide’s examples: Transformer 0.05B parameters (2017), BERT 0.34B (2018), GPT-2 1.5B (2019), GPT-3 “170B” as printed (2020), Switch Transformer 1.6T (2021). Training “requires massive amounts of training data [and] large computational resources”. Lecture 7 slide 13 gives a recent example: DeepSeek-V4-Flash has 284B parameters, uses about 13B per token, and was pre-trained on more than 32 trillion tokens. “Training a frontier model from scratch is beyond a typical laptop”, which is why most users prompt or fine-tune an existing model (chapter 20).

A tiny worked example

1. Cross-entropy for one word (slide 5’s sentence). The input is “So long and thanks for”, and the true next word is “all”. We use the natural log here; the slide just writes “log”.

Rows = how much probability the model gave the true word “all”; columns = the resulting loss.

P(model says “all”) Loss \(= -\ln P\)
1.0 0 (perfect, “loss is minimized if we … predict with probability one the next word”)
0.9 0.105
0.3 1.204
0.01 4.605

By hand: \(-\ln(0.3) = 1.204\). The less probability the true word gets, the bigger the penalty.

2. Averaging over a sequence (slide 5). Suppose that at three positions the true next word got probabilities 0.5, 0.2 and 0.4. The losses are 0.693, 1.609 and 0.916. The sequence loss is their average: (0.693 + 1.609 + 0.916) / 3 = 1.073.

3. Gradient descent on \(L(v) = v^2\) (slide 8). Start at \(v = 2\). The slope is \(\nabla L = 2v\), so the update is \(v' = v - \eta\,2v\). We pick two learning rates (our choice; the slide shows dots, not numbers).

Rows = step number; columns = learning rate η; each cell = the value of \(v\) after that step.

Step η = 0.1 (small) η = 0.9 (large)
0 2 2
1 1.6 −1.6
2 1.28 1.28
3 1.024 −1.024
4 0.819 0.819

By hand, step 1 with η = 0.1: \(2 - 0.1 \times 2 \times 2 = 2 - 0.4 = 1.6\). With η = 0.9: \(2 - 0.9 \times 4 = -1.6\), so it jumps right over the minimum at 0. A small η creeps slowly downhill (the slide’s green dots). A large η bounces from side to side (the red dots).

4. Backpropagation on the slide’s graph (slides 10–11, 13). Let \(c = a + b\), \(d = b + 1\), \(e = c \times d\), with \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\). Then \(c = 3\), \(d = 2\), \(e = 6\). Each edge carries a local derivative: \(\partial c/\partial a = 1\), \(\partial c/\partial b = 1\), \(\partial d/\partial b = 1\), \(\partial e/\partial c = d = 2\), \(\partial e/\partial d = c = 3\).

The derivative of \(e\) with respect to \(b\) is “the sum over all possible paths” from \(b\) to \(e\), multiplying the edges along each path.

In words: to find how much \(e\) changes when \(b\) changes, follow each road from \(b\) to \(e\), multiply the numbers along that road, then add the roads together.

\[\frac{\partial e}{\partial b} = 1\times 2 + 1\times 3 = 5\]

Path via \(c\): \(1 \times 2\). Path via \(d\): \(1 \times 3\). In the same way \(\partial e/\partial a = 1 \times 2 = 2\). Reverse mode starts at \(e\) and works backwards, so one pass gives the derivative of \(e\) with respect to every node (a, b, c, d). That is backpropagation.

5. Epochs and mini-batches. With 10,000 training sequences and mini-batches of 100, one epoch (one full pass) contains 10,000 / 100 = 100 weight updates.

The formula, symbol by symbol

In words: the penalty at one position is minus the log of the probability the model gave to the true next word.

\[L_{CE}(\hat y_t, y_t) = -\log \hat y_t[w_{t+1}]\]

  • \(\hat y_t\) = the model’s probability vector over the whole vocabulary at position \(t\).
  • \(y_t\) = the “correct” distribution: all the weight on the true next word.
  • \(w_{t+1}\) = the true next word in the training text.
  • \(\hat y_t[w_{t+1}]\) = the probability the model gave to that true word.
  • \(-\log\) = turns a probability near 1 into a loss near 0, and a probability near 0 into a big loss.

Read aloud: “The loss at position t is minus the log of the probability the model gave to the word that really came next.”

In words: move every dial a small step (of size \(\eta\)) in the downhill direction of the loss.

\[v \to v' = v - \eta \nabla L\]

  • \(v\) = the parameters (weights) now; \(v'\) = the parameters after one step.
  • \(\nabla L\) = the gradient: for each parameter, how much the loss rises if that parameter rises a little.
  • \(\eta\) = the learning rate, or step size.
  • The minus sign means “go against the slope”, which is downhill.

Read aloud: “New weights = old weights minus learning rate times the slope of the loss.”

Slide inconsistency. The mini-batch SGD algorithm on slide 16 prints line 10 as “θ ← θ + η_k ĝ” with a plus sign (θ = all the dials, ĝ = the slope estimated from one mini-batch). For minimising a loss it must be a minus, as on slide 9. In the exam write \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta_k \hat g\).

How this shows up on the exam The 2025 exam had T/F (f): “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning” → FALSE. The right word is self-supervised (the text itself supplies the right answers) (L9b slide 4). Other likely T/F items:

  • “Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation / the chain rule” → TRUE. Backpropagation (the method that works out how much each dial in the model caused the error) is the same thing as reverse-mode differentiation. It rests on the chain rule (the school-maths rule for slopes of linked steps).
  • “A mini-batch of size one is standard gradient descent” → FALSE. A mini-batch is the small handful of examples used for one learning step. A handful of one is called online training. Standard gradient descent uses all the data in each step.
  • “An epoch is one pass through the full training set” → TRUE. An epoch is one full read-through of all the training data.
  • “Teacher forcing feeds the model its own predictions” → FALSE. Teacher forcing (a training trick) feeds the model the true earlier words, not its own guesses.
  • “Fine-tuning a sentiment classifier needs labelled data” → TRUE. Fine-tuning (extra training for one task) a model that tells positive from negative texts needs texts already tagged positive or negative.

A short question might ask “Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised?” or “Explain the role of the learning rate” (the size of each learning step).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For “self-supervised”, make three points. (1) The model predicts the next word, or a hidden (“masked”) word. (2) The right answer (the target) comes from the text itself, so nobody has to label data by hand. (3) The loss is cross-entropy (a penalty that is big when the model gave the true word a low chance) against the true next word. It is made smaller by gradient descent (stepping downhill on the error) with backpropagation (working out each dial’s share of the blame).
  • Then contrast. Unsupervised methods, such as LDA (a topic model that finds themes), have no target at all. Fine-tuning or SFT (supervised fine-tuning) is supervised: it learns from labelled examples.
  • For the learning rate (how big each downhill step is): too high overshoots or bounces around; too low is slow. Make it smaller over time, or use adaptive optimisers (methods that adjust the step size by themselves), such as Adam.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Writing “unsupervised” for LLM pre-training (the first, big training stage). It is self-supervised.
  • Saying the model is trained on human-labelled data at the pre-training stage. Pre-training uses plain text with no labels.
  • Copying the plus sign from slide 16. The update rule there has a typo: it must be a minus, \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta_k \hat g\) (move the dials against the slope, so you go downhill).
  • Saying the LLM keeps learning while you chat with it. Its weights (the learned dials) are fixed when it answers (L7 slide 10).
  • Mixing up epoch (one full pass through all the data) and mini-batch (a small handful of examples for one step).

Key terms to use

  • self-supervised pre-training (first training; text supplies its own answers)
  • next-token (or masked-word) prediction (guess the next or hidden word)
  • cross-entropy loss (penalty for a low chance on the true word)
  • average loss over the sequence (penalty averaged across all the words)
  • gradient (direction and steepness of the error slope)
  • gradient descent (step downhill on the error, again and again)
  • learning rate η (size of each downhill step)
  • backpropagation = reverse-mode differentiation = chain rule (work backwards to blame each dial)
  • computational graph (map of all the calculation steps)
  • stochastic gradient descent (downhill steps using random bits of data)
  • mini-batch (small handful of examples per step)
  • epoch (one full pass through all the data)
  • online training (one example per step; very noisy)
  • teacher forcing (show the true earlier words during training)
  • learning-rate decay (step size shrinks over time)
  • Adam/RMSProp/AdaGrad (optimisers that adjust their own step size)
  • non-convex (error landscape with many hills and valleys)
  • vanishing/exploding gradients (slopes shrink to nothing or blow up)
  • shuffling (mixing the order of examples each epoch)
  • supervised fine-tuning (SFT) (extra training on example instructions and answers)
  • preference optimisation (rewarding the answers people prefer)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Estimated” here means “trained” (how the model’s dials get set). “Unsupervised learning” means learning with no right answers at all, only spotting patterns. Is that how LLMs (large language models such as ChatGPT) are trained?

    False. Why: the course calls it self-supervised. There is a right answer every time: the next word in the text. The model guesses it, and a penalty called cross-entropy measures how wrong the guess was. It is like a book with a sticky note over the next word: you guess, lift the note and check. Nobody wrote an answer key, but the book itself is the answer key. (Source: L9b slide 4)

  2. T/F: “If the mini-batch size equals the full sample, we essentially perform standard gradient descent.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Gradient descent is learning by small steps downhill on the error. A mini-batch is the handful of examples used to decide each step. If that handful is the whole data set, is that ordinary gradient descent?

    True. Why: ordinary gradient descent looks at all the data before each step, so a “handful” that contains everything is the same thing. It is like tasting soup: a spoonful is a mini-batch, and tasting the whole pot is the full sample. (Source: L9b slide 6)

  3. T/F: “Reverse-mode differentiation gives the derivative of the output with respect to every node in one pass.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A derivative says how much the result changes if you nudge one thing. A node is one step in the model’s chain of calculations. Does one backward sweep through the chain tell you this for every step at once?

    True. Why: that is what reverse-mode differentiation (backpropagation) does. Think of a factory line that makes a faulty product: one walk back from the end, station by station, tells you how much each station added to the fault. (Source: L9b slide 13)

  4. T/F: “The cross-entropy loss is zero when the model gives the true next word probability one.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The cross-entropy loss is the penalty for a guess, worked out as minus the log of the chance the model gave the true word. “Probability one” means the model was 100% sure of the right word. Is the penalty then zero?

    True. Why: the log of 1 is 0, so the penalty is \(-\log 1 = 0\). A weather forecaster who said “100% rain” on a day it rained loses no points. (Source: L9b slide 4)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised, and how does it differ from fine-tuning a sentiment classifier?

    Model answer: In pre-training the model reads ordinary text and predicts the next (or a masked) word. The true word is taken from the text itself, so no one has to label data. The prediction is compared with the true word using a cross-entropy loss, and the weights are updated by gradient descent and backpropagation. So there is a target, as in supervised learning, but it is generated from the data, hence “self-supervised”. Fine-tuning a sentiment classifier is ordinary supervised learning: it needs texts already labelled as positive or negative (L9b slides 4, 22).

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: In its first training, the model guesses the next word of normal text, and the text itself shows the right word. So nobody has to mark up any data by hand. The model checks how wrong it was and adjusts its dials a little each time. Teaching it to spot positive or negative reviews is different: for that, people must first tag example reviews as positive or negative.

Sources: Lecture 9b LLMs: Training and fine tuning (Lecture_llm_trainingandfinetuning.pdf), slides 4–19 and 22; Lecture 7 Introducing LLMs (Lecture_llm_intro.pdf), slides 7, 9, 10, 13.

20. Fine-tuning vs prompt engineering vs embeddings, RAG, zero-/few-shot and alignment

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(e) (fine-tuning vs prompt engineering, 5 points) and 2025 T/F (j) (zero-shot); also the natural toolbox for the business-case reflection.

Start from zero

The problem. A bank gets thousands of customer complaints every week. Some are about card fees, some about the app crashing, some about loans. The bank wants an LLM to sort each complaint into the right bin, so the right team sees it fast. A ready-made LLM already knows a lot of language. But it has never seen this bank’s bins or its customers’ way of writing. So how do you get it to do this one job well? There are two big options: change what you tell the model, or change the model itself. This chapter is about choosing between them, plus two in-between options.

How it works, step by step.

Option 1: prompting (write the model better instructions; its insides stay untouched).

  1. Write clear instructions: “Sort this complaint into one of: fees, app, loans. Reply with one word.”
  2. If you give no solved examples, that is called zero-shot. If you add one or a few solved examples to the instructions, that is few-shot.
  3. Send the instructions plus the complaint to the model. It answers. Nothing inside the model changed. Tomorrow you can rewrite the instructions and try again.

Option 2: fine-tuning (send the model back to school on your own examples; its insides change).

  1. Collect many complaints that staff have already sorted by hand. These are labelled examples.
  2. Bolt a small new output part, called a head, onto the model. Its only job is to choose between fees, app and loans.
  3. Train it with the same loop as chapter 19: show a complaint, let the model guess the bin, measure how wrong it was, nudge the dials, repeat.
  4. You decide which dials may move. Either only the new head’s dials (the rest are frozen, locked in place), or all the dials in the model.
  5. Afterwards, the model’s insides are different. It has become a specialist in your bins.

Two in-between options (insides untouched).

  1. RAG: a search step finds the relevant documents (say, the bank’s fee rules) and pastes them into the instructions before the model answers.
  2. Embeddings: ask the model only for its “number summary” of each complaint. Then train your own small, simple sorter on those numbers.

A tiny example by hand. The complaint is “You charged my card fee twice this month.”

Zero-shot prompt. “Sort this complaint into one of: fees, app, loans. Reply with one word.” A capable model should reply “fees”. Dials changed: 0.

Few-shot prompt. The same instruction, plus one solved example: “Example: ‘The app crashes when I log in.’ → app”. Dials changed: still 0. The model copies the pattern it sees in the instructions.

Head-only fine-tuning, in miniature. Imagine the model’s summary of each complaint is a list of only 4 numbers. (Real models use far more; the chapter’s example below uses 1,024.) The new head must turn those 4 numbers into one score for each of the 3 bins.

  1. Each bin needs one dial for each of the 4 summary numbers: 4 × 3 = 12 dials.
  2. Each bin also gets one extra “starting value” dial, called a bias: 3 more.
  3. Total: 12 + 3 = 15 new dials. Only these 15 are trained. Every other dial in the model is frozen.

At real size. The worked example further down does the same count for a summary of 1,024 numbers and 2 labels (positive, negative): 1,024 × 2 + 2 = 2,050 new dials. For the bank’s 3 bins it would be 1,024 × 3 + 3 = 3,075. That is still less than 0.001% of the 340 million dials in the model. That is why head-only fine-tuning is cheap, and full fine-tuning (moving all 340 million) is expensive.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Prompting is good for starting fast and cheap, with no labelled data and no training. It breaks when you need the same behaviour every time at huge volume: it can be inconsistent, you pay for every token on every request, and only so much fits in the instructions.
  • Fine-tuning is good for a stable, high-volume task: you get a consistent specialist. It breaks when you lack labelled data, computing power or skills, or when the bins keep changing (you must train again).
  • RAG is good for answers that must rest on your own up-to-date documents. It breaks when the search step finds the wrong document.
  • None of them guarantees correct answers. Always check against a sample that people have sorted by hand.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that has learned from huge amounts of text to predict what comes next.
  • pre-trained LLM: a model that has already done its big general training (chapter 19) and “knows language” but not your task.
  • weight / parameter: one adjustable number (a dial) inside the model. Changing weights = changing the model’s insides.
  • fine-tuning: extra training of a pre-trained model on your own labelled examples, so its weights change. Like sending a trained nurse on a short course to specialise in one ward.
  • transfer learning: reusing what a model learned on one task to help with another. Like a violin player learning viola faster than a beginner.
  • domain: a field or type of data, such as “bank complaints” or “film reviews”.
  • head (model head, task head, problem-specific head): a small output part bolted onto the top of the model for one specific job. Like a new attachment on a drill.
  • language modelling head (LM head): the usual head that scores every word in the vocabulary as the possible next word (chapter 18).
  • logits: the raw scores a head gives each option before they become probabilities.
  • softmax head: a head that ends with softmax, so it gives one probability per label, adding up to 1.
  • label / labelled data / “already classified”: examples that come with the right answer written down by a person, such as a review marked “negative”.
  • supervised training: training on labelled examples, with the right answers as the target.
  • BERT / Bidirectional Transformer Encoder: a model family that reads the whole text in both directions. Often used for understanding tasks such as sentiment.
  • [CLS] token: a special token placed at the start of the text in BERT. Its final numbers act as a summary of the whole text.
  • embedding / vector: a list of numbers that stands for a word or a whole text. A “sequence-level embedding” is one such list for a whole text.
  • sentiment: the feeling in a text, such as positive or negative.
  • frozen layers / head-only fine-tuning: all the old dials are locked; only the new head’s dials are trained.
  • full fine-tuning: both the new head and all the old dials are trained.
  • bias (in “2 biases”): one extra dial per output that sets its starting level, like the “zero” setting on a kitchen scale.
  • SGD: stochastic gradient descent, the “nudge the dials downhill using a small random batch” method from chapter 19.
  • prompt: the text you send to the model: instructions, examples, documents and the question.
  • prompt engineering: the skill of writing prompts that get good, reliable answers. Like writing a clear brief for a new colleague.
  • system prompt: standing instructions sent before the user’s text, such as “Reply ONLY with JSON.” Like the house rules on a staff noticeboard.
  • context: everything the model can see in this request: the prompt, examples and any pasted documents. It disappears after the answer.
  • context window: the most tokens the model can read at once (chapter 18).
  • token: one small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. Providers charge per token.
  • tone: the style of the answer, such as formal, friendly or short.
  • output format / JSON: the exact shape the answer must have. JSON is a strict text format that other programs can read, like {"sentiment": "negative"}.
  • edge case: an unusual example that doesn’t fit the rules neatly, such as a lukewarm review.
  • temperature 0: the setting where the model always picks its most likely next word, so the same input gives the same answer (chapter 18).
  • zero-shot: asking the model to do a task from instructions alone, with no examples and no change to its weights. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • few-shot: putting one or a few solved examples in the prompt. Still no change to the weights.
  • chain-of-thought: asking the model to reason step by step before giving its final answer. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • latency: waiting time before the answer arrives.
  • grounding: telling the model to answer only from a text you give it. Like an open-book exam where you may only use the book on the desk.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): a search step (the retriever) finds relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt, then the model writes the answer. Like a librarian handing the consultant the right folder first.
  • retrieval / retriever: finding relevant documents / the search tool that does it.
  • tf-idf: a word-count-based way of scoring how relevant a document is to a search, from earlier in the course.
  • hallucination: the model stating something false with confidence, such as a made-up quote.
  • embedding extraction / “average of the last 4 layers”: taking the model’s number lists for your texts and using them elsewhere. With BERT, people often average the lists from its last 4 layers.
  • API: a web service your program sends text to and gets results back from. Like a vending machine for model outputs.
  • downstream task: the later task you actually care about, such as sorting complaints, that uses the model’s output.
  • classifier: a model that puts things into categories.
  • Naive Bayes: a simple, fast word-counting classifier from Lecture 3.
  • clustering: grouping similar texts together without labels.
  • alignment: teaching a model to follow instructions and give helpful, safe answers. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • SFT (supervised fine-tuning): training on examples of instructions paired with good answers.
  • preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: training where answers people prefer are rewarded.
  • RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback): the common name for training a model on human ratings of its answers. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • provider: the company that makes and runs the model.
  • compute / GPU: compute = computer power. A GPU is a special chip that does the heavy maths of training fast.
  • over-fitting: memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern.
  • validate / hand-labelled sample / benchmark: validate = check how often the model is right. A hand-labelled sample is a set of examples people sorted, used for checking. A benchmark is a simple method to compare against, like “always guess the biggest bin”.
  • volume: how many items you need to process, such as 100,000 reviews a month.

The idea in plain words

You have a pre-trained LLM that already “knows language”. You want it to do your job, for example labelling customer reviews as positive or negative. There are four broad ways to get there:

  1. Ask it better (prompt engineering). Change only what you say to the model: clear instructions, the exact output format, an example or two, the relevant document. The model itself does not change.
  2. Give it the right documents (RAG). A search step finds relevant text and pastes it into the prompt. Still no change to the model.
  3. Use its embeddings. Pull out the model’s number-vectors for your texts and feed them to your own, simpler model.
  4. Re-train it a bit (fine-tuning). Bolt on a small new output layer (a “head”) for your task and train on labelled examples. You update either only that head or the whole model. Now the weights do change.

The single most important sentence: “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.” (Lecture 7 slide 10).

Analogy You hire an experienced consultant (the pre-trained LLM). Prompting is writing them a clear brief with a sample of what you want. RAG is handing them the right folder of company files before they start. Using embeddings is asking them only for their notes and doing the final judgement yourself. Fine-tuning is sending them on a training course for your company’s task, so they come back changed. The first three leave the consultant as they were. Only the course changes them.

The exam definition

Fine-tuning (L9b slide 20). “Fine tuning is an instance of the more general transfer learning approaches.” Transfer learning means using “a model trained for solving a task in one domain to solve a different task in another domain”. Fine-tuning:

  • “involves adding a problem specific head to an otherwise pre-trained LLM” (a small new output part made for your task);
  • means you “re-train the model on this new task”;
  • updates “all of the model parameters or only the parameters in the new model head”.

Fine-tuning example (L9b slides 21–22). The usual language-model head (logits over the vocabulary, i.e. one raw score per possible next word) is replaced by a new head. To classify the sentiment of “[CLS] entirely predictable and lacks energy”:

  • use a pre-trained Bidirectional Transformer Encoder (BERT-type);
  • let the [CLS] token denote the sequence-level embedding (the special start token whose numbers summarise the whole text);
  • add a new softmax head on top of it (an output part that gives one probability per label);
  • “Use SGD to train the new parameters in the model and potentially update the pre-trained parameters as well”.

This “requires supervised training and training data already classified”.

Alternatives to fine-tuning (L9b slide 23).

  1. “Prompt engineering”.
  2. “Extract the word embedding vectors from the LLM directly and work with these on the down stream task of interest” (take the model’s number lists and use them in the later task you care about). With BERT it is common to take “the average of the last 4 layers”. Many LLMs also offer “API solutions to get the actual word embeddings” (a web service you send text to and get number lists back).

Context vs weights (L7 slides 10, 20). “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.” “RAG: add retrieved evidence to context.” “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights. Neither guarantees accuracy.”

Prompt engineering: what the course files actually show. There is no slide list, because it lives in Lecture 11. The course files give three sources:

  • Assignment evaluation guidelines 2024/2025: “Core skills include providing appropriate context and tone and chain-of-thought input.”
  • Notebook 4, cell 17 lists the techniques you practised to get valid JSON, “one change at a time”:
    1. set temperature 0 (always pick the most likely word);
    2. a system prompt (standing instructions sent before the user’s text) that spells out the exact output format (Reply ONLY with JSON of the form {"sentiment": "positive|negative|mixed", "aspect": "..."}. No other text.);
    3. “add an example to the system prompt (few-shot)”;
    4. tell the model what to do with edge cases (unusual examples, e.g. lukewarm reviews).
    Cells 19–24 add grounding (tying the answer to a given text: “Answer using ONLY the provided excerpt. If the excerpt does not contain the answer, say that it does not.”) and RAG (a search step pastes relevant documents into the prompt).
  • Lecture 7 slide 9 gives the training steps after pre-training (calling them “alignment” is [Not in course files — general knowledge]; slide 9 does not use the word): supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on “examples of instructions and desired responses”, then preference optimisation / reinforcement learning (“improve responses using preferences or rewards”).

Zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, alignment. The course files only name “few-shot” (Notebook 4) and “chain-of-thought input” (the evaluation guidelines). The definitions below are standard.

  • Zero-shot [Not in course files — general knowledge]: the model does a task from instructions alone, with no examples in the prompt and no change to the weights. Notebook 4’s starting prompt “Classify the review. Reply in JSON.” is a zero-shot prompt.
  • Few-shot (named in Notebook 4 cell 17): include one or a few worked examples (input → desired output) in the prompt. Still no weight changes. The model copies the pattern from its context.
  • Chain-of-thought [Not in course files — general knowledge]: ask the model to reason step by step before giving the final answer (“think step by step”). This often helps multi-step problems. Related course point (L7 slide 11): models can “spend extra computation before returning a final answer”, which “increases latency and resource use”, and “a persuasive explanation does not guarantee correctness”.
  • Alignment / RLHF [Not in course files — general knowledge]: after pre-training, the model is taught to follow instructions and give helpful, safe answers. This is done by SFT and then by learning from human preference ratings (reinforcement learning from human feedback). The course’s own words are “supervised fine-tuning” and “preference optimization / reinforcement learning” (L7 slide 9). This changes the weights, but it is done by the model provider, not by you.

Why 2025 T/F (j) “zero-shot involves re-estimating only the final output layer” is FALSE. Zero-shot means no re-estimation at all: the weights stay fixed and you only write instructions. Re-estimating only the final layer is head-only fine-tuning (L9b slide 20: “only the parameters in the new model head”). That is a training method which needs labelled data. The statement swaps a prompting idea for a fine-tuning idea.

A tiny worked example

Task: label the review “entirely predictable and lacks energy” (the L9b slide 22 example) as positive or negative, for a firm with many reviews. Here are the five routes, and what each one needs, for this exact review.

  • Zero-shot prompt. System prompt: “Classify the review as positive or negative. Reply ONLY with one word.” Weights changed: none. Labelled data: none, though a few labelled reviews are still needed to check accuracy.
  • Few-shot prompt. Same instruction plus one worked example in the allowed labels, e.g. “Example: ‘A gripping, beautifully acted film.’ → positive”.
