(Notebook 4 cell 17 uses the same idea with its own example, ‘Great screen, awful speakers.’ → mixed, because its label set includes “mixed”.) Weights changed: none.
  • RAG. Not really needed for sentiment. It fits questions like “What does our return policy say?”: a retriever pastes the policy text into the prompt. Weights changed: none.
  • Embeddings + own model. Send each review to the LLM and take its embedding (e.g. the average of BERT’s last 4 layers, slide 23). Then train a simple classifier of your own (a supervised model that sorts texts into categories, as in Lecture 3) on, say, a few hundred labelled reviews. The LLM’s weights: unchanged. Your small model is trained.
  • Head-only fine-tuning. Put a softmax head with 2 outputs on the [CLS] vector. Suppose the vector has length \(d = 1024\), the size used by the 0.34B-parameter BERT on slide 19 [Not in course files — general knowledge: d = 1024]. Then the head has \(1024 \times 2\) weights \(+ 2\) biases \(= 2{,}050\) new parameters. That is about 0.0006% of 340 million. Only these 2,050 numbers are trained, on labelled reviews.
  • Full fine-tuning. Same head, but SGD also updates all ~340 million pre-trained weights. This is the most flexible and the most expensive in compute and data.

Hand check: \(2{,}050 / 340{,}000{,}000 \times 100 = 0.0006\%\). This is why head-only fine-tuning is cheap. Full fine-tuning can adapt deeper, but costs far more.

Comparison table. Rows = the approach; columns = what changes, what data it needs, how costly it is, and when to use it.

Approach What changes Data needed Cost / skill When to use
Prompting (zero-/few-shot, format, chain-of-thought) Only the context (instructions, examples). Weights fixed. None to start; a small labelled set to check quality Cheapest to try; pay per token at run time; no training Quick start, changing tasks, few or no labels, a capable general model
RAG Context: retrieved documents are added to the prompt. Weights fixed. A document collection plus a retriever (a search tool, using tf-idf word matching or embeddings) Build and maintain search; longer prompts cost more tokens Answers must rest on company or up-to-date facts; reduces hallucination (confident made-up answers) but “neither guarantees accuracy”
Embeddings + own model Nothing in the LLM; you train a separate small model on its vectors Labelled data for your small model Moderate; the small model is cheap to run and easy to validate Classification, clustering or search at scale; when you want a transparent, cheap downstream model
Head-only fine-tuning A new task head (e.g. softmax on [CLS]); all other weights frozen Labelled training data (“already classified”) Low–moderate training cost; needs ML skills A stable, high-volume task with labels; limited compute
Full fine-tuning The new head and all pre-trained weights More labelled data Highest: GPUs (special maths chips), expertise, risk of over-fitting (memorising instead of learning) Prompting and head-only are not accurate enough, the domain is special, and the volume justifies the cost

Sources: L9b slides 20–23; L7 slides 10, 20; Notebook 4 cells 17–25.

Applying it to the course’s business case (Assignment 4.2 c). A firm wants to classify 100,000 reviews a month. Prompting a small local model takes 5–30 seconds per review on a laptop (Assignment slide 23), so the per-review cost and time add up fast at that volume. Naive Bayes (Lecture 3, a simple word-counting classifier) is fast and cheap but needs labels. Fine-tuning becomes worth it when you have (or can create) a labelled set, the task is stable, and the volume is high enough that a cheaper, faster specialised model pays back the training effort. Whatever you choose, validate it against a hand-labelled sample and a simple benchmark.

How this shows up on the exam The 2025 exam’s Q4(e) asked for the difference between fine-tuning and prompt engineering (5 points). Fine-tuning is extra training that changes the model. Prompt engineering is writing better instructions. The graders’ guideline said: fine-tuning re-estimates part of the model or extra layers (re-sets some of its dials, or new ones added on top); prompting keeps the weights and improves the context (leaves the dials alone and improves what the model is told). The 2025 T/F (j) was: “zero-shot involves re-estimating only the final output layer” → FALSE. Zero-shot means asking with no examples, and it changes nothing inside the model. Likely new items:

  • “RAG updates the model’s weights” → FALSE. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: a search step pastes relevant documents into the prompt) only changes what the model reads (L7 slide 20).
  • “Fine-tuning is a form of transfer learning” → TRUE. Transfer learning means reusing a model trained on one job for a new job (L9b slide 20).
  • “Few-shot prompting changes the model’s parameters” → FALSE. Few-shot means putting a few examples in the prompt; the parameters (dials) stay the same.
  • A business-case question asking which approach a firm should use, and why.

What a top-grade answer must include For fine-tuning vs prompting:

  1. Fine-tuning = transfer learning (reusing a trained model for a new job). You add a task-specific head (a small extra layer for your task, e.g. a softmax on the [CLS] token for sentiment). Then you re-train with labelled data (examples already tagged with the right answer). You update only the head or all parameters, so the weights change.

  2. Prompting = the weights stay fixed. You improve the context (everything the model reads before it answers): instructions, format, tone, examples (few-shot), chain-of-thought (asking it to reason step by step), retrieved documents.

  3. One line of judgement. Prompting is fast and needs no labels, but it is harder to control and limited by the context window (how much text the model can read at once). Fine-tuning needs data, compute (computer power) and skills, but at high volume it can give a consistent, cheaper specialist model.

  4. If you have room, mention the third route: extracting embeddings (taking the model’s number lists for your texts and using them in your own model) (slide 23).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying zero-shot or few-shot “trains” the model. It does not change the model at all.
  • Saying RAG or uploading a file teaches the model for good. It only changes the context (what the model reads this time).
  • Forgetting that fine-tuning needs labelled data (examples tagged with the right answer).
  • Describing only one side of the comparison.
  • Claiming fine-tuning always beats prompting.
  • Presenting zero-shot or chain-of-thought definitions as quotes from the slides. They come from Lecture 11 or general knowledge.

Key terms to use

  • transfer learning (reusing a trained model for a new job)
  • pre-trained LLM (big model already trained on lots of text)
  • fine-tuning (extra training that changes the model’s dials)
  • problem-specific (task) head (small extra layer added for your task)
  • [CLS] token (special first token that summarises the text)
  • softmax head (layer turning scores into chances per label)
  • update all parameters vs only the head (re-train everything, or only the new layer)
  • labelled / “already classified” data (examples tagged with the right answer)
  • supervised (learning from examples with right answers)
  • prompt engineering (writing better instructions for the model)
  • system prompt (standing instructions given before the user’s text)
  • context (everything the model reads before answering)
  • output format (the exact shape the answer must have)
  • tone (the style of voice of the answer)
  • zero-shot (instructions only, no examples)
  • few-shot (a few worked examples in the prompt)
  • chain-of-thought (asking the model to reason step by step)
  • grounding (answer only from a text you supply)
  • RAG (search step pastes relevant documents into the prompt)
  • “context vs weights” (prompting changes the input; fine-tuning changes the model)
  • embedding extraction (average of last 4 layers / API) (take the model’s number lists for your texts)
  • SFT (supervised fine-tuning on example instructions and answers)
  • preference optimisation / RL (alignment) (rewarding the answers people prefer)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Zero-shot learning involves re-estimating only the final output layer of the model.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Zero-shot means asking the model to do a task with instructions only, no examples. “Re-estimating only the final output layer” means re-training the model’s last layer. Does zero-shot re-train that last layer?

    False. Why: zero-shot changes no weights (dials) at all; you only write a request. Re-training only the last layer (the head) is a kind of fine-tuning, called head-only fine-tuning. It is the difference between briefing a consultant on a new task and sending them on a training course. (Source: L9b slide 20)

  2. T/F: “Retrieval-augmented generation changes the model’s weights.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a set-up where a search step finds relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt. The weights are the model’s learned dials. Does RAG change those dials?

    False. Why: RAG only changes what the model reads this time. The slide puts it this way: “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights”. It is like handing a consultant the right folder before a meeting: they are better informed today, but they have not been retrained. (Source: L7 slide 20)

  3. T/F: “When fine-tuning, one can update all model parameters or only the parameters in the new head.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Fine-tuning is extra training for one task, and the new head is the small layer added on top for that task. The parameters are the model’s dials. Can you choose to re-train either all the dials or only the new layer’s dials?

    True. Why: both options exist. You can re-train every dial in the model, or leave the old dials as they are and train only the new layer on top. It is like either retraining a whole team or only training the new person who joined it. (Source: L9b slide 20)

  4. T/F: “Adding an example of the desired answer to the system prompt is called few-shot prompting.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The system prompt is the standing set of instructions given to the model before the user’s text. If you put a worked example of a good answer in there, is that called few-shot prompting?

    True. Why: few-shot means showing the model one or a few examples of what you want. It is like showing a new colleague one finished report before asking them to write the next one. (Source: Notebook 4 cell 17)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): Describe the difference between fine-tuning and prompt engineering.

    Model answer: Fine-tuning is transfer learning: we take a pre-trained LLM, add a problem-specific head (for example a softmax layer on the [CLS] embedding for sentiment) and re-train on labelled data. Either only the new head or all parameters are re-estimated, so the model’s weights change. Prompt engineering leaves the weights unchanged and instead improves the context the model sees: clear instructions, the required output format and tone, examples (few-shot), step-by-step reasoning, or retrieved documents. Prompting is quick and needs no labelled data but is less controllable. Fine-tuning needs data, compute and skills but can give a more consistent specialist model for a stable, high-volume task.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Fine-tuning takes a trained model, adds a small layer for your task, and trains it more on examples with the right answers, so the model itself changes. Prompt engineering leaves the model as it is and gives it better instructions, examples or documents to read. Prompting is quick and needs no tagged examples, but the results are harder to control. Fine-tuning takes data, computer power and skill, but for a big, steady task it can give a more consistent specialist.

Sources: Lecture 9b Training and fine tuning, slides 20–23; Lecture 7 Introducing LLMs, slides 9, 10, 20; Interactive Notebook 4, cells 14–25 and 28; Assignments 2026 slides 20, 22; 2024/2025 assignment evaluation guidelines. Note: the Lecture 11 slides (“Prompt engineering and model alignment”, 16 Nov) are not in the course folder. If you took notes in that lecture, use its exact terms next to this chapter.

21. Lessons from running a real LLM locally (Interactive Notebook 4)

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — rarely asked directly, but excellent, concrete material for the business-case reflection (2025 Block 5, 20 points) and for T/F items on tokens, temperature and RAG.

Start from zero

The problem. Reading about LLMs is one thing. Using one for real work is another. Imagine a Norwegian company that wants an LLM to label customer reviews and to answer staff questions from its handbook. Before spending money, the managers want to know five things. What will it cost? Will it give the same answer twice? Can its answers be fed straight into other software? Will it make things up? And can it find the right page of the handbook when someone asks in their own words? The course notebook tests all five with a small, free model running on your own laptop.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Get a small model. Download a free model (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct) once from Hugging Face, a website where people share models. After that it runs on your laptop, with no account and no internet service.
  2. Cost test (tokens). Feed in the same sentence in English and in Norwegian. Count how many pieces (tokens) each one is cut into. More pieces means more cost.
  3. Same-answer test (temperature). Ask the same question three times. Count how many different answers come back at each temperature setting.
  4. Software-ready test (JSON). Ask the model to label 4 reviews in a strict, machine-readable format. A small checking program counts how many replies are usable. Then improve the instructions one change at a time.
  5. Making-things-up test (hallucination). Ask the model to quote a real speech. Try three ways: with no source text, with the right source text, and with the wrong source text.
  6. Find-the-page test (RAG). Chop many speeches into short chunks. Let a word-matching search pick the best chunks and paste them into the prompt. Check whether the search still finds the right chunk when the question uses different words.
  7. Turn each result into a business rule.

A tiny example by hand.

Why the model needs a search step at all. The collection of speeches is about 2 million tokens long. The model can read at most 32,768 tokens at once. Divide: 2,000,000 / 32,768 = about 61. So the speeches are about 61 times too long to fit. The model can only be shown a few chosen chunks, and a search step has to choose them.

Why the search step misses reworded questions. Take three short chunks (the same toy example as further down). First, the search tool throws away very common “stop words” such as “we”, “will”, “for”, “the”, “our”, “must” and “more”. What is left:

  • Chunk A: protect, social, security, elderly.
  • Chunk B: build, roads, bridges.
  • Chunk C: schools, need, better, teachers.

Now count, by hand, how many words each question shares with each chunk.

  • Question 1 asks about “Social Security for the elderly”. It shares 3 words with chunk A (social, security, elderly), 0 with B and 0 with C. So chunk A wins. Correct.
  • Question 2 asks the same thing in other words: “pensions for old people”. The words “pensions”, “old” and “people” appear in no chunk. It shares 0 words with A, 0 with B and 0 with C. Every chunk scores 0, so the search has nothing to go on. The model then gets the wrong text, or none.

This is the notebook’s key point: a word-matching search only finds the same words, not the same meaning.

What it’s good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: it is free, runs offline, and keeps company data on your own machine.
  • Good: a tiny model makes the typical LLM failures easy to see before you scale up.
  • Breaks: a small model on a laptop is weak and slow, around 5–30 seconds per review.
  • Breaks: passing a test on 4 reviews proves little about 100,000. The wrong source text can be worse than no source, and word-matching search misses reworded questions.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that predicts text one token at a time.
  • notebook / cell: a notebook is a document that mixes code and explanations and runs in a web browser. A cell is one box of code or text in it. Like a recipe book where each step can be “cooked” by pressing a button.
  • code / Python: instructions written for the computer. Python is the programming language the notebook uses.
  • Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct: the name of the small model used. “0.5B” means half a billion dials (parameters). “Instruct” means it was trained to follow instructions and chat.
  • parameter / weight: one adjustable number (dial) inside the model, set during training.
  • Hugging Face: a website where people share models, like an app store for AI models.
  • account / API key / cloud: the usual way to use a big model: sign up (account), get a password for programs (API key), and send your text to the provider’s computers over the internet (cloud). The notebook needs none of these.
  • local deployment / open weights: running the model on your own computer, which is possible because its dials (weights) are published for anyone to download.
  • per-token fee: what online providers charge: a small price for every token in and out.
  • privacy: keeping data away from outsiders. Running locally means your text never leaves your machine.
  • token: one small piece of text, often a word, sometimes part of a word or a number.
  • tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens. Like a butcher with a fixed set of cuts.
  • subword token: a token that is only part of a word. A long Norwegian word may be cut into several of these.
  • tokens per word: how many tokens, on average, one word turns into. Higher means more cost.
  • effective price: what a document really costs once you count its tokens. Same price per token, but more tokens per word, means a higher bill.
  • leading space: the space in front of a word. ” bank” (with a space) and “bank” count as different tokens.
  • len(text.split()): a line of code that counts words by cutting the text at the spaces.
  • context window: the most tokens the model can read at once (here 32,768). Like the size of a desk.
  • corpus / SOTU: a corpus is a collection of texts. SOTU is the State of the Union speeches by US presidents, the corpus used here.
  • temperature (T): the “boldness” dial for picking words (chapter 18). Low = predictable, high = varied.
  • greedy (T = 0): always pick the single most likely next word, so the same question gives the same answer every time.
  • seed: a starting number for the computer’s random dice. A different seed gives different rolls.
  • N_SAMPLES: a setting in the code: how many times to ask the same question (here 3).
  • JSON / machine-readable: JSON is a strict text format such as {"sentiment": "positive"}. Machine-readable means other software can read it without a human.
  • system prompt: standing instructions sent before the user’s text, like house rules.
  • explicit output format: spelling out exactly what shape the answer must have.
  • few-shot example: a solved example placed in the prompt to show the pattern (chapter 20).
  • label set: the list of allowed answers, such as positive / negative / mixed. Choosing it is a business decision.
  • edge case / lukewarm: an example that doesn’t fit the labels neatly, like “It’s fine, I guess.”
  • format checker / json.loads: a small program that tests whether each reply is valid. json.loads tries to read a reply as JSON and fails if it is broken.
  • validation sample: a set of examples people have labelled by hand, used to check how often the model is right.
  • benchmark / majority class: a simple method to compare against. “Majority class” means always guessing the most common label.
  • Naive Bayes: a simple, fast word-counting classifier from Lecture 3, often used as a benchmark.
  • hallucination: the model stating something false with confidence, such as an invented quote.
  • grounding / excerpt: giving the model a source text (an excerpt) and telling it to answer only from that. Like an open-book exam.
  • STRICT instruction: the notebook’s firm extra instruction: if the answer is not in the excerpt, say so.
  • scoreboard: the notebook’s simple check of whether the reply contains the real words of the speech.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first search for relevant chunks, then paste them into the prompt, then let the model answer.
  • retriever: the search tool inside RAG.
  • chunk / CHUNK_SIZE: a short slice of a long text. CHUNK_SIZE sets how many words each slice has.
  • top-k chunks / TOP_K: the k best-matching chunks that get pasted into the prompt.
  • stop words: very common words like “the”, “for”, “we” that a search tool ignores.
  • tf-idf / TfidfVectorizer: a way of scoring words: a word counts more if it is frequent in this chunk but rare across all chunks. TfidfVectorizer is the code tool that does it.
  • vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order. Here, one number per vocabulary word for each chunk.
  • document-term matrix: a table with one row per chunk and one column per word, each cell showing how much that word counts in that chunk.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a bag of word counts, ignoring word order.
  • dot product: multiply two lists number by number and add up. If two texts share no words, it is 0.
  • cosine similarity: a 0-to-1 score of how alike two word-lists are, built on the dot product. 0 = nothing in common.
  • argsort: a code command that puts scores in order, used to pick the top chunks.
  • GENERATE = True: a switch in the code. When on, the retrieved chunks are sent to the model to write an answer.
  • literal-word matching vs dense embeddings: matching the exact same words, versus matching number lists that capture meaning (Interactive Notebook 3). Dense embeddings can often tell that “pensions” and “Social Security” are related.
  • paraphrase: saying the same thing in other words.
  • hit rate: how often the retriever finds the right chunk.
  • pipeline: the whole chain of steps around the model: input, model, checks, output.
  • T/F: a True/False exam question.
  • reflection (business case): the exam’s longer question where you propose methods for a firm and discuss their pitfalls.

The idea in plain words

The notebook runs a small real LLM, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (half a billion dials, trained to follow instructions), downloaded once from Hugging Face (a website for sharing models), on your own laptop: “no account, no API key, no cloud”. It then asks five practical questions a business would face:

  1. Tokens: does the same sentence cost more in Norwegian than in English?
  2. Temperature: ask the same question three times. Do you get the same answer?
  3. JSON: can a prompt make the model return machine-readable output every time?
  4. Hallucination: does the model quote a speech correctly with no source, the right source, or the wrong source?
  5. RAG: does a word-matching retriever find the right passage when you ask in other words?

The answers turn into five business rules: tokens are the unit of cost; use temperature 0 for extraction; always check the output with code; ground the model in the right source; and RAG is only as good as its search step.

Analogy It is like test-driving a small car before buying a fleet. The small car is not the best car, but every weakness you notice (fuel use, how it handles in snow) tells you what to check before you put 100 of them on the road. In the same way, the tiny 0.5B model makes the typical LLM failures easy to see.

The exam definition

These are the notebook’s takeaways (cell 28), in its own words:

  • “Tokens are the unit of cost and of context. Languages and formats the tokenizer saw less of (Norwegian, numbers, codes) cost more tokens per word.”
  • “Temperature trades predictability for variety. Use 0 for extraction and classification; higher values only when you want variety.”
  • “A system prompt with an explicit format makes output far more reliable — but not perfectly so. ‘Reliable’ has to be checked by code around the model, and the label set is a business decision.”
  • “Without context the model dodges or hallucinates. The right context (at temperature 0) fixes it. The wrong context can be worse than none.”
  • “RAG is only as good as its retriever. Literal-word retrieval misses paraphrases.”

Plus the reason the model needs retrieval at all (cell 22): the State of the Union corpus is about 2 million tokens, and the model’s window is 32,768 tokens. So you retrieve the most relevant chunks with tf-idf + cosine similarity (word-matching search, see the example above) and feed only those.

A tiny worked example

Q1, tokens (cells 6–9). The three test texts have 10, 7 and 8 words (counted with len(text.split()), as the notebook does):

  • English: “The central bank raised the interest rate to fight inflation.”
  • Norwegian: “Sentralbanken hevet renten for å bekjempe inflasjonen.”
  • Numbers: “Invoice 2024-11-07: NOK 1,234,567.89 due within 30 days.”

The tokenizer (the tool that cuts text into tokens) “was built mostly from English text”. So common English words are often a single token, while Norwegian words like “Sentralbanken” and number strings get chopped into several pieces. When run, the Norwegian sentence shows more tokens per word than the English one. You pay per token, and the context window is counted in tokens. So the effective price of a Norwegian document is higher, even at the same price per token. That answers the notebook’s “Think” question about two providers. A small detail from cell 8: a leading space is part of the token, so ” bank” and “bank” are different tokens.

Q5, retrieval: why rewording fails. This is a toy example we made, run with the same tools as cell 24: TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english") and cosine_similarity. It uses three short “chunks”:

  • A: “We will protect Social Security for the elderly.”
  • B: “We must build more roads and bridges.”
  • C: “Our schools need better teachers.”

Rows = query; columns = cosine similarity with each chunk, plus the query words the index knows.

Query A B C Query words the index knows
“…promise about Social Security for the elderly?” 0.866 0 0 social, security, elderly
“…promise about pensions for old people?” 0 0 0 (none)

Why the second row is all zeros, by hand: after stop words are removed, “pensions”, “old” and “people” appear in no chunk. Cosine similarity is built on a dot product, and the dot product only adds up words that appear in both vectors. With no shared words the dot product is 0, so the cosine is 0. The retriever finds nothing, and the LLM is then fed irrelevant text. This is the notebook’s point: “tf-idf only matches literal words. Modern RAG systems use dense embeddings (Interactive Notebook 3) to match meaning.” (Dense embeddings are number lists that capture what a text means, not which words it uses.)

Reading the course code

Notebook 4, cell 24 (mini-RAG), key lines simplified:

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
X = tfidf.fit_transform(chunk_text)
sims = cosine_similarity(tfidf.transform([QUESTION]), X)[0]
top = sims.argsort()[::-1][:TOP_K]
  • Line 1 sets up a tf-idf weighting (chapter on tf-idf) that drops English stop words.
  • Line 2 builds the document-term matrix (a table: one row per chunk, one column per word) of all speech chunks (each chunk is CHUNK_SIZE words, labelled “president, year”) and weights it by tf-idf.
  • Line 3 turns the question into a tf-idf vector with the same vocabulary and computes its cosine similarity with every chunk.
  • Line 4 sorts the scores (argsort, then reversed so the biggest comes first) and keeps the TOP_K most similar chunks.

If GENERATE = True, these chunks are pasted into the prompt with the system instruction “Answer using ONLY the provided excerpts, and mention which president and year”, at temperature=0. When run, it prints the number of chunks, each retrieved chunk with its similarity score, and “Query words the index knows”.

The other experiments, briefly:

  • Q2, temperature (cells 10–13): the same question is asked N_SAMPLES = 3 times with different seeds (different starting points for the random dice), and the cell prints “k distinct answers out of N”. At T = 0 (greedy) all answers are identical. They become more varied as T rises, and stop making sense at high T (try 2.0).
  • Q3, JSON (cells 14–17): a checker (json.loads, which tries to read the reply as JSON, plus key and label checks) scores how many of 4 reviews give usable output. You improve the score with T = 0, an exact format, a few-shot example and edge-case rules (chapter 20). The hard case is “The app is fine, I guess. Nothing special.” It is lukewarm, so it fits none of positive/negative/mixed neatly. That is a label-set decision, “a business decision, not a coding one”.
  • Q4, hallucination (cells 18–21): the model is asked to quote Gerald Ford’s 1975 address; the scoreboard checks for his real words “not good”. With no context the model “predicts plausible text; it does not look things up”, so it dodges or invents. With the right excerpt at T = 0 it can quote correctly. With the wrong excerpt (Washington 1791) the small model may present that text as the answer, even with the STRICT “say so if it is not there” instruction.

What this means for business use

These points link the notebook to Lecture 7’s use-case slides, and they are ready-made reflection material:

  • Cost is counted in tokens, and depends on language and format. Budget for Norwegian text and for numbers and codes.
  • Pick the temperature to suit the task. Use 0 for extraction or classification (invoice amounts, review labels). Use a higher value for creative work (ten campaign slogans).
  • Build checks around the model. 4 out of 4 valid JSON does not prove 100,000 out of 100,000 (cell 17 “Think”). Add a format checker, a hand-labelled validation sample, and a benchmark (a simple method to beat, e.g. Naive Bayes, or “always guess the biggest class”). This matches L7 slide 18 (“Verifiable Results”, “Manageable Errors”).
  • Ground the model, and test the retriever. Hallucinations “sound confident” (L7 slide 26). The wrong context can be worse than none, so measure the retrieval hit rate (how often the right chunk is found) for literal and reworded questions (Assignment 4.2 a). Consider embedding-based retrieval for paraphrases.
  • Weigh the risk against how easy errors are to check (L7 slide 19). Summarising survey feedback is low-consequence but hard to check, so inspect examples. Anything that triggers payments needs human approval.
  • Running locally keeps data on your own machine (privacy) and has no per-token fee. But a small model is weaker and slow: 5–30 seconds per review on a laptop (Assignment slide 23).

How this shows up on the exam Directly, as True/False items such as these:

  • “A Norwegian sentence typically costs fewer tokens than its English translation” → FALSE. Tokens are the word pieces the model reads and charges for. Norwegian words get chopped into more pieces, so Norwegian costs more.
  • “At temperature 0 the model gives the same answer every time” → TRUE. Temperature 0 means greedy decoding (always taking the top word), so there is no randomness.
  • “A tf-idf retriever will find a passage about ‘Social Security for the elderly’ when asked about ‘pensions for old people’” → FALSE. A tf-idf retriever (a search tool that matches the exact words used) finds literal word matches only, and these two phrases share no words.

Indirectly, in the 2025 Block 5 reflection question. It asked you to analyse 1,000+ free-text survey answers about how customers see a firm, and to propose at least two methods with motivation and pitfalls (what could go wrong). Notebook 4 gives you concrete pitfalls straight from the course: hallucination (the model inventing facts), format failures (answers in the wrong shape), label-set choices (which answer options to allow), token cost in Norwegian, retrieval missing paraphrases (the search tool missing questions asked in other words), and validating against a benchmark (checking the LLM beats a simple method).

What a top-grade answer must include When you propose an LLM in a business case, give three things.

  • How you will use it. Either a prompted classifier (the LLM sorts each text into a label because you asked it to) at temperature 0, with an explicit output format and a few-shot example. Or RAG (a search step pastes the right documents into the prompt), grounded in company documents (told to answer only from them).
  • How you will validate it (check that it works): a hand-labelled sample (texts a person has tagged with the right answer), accuracy against a benchmark such as Naive Bayes (a simple word-counting classifier) or the majority class (always guessing the most common label), and a code check of the format.
  • At least one specific pitfall: hallucination (made-up facts), wrong context (the wrong document pasted in), Norwegian token cost, lukewarm or sarcastic answers that fit no label, retrieval missing reworded questions.

Tie it to the grading criteria in Assignment slide 24: evidence, understanding, honest evaluation, judgement.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Treating the LLM’s output as automatically correct.
  • Saying “use an LLM” without saying the temperature, the output format or how you will check it.
  • Forgetting that tokens (word pieces), not words, set the cost.
  • Assuming RAG solves hallucination. It only helps if the search step finds the right text.
  • Quoting notebook numbers that were never printed. The notebook has no saved outputs.

Key terms to use

  • subword tokens (word pieces the model reads)
  • tokens per word (how many pieces each word becomes)
  • effective price (real cost once you count the tokens)
  • context window (32,768 tokens) (most text the model reads at once)
  • temperature 0 / greedy (always pick the top word; no randomness)
  • system prompt (standing instructions given before the user’s text)
  • explicit output format (the exact answer shape, e.g. JSON)
  • few-shot example (a worked example shown in the prompt)
  • label set (the list of allowed answers)
  • format checker (small program that tests each reply is valid)
  • validation sample (texts a person tagged, to check the model)
  • benchmark (a simple method the LLM must beat)
  • hallucination (confident-sounding but made-up answer)
  • grounding (answer only from a text you supply)
  • STRICT instruction (if the answer isn’t there, say so)
  • retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (search step pastes relevant text into prompt)
  • chunk size (how long each cut-up piece of text is)
  • top-k chunks (the k best-matching pieces passed on)
  • tf-idf + cosine similarity (match texts by shared, rarer words)
  • literal-word matching vs dense embeddings (same words vs same meaning)
  • hit rate (how often the right chunk is found)
  • local deployment / open weights (Hugging Face) (free model run on your own computer)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “In Notebook 4, the retriever uses dense embeddings to find relevant passages.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The retriever is the search step that finds the bits of text to hand the model. Dense embeddings are lists of numbers that capture a text’s meaning, so they can match texts that use different words. Does the notebook’s search work by meaning?

    False. Why: it uses tf-idf + cosine similarity, which matches texts by the words they share (a bag-of-words method that ignores meaning and word order). Dense embeddings are suggested as the better choice. It is like a librarian who only finds books whose titles contain your exact words, instead of one who understands what you mean. (Source: Notebook 4 cells 22, 25)

  2. T/F: “Giving the model the wrong source text can be worse than giving it no source at all.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The source text is the passage you paste in for the model to answer from. Can a wrong passage do more harm than giving no passage?

    True. Why: with a wrong passage, the small model may present that passage as the answer, even when told to say so if the answer is not there. With no passage, it dodges or makes things up, but at least it is not handed false facts to repeat. It is like being handed the wrong map: you may end up further away than if you had no map. (Source: Notebook 4 cell 28)

  3. T/F: “Because the SOTU corpus is larger than the model’s context window, the notebook retrieves a few chunks instead of feeding all speeches.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The SOTU corpus is the collection of US State of the Union speeches. The context window is the most text the model can read at once. Since all the speeches are too long to fit, does the notebook pick out a few short pieces (chunks) instead?

    True. Why: the speeches add up to about 2 million tokens (word pieces), but the model can read only 32,768 at once. It is like a suitcase: you cannot pack the whole wardrobe, so you pick the few clothes you need for this trip. (Source: Notebook 4 cell 22)

  4. T/F: “Once a prompt gives 4 out of 4 valid JSON replies, the pipeline can safely run on 100,000 reviews without checks.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: JSON is a strict text format that other programs can read. A valid JSON reply is one in the right shape. The pipeline is the whole automatic process. If 4 test replies come out right, can you run it on 100,000 reviews and stop checking?

    False. Why: 4 good replies do not prove 100,000 good replies. The notebook says reliability “has to be checked by code around the model”. It is like a new driver who parked well 4 times: that does not mean you never need to look again. (Source: Notebook 4 cells 17, 28)

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): A Norwegian company wants an LLM to answer staff questions from its internal handbook. Name two risks shown in Notebook 4 and how to handle them.

    Model answer: First, the model hallucinates when it lacks the facts, so it should be grounded with RAG: retrieve the relevant handbook passages and tell it to answer only from them, at temperature 0. Second, the retriever can miss questions asked in other words. A tf-idf retriever only matches literal words, so “pension” will not find “retirement benefits”. Embedding-based retrieval and a test of the hit rate on reworded questions reduce this. Norwegian text also costs more tokens per word, which raises cost and fills the context window faster.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Risk one: when the model does not know the facts, it makes them up. So you find the right handbook pages, paste them in, and tell the model to use only those pages, with no randomness. Risk two: a word-matching search misses questions asked in different words, so use a search that understands meaning and test how often it finds the right page. Also, Norwegian text costs more and fills the model’s reading space faster.

Sources: Interactive Notebook 4 A Real LLM on Your Laptop (GRA4164_Interactive_4_A_real_LLM_on_your_laptop.ipynb), cells 0–28; Assignments 2026 slides 20–24; Lecture 7 slides 18–20, 26. The notebook has no saved outputs, so no token counts or scores from it appear here.

Part VI — Putting it together

22. Choosing the right method for a business case (the reflection question)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 20 of 100 points in 2025, and the question that most separates a C from an A.

Start from zero

The problem. A company has a pile of text it can’t read by hand: 1,000 survey answers, 50,000 product reviews, or years of news articles. Management asks a simple question, like “do customers like us?” or “what are people complaining about?”. The exam’s last question (20 of 100 points) gives you a situation like this. It asks which tools from the course you’d use, why, and what could go wrong. You don’t need maths for it. You need to know what each tool does, in one sentence, and when it fits.

The toolbox, one plain sentence per tool. Every tool turns a pile of text into something a manager can read: a score, a label, or a list of themes.

  1. Dictionary (word list): you write a list of words yourself, e.g. positive = {good, great, love} and negative = {bad, slow, rude}, then count how often they appear in each text. More positive than negative words means a happier text. (Ch. 7)
  2. Boolean search: a search rule with AND / OR / NOT, like in a library catalogue: an article counts only if it contains “economy” AND “policy” AND “uncertain”. You count how many texts match each month. (Ch. 7)
  3. tf-idf + cosine similarity: a way to score how similar two texts are by the distinctive words they share. Common words like “the” count for almost nothing; rare, telling words count a lot. Use it to find texts that look like a reference text. (Ch. 4–5)
  4. Naive Bayes: a spam-filter-style sorter. You first label some texts by hand (e.g. 300 answers marked “happy” or “unhappy”). It learns which words show up in each group, then sorts all the new texts. (Ch. 9)
  5. Regularised (text) regression, e.g. Lasso: predicts a number (like a 1–10 satisfaction score) from the words in a text. It is built to ignore most words and keep only the few that really matter, so it doesn’t fool itself when there are more words than texts. (Ch. 8)
  6. Topic model (e.g. LDA): the computer sorts all the texts into themes by itself, like sorting mail into piles without being told the piles. You then read each pile’s top words and name it (“delivery”, “price”, “staff”). (Ch. 10)
  7. Word embeddings (e.g. word2vec): gives every word a spot on a “meaning map”, so that similar words sit close together (“cheap” near “inexpensive”). Useful for finding synonyms you forgot to put in a word list. (Ch. 13)
  8. Fine-tuned language model (e.g. BERT): take a ready-made model that already “reads” well, and train it a bit more on your hand-labelled examples. It understands context (“not good” is negative), but needs labels and computing power. (Ch. 20)
  9. Prompted LLM (like ChatGPT): don’t train anything; write clear instructions (“Label this answer as positive, negative or neutral”) and maybe give a few examples. Fast, but it can make things up, so you must check it against texts you labelled yourself. (Ch. 20–21)

How to choose, in three questions.

  1. Do you already know what you’re looking for? If yes (e.g. “mentions of climate”), use a word list or Boolean search. If no (“what are people talking about?”), use a topic model.
  2. Do you have texts with answers attached? Examples: star ratings next to reviews, or a few hundred answers you labelled by hand. If yes, you can train a sorter (Naive Bayes, fine-tuned model) and check any method’s accuracy.
  3. Does context matter? Negation (“not good”), sarcasm, or words with two meanings call for a language model (fine-tuned or prompted) rather than word counting.

A great answer picks two tools that do different jobs. For example, one measures how people feel and the other finds what they talk about. It says why each fits this firm and is honest about where each can go wrong.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Supervised: the method is told the answer in advance. Usually that means you give it examples with the right answer attached (texts already labelled “happy” or “unhappy”), like a student learning with an answer key. In this course, word lists also count as “supervised”, because you fix the rule yourself (“count these words”) and the computer learns nothing on its own. The course’s phrase for this is “we know the functional form”: you know exactly what output you’ll get for any input.
  • Unsupervised: no answers and no rule. The computer finds the structure itself (e.g. topic models finding themes).
  • Self-supervised: the answers come free from the text itself (hide the next word, guess it). This is how word embeddings and LLMs learn.
  • Label: the right answer attached to a text, e.g. “positive”, or a star rating.
  • Classify / classifier: sort texts into boxes (positive / negative, spam / not spam).
  • Baseline: the simplest possible method, used as a yardstick. If the fancy method can’t beat “always guess the most common answer”, it’s useless.
  • Validation / out of sample: checking a method on texts it hasn’t seen, compared with answers you trust. Like testing a student on new exam questions, not on the ones they memorised.
  • Overfitting: a method that memorises its examples instead of learning the pattern, so it looks perfect on old data and fails on new data.
  • Pitfall: a way the method can go wrong in this particular case.
  • Normalise: make texts comparable, e.g. count hits per 1,000 words, so long texts don’t win automatically.
  • K (number of topics): how many piles you ask the topic model to make. You choose it, and the results change with it.
  • Seed instability: run a topic model twice and you may get slightly different piles, because it starts from a random point.
  • Polysemy: one word, several meanings (“green” = a colour, or eco-friendly).
  • Negation / sarcasm: “not good” means bad; “great, another delay” means bad. Word counting gets both wrong.
  • Hallucination: an LLM confidently making something up.
  • GDPR: the EU’s data-protection law. Sending customers’ answers to an outside AI company may break it. [Not in course files — general knowledge, apart from the course’s mention of GDPR among LLM issues.]
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first look up the relevant documents, then give them to the LLM with the question, so it answers from real sources.
  • Index (= 100 in a base period): a number scaled so that a chosen starting month equals 100. Then 120 means “20% more than at the start”.

The idea in plain words

The reflection question gives you a business situation with text in it and asks: which tools from this course would you use, why, and what could go wrong? Think of yourself as a carpenter with a toolbox. Each tool from the course is good at one job:

  • dictionary
  • Boolean search
  • tf-idf + cosine
  • Naive Bayes
  • regularised regression
  • topic model
  • word embeddings
  • a fine-tuned LLM
  • a prompted LLM

The examiner checks three things:

  1. Did you pick tools that fit this job?
  2. Can you say what number each tool will produce for the client?
  3. Do you know where each tool breaks?

Analogy

A doctor does not prescribe every medicine in the pharmacy. They pick two or three that fit the diagnosis, explain why, and warn about side-effects. Your answer should read the same way: diagnosis (what the firm wants to know), prescription (two or three methods), side-effects (pitfalls in this case).

The exam definition (what the graders say they want)

  • 2025 evaluation guideline: “A good answer should mention methods that are well motivation[sic] and relevant for the problem, and also identify one or more pitfalls with the proposed method in the current context. Would then be great if the methods complement each other in that regard.”
  • Assignment evaluation guidelines (2024/2025): students should “know when the different tools might be appropriate to apply”, understand “how different pre-processing steps, and other modelling choices, might affect the answers”, and “critically reflect on in which situations this might be more relevant than using … the other tools learned about in this course”. For a business case: “Provide a well explained motivation for why and how to use text data in this case” and “Identify and critically discuss how the methods learned about in this course can be used.”
  • BI grade A: “excellent judgement and a high degree of independent thinking.”

The method chooser (one table to memorise)

If the firm wants… Use Supervised? Gives you (the number) Main pitfalls
To track a concept it can name in advance (uncertainty, ESG, a product) Boolean search / dictionary (Ch. 7) “Supervised” in the course’s sense: you set the rule yourself, nothing is learned (see “What the words mean” above; slide 7) Hits or tone per document, normalised (e.g. per 1,000 words; index = 100 in a base period) Subjective word lists; must know what to search for; polysemy, synonyms, negation, sarcasm; language
To find documents similar to a reference text, or to each other tf-idf + cosine similarity (Ch. 4–5); Engle et al. climate index Unsupervised measure Similarity score 0–1 per document Literal word overlap only (misses paraphrases); depends on preprocessing
To discover what people talk about (unknown themes) Topic model: LDA, LSA/SVD (Ch. 10) Unsupervised Topic shares per document; top words per topic Choice of K; seed instability; labels are your interpretation; needs enough text
To predict a category (positive/negative, spam, party) from text, with labelled examples Naive Bayes (Ch. 9); regularised logistic regression (Ch. 8) Supervised Predicted class / probability; accuracy vs baseline Needs labels; overfitting when p ≫ n; leakage in the train/test split
To predict a number (GDP growth, a rating) from text Regularised text regression, Lasso/Ridge (Ch. 8) Supervised Fitted value; out-of-sample R² p ≫ n: in-sample fit is meaningless; use cross-validation
To measure meaning and similarity between words; track how meaning changes Word embeddings: PMI + SVD, word2vec (Ch. 13) Self-supervised Word vectors, cosine similarity, analogies Needs a big corpus (or a pre-trained model); static vectors ignore context; noise over time
Context-aware classification at high accuracy, with labelled data Fine-tune a BERT-type model with a new head (Ch. 20) Supervised Class probabilities per document Needs labelled data and compute; less transparent
Fast classification/extraction with no or few labels Prompt an LLM, zero-/few-shot, with format + temperature 0; RAG for documents (Ch. 20–21) No training Labels/fields per document Hallucination, inconsistency, cost per token, privacy/GDPR if sent to an external provider; must validate on a labelled sample

A 6-step template for the reflection answer

  1. Restate the goal as measurable outputs. Example: “a tone score per respondent; the share of answers about ESG”. One or two sentences.
  2. Describe the data and preprocessing, with one judgement call. For example, keep “not”, since stop-word lists remove it and flip meaning (“not good” → “good”; Interactive 1).
  3. Method 1: the simple, transparent baseline (dictionary/Boolean, or tf-idf + cosine). Cover what it does, why it fits here, the number it delivers, and its pitfalls in this case.
  4. Method 2: a method that fixes method 1’s main weakness. Unsupervised discovery (LDA) if method 1 needs known words; contextual models (fine-tuned BERT or a prompted LLM) if method 1 cannot handle context. Cover the same four points.
  5. Validation: use any labels you have to check every method. Survey ratings, star ratings and a hand-labelled sample all work. Compare against a simple baseline, and evaluate out of sample.
  6. Wider pitfalls: representativeness of the texts, language, privacy/GDPR, cost, explainability to management.

A tiny worked example — a second case, outlined

Case (our own illustration): a Norwegian bank wants a monthly indicator of how much climate risk is discussed in Norwegian news about its borrowers.

  • Goal → numbers: a monthly index (base = 100) and a per-firm score.
  • Method 1 — tf-idf + cosine similarity to a climate reference text, as in Engle et al. (2020): the WSJ Climate Change News Index (Lecture 2, slide 23; the course data even includes climate_reference.txt). It is transparent and needs no labels. Pitfall: it works on literal word overlap, so Norwegian-language news needs a Norwegian reference text, and paraphrases are missed.
  • Method 2 — Boolean “transition risk” search in the spirit of EPU (Lecture 3, slide 8). For example: (climate OR emissions OR carbon) AND (regulation OR tax OR policy), normalised by the number of articles per month. Pitfall: the word lists are subjective, and polysemy is a problem (“green” as a colour).
  • Method 3 (complement) — word embeddings to expand the word list with near-synonyms (cosine-nearest neighbours of “emissions”; our suggestion). The course shows that embeddings can measure exactly this: Kapfhammer, Larsen & Thorsrud (2020), “Climate risk and commodity currencies”, which measures transition risk for Norway with word embeddings (Lecture 6, slide 31). Pitfall: embeddings need a large corpus, and meanings drift over time.
  • Validation: read a random sample of high-scoring and low-scoring articles; check the index spikes at known events (e.g. the Paris Agreement).

How this shows up on the exam

In 2025 this was Block 5 (20 points, ½–1 page). Expect a new business setting, such as customer reviews, news, reports, emails or survey answers. The question gives an explicit list of what to cover: motivation (why this method fits), problem solved, and pitfalls (what could go wrong). Earlier blocks of the exam also test “when is method X appropriate” (when is it the right tool).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • At least the number of methods asked for (two), each one from the course and named precisely.
  • For each method: why it fits this firm, the concrete output (what number management actually gets), and at least one pitfall that is specific to this case.
  • Methods that complement each other (cover each other’s weak spots). For example: one supervised (learns from tagged examples) and one unsupervised (finds patterns with no tags); one transparent (easy to see why it decided) and one context-aware (understands word order and meaning); or one that checks the other.
  • A validation step (how you will check the results are right) and one preprocessing judgement (a choice about cleaning the text first, e.g. whether to remove stop words).
  • About one page, organised with short headings or bold method names.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Listing methods without linking them to the firm’s questions.
  • Generic pitfalls (“the model may be wrong”) instead of pitfalls tied to the case. Examples: answers in several languages, a small corpus (too few texts), negation (“not good”), survey selection bias (the people who answer are not typical customers), GDPR (the EU data-privacy law).
  • Proposing an LLM as magic: no check of its results, no mention of hallucination (made-up answers) or cost.
  • Ignoring labels that are already there (survey scores, star ratings). They make supervised learning and checking possible.
  • Going far beyond the length limit.

Key terms to use

  • supervised / unsupervised / self-supervised (learns from tags / no tags / text supplies answers)
  • dictionary-based (count words from a hand-made word list)
  • Boolean search (find texts with AND / OR / NOT rules)
  • normalisation (clean text: lower case, remove punctuation, etc.)
  • tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more)
  • cosine similarity (how alike two texts’ word profiles are)
  • topic model (LDA) (finds hidden themes in many texts)
  • number of topics K (how many themes you tell LDA to find)
  • Naive Bayes (simple word-counting classifier that learns from labels)
  • regularisation (penalty that stops a model over-fitting)
  • out-of-sample validation (test on texts the model never saw)
  • baseline (simple method your model must beat)
  • fine-tuning with a classification head (extra training with a new labelling layer)
  • prompt engineering (zero-/few-shot, chain-of-thought) (writing instructions; no examples / some examples / step-by-step)
  • RAG (search step pastes relevant documents into the prompt)
  • hallucination (confident-sounding but made-up answer)
  • GDPR (EU law on handling personal data)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “An unsupervised topic model is the best choice when the firm already knows exactly which concept it wants to track.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: An unsupervised topic model (such as LDA) reads many texts and finds the themes in them by itself, with no hints. “Already knows which concept it wants to track” means the firm knows what it is looking for, for example “complaints about delivery”. Is a theme-finding tool the best pick in that case?

    False. Why: when you know the concept and its words, a dictionary approach (counting words from your own list) or a Boolean search (rules like “delivery AND late”) does the job directly. Topic models are for discovering themes you did not know about. If you know you are looking for your keys, you search your pockets; you do not sort the whole house to see what turns up. (Source: Assignment 2, Q2.2c framing; Lecture 3)

  2. True or false: “If a survey contains star ratings next to the free text, these can be used to train or validate a text classifier.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Free text is what people wrote in their own words. A text classifier is a model that sorts texts into groups, such as happy or unhappy. “Train or validate” means teach it or check it. Can the star ratings be used for that?

    True. Why: the stars are labels (ready-made right answers next to each text). So supervised learning, such as Naive Bayes or fine-tuning, becomes possible, and you can check the model against them. It is like a set of practice questions that comes with the answer sheet. (Source: Lecture 3 slides 22–27; training slide 22)

  3. Short answer (2–5 sentences): A retailer receives 50,000 product reviews per month with star ratings and wants to know why customers are unhappy. Name two complementary methods.

    • Model answer: First, use the star ratings as labels to train a supervised sentiment classifier. Naive Bayes on word counts is a transparent baseline; a fine-tuned BERT-type model with a classification head handles negation and context better. Evaluate both out of sample against the majority-class baseline. Second, run LDA on the low-rated reviews to discover the themes behind dissatisfaction (delivery, size, quality), giving topic shares that can be tracked monthly. The classifier measures how unhappy customers are, and the topic model explains why. Pitfalls: topics depend on K and the random seed, and ratings are noisy labels.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Method one: use the stars as answers to teach a model to tell happy from unhappy reviews. Start with a simple word-counting model, try a stronger one that understands phrases like “not good”, and test both on reviews they have not seen. Method two: take only the bad reviews and let a theme-finder show what people complain about, such as delivery or size. The first says how unhappy people are, the second says why, but the themes can shift with your settings and star ratings are not always accurate.

Sources: 2025 exam Block 5 and its evaluation guideline; assignment evaluation guidelines 2024/2025; Lecture_bow_based_methods.pdf (method map slides 4–6; dictionaries 7–12; regressions 15–19; Naive Bayes 22–27; topic models 31–59); Lecture_neuralnets_wordembeddings.pdf; Lecture_llm_intro.pdf slides 18–27; Lecture_llm_trainingandfinetuning.pdf slides 20–23; Interactive notebooks 1–4.

23. One-page exam-day cheat sheet

In plain words. This page is a recap, not a lesson. It only makes sense after you have read the chapters, and every term in it is explained there in its “Start from zero” section. Use it the night before the exam to jog your memory.

Pipeline (L1): collection → preprocessing (lowercase, punctuation, tokenize, stop words, numbers, stem/lemmatize) → features (BoW, tf-idf, embeddings) → model (classification, clustering, topics, LLMs) → interpretation. Four challenges: big data, noisy text, ambiguity (“bank”), ethics (bias, privacy, black box).

Bag-of-words and the DTM (L2): word order ignored, words treated as independent. DTM \(C\) is \(n\times p\) (documents × vocabulary), entries = counts \(c_{ij}\); sparse and large. N-grams keep local order (“low unemployment”).

Normalisations (L2 slides 16–17):

  • Row: \(x_i=c_i/m_i,\ m_i=\sum_j c_{ij}\) (removes length).
  • Binary: \(x_{ij}=1_{c_{ij}>0}\) (removes repetition).
  • tf-idf: \(\mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}_{ij}=c_{ij}\log(n/d_j)\), with \(d_j\) = number of documents containing \(j\). A word in all documents gets 0. Rare words are up-weighted.
  • scikit-learn: \(\ln\frac{1+n}{1+d_j}+1\), rows scaled to length 1.

Similarity (L2 slide 22):

  • Cosine: \(\cos\theta=\frac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}\) (angle only; 1 = same direction, 0 = orthogonal).
  • Euclidean: \(\sqrt{\sum(a_i-b_i)^2}\), which is driven by document length.
  • Slide example: Euclidean 1.46 vs 1.35, cosine 0.99 vs 0.84.

Method map (L3):

  • Dictionary/Boolean: “supervised” because the function is known. Most used in economics and finance.
  • Text regression: \(p(y|c)\). Naive Bayes: \(p(c|y)\). LSA, LDA: unsupervised, latent topics.

Boolean/EPU: (uncertain OR uncertainty) AND (economic OR economy) AND (≥1 of regulation, federal reserve, deficit, congress, legislation, white house); monthly counts over 10 US newspapers, scaled, mean 100 over 1985–2009. Dictionary: tone = #pos − #neg, normalised; Loughran–McDonald for finance. Weaknesses: subjective, must know what to search for, polysemy, synonyms.

Text regression (L3 slides 15–18, 34): \(n\ll p\) (curse of dimensionality) → penalised regression. Lasso: \(\min\{l(\alpha,\beta)+n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\}\). \(\lambda=0\) gives OLS; a larger \(\lambda\) shrinks coefficients to 0. Choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation (or AIC/BIC). Judge by out-of-sample R², never in-sample.

Naive Bayes (L3 slides 22–26):

  • Formula: \(v_{nb}=\arg\max_k P(v_k)\prod_j P(c_{ij}|v_k)\).
  • Prior: \(n_k/n\). Likelihood: \(\frac{count+1}{\text{words in class}+p}\) (Laplace smoothing).
  • “Naive” = BoW + independent words. “Bayes” = Bayes’ rule.
  • For categorical outcomes. Slide example: 0.27 vs 0.73 → class b.

Topic models (L3): topic = cluster of words; a document = a mixture of topics.

  • LSA: \(C=USV'\), keep \(K\), \(F=U_{1:K}S_{1:K}\), \(L=V_{1:K}\). Non-probabilistic; values unrestricted.
  • LDA (Blei et al. 2003): generative story.
    1. Draw the document’s topic mix.
    2. For each word, draw a topic, then draw a word from that topic.
  • LDA weights are probabilities: each document’s topic weights sum to 1 (rows of \(V\)), and each topic’s word probabilities sum to 1 (columns of \(\Theta'\)). Dirichlet priors give sparsity.
  • Choose K; check seed stability.

n-grams (L4): \(P(c_n|c_{n-1})=\frac{count(c_{n-1},c_n)}{count(c_{n-1})}\); add-one smoothing for unseen pairs. Loss = average negative log-likelihood; perplexity \(=e^{\text{Loss}}\) (uniform over 27 → 27). Temperature: low = sharper, high = flatter.

Embeddings (L6):

  • “You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth).
  • PMI: \(M_{ij}=\log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_ip_j}\) (\(p\times p\)). PPMI = max(PMI, 0). Rare words get high weight, so use add-one smoothing.
  • Truncated SVD on \(M\): rows of \(U\) = embeddings.
  • word2vec (Mikolov 2013): 2-layer network. CBOW (context → word) vs Skipgram (word → context).
  • One-hot \(x\) selects a column of \(W^1\) (\(K\times p\), \(K\approx300\)) = the embedding. Negative sampling.
  • word2vec is static; BERT is contextual.
  • King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen.

LLMs (L7):

  • Next-token predictor.
  • Pipeline: pre-training (self-supervised) → SFT (supervised) → preference optimisation/RL.
  • “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.”
  • Tokens ≠ words (sub-words via BPE: repeatedly merge the most frequent pair).
  • Context window. Hugging Face = open-source hub.
  • Critical issues: sustainability (energy for training and inference, water, chips); ownership & control (monopoly, open weights); reliability (hallucination, bias); responsibility (bias, abuse, prompt injection, Tay; slide 23); privacy & security (GDPR, EU AI Act). Copyright/data without permission is accepted by the 2025 guideline.

Transformer (L8–L9):

  • Projections: \(q_i=x_iW^Q,\ k_i=x_iW^K,\ v_i=x_iW^V\).
  • Score: \(\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}\). Weights: \(\alpha_{ij}=\) softmax. Output: \(\boldsymbol\alpha_i=\sum_{j\le i}\alpha_{ij}v_j\).
  • Query = what I look for; key = what I offer; value = my content.
  • Causal (past only; future masked with \(-\infty\)) vs bidirectional.
  • Multi-head = parallel heads → richer relations.
  • Block: attention → add & norm → feed-forward → add & norm.
  • Positional embeddings are added because attention is order-blind (“cat chased dog”). Sinusoidal: \(PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})\).

Input/output and training (L9):

  • Input: one-hot × E, plus positions.
  • LM head: softmax over the vocabulary.
  • Decoding: greedy, random, top-k, temperature softmax\((u/\tau)\).
  • BERT max 512 tokens. Encoder vs decoder; cross-attention (Q from decoder; K, V from encoder).
  • Training: self-supervised, cross-entropy \(-\log\hat y[w_{t+1}]\).
  • Gradient descent: \(v\to v-\eta\nabla L\). Backprop = chain rule. SGD/mini-batch/epoch.
  • Fine-tuning = transfer learning: new head; update all parameters or the head only; needs labels.
  • Alternatives: prompt engineering; extract embeddings.
  • Zero-shot = instruction only, no examples, no weight change [Not in course files — general knowledge]. Few-shot = examples in the prompt (Interactive 4).

24. Answer-writing strategy for each question type

Type (2025 example) Command words Recipe for full marks Length
True/False (Block 1) “Answer only whether…” Find the one claim; look for a twist: wrong job for a method, weakness sold as a strength, benefit flipped, wrong definition, near-miss term (unsupervised vs self-supervised). Write only True/False. 1 word
Define (2a, 3a, 3c) “What is…”, “underlying assumption” Core idea in course words → structure or formula with dimensions → one-line example → one consequence. Answer every half of a two-part question in its own sentences. 3–5 sentences
Describe + motivate (2b, 4b, 4c) “Describe…”, “Include the motivation”, “Why” For each item: what it is + why you’d use it (the problem it solves). Give exactly the number of items asked for, or one more at most. 4–6 sentences
Describe with course example (2c) “Use a concrete example discussed in this course” General recipe, then the course’s example by name with its details (EPU terms, normalisation, newspapers). 4–6 sentences
Intuition (4d) “Describe in intuitive terms” An example sentence (“bank”, “it” → “animal”) → the analogy (database Q/K/V) → the steps in words → why it helps (long range, parallel, interpretable). 5–7 sentences
Compare (2d, 3b, 4e) “difference/similarity”, “biggest conceptual difference” One line per method → an explicit contrast sentence (“X changes the weights; Y changes the context”) → the shared ground → when to use which. Obey “max two sentences”. 2–6 sentences
Draw (3d) “Make an graph” [sic] Labelled axes, arrows from the origin, angle marks, cos ≈ 1 vs cos ≈ 0 written on the drawing, one sentence that length doesn’t matter. Drawing + 2 lines
Discuss issues (4a) “Discuss shortly two” Name each issue (E/S/G) → mechanism (why it arises) → consequence or mitigation. Two good issues beat five listed ones. 2 short paragraphs
Reflection (5) “Propose at least two methods… motivation, problem, pitfalls” Use the 6-step template from Ch. 22, with bold method names as headings. ½–1 page

Always:

  • Use the course’s vocabulary.
  • Answer every part.
  • Give one concrete course example when you can.
  • Leave 10–15 minutes to re-read the T/F answers and check every sub-question was answered.
  • Write legibly. It is a hand-written exam, so short, clear sentences beat long ones.
